# Changelog

All notable changes to Luxar are documented in this file.

## [Unreleased]

## [2026.09.22] - 2026-09-22

### September 2026

#### Seven cell-tracking crops are pinned for publication

Seven of the nine annotated crops behind `gsplats_cell_tracking` are uploaded to
the `cc-by` draft and pinned in the demo-data manifest: per crop, the finished
4D Gaussian-splat volume with its LOD ladder plus the lineage-track geometry.
The record is not public yet, so the demo still takes its existing Kaggle path
for now. Once the record is published, these pins make the default six-crop path
need no credentials, no 4 GB download and no GPU.

The seven are the crops with a complete 100-timepoint fit cache at the demo's
default 60,000 seeds. They cover the default `--datasets 6` with one spare;
`--datasets 8` or `9` still falls back to the Kaggle path, which the loader
already treats as a supported partial-record state rather than a fault, and
announces by name.

Splat counts run 2.2M to 4.6M per crop over the 100 timepoints, 632.4 MB in
total. The archive characteristics record the declared 100 × 64 × 256 × 256
uint16 source grid, so the publication table can state compression honestly.
The archives carry no PSNR, so the record leaves both quality columns empty
rather than guessing: the bundle builder loads its per-timepoint fits without
statistics, so none reach the combined 4D store. The quality choice behind them
is documented where it was measured — `DEFAULT_SEEDS` in the demo records a nuclei-masked K
sweep (37.41 dB at 12,126 splats rising to 40.29 dB at 120,000, about +1 dB per
doubling with no plateau) and explains why 60,000 is the balance point.

Pinning a hosted-only dataset means editing `data_manifest.json` itself: with no
in-repo directory to scan, the generator preserves the committed list, and a
`files=` in the generator's spec would be silently discarded. The spec now says
so, and the bundle builder now points at the committed manifest rather than the
generator spec.

#### The demo payloads leave the repository

27 Git-LFS files — 409.9 MB — are gone from `demos/data/`, and the manifest's
dual checksum contract goes with them. Every clone has been paying that
bandwidth to carry a second copy of data the Zenodo records already serve.

With no file in the tree for a repo digest to describe, `hosted_sha256` becomes
`sha256` and the hosted-specific fields are dropped. The direction matters and is
the only safe one: `download_sha = hosted_sha or sha`, so keeping the repo digest
and dropping the hosted one would make every fresh download match nothing and be
quarantined. Nothing about how the fetch reads a pin changes.

Four payloads carried only a repo `sha256` and were previously thought to block
this. They do not: their hosted copies were measured byte-identical, so that one
digest already describes the record copy and needed no re-pin —
`3d_umap_coords_human.parquet`, `3d_umap_coords_mouse.parquet`,
`census_umap_1m.npz` and `zebrafish_4d.gsplats.zarr.zip`.

`dipc_genome/dipc_gm12878.npz` stays. Its bucket is `regenerate` and it is on no
record, so deleting it would leave a pin nothing can satisfy.

The 19 demos that now resolve exclusively from records no longer advertise a
`git-lfs` local-data requirement in the catalogue. Dip-C remains the sole
LFS-backed demo.

A cache populated from the old in-repo copies no longer matches the collapsed pin
and is re-downloaded once — 23 of 36 files on a developer machine. Recording each
outgoing repo digest in `superseded_sha256` would avoid that, at the cost of
spending the single honoured fallback slot on the older generation; that trade is
left open rather than assumed.

#### A failed progressive-LOD commit no longer strands the node

A progressive loader appends each streamed LOD level to its ladder as soon as
the data arrives, before the caller has concatenated, projected and committed
it. When that commit threw, the cursor had already moved — so the retry resumed
from the advanced cursor and attempted a *larger* allocation than the one that
had just failed, and on reaching the last rung flipped `hasMoreLODs` to false.
The refinement loop then dropped the node, its 3-strike failure cap was never
reached, no notification fired, and the node froze permanently at its last
committed rung while the data-loading monitor still reported a complete ladder.

The hosted Cosmicflows/Laniakea demo showed exactly this: basins reporting
"LOD 7/7 ~100%" while drawing a coarse prefix, with the recovery retries
themselves driving the tab further out of memory.

Each progressive loader now records its level count at pass start and unwinds
to it when a commit fails, so a retry re-attempts the same prefix instead of
escalating. Failures now reach the cap and are reported rather than passing
silently. All four geometry types carried the identical defect and all four are
fixed.

#### Progressive LOD refinement now stops at a memory ceiling instead of an out-of-memory crash

An additive LOD ladder is prefix accumulation, so its terminal state is 100% of
the node — on every node, always. That bounds first paint, but it bounded
nothing at rest: refinement drove every loader to its last rung with no notion
of what the scene could afford. The Cosmicflows/Laniakea demo (10 line nodes,
11.4 million segments) climbed its ladders until the tab ran out of memory.

The viewer already measured this pressure when _loading_ a scene, but that gate
releases as soon as each node's first paint completes, and refinement is
scheduled afterwards — so by the time the ladders climbed, nothing held a
budget at all.

Refinement now shares one residency ceiling across the sweep-registered
progressive leaves of all four geometry types, sized from the same device-heap
signal the load-time gate uses. Lazy `lod_group` levels are not registered in
those sweeps and remain outside this accounting. The gate is a refusal, never an
eviction: tracked leaves at the ceiling stop adding detail and keep everything
already drawn, so the scene settles at a legible partial view instead of dying.
Where the ceiling is reached, the console says so once, naming the budget and
the tracked measured footprint, without repeating on later view changes.

Sharing one budget across the four types is deliberate — Laniakea's ten line
nodes are each individually affordable and only collectively fatal, so per-type
budgets would have admitted all of them. Browsers without a heap-limit signal,
including Firefox and Safari, use the device-class fallback pool and therefore
receive a ceiling too. The shared working-set calculation is capped at 512 MiB,
so sufficiently large desktop heaps resolve to the same ceiling rather than
scaling without bound.

Superseded or otherwise uncommitted refinement passes now release the previous
cumulative payload they used for prefix-append detection instead of retaining
that abort-path lineage until another pass happens to replace it.

The Scene-Graph monitor now reports the number of ladder rungs actually
committed on screen, rather than the loader cursor. Failed or superseded commits
therefore no longer make a stalled node appear fully refined.

#### Warm-cache refinement now respects the residency ceiling within a pass

Progressive Points, Lines, GSplats, and Mesh refinement now receive a per-pass
share of the shared budget's remaining byte headroom, with enough allowance for
one estimated rung, and stop after the first rung that spends it. Cached ladders
can no longer climb through several resident rungs under one admission before
the ceiling is measured again. The budget reconciles each loader's measured
post-pass footprint before considering the next node.

#### Make constrained GPU residency budgets bind

The shared GPU buffer-pool and LOD-retention byte budget no longer clamps a
measured small-device value up to 512 MB, where stranded growth buffers could
remain below the eviction threshold forever. Twenty-five percent of
`navigator.deviceMemory` now has only a 2 GB ceiling; 512 MB is used solely when
no memory signal exists.

An explicit `?cacheBudgetMB=` value (including the native launcher's
`LUXAR_CACHE_BUDGET_MB` setting) also supplies the cache pool's implied
non-cache remainder as an automatic GPU residency signal. It replaces the
heap-derived remainder in either direction, so the launcher's 2048 MiB default
resolves to 1432 MB while smaller values constrain it. Measurable Chromium heap
tiers use the same remainder derivation, allowing roomy desktops to scale past
the eager loader's unrelated 512 MiB cap up to the existing 2 GB ceiling.

#### GPU geometry budgets scale with available heap

The automatic GPU-geometry byte budget now derives directly from the shared
non-cache heap remainder instead of inheriting the eager loader's unrelated
512 MiB burst cap. Roomy Chromium heaps therefore keep scaling — a 4 GiB heap
resolves to about 1.37 GB — until the module's existing 2 GB ceiling applies;
the eager-loader and refinement-residency caps remain unchanged.

Explicit cache-pool overrides and the mobile WebKit device-class fallback now
use that same remainder derivation. The native launcher's 2048 MiB default
implies about 1.43 GB of GPU geometry rather than 716 MB; this comes from the
configured pool split and is equivalent to the remainder from roughly a
4.2 GiB heap under the same model, rather than a measurement at that budget.
Mobile devices keep their independent 128 MiB safety cap as a peer minimum,
while a smaller measurable Chromium heap can still bind below it.

#### Hosted demo datasets now credit their original data sources

The DESI, CELLxGENE Census, human and mouse peak-UMAP, and neuromast hosted
datasets now identify the publications or unpublished source data behind their
derived artifacts. Their citations were resolved against Crossref and arXiv,
and the public demo credits now use the corrected publication years and
provenance wording consistently.

#### Surface accelerator fallback failures instead of hiding them

Unexpected CUDA volume-render and Numba spatial-ordering failures now report the
exception type and message before falling back to the portable implementation.
Missing optional backends and CUDA-unsupported dimensions remain quiet, and the
CUDA warning is emitted only once per process. Image-overlay decode failures now
preserve the underlying imageio error in the validation message.

#### The README gallery is hosted now, and pinned to the bytes rather than a path

The 58 committed gallery tiles — 181 MB of git-LFS across 29 demos — are gone,
and the README points at `data.luxarviewer.dev/media/<sha256-prefix>.<ext>`
instead. HEAD's git-LFS drops from 599.5 MB to 418.6 MB, which matters because
GitHub's free tier allows 1 GB of bandwidth a month and a public clone pulls
HEAD's LFS objects: at the old size the second clone of the month exhausted the
quota, and an exhausted quota fails CI as readily as it fails a visitor.

The keys are content-addressed rather than dated, because retention by wave
count is a countdown — a tag pinned to `…/media/<wave>/` breaks after N
refreshes, which is a slower version of the problem being solved. A key that
names its own bytes cannot rot, and a refresh uploads only what actually
changed.

`scripts/gallery/media-manifest.json` is committed alongside, carrying each
object's key, byte count, full sha256 and content type. It is what generates the
README's URLs and what the harness maps a key back through — but it also keeps
"what did the gallery look like at this commit" answerable from the repo alone,
which is the one thing deleting the tiles would otherwise have destroyed.

Two consumers followed the id into the manifest. `GALLERY_ONLY=readme` used to
recover demo ids from README paths and now recovers them from keys, treating an
unmapped key as an error rather than quietly capturing a smaller set than the
README shows. The tile-staleness report used to blame each committed tile and
now dates each demo from the blamed lines in its own media-manifest entry, so a
partial re-capture or unrelated manifest edit does not re-date the rest.

#### The neuromast demo now cites the data author's requested paper

The hosted neuromast dataset's manifest and top-level acknowledgment now cite
Erzberger et al. (2020), *Nature Physics* 16:949-957, at Adrian Jacobo's
request. The credit continues to identify the iSIM imaging itself as unpublished.

#### Restore the downloads helper package to built wheels

Built wheels once again include `luxar.demos._support.downloads`, so the
installed `luxar` command can import and run. An over-broad `.gitignore` rule
had silently removed that tracked subpackage from Hatchling's wheel inputs.

The packaging guard now checks tracked package files against the same root
`.gitignore` scope Hatchling uses, without false failures from Git negations or
developer-local exclusion files.

#### Pull requests now name the integration branch explicitly

The contributor Quick Start and release-version helper now target `dev`
explicitly instead of inheriting the repository default. The release hint also
spells out that `make release` runs from `main` after the version bump has been
promoted.

#### Dispatch promotion repair windows on dev

Promotion repair windows are now requested explicitly on `dev` instead of running from
default-branch cron events. Each dispatch tests the exact dev commit receiving its check
contexts, defaults to the required Python 3.12 leg, and repairs cancelled required checks
from superseded dev push runs. Merge pushes continue to exercise the full supported
Python matrix.

#### Coverage gates that actually gate

Both coverage floors had drifted far enough below the measured numbers to stop
enforcing anything: Python sat at `fail_under = 80` against 92% measured, and the
viewer at 71/71/74/61 against 88/87/85/82. The viewer could have lost a third of
its tests and stayed green.

Three measurement defects had to be fixed before the floors could be set honestly.
The Python `exclude_lines` entries are regexes searched against every physical
line, and a hit inside a multi-line statement is attributed to that statement's
first line — so the unanchored `"pass"` deleted whole function bodies from the
report wherever a `passes` substring or a `*_per_pass` parameter name appeared,
76 files and roughly 1,102 statements of them. It was hiding well-tested code
rather than thin code, which is why nobody noticed. On the viewer side, vitest 4
removed `coverage.all` and `include` defaults to "files some test imported",
leaving 45 source files outside every threshold — so adding an untested module
could raise the reported number. And a vitest glob threshold matching zero files
reports `pct: "Unknown"`, which compares false against any floor and passes
silently, turning a renamed directory into a gate that inspects nothing.

Floors are now Python 89 and viewer 86/85/84/80, plus thirteen per-subtree floors
so a healthy subtree cannot be dragged down by the global average. Because a floor
set once decays, `check-coverage-slack.mjs` now fails `check:ci` whenever any floor
drifts more than three points under measured, rejects empty globs, and prints the
exact replacement value; thresholds live in a single module shared by the config
and the guard so the two cannot disagree.

A narrow `tsl-parity` job also puts the TSL/GLSL shader parity spec into CI for the
first time. Roughly five thousand lines of the rendering cone were counted in the
coverage metric while being gated by nothing.

Gaussian-splat fitting now seeds residual-percentile sampling from
`DynamicOpsConfig.seed` and advances both dynamic-operation samplers with each
relocation step. Seeded fits are now reproducible across those steps, and their
output may differ from stores fitted with earlier versions.

#### Built demo scenes record the exact verified input artifacts

Manifest-backed demos now stamp a canonical `input_digests` map on the scene
root, keyed by artifact basename. The resolver preserves the sha256 of the bytes
it actually accepted — including a superseded positional-pair fallback — so a
built scene can be traced to its precise input generation without reconstructing
the answer from cache state or logs.

#### The CI queue watchdog can see obsidian work inside queued runs

`queue-watchdog`'s repository-wide liveness scan listed only runs whose
**run-level** status was `in_progress`. GitHub reports a run as `queued` while any
one of its jobs is still queued, even as its other jobs execute — and on a push or
the daily full-matrix schedule `max-parallel` deliberately holds one Python leg
queued — so the runs carrying live obsidian legs were exactly the ones the scan
never listed. The fuller the box, the more certain the watchdog was that the box
was dead, and it cancelled whichever healthy run happened to be inside its
ten-minute window: three PRs lost required contexts that way in a single morning,
and a leg cancelled while queued cannot be revived by re-running failed jobs.

The scan now covers both run-level statuses. Covering two statuses out of one
first-come run budget would have reproduced the same failure from the other side —
a full page of queued runs could spend the whole budget and hide the `in_progress`
pass, whose absent evidence reads as a dead box — so `--max-runs` is still spent
first-come, less one run reserved for each status still to come. Every pass is
therefore guaranteed at least a look, no pass is capped while budget remains, and
the worst-case job fan-out per scan is unchanged, the added cost being one
runs-list call; the expected cost does rise, since it is now the queued runs that
are numerous. `--stop-after-running 1` still short-circuits on the first active
job, and `queued` is scanned first because that is where the evidence usually is.

#### Compiled point scenes can be read back through their authored structure

`LuxarScene.get_points(..., flatten=True)` now reconstructs the finest point
cloud from substitutive LOD, spatial partitions, and disjoint additive
increments. `get_point_array(..., flatten=True)` reads one field without
materializing unrelated shared arrays. The DESI scene repair path now uses this
supported reader surface instead of reaching into the encoding decoder.

#### Slice-even additive ordering for gsplat nodes the viewer slices

A gsplat node with a hidden dimension is shown one coordinate at a time, but an
additive rung is sized against the whole node — and because a rung is a global
contribution-ordered prefix, it does not divide evenly either: it piles onto
whichever coordinates carry the signal. The NEXRAD supercell demo authored an
absolute `breakpoints="stream:20000"` first rung over 82 radar scans and 817,989
splats; where that spec actually computed, its 5th-percentile scan held 4 splats,
which `scripts/check_demo_ladders.py` fails on both its absolute first-paint
floor and its rung-0 share floor.

`make_additive_lod` and `compute_additive_order` now take `slice_dims=`, a list
of centre columns whose distinct combinations the viewer slices. The ordering
chosen by `method=` is re-emitted round-robin across those slices, so after `R`
passes every prefix holds `min(slice size, R)` elements of each slice: an equal
*absolute* budget per slice, with any slice smaller than the budget carried
whole. It is a modifier rather than a new ordering method — it composes with all
of them, and the order *within* a slice stays whatever the method produced, so
each coordinate still paints bright-core-first rather than evenly thin. It is
also deterministic, which sizing alone is not: that stack's sparsest scans hold
562-774 splats, so the 250-element floor needs about a third of the sparsest one,
and a uniform random permutation is proportional only in expectation — over seeds
0-7 an `n_lods=3` random ladder cleared the floor five times in eight.
Because `slice_dims` names raw pre-`dim_order` centre columns, selecting a scene
position can accidentally target a continuous coordinate; a high-cardinality
selection now warns instead of silently degrading to a near-no-op interleave.

One trap surfaced on the way, worth knowing if you author a stacked gsplat
scene: an `additive_lod=` spec is silently a **no-op** on a dataset built with
`GSplatData.combine_as_new_dimension` from sources that already carry ladders.
The combine *merges* those ladders rather than dropping them — rung *i* of every
source becomes rung *i* of the stack — so the result arrives with rungs to spare
and `resolve_additive_axis_gsplats` takes its pass-through branch, which computes
only when the level holds one rung or `recompute=True` is set. What survives is a
per-source equal-count ladder, which is exactly proportional per slice and so
starves a sparse slice just as a global prefix does. Pass `recompute=True`
alongside `slice_dims=`; the store's tell for the shadowed case is an
`additive_0/lod_stats` carrying `n_sources` and no `lod_method`.

The NEXRAD demo now authors
`additive_lod=dict(n_lods=4, slice_dims=[3], recompute=True)`, whose rung 0
delivers a measured 2,744 splats per scan (a nominal 204,497/82 = 2,494, raised by
the 12 scans small enough to be carried whole) and therefore carries the
5th-percentile scan complete at 774; without the flag the merged per-frame ladder
left it at 774/4 = 194, still under the floor. Replacing 82 per-frame `greedy`
orderings with one global `self_energy` one did not cost per-scan quality —
measured as each scan's share of its own self-energy captured at rung 0, the mean
rose 0.9099 → 0.9247 and the worst scan 0.8188 → 0.8290. The demo authoring gate
grew a sibling that
walks the gsplats adders too — the older check only read `add_points` and
`add_lines`, which is why an absolute first rung on a sliced gsplat node was
invisible to it — and it requires both spellings separately: `slice_dims=`, so the
ladder is authored slice-aware, and `recompute=True`, so the spec actually runs.
The second looks redundant on a flat fit and costs nothing there, which is the
point: a static check cannot tell a stacked dataset from a flat one, so the gate
asks for the harmless flag rather than leaving the shadowing undetectable.

#### GSplats `array_ref` resolution is now covered by a test, and #2490's diagnosis retracted

Issue #2490 reported that the viewer does not resolve `array_ref` for gsplat
`centers`, on the strength of a hosted render A/B in which the DESI
`By redshift` layer settled at 348,558 elements against the published store's
7,116,524 — a 243x gap that appeared exactly when the re-laddered scene started
deduplicating its coarse-level `centers` across the two layers.

It resolves them. A controlled A/B settles it: two locally-served stores built
from the same 2M points, the same LOD recipe and the same colours, differing
only in which layer was written first — and therefore only in which layer's
`centers` are `array_ref`s. Toggling the layer produced identical totals
(66,438 -> 70,438 in both arms), identical per-node draw counts
(`child_0` 31,219, `child_1` 4,000 in both) and identical request counts
(1,239 ok / 9 failed in both). The hosted gap is a measurement artefact: on that
scene `totalElements` swings 320k <-> 6.2M *within a single run* in both stores
as the 512 MiB refinement residency ceiling and the GPU buffer pool trade
nodes, and the regenerated leg logged 7x the aborted requests. Two 9.75M-point
layers do not fit that budget; which nodes win the race is not deterministic.

What was true is the coverage gap the issue identified. The suite covered
`array_ref` through `ArrayDecoder.decode` (whole-array, Points `colors`,
uniformly-quantized `rgb_uint8` target) and not at all through the gsplats RANGE
path (`loadArrayRanges` -> `loadRangesResolvingRef` -> `resolveArrayRef` ->
`loadPerChannel` / `loadQuantized`), where the targets use per-channel and uniform
quantization. So a `(0, 3)` ref resolved against the wrong metadata could decode
corrupt values without an error, and no test would have caught it. A new fixture
and test close that: the deduplicated layer must decode centers and amplitudes
bit-identically to the layer that owns them, non-vacuously, with the store's own
`array_ref` encoding asserted so the test cannot quietly stop covering refs.

#### Additive GSplat ladders use bounded multi-rung lookahead

After the first coarse rung paints, the viewer now initializes the remaining
GSplat ladder indexes together and keeps up to three later rungs in flight when
the decompressed-chunk cache has room. Static hosted scenes reach full detail
without serializing every rung's metadata round trip, while playback stays at
one-rung lookahead and view changes cancel obsolete speculative reads.

#### Complexity ratchet fails closed on Ruff scan drift

The C901 baseline now fingerprints Ruff's resolved settings, rejects nested
Ruff configurations, and verifies that every existing baselined file remains in
Ruff's scan set. Configuration edits and partial subtree drops therefore fail
the gate instead of being reported as paid-down complexity debt; both Ruff
ratchets share the same trust guards so their protections cannot silently drift.

#### Defect-bearing lint rules are now ratcheted

Ruff's `flake8-bugbear` family and `RUF012` are enforced as a baseline-driven
ratchet by `scripts/check_lint_ratchet.py`, wired into `hatch run lint` and
`make check-all`. CI enforces the same check through its repository-level pytest.
Existing violations are tolerated via
`scripts/lint_baseline.json`; a file that newly breaks one of these rules, or
gains another violation of a rule it already breaks, fails the check.
The baseline also fingerprints Ruff's normalized root resolved settings and
refuses nested Ruff configs, so a configuration change cannot silently hide
findings.

These are the rules that describe silently-wrong code rather than untidy code:
mutable defaults shared across calls, closures capturing a loop variable by
reference, `warnings.warn` blaming the wrong line, `raise` inside `except`
dropping the cause, and `zip()` truncating to its shortest input. They could not
simply go into `[tool.ruff.lint] select` — there are 473 pre-existing
violations, 290 of them `zip()` without `strict=`, whose fix changes behaviour
(`strict=True` raises) and is therefore a decision per call site rather than a
mechanical sweep.

`B008` needed no baseline at all. All 83 findings were `typer.Option(...)` /
`typer.Argument(...)` in a parameter default — the documented Typer idiom,
evaluated once at import on purpose — so `extend-immutable-calls` now declares
those two calls immutable and the ratchet gates the rule at zero.

One live defect fell out of the measurement and is fixed: `stats/generate_stats.py`
passed `maxsplit` positionally to `re.split`, which Python 3.13 deprecates.

#### Viewer CI reports every gate and coverage erosion

The viewer merge gate now runs independent static and coverage checks before
reporting ordinary failures together. It still stops immediately when a
subprocess is killed, and skips the slack check when a failed coverage run
produced no summary to inspect. Local runs can retain fail-fast behavior with
`check:ci -- --bail`.

Coverage floors now carry keyed recorded measurements with a fail-closed shape
check. The guard surfaces meaningful movement in either direction as GitHub
Actions annotations and can print a paste-ready recorded-baseline block with
`check:coverage-slack -- --print`.

#### Repository gates now inspect their full intended scope

The documentation gate now scans nested Python and TypeScript modules, while
excluding test directories from API-documentation coverage. Demo-scene credit
and LOD checks gain `--require-scenes` for callers that expect built outputs and
no longer report a normal pass after inspecting nothing.

Python linting now covers the repository's scripts and support files, requires
Ruff formatting, and pins Ruff to the 0.16 series. Rust checks now propagate
Clippy failures. Wheel builds gain `hatch run check-wheel`, which verifies
package completeness, build exclusions, bundled viewer assets, Git LFS pointer
stubs, and PyPI's per-file size limit in both pull-request and release builds.

#### Ratchet TypeScript correctness and complexity debt

Viewer linting now rejects new floating or misused promises, invalid awaits,
unsafe implicit stringification, and production functions that exceed the
complexity, size, nesting, or parameter limits. Existing findings are recorded
as per-file counts in ESLint's native suppressions file, so new debt fails CI
without requiring the current backlog to be fixed in the same change.

Paying down a finding now fails lint until the suppressions file is pruned. Run
`pnpm lint:prune` to tighten the recorded count and commit the updated baseline
with the cleanup.

#### Surface loader/cache promise failures

The viewer now catches and reports rejected background prefetches and queued
view-state re-entries instead of leaving unhandled promises that can silently
stall loading. Retry exhaustion also preserves details from non-`Error` values
thrown by fetch implementations.

#### Unbreak the viewer lint gate on dev

The scene-identity watchdog tests recorded probe URLs with `String(input)` on a
`RequestInfo | URL` parameter. That predates the type-aware ESLint rules, which
landed in a parallel branch, so the two met for the first time on dev and left
`typescript-tests` red for every branch cut afterwards. The stubs now resolve
the fetch input to its URL explicitly, which also keeps a `Request`-shaped call
readable in an assertion diff instead of printing `[object Request]`.

#### Keep fitting config bundles faithful and composable

`OptimConfig`, `LossConfig`, and `ConstraintConfig` can now be unpacked directly
into `fit_gaussian_splats`, individually or together. Their defaults match the
fitter's public signature: `gradient_clip` changes `1.0` → `None`, `patience`
changes `25` → `15`, `lr_reduction_factor` changes `0.98` → `0.9`, and
`sigma_min_diag` changes `None` → `DEFAULT_SIGMA_MIN_DIAG`.
`boundary_penalty` is removed from `LossConfig` and remains on
`ConstraintConfig`, so each fitter keyword belongs to only one bundle.

The published gsplat format references also consistently identify v3.4 as the
current readable and writable format, including the `screen-area` selector
produced when legacy LOD metadata is migrated.

#### A capture is no longer reported ready when a memory ceiling truncated it

Progressive refinement stops scene-wide once tracked residency reaches the
refinement byte ceiling, and the GPU buffer pool sheds pooled geometry —
levels the LOD registry demoted from active included — when it goes over its
VRAM byte budget. Either leaves a scene whose element counts are a property of
the run rather than of the store — `desi_galaxies` authors 9.75M points, of
which one layer's finest level alone is 446 MiB of the 512 MiB ceiling, so it
settles wherever the refinement order happened to land. Until now the only
signal was a single console warning, and `summarizeCaptureReadiness` reported
`ok: true` for such a scene, so every capture tool and A/B comparison
downstream believed the truncated counts.

`RefinementResidencyReporter` now records every refusal (distinct paths, plus
the first verdict's reason and byte figures) in addition to logging the first
one, and the GPU pool counts byte-budget evictions separately from ordinary LRU
recycling. Both surface on `__luxarDebug.getState()` — as
`refinementResidency` and `gpuPool.byteBudgetEvictions`, the latter finally
wiring up a `gpuPoolStats` provider that had been declared but never passed —
and `summarizeCaptureReadiness` refuses on either, naming the first refusal's
verdict, the resident and budget figures and the path that stopped first. Note
that a byte-budget eviction does not on its own prove rendered geometry was
lost, and does not fire at all when active bytes alone exceed the budget; it
says the pool's residency was decided by the machine, which is enough to make
the capture incomparable.

Both accumulate for the life of the scene loader with no reset: they answer "did
this happen at some point while this scene was loaded", not "is it true right
now", so a scene that stopped once and later refined fully is still refused —
refinement order is path-dependent, so that run settled on a composition the next
would not reproduce. Scope is the loader, not the page: an in-page dataset switch
builds a fresh loader, reporter and pool, so the next scene starts clean with no
reload.

#### Foreground-weighted calibration for sparse volumes

`luxar gsplat cal` can now select K* with foreground-weighted held-out PSNR,
using a dependency-free Otsu foreground mask and recording the mask metadata in
`cal.json`. CLI tables and PDF reports follow the selected metric, while updated
guidance clarifies that gain-over-predict-zero selects the same K* as min-max
PSNR and directs sparse or deconvolved volumes to the weighted metric instead.
Intensity feature counting and content tiling now share the same dependency-free
Otsu threshold as calibration; installs with scikit-image are unchanged, while
plain `luxar[gsplats]` installs no longer treat every value above the floor as
foreground.

#### Mesh and shading are documented

`luxar.mesh` and `luxar.shading` are public packages — both declare `__all__` —
that had no presence in the API reference at all, while `docs/api/cli.rst`
carried thirteen `automodule` entries for CLI internals. Both now have pages,
listed in the index toctree and in a new "Geometry & Appearance" group in the
Packages Overview. `bake_ambient_occlusion`, the sanctioned way to make emissive
geometry read as three-dimensional, is findable.

The `luxar mesh` command group is documented for the first time. It has shipped
`import` and `lod` for some time, and the string `luxar mesh` appeared nowhere
in CLAUDE.md; the root README covered the Python mesh API thoroughly but never
mentioned that a classical mesh file could be imported at all. The two LOD
recipes are spelled out, because they are not interchangeable: `levels`
decimates into coarse levels that replace one another, while `reveal` writes an
additive ladder of disjoint face groups. A surface has no coarse prefix, which
is why a mesh cannot have both.

A new test keeps this from recurring: every top-level `luxar.*` package that
declares `__all__` must be named by an autodoc directive somewhere under
`docs/`. Both sides are derived from the tree rather than listed by hand, so a
new public package cannot be added without a page.

Separately, `grimp`, import-linter's Rust graph engine, is explicitly capped so
its upgrades are reviewed independently. The cap is now below 3.18: version
3.16 initially omitted the macOS arm64 wheel for standard CPython 3.14, forcing
a source build that needs rustc 1.94, but upstream backfilled those wheels for
3.16 and 3.17 on 2026-09-11.

#### The encoding vocabulary can no longer be misspelled

Luxar's on-disk encoding names carry two bit-width suffix conventions — the
per-channel family writes `_uN`, the scalar / bounded / lut / rgb families write
`_uintN` — and several documents used the wrong sibling of a real name,
including the published gsplats format spec and a docstring forty lines above
the code that emits a different name. The affected prose is corrected.

The conventions themselves stay. Both spellings are live in published stores, so
renaming either would invalidate every published store and checksum-pinned
record; `format-contract/contract.yaml` now records that measurement and the
reasoning, rather than leaving the split looking like an oversight.

Two gates enforce it instead. One asserts that no document names an encoding
absent from the contract, deriving the wrong-convention siblings from the
contract itself so a new encoding is covered as soon as it is added. It reads
prose deliberately: a misspelling reaches a docstring before it reaches an
f-string. The other closes the reverse direction of the existing emitted-names
check — every quantized name in the contract must be reachable by some producer,
or recorded as unreachable with its reason. Existing producer tests covered
individual names, but nothing enforced that reverse subset across the complete
contract, so a dead entry or a whole family disappearing from the producer
surface could go unnoticed.

#### Redistributed bundles now carry their third-party licence notices

The compiled viewer is redistributed four ways — the npm package, the wheel's
`luxar/_viewer_dist`, `luxar export` folders and the native launcher bundles —
and none of them carried a notice for any of the third-party code inside. The
production build emitted nothing because it runs no plugins, so only Luxar's own
BSD-3 licence existed anywhere in the tree. MIT, Apache-2.0, MPL-2.0 and BSD all
require their notices to accompany a binary redistribution.

The build now generates `THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.txt` from what it actually
consumes: the pnpm production closure, the cargo build graph of the WASM module,
and the colormap generator's own tables. Nothing is listed by hand, so a new
dependency cannot ship without its notice, and the generator refuses to write a
file it cannot complete rather than emit a plausible-looking partial one. Luxar's
own licence is embedded in it, because an export folder travels on its own.

`luxar export` now refuses to produce a folder whose notices are missing, rather
than warning: the folder otherwise looks complete to whoever receives it.

Separately, `scripts/generate_builtin_colormaps.py` no longer deletes four
shipped colormaps. `builtins.py` credits it as the generator, but running it
dropped `orange`, `bop_blue`, `bop_orange` and `bop_purple` from both the Python
and the TypeScript output without saying so — two hardcoded name lists had to
agree and did not. The grouping is now derived from the generated set and
asserts that nothing goes unwritten, and a test holds the round trip the file's
own header promises. No colormap data changed.

#### The browser support matrix says what was measured

Two READMEs listed four browsers as fully supported, with version floors, while
the Playwright config declared a single project — Firefox and WebKit were
commented out, so the claim had never been run even once.

It has now been run. Chromium, Firefox and WebKit all pass the E2E smoke subset,
but WebKit's OPFS store fails its init probe, so it renders correctly while
running **without the on-disk chunk cache** — nothing persists between sessions.
That is exactly the kind of difference a "supported" column hides, and it
matters most for the large datasets the old table was recommending a browser
for.

The version floors are gone: there is no `browserslist` and the build targets
`esnext`, so no floor follows from the toolchain and the numbers were never
derived from anything. The claim that Firefox decompresses WebAssembly twice as
fast is gone too — it appeared exactly once in the repository with no benchmark
behind it, and a specific number nobody measured reads as though somebody did.

Firefox and WebKit are now real Playwright projects rather than comments,
opt-in behind `LUXAR_E2E_BROWSERS=all` so the default suite still runs one
engine. `pnpm test:e2e:browsers` reproduces the measurement, and a new check
refuses to let either README name an engine the suite cannot run, or state a
version floor.

`luxar export --native` now names its `make build-launchers` prerequisite in the
CLI reference.

#### Changelog entries are filed under the month they were written

At release-prep the fold used to put every pending fragment under whichever
month it happened to run in. With 440 fragments waiting across two months, that
would have mis-dated 408 of them into a single unnavigable heading. Each entry
now goes under the month of the commit that added it, and a fragment git cannot
date fails the fold rather than being filed under the wrong month — committing
it is the fix, and `--month` remains the explicit override.

`make changelog-release` is new: it renames `## [Unreleased]` to
`## [<version>] - <date>` and opens a fresh empty one, so `CHANGELOG.md`
accumulates release history instead of a single ever-growing section. The
version comes from `__version__`, and the date is derived from it when it looks
like a CalVer date, so the header cannot contradict itself when the cut runs on
a different day from the version bump. It refuses while fragments are still
pending, because folding after a cut would ship those entries under the next
version.

#### The viewer now says which build it is

Every viewer bundle carries its version, commit and build time. `window.__luxarBuild`
is attached before init and without needing `?debug`, a startup log line reports the
same, and `index.html` gets a `<meta name="luxar-build">` tag that survives a bundle
which fails to boot — greppable in an unzipped wheel or an emailed `luxar export`
folder. Embedders can read it directly through the new `buildInfo()` export.

The stamp is applied once at Vite build time and so reaches the dev server, the PyPI
wheel, `luxar export` output, the npm library bundle and the hosted site together. It
never fails a build: a checkout with no git history is stamped `commit: "unknown"`
rather than erroring, and a dirty tree is marked as such so a dev build cannot point
a reader at source that is not what ran.

This also replaces `__luxarDebug.version`, which was the hardcoded string `'1.0.0'`
in two places — a wrong version being a worse diagnostic than no version, since the
claim looks authoritative.

A new `check-build-identity` gate reads the emitted files and fails if a bundle ships
unstamped or with a version that disagrees with `package.json`. It runs inside the
existing `wheel-viewer` and `release-readiness` CI jobs.

#### The viewer's build and gate scripts are now linted, formatted and type-checked

`pnpm lint`, `pnpm format` and `pnpm typecheck` covered `src/` and nothing else, leaving
5,774 lines across 37 files — every Playwright config, both Vite configs, both Vitest
configs and every `.mjs` gate script — outside all three tools. The selection was
adverse: those are the scripts that enforce the other gates.

All three scopes now reach the package root, and a new `check-lint-scope` test fails
when a source file lands outside them again, so the gap cannot silently reopen.

Widening the scope found one dead setting and one type mismatch: `minWorkers` in the
Vitest config is not an option in Vitest 4, while a working GitHub reporter entry had
the wrong tuple type.
It also exposed that Playwright 1.62 honours the screenshot comparison's 10-second
runtime timeout without declaring that option in its public config type, and found five
`eslint-disable` directives in a benchmark script that had never suppressed anything,
because nothing had ever linted the file.

The coverage thresholds module now has declarations, so TypeScript consumers check
its exports and value shapes instead of importing them as `any`; the runtime slack
guard remains responsible for rejecting misspelled metric names.

#### The `core` ↔ `io` import cycle is gone, and cannot come back

`luxar.core` and `luxar.io` were mutually dependent. The `core` → `io` direction ran
through fourteen function-local imports reaching into the *private* `io._compiler`
tree — and being function-local is exactly what hid it, since mypy does not follow
deferred imports for cycle purposes and neither existing import-linter contract looked
at this pair.

The shared code has moved to where both callers can reach it without either depending
on the other. Eighteen pre-write validators — the gates a geometry writer and the
pre-split path in `core.group.compositing` must run *identically*, or a wrong-length
channel rides the per-part slicer into every part — now live in `luxar.validation.writing`.
The `json_safe_value` attr-coercion helper, needed by `core`, `io` and `gsplats` alike,
moved to `luxar.typing_utils.json_safe`. Nothing changed about what any of them do.

A new `core must not import io` import-linter contract makes it permanent. It was
verified by reintroducing the cycle in both forms — a module-level import and the
deferred, inside-a-function form that hid the original — and watching it fail on each.

#### Viewer load and render performance

The viewer now measures how many elements each data node projects per drawing-buffer pixel and acts on it: additive, luminous and volumetric nodes that are denser than a few elements per pixel are thinned on the GPU with a hashed keep-fraction ladder and brightness compensation (a **Density Guard** toggle in the Performance popover turns it off per scene, with a live readout of how many nodes are thinned and how far; `?noDensityGuard` does the same for one session; the data monitor's scene graph marks each thinned node with a lattice-glyph `1/K` chip beside its LOD chip, since thinning changes what is drawn, not what is resident; the draw-order chip likewise trades the word `transparent`/`opaque` for a bucket glyph, with the full explanation in both tooltips), and the refinement loop defers additive rungs a node cannot show until the camera moves in. On the 1.5 M-point dense example this takes a framed view from 43 ms to the display's 8 ms frame budget at the same mean luminance; the 14.8 M-splat pathology slide drops from 114 ms to 67 ms per frame.

Startup no longer runs the load pass twice: the post-load slice update is skipped when the view state is unchanged, which removes the second query/decode/commit of every node (main-thread long tasks −65 to −70 % on the audited scenes) and lets the first refinement run finish instead of being cancelled. Large 3-D gsplat nodes project in a worker, the OPFS write queue accepts a much deeper burst of small chunks while bounding retained pending bytes to the larger of the L1 cache budget and 64MB, points and lines loaders skip the 404 probes for optional arrays the store listing rules out, blend-mode warm-up shares one compiled keeper per program variant across nodes (400 → 4 idle callbacks on the 100-node benchmark), and the adaptive-DPR controller stops learning from frames while the viewer is still loading or refining.

Observability landed first: `__luxarDebug.getPerf()` exposes a load timeline (`loadStart` → first commit → `sceneLoaded` → `refinementComplete`), renderer counters, adaptive-DPR diagnostics, projected density per node, cache and warm-up stats, and an `isSettled` flag probes can wait on; `pnpm test:perf:e2e -g "viewer audit"` reproduces the audit's measurements against the production bundle and `scripts/perf-diff.mjs` diffs two runs. `luxar info --stats` warns when a store's mean chunk is small enough to be round-trip bound on an HTTP/1.1 host such as `luxar serve` (10.6 s vs 4.0 s over HTTP/2 for the same 1.5 M points at 25 Mbps / 30 ms).

A pre-existing picking bug surfaced by the change was fixed on the way: pick materials of nodes registered after the scene load never bound their element texture, so first-load hovers on points and lines resolved nothing.

#### `poisson-disk` LOD ordering is no longer quadratic

Authoring a Points or Lines ladder with `additive_lod=dict(method="poisson-disk", …)`
was O(N²), not the O(N) its docstring claimed. The cell grid used to accelerate the
rejection test held *every input point* rather than only the accepted samples, and at
the coarsest radius that grid is just a few cells across — so the neighbourhood scan
covered the whole dataset and every candidate was tested against every point. On a
million points it extrapolated to about four and a half hours.

The grid now holds accepted samples only, which is what Bridson's algorithm calls for.
Cost per point is now flat from 10K to 1M points. The constant is hardware-bound — the
Bridson walk is a sequential interpreted loop — and measures 25 µs/point at
`n_lods=6` on an Apple M-series core against about 100 µs/point on a slower x86 one,
or roughly 25 to 100 seconds for a million points instead of hours.

The output is unchanged, and deliberately so: the neighbourhood search was already
correct, only the set scanned inside it was wrong. The permutation and per-level counts
are bit-identical to before across 320 configurations spanning eight point
distributions, and a new `test_cost_grows_linearly_with_n` fails if the quadratic ever
returns.

#### Wheel input is normalized across browsers

`WheelEvent.deltaY` only means something alongside `deltaMode`, and the viewer read
it as if it were always pixels. Chromium and WebKit report one notch as
`deltaMode = 0` with `deltaY = 100`; Firefox reports the same notch as
`deltaMode = 1` (lines) with `deltaY = 3`. Every wheel path that consumes the
magnitude therefore ran about 32x weaker there: wheel zoom moved 0.15% of the
distance to the target per notch instead of 5%, which in practice felt like a dead
wheel, and Ctrl+wheel FOV was off by the same factor at 0.15 degrees per notch
instead of 5. Shift+wheel view-axis roll had it too.

The three magnitude-consuming entry points — orbit/ortho wheel zoom, Shift+wheel
roll, Ctrl/Cmd+wheel FOV — now convert the delta to a pixel equivalent first, with
a line worth 16 px and a page worth the canvas's own height (falling back to a
nominal 800 px for an element that has not been laid out yet). Pixel-mode events
pass through verbatim and unclamped, so Chromium and WebKit behaviour is exactly
what it was and neither the per-scene Zoom Speed nor the global Zoom Sensitivity
needed re-tuning; a fast trackpad fling still arrives whole. The one exception is a
NaN or infinite delta, which is now dropped in every mode rather than passed on —
pre-fix an infinite one jumped the camera its full distance to the target in a
single event. Only the converted line and page deltas are capped, at 200 px — two
Chromium notches, the largest single step worth allowing — so a page-mode event on
a tall canvas or a driver reporting an absurd line count cannot produce one enormous
jump. Firefox's ordinary 3-line notch lands at 48 px, nowhere near that cap — the
same ballpark as Chromium's 100 px rather than exact parity, and the remaining
difference in feel is what the Zoom Sensitivity slider is for.

Normalization sits at the wheel handlers, not inside the zoom math, which is shared
with pointer-drag dolly — those deltas are real screen pixels and must stay raw. Fly
controls take only the sign of the wheel delta and are unaffected; the comment there
claiming to "normalize deltaY across browsers" was the mislabel that let this sit
unnoticed, and now says what it actually does.

#### `luxar gsplat info` no longer loads a whole store to describe it

Pointed at a partition or nested `.gsplats.zarr`, `info` decoded every array of every
leaf into memory — three separate times. Once for a flat load that raises for a tree
and was discarded, once as a validity check whose result was thrown away, and once for
the summary itself. On a 10-part store of 960,000 splats occupying 6.4 MB on disk, that
was 120 decode calls and 115 MB of arrays, to print 25 lines of metadata. The
operational record has the same shape reaching 116 GB of memory on a 13 GB store.

Everything `info` prints about a tree — its kind, dimensionality, per-leaf splat counts,
bounds and fitting record — lives in the store's attributes and array metadata, so it is
now read from there. The same store decodes nothing at all, and `info` additionally
reports what a full load *would* materialise.

#### The package now has a layering contract

`import-linter` declared three narrow rules and reported them kept across 1,026 files —
green, while the dependency graph carried ten mutually-cyclic subpackage pairs. There
was no contract describing which package may import which.

There is one now, and its order was chosen by measurement rather than assertion: every
ordering of the packages whose position was in question was scored by how many imports
point the wrong way up the stack, and the declared order is the minimum. Where two
orders tied, the tie was broken on what the imports mean — `gsplats` sits below `core`
and `io` because those consume the splat data model, not the other way round.

The 35 imports that still point the wrong way are listed as dated debt rather than
hidden. That list can only shrink: `import-linter` rejects an entry that no longer
matches anything, and a new `check-layer-order` gate pins 35 as the maximum, so a new
violation cannot be hidden by adding a matching ignore. The same gate re-checks that
the declared order is still the best available, so a structural change that argues
for a different architecture says so instead of quietly accumulating exceptions.

#### Six fit parameters had drifted to different defaults in different places

The Gaussian-splat fit schema is restated along its call chain, and nothing checked that
the restatements agreed. `prepare_fit_config` — public API — disagreed with
`fit_gaussian_splats` on five defaults, and a `FitConfig(...)` that supplied its required
fields while omitting `max_eccentricity` disagreed on a sixth: it left the limit unset,
while every documented default said 10.

All six now match the documented entry point. No internal path was affected —
`fit_gaussian_splats` passes those parameters explicitly — so the divergence only ever
reached callers who used the lower-level functions directly, which is why it went
unnoticed.

A new schema-agreement test derives both sides and fails on any shared parameter whose
default differs, so adding a knob in one place and not another goes red. It also pins
the published contract for `OptimConfig`/`LossConfig`/`ConstraintConfig`: unpacking a
default bundle into `fit_gaussian_splats` must change nothing.

#### Remote-control embedder API: `flyTo`, rendering and layer setters, `getViewerState`, `camera-changed`

A Luxar viewer can now be driven from an external program without the built-in
UI. `LuxarApp.flyTo(pose, { durationMs, easing })` transitions smoothly to a
camera pose captured with `getCameraPose()`, interpolating in the orbit
parameterisation (the focus target moves linearly while the viewing direction is
slerped and the distance log-interpolated) so the camera arcs around the scene
instead of cutting through it, and lands on the pose exactly. Any input on the
canvas or keyboard cancels the flight where it is — the visitor's own hand always
wins — and the promise reports whether the flight completed.

`setRenderingSettings(patch)` rides the exact path an authored `viewer_config`
takes at load, so anything a scene author can bake a controller can set live, with
the same validation and side-effects; `setLayer(path, patch)` and `getLayers()`
expose the Layers panel's per-layer appearance through the panel's own
state-manager and apply-engine route; `getViewerState()` bundles dataset, camera,
slice position, rendering and layers in one call; and a new `camera-changed`
event streams the pose as it moves. `docs/guides/specs/REMOTE_CONTROL_SPEC.md`
records the design and the follow-on phases (WebSocket hub in `luxar serve`,
kiosk permissions in `viewer_config`).

Scenes can also now author **story waypoints**: `ViewerConfig(waypoints=[Waypoint(
when={"story": 1, "time": (10, 20)}, camera=CameraConfig(target_node="cluster_7"),
duration_ms=2500)])` binds a camera pose to a position along the hidden
dimensions, using the same `visible_range` rule overlays use (exact within ±0.5,
inclusive ranges, first match wins). A hidden discrete "story" dimension thus
carries a whole guided tour — colours in the data, captions as dimension-aware
overlays, and now the camera — driven by the `[` / `]` keys, the slider or an
external controller calling `setDimensionValue`. The viewer snaps to the
matching waypoint at load and flies on a change of match; fields a waypoint
leaves out keep the live camera's value, so a waypoint can re-aim without
moving, and an optional `rendering` block applies snake_case `ViewerConfig`
overrides on arrival. Waypoints compose with the orbit turntable: while
auto-rotate is on, a story step keeps the live viewing direction and only moves
the point the camera spins around, so the spin never pauses (`flyTo` exposes
this as `keepOrientation`). `CameraConfig` gains an ortho `zoom`, since under an
orthographic projection zoom, not distance, is what frames tighter. Under dynamic
clipping, flights and `setCameraPose` leave `near`/`far` to the per-frame updater,
which owns them; interpolating a pose's captured planes had clipped geometry away
mid-flight until landing.

A new demo, `esm3_protein_stories`, is the reference scene for all of this: the
ESM C Swiss-Prot 3D UMAP with a hidden `story` dimension that flies through ten
protein-family clusters — hemoglobin, photosystem II D1, Hsp70/DnaK, the viral
surface proteins, the prion protein — each highlighted in its own layer and
captioned with a panel of sourced facts closing on an open question, and wrapped
in a faint translucent marker shell built from the existing mesh model. It reads
the landscape demo's cache and opens with the turntable on.

Overlays gain a fourth type: `Scene.add_video` stores a WebM or MP4 beside the
overlay (like an image) and the viewer renders it as a muted, looping `<video>`
that plays only while its `visible_range` matches, so a dozen clips cost one
decode at a time. A VP9 WebM with an alpha channel renders transparent in Chrome
and Firefox; an optional poster covers Safari. The stories demo uses it to show a
representative PDB structure turning beside each story as a matte clay surface
in pastel shades of the story's own colour, standing on its longest axis and
turning once in 30 s. PyMOL computes the surface once; a moderngl offscreen GPU
renderer shades the 900 frames with screen-space ambient occlusion in about a
millisecond each (PyMOL's own ray tracer, the first implementation, needed five
and a half hours for the set). PyMOL is the demos' one deliberate non-pip
dependency, gated with an install hint rather than a hard requirement.

#### Fit parameters now cross the internal pipeline once (#2539, part 1/2)

`fit_gaussian_splats` remains the explicit documented API, but its raw fitting
parameters now enter a `FitParameters` dataclass before crossing
`GaussianSplatFitter.fit` and `prepare_fit_config`. Those two internal hops no
longer repeat 43 defaults apiece, so a new fit knob has one public signature and
one parameter field rather than three independently drifting signatures.

Direct low-level callers now pass `FitParameters(V=..., ...)` to
`GaussianSplatFitter.fit`, and `prepare_fit_config` accepts the same bundle. The
validation order and normalized `FitConfig` output are unchanged; the schema gate
now checks that the bundle covers every entry-point parameter not handled by the
wrapper and that every default still agrees.

#### Fit validation no longer lives in one guard wall (#2539, part 2/2)

`prepare_fit_config` now delegates input normalization and ordered validation to
focused helpers below the complexity ceiling. An all-pairs equivalence harness
pins every recorded validation failure against every later one, so exception
types, messages, and first-error precedence remain unchanged as the checks evolve.

#### `batch-fit run` gains `--calibration-samples`, and `submit`'s `--gpus` becomes `--gpus-per-task`

`batch-fit run` and `batch-fit submit` plan the same job and differ only in who
executes the tasks, but each mapped its flags onto the planner's config objects in
its own code. The copies drifted: `--calibration-samples` was declared on `submit`
only, while the local path consumes it — a local `--denoise` run with a deferred
percentile floor always calibrated `h` on 5 timepoints, with no way to ask for more.
The flag now exists on both, with the same default, so nothing changes unless you
set it.

`--gpus` meant two different things on the two commands: on `run` it selects which
local devices to use (`auto` | `all` | `cpu` | `0,1,3`), on `submit` it was a count
of GPUs to request per Slurm task. So `--gpus 2` meant "use card #2" on one and "two
GPUs per task" on the other, and `--gpus auto` was a parse error on `submit`. The
Slurm one is now `--gpus-per-task`, which is also the directive it generates. `run`'s
`--gpus` is unchanged.

Both commands now build their configs through one shared mapper, and a new agreement
test fails if a second mapping site appears, if a flag reaches one command and not
the other, or if the two disagree on a shared default or public spelling.

#### The offline capture loop is six named stages instead of one 676-line method

`runOfflineCaptureLoop` — the code that produces the gallery stills and turntable
videos — was a single 676-line method nested twelve blocks deep, three quarters of
its module. It is now 164 lines that read as the sequence it always was: preflight,
driver and context, overlay, frame loop, LOD settle, teardown. Each stage is its own
file, and the LOD quiescence drain in particular is now reachable on its own rather
than behind a driver, an animation controller and a DOM overlay.

Nothing about the capture behaves differently. The fifty-three existing behavioural
tests were left untouched and stayed green through every step of the extraction,
which is what makes that claim checkable rather than asserted. All eight of the
file's lint suppressions — one complexity, six depth, one function length — are
gone rather than re-keyed.

#### The CUDA and Metal backends could not be built at all — fixed

Both native build paths pinned `-std=c++17`, in the position where PyTorch appends
its own `-std=c++20` first and the last flag wins. Current PyTorch refuses to be
compiled below C++20 outright (`#error C++20 or later compatible compiler is
required`), so this did not merely relax the standard — it stopped the extensions
compiling. The Metal package builds itself the first time you use it, so the failure
landed on users of `luxar[gsplats]` on Apple silicon rather than in any build.

Both are now on C++20, verified by rebuilding the Metal extension end to end and by
compiling the CUDA bindings against PyTorch's headers at each standard.

`make check-native` is the check that would have caught it: it checks every shipped
CUDA and Metal translation unit when the relevant toolchain is present, without
needing a GPU, and reports each toolchain it cannot find rather than passing
silently over it. CI requires the host-C++ arm; #2544 tracks macOS and CUDA-toolkit
coverage for the Metal and `nvcc` arms.

The numeric parity tests against the PyTorch reference do already exist for both
backends, and are substantial; they are skipped without a GPU, so they never run
automatically. Both backends' READMEs now say plainly what is and is not verified,
rather than leaving it to be assumed.

#### Python static checks can no longer silently miss CI

CI now invokes the declared `lint`, import-layer, and version-check Hatch scripts
instead of restating their commands. A repository-level test also rejects any new
`check-static` member that is neither invoked by a workflow that gates pull requests
nor carrying a documented exemption.

#### `import luxar.validation.types` works, and ~40 dead typing names are gone

`luxar/__init__.py` bound the name `validation` to `validation/base.py` rather
than to the subpackage, so `import luxar.validation.types` raised
`ImportError: cannot import name 'types' from 'luxar.validation.base'` — and the
same for six other submodules. Internal code never hit it, because
`from luxar.validation.x import y` goes through the import system rather than the
attribute, and neither did the docs, because Sphinx resolves via `sys.modules`.
Only the form a user would reach for was broken. A second re-export existed
beside it purely as the escape hatch, with no readers at all; both are gone and
the subpackage is bound directly.

`validate_node_type()` rejected `"mesh"`. It checked against a hand-copied tuple
of five `NodeType` values where the enum has six, so a public validator refused a
first-class geometry type that the contract-reading validator next door accepted.
The node-type and physical-unit vocabularies are now derived from their enums,
which removes the last two of four separate copies of the unit list.

`luxar.typing_utils.config` is deleted. Three of its ~30 public names had a
reader: two were aliases of constants that already existed, and the third moved
next to its single caller. `typing_utils.protocols` loses the six names nothing
referenced, and `typing_utils.constants` loses thirteen — including a duplicated
point-count pair that disagreed with its twin, and a compression-level trio that
agreed with neither the real codec policy nor the validator that used to sit
above it.

#### The writer protocol now type-checks the compiler that implements it

`ZarrWriterProtocol` declares the contract every Zarr writer must satisfy, and
its one implementation had opted out of it: all four geometry write methods on
`LuxarZarrCompiler` carried `# type: ignore[override]`, so nothing verified the
417-line interface against the code behind it.

Two disagreements were hiding there. `io/writer.py` defined its own
`PositionArray` and `ColorArray` — wider than the same names in
`typing_utils.aliases`, in a module that also imports from it — so the protocol
and the compiler were annotated from two different vocabularies and could not
agree. Writing a store per candidate dtype settled which was right: the write
path really does accept float16 positions, uint8 and uint16 colors, and
float16/uint8 scalar attributes, so the narrow annotations were the fiction.
There is now one definition of each, threaded from the public method down
through the geometry writers, spatial ordering, dataset writers and validators.

The second was a plain bug. The protocol's `write_mesh` omitted the eleven
texture parameters the compiler takes between `scalars` and `shading`. Those are
positional-or-keyword, so their absence renumbered every argument after them: a
caller typed against the protocol and passing `shading` positionally would have
set `uvs` instead.

Nothing about how data is written changed — these are annotations. What changed
is that mypy now checks all four methods, and a new test pins the parameter
names, order and defaults of all sixteen declared methods, plus the input dtypes
the aliases promise.

#### The partial-extend tolerance is decided in one place again

`GEOMETRY_DESCRIPTORS` is the viewer's table of what each geometry kind needs
from the shared scene-loader machinery, and it exists specifically so a per-type
capability is a table entry rather than the presence of an `if`.
`applyPartialExtendTolerance` had escaped it: twelve call sites hardcoded the
boolean — the four node loaders, the four leaf handlers, the four LOD-refinement
loops — and only two read the table. Lines, the one kind that opts out, wrote
`false` in three separate places with three separate comments explaining why.

Nothing was visibly broken, which is the point: a wrong value there is not a
crash but a clipping result quietly too generous or too tight, on one geometry
type, in one code path. All twelve now read one table, which the descriptor also
sources from, and a test fails on any new hardcoded site.

#### Two E2E specs that #2494 exposed rather than broke

`test-fixtures-rendering.spec.ts`'s "should detect and report console errors"
navigates to a dataset that does not exist, which is the whole premise of the
test. It used to pass because the viewer quietly opened the dataset browser
instead; since the URL-suffix short-circuit the viewer honestly attempts the
load and logs four errors for the failure, and the fixture's automatic
console-error gate failed the teardown even though every assertion in the body
passed. The test now carries the fixture's per-spec `ALLOW_CONSOLE_ERRORS`
annotation. Not a new entry in `DEFAULT_ALLOWED_CONSOLE_ERRORS`: "Failed to load
scene" is the most important error the viewer can log, and forgiving it there
would blind the sixty-odd specs that share the fixture. The test also counted
warnings as errors — once in its page-console listener and again when tallying
the interceptor's buckets — so a single unrelated warning could satisfy it on
its own. The verdict now needs a genuine error from one side or the other, and
the warning counts stay in the diagnostic output.

`worker-wasm-integration.spec.ts` asserted that `DataWorker ready` appears in
the in-page console buffer. That line is logged from inside the data worker, and
the interceptor only patches the main-thread console, so it could never appear
there — the assertion sat behind an `if (hasWorkers)` guard that had always been
false. Moving pool creation to an eager warm-up at scene load put
`Worker N/M ready` in the buffer, flipped the guard true, and the dead assertion
finally ran. It now waits unconditionally for `Worker pool ready with N
worker(s)`, which is logged on the main thread and only after a pool comes up
with at least one worker. The test is renamed to what it verifies: neither
assertion ever established that a query was *offloaded*, which would need a
worker-served-query counter on the debug interface. The redundant sibling
"should create worker pool successfully" — same dataset, same probe, same final
assertion, same vacuous guard — is dropped.

#### Luxar's console output can now be turned down, or off

Everything below the CLI narrates through arbol — 547 `aprint` calls across
`gsplats`, `io` and `core` — which is the right default for a long CLI run and
the wrong one in a notebook cell or a napari plugin. There was no way to say so:
no `verbose` or `quiet` parameter on `Scene.save()` or `fit_gaussian_splats()`,
and no switch that was part of Luxar's own API.

```python
import luxar

luxar.set_verbosity("silent")     # process-wide: silent | summary | normal | full
with luxar.verbosity("summary"):  # scoped, restores on exit
    scene.save()
```

`"full"` remains the default, so nothing changes for code that does not call
this. An integer sets an explicit tree depth. Note that `0` is *not* silence —
arbol at depth 0 still prints top-level lines plus a truncation notice for each
section it truncates at the cap — so pass `"silent"`; a bool is refused outright
because `set_verbosity(False)` reads as quiet but would resolve to that
non-silent depth 0.

Warnings routed through `arbol_warnings()` now fall back to Python's standard
stderr display whenever arbol output is disabled or the current section is
below its depth cap, instead of being dropped. This also applies to existing
callers that set a finite `Arbol.max_depth` without using the new verbosity API.

The setting drives arbol's own switches, which are class attributes, so it is
process-global rather than per-call and is not thread-safe. Both constraints are
documented on the module. A per-call argument and a `logging` bridge remain
possible later; neither is needed to make the output silenceable.

#### One copy of the LOD-refinement plumbing instead of four

The viewer's four progressive-LOD refinement wrappers — one per geometry type —
were 83-91% identical after name normalisation. Each carried its own copy of the
admission gate, the abort-versus-failure catch block with its pass rollback and
backoff counting, the residency bookkeeping, and the four loop-progress
callbacks. Only the load-and-commit body genuinely differs, and it still lives
per geometry, because parameterising it would trade four readable flows for one
function with a strategy argument.

The saving in lines is small — 43 — and that is not the point. One coupled
invariant in particular now lives in one place: the gate's decline reasons must
match the progress callbacks' exclusions, because a budget-declined loader still
reports having more levels, so leaving it out of the "is anyone still working?"
check means the refinement loop never terminates while holding the update lock.
That pairing used to be restated four times.

Nothing about how refinement behaves changed. The four wrappers were already
covered by one shared behavioural contract, which is what made collapsing them
verifiable: each of three deliberate regressions introduced into the extracted
code fails in all four geometries and passes again when reverted.

#### `LUXAR_TRACEBACK=1` gets the traceback back out of a failed command

Seventeen CLI error handlers printed one line and exited. That is the right
default — a stack trace is noise when the cause is "file not found" — but there
was no way to opt out, so a genuine bug inside the library arrived as one line
with nowhere to go next. Eight of them discarded the exception chain as well,
two via `raise ... from None`, which erases the implicit context too.

Setting `LUXAR_TRACEBACK=1` now re-raises the original exception with its
traceback intact, and the one-line message says so, so it is discoverable at the
moment you need it:

```
❌ Error reading info for /tmp/notastore.luxar.zarr: No group found in store …
   (set LUXAR_TRACEBACK=1 and re-run for the full traceback)
```

An environment variable rather than a flag, because a Typer callback option has
to precede the subcommand — a poor shape for something you reach for after a
command has already failed. `LUXAR_TRACEBACK=1 luxar …` re-runs what you just
typed. `LUXAR_TRACEBACK=0` (and `false`/`no`/`off`) mean off, so exporting it
does not pin it on.

A separate group of about two dozen handlers already prints a traceback
unconditionally, which is the opposite complaint — a missing file should not come
with a stack trace. Making those opt-in too is a behaviour change for two dozen
commands and is left for its own change (#2553).

#### CLI tracebacks are opt-in for interactive commands

Interactive `luxar gsplat` commands now report a concise error by default instead
of attaching a Python traceback to routine failures. Set `LUXAR_TRACEBACK=1` when
re-running a command to see the original traceback. The long-running fit and batch
entry points still print tracebacks unconditionally so unattended GPU and Slurm
logs remain useful for post-mortem diagnosis.

Fatal error lines also fall back to stderr when process-wide arbol verbosity hides
normal narration, preventing a silent exit 1.

#### Integral quantized arrays decode without truncation bias

The Python decoder now rounds reconstructed values and clamps them to the target
range before restoring an integral `original_dtype`, matching nearest-integer
quantization semantics instead of systematically truncating values toward zero.
Floating-point decoding and the CUSTOM encoder's historical truncating write path
are unchanged.

#### Demo download credentials no longer follow unsafe redirects

`robust_download()` and `download_zip_member()` accepted arbitrary HTTP headers
for authenticated datasets. Requests already removed `Authorization` when a
redirect changed host, port, or downgraded HTTPS to HTTP, but custom credential
headers such as `api-key` kept following the redirect. Both download paths now
apply requests' own authorization policy to every caller-supplied header while
retaining its safe default-port HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade exception.

#### Mesh physical materials, Phases 1 and 2: `material="physical"`, glass, live knobs

A mesh can now opt out of the house shader's light-free, view-anchored key and
into three.js's physically based material — `MeshPhysicalMaterial` on WebGL,
`MeshPhysicalNodeMaterial` on WebGPU — with `add_mesh(..., material="physical")`
and the knobs `roughness`, `metalness`, `clearcoat`, `clearcoat_roughness`,
`iridescence`, `sheen` (each in `[0, 1]`) and `sheen_color`. That unlocks what the
house model could never express: polished and brushed metals, a pearlescent
shell, velvet, and a true view-relative Fresnel rim from `clearcoat` on a dark
translucent base — the marker-shell look the protein-stories demo wanted. The
viewer lights these from a scene environment (a prefiltered `RoomEnvironment`)
that is built lazily on the first physical mesh and never otherwise, so every
existing scene keeps `scene.environment` empty and renders exactly as before;
house materials do not read it in any case.

Phase 2 adds the glass family: `transmission` (`[0, 1]`), `ior` (`[1, 2.333]`),
`thickness`, `attenuation_color` with `attenuation_distance`, and `dispersion`,
rendered by three's stock transmission pass on both backends. Glass refracts the
background and other meshes — not Luxar's points, lines or splats, which three's
pass never sees and which stay crisp on top, in front of or behind the glass, on
both backends (a transmissive mesh is ordered first within its `layer_order` band
so WebGPU, where glass shares the transparent list with the emissive layers,
cannot paint over a cluster that sorts behind it). The Layers panel's physical
knob listing became live sliders: dragging `Transmission` on a metal turns it to
glass, an `Attenuation distance` slider's top stop means "none", and Reset
restores what `add_mesh(...)` authored.

Authoring is fail-loud: a physical knob without `material="physical"` is refused,
a physical mesh refuses the house-shader knobs, `blending_mode`, a colormap, a
texture and `shading="none"`, and `thickness` / `attenuation_*` / `dispersion`
are refused without a `transmission` above zero — none of these means anything in
those pairings. `shading` smooth/flat and `alpha_cutoff` are kept — the first is
a property of any lit surface, the second maps onto three's `alphaTest`.
Translucency is read off the data (an `opacity` below 1, a `transmission` above
0, or per-vertex alpha without a cutoff); a physical mesh is never
triangle-sorted but keeps its `layer_order` band, picks through the house
mesh-pick material, and works with partitions, LOD groups and nD slicing as any
mesh does.

Ships with `demo_mesh_physical_materials` (nine spheres — house shader, clearcoat
shell, gold, steel, pearl, velvet, clear glass, amber glass, dispersive crystal —
in front of a checkerboard for the glass to bend, with emissive clusters inside
the shell and the clear glass), a public `luxar.mesh.primitives.icosphere()`, and
a real-WebGPU-versus-WebGL screenshot A/B script
(`scripts/ab-webgpu-vs-webgl.mjs`, judged by structural similarity).

#### L2 write queue keeps a bound without throwing away the cache

The viewer's background OPFS write queue capped the bytes its pending writes retain at the larger of the resolved L1 budget and 64MB. That charged the queue for memory it does not own: a pending write holds the very same buffer the L1 entry holds, so while the entry is L1-resident it costs one extra reference rather than a second copy, and the only genuinely extra retention is the set of writes whose L1 entry has since been evicted. On a machine whose L1 resolves to around 100MB the cap therefore bound at roughly half of what a large scene streams, and the L2 tier silently went back to dropping most of its writes — a second visit re-fetched nearly the whole store.

The allowance is now derived from the heap headroom left outside the cache pool, the same model the eager loader's working-set budget uses: a quarter of that remainder, capped at 512MB, and 256MB where no memory signal exists at all. On a 4GiB Chrome heap that resolves to 328MiB, which clears both the 214MB the largest audited scene streams before the old cap binds and that scene's 277MB whole-store ceiling — by 1.18× on the latter, so the margin is real but not large. The allowance is heap-relative by design: below roughly a 2.6GiB heap it binds again for that scene and writes are dropped, which is the correct behaviour when the memory to retain them is not there. The eager working set takes half of the same remainder and the last quarter is claimed by neither.
