Overflow also drops the arriving write instead of the oldest pending one — the queue drains from the oldest end, so evicting there kept discarding the write that was about to run and left a scattered remnant on disk, whereas dropping the arrival lets that end drain in order and leaves contiguous runs a warm revisit can serve from. The tradeoff is locality rather than drop count: uniform-size writes drop equally under either policy, while mixed sizes can favour either one. A large arrival no longer displaces several small pending writes, but a large pending write can hold off several smaller arrivals. The opt-in performance bench now asserts the drop counter is zero — at the end of every cold repetition as well as during the load, and on the warm revisit — and separately flags an allowance that no longer covers what the scene streamed, recording the resolved allowance in its result row. A cap that binds again is therefore visible as a bench failure instead of only as a slower second visit.

#### Density guard: threshold knob, held-rung marker, audit record

`?densityCap=N` overrides the density guard's elements-per-pixel threshold for one session, for both the shader thinning ladder and the refinement rung gate, so a threshold sweep is one URL edit per arm; the Performance popover's Thinning row shows the cap in force. In the data monitor's scene graph a pending detail level the loader is deliberately holding back, either because the density guard deferred it at the current framing or because loading it would cross the residency ceiling, now shows a pause glyph instead of the streaming hourglass, with the reason in its tooltip, and the header counts such nodes as `held` rather than `refining`. The September 2026 viewer performance audit that drove these changes is preserved under `docs/guides/developer/`.

#### Bloom renders as a glow again on the WebGPU renderer

On the opt-in WebGPU renderer, bloom came out as a flat dim wash rather than a
glow. The bloom pyramid's upsample pass accumulates each smaller mip into the
larger one by drawing it with additive blending, and that blend is the whole
accumulation mechanism — without it every upsample overwrote its destination mip
and only the last, weakest contribution survived.

The cause was in `buildMaterial`, the helper both backends construct their
post-processing materials through: the WebGPU branch forwarded only the uniform
table to the TSL factory and discarded the rest of the requested state, so the
returned material kept its default `NormalBlending` while the WebGL branch
honoured the `AdditiveBlending` the bloom chain asked for. The render state
(`blending`, `depthTest`, `depthWrite`, `transparent`, `toneMapped`, `side`) is
now resolved once and applied on both branches, which fixes bloom and closes the
same trap for every material the WebGPU port gains next. The other five keys were
silently dropped too, and were harmless only by coincidence: the bloom and FXAA
factories happen to set matching `depthTest`, `depthWrite` and `transparent` on
themselves, `side` was never set by any of them but its material default already
matched, and `toneMapped` is not read on that backend at all.

#### Shift+wheel roll survives browser axis swapping

Orbit and fly controls now read the horizontal wheel delta when a browser moves a
Shift+wheel gesture off the vertical axis, allowing the advertised view-axis roll
to consume that swapped-axis input. Vertical deltas still take precedence when
both axes carry motion, and zero-delta events no longer wake the render loop.

The fallback is deliberately opt-in: ordinary horizontal trackpad scrolling still
does not zoom, change FOV, or move the fly camera forward. The three slider wheel
handlers that already carried the same fallback now share the central helper.

#### Sound layer: `sound` nodes, the viewer's audio engine, and a narrated stories demo

A scene can now be heard as well as seen. `scene.add_sound(name, clip, …)` writes a first-class `sound` node — an MP3 or AAC clip stored as an opaque file inside the node group, with an optional nD `positions` array — and the viewer plays it through Web Audio via three's `AudioListener`, `PositionalAudio` and `Audio`, with no new dependency. A sound is *heard, not drawn*: it joins the format contract's `node_types` but none of the geometry tables, carries no appearance attrs, and never stretches the scene bounds. Its audibility is the same hidden-dimension slab rule that decides which points are visible, so `hidden={"story": 3}` binds a clip to a story step and `extend_to_all` works as for points; a clip with no positions plays everywhere, and a spatial clip plays from its place in the scene and gets louder as the camera approaches. Triggers are `continuous` (looped while audible, fading on the slab edge) and `once` (each time the node becomes audible); three buses — `ambient`, `voice`, `effects` — carry per-scene gains from `ViewerConfig.audio`, and the voice bus ducks the ambient bed while a narration plays. Every clip must record its `license`, `attribution` and `source_url`; Ogg is refused because Safari cannot decode it; the clip bytes are folded into `content_hash` through the same payload step that covers overlay images.

In the viewer a **Sound** button appears in the rail only when the loaded scene has sound nodes (click mutes, right-click opens a mixer), the mute and master gain persist across scenes, and a one-time "Tap to enable sound" gate covers browsers that refuse to start audio without a gesture (a kiosk launched with `--autoplay-policy=no-user-gesture-required` never sees it). The embedder API grows `getAudioState()`, `setAudio()`, `playSound()`, `stopSound()`, an `audio` block in `getViewerState()`, and `sound-started` / `sound-ended` events.

The `esm3_protein_stories` demo is the reference scene: a CC0 ambient pad plays under the whole tour and each story is narrated on arrival by its authored spoken script, synthesised when the scene is built (`luxar.demos._narration`: OpenAI TTS when `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set, the macOS system voice otherwise, a warning and no narration on a box with neither), cached by engine, voice and text so an unchanged story never re-synthesises. `--no-audio` builds the scene without the layer.

Fixed along the way: enumerating a group that holds a plain payload file (an overlay image, now also a sound clip) made zarr warn, which under `-W error` failed every such compile at finalize; the warning is scoped out at the finalize boundary and in the reader.

**Phases 2–4 of the spec land in the same PR.** `trigger="on_arrive"` / `"on_depart"` play when a story flight lands on / leaves the `viewer_config.waypoints` entry the node's row belongs to: the waypoint driver now emits `waypoint-departed { index }` and `waypoint-arrived { index, completed }` on the embedder bus (a flight the visitor cancels still arrives; one superseded by the next story never does), and the same slab kernel that decides audibility decides membership, so `extend_to_all` and `nd_transform` hold for triggers too. `attach_to="<node name>"` makes a source follow another node's bounding-box centre — "the cluster hums" without authoring coordinates. Sound nodes authored with `layer=True` are rows in the Layers panel: the eye mutes the node (a group's eye silences every sound under it), an inline slider sets its gain, and the tooltip shows the clip's provenance; `LayerSummary` / `LayerPatch` carry `gain`. The Recording panel's real-time WebM path records the mix the listener hears when "Include Audio" is on (an Opus-capable mime is requested first; frame-by-frame captures stay silent). `ambisonic="foa"` marks a first-order ambisonic **field** — a 4-channel AmbiX AAC clip decoded to stereo through a dependency-free rotate-and-decode graph (nine gains over the dipoles, a virtual-cardioid pair) and turned against the camera every frame, so a bed stays fixed to the world as the visitor turns. Omnitone was not adopted: it decodes to binaural only, fetches its HRIRs from a CDN at runtime, and is unmaintained.

In the stories demo the narration is now `on_arrive` and the ambient bed is re-encoded as an ambisonic field at build time when the box has a decoder and an AAC encoder (`afconvert` on macOS, or `ffmpeg`); `luxar.demos._audio_synth` holds the synthesis, encoding and AmbiX helpers.

#### Scene environments for physical meshes: the data is the light (Phase 4)

A physical mesh is lit by an environment, and until now that environment was
always three's neutral room. `viewer_config.environment` picks the source:
`room` (the default, unchanged), `hdri` (an equirectangular image, `url`), or
`scene`, in which case the viewer captures a cube map from a probe inside the
scene itself — the centre of the bounds, a node's bbox centre (`node:<path>`) or
a literal `(x, y, z)` — so a chrome sphere reflects the point cloud around it and
a glass shell tints the data behind it. The capture hides the physical meshes for
its six draws, is redone when geometry commits, a slice moves or an appearance
changes, only once the loader has settled, and never per frame or on camera
motion; both backends re-prefilter the cube in place. `resolution` (16 to 1024,
default 128) and `intensity` complete the config.

A published scene should not pay for a live capture on every visit, so the
capture can be baked. `luxar env bake scene.luxar.zarr` serves the store and the
built viewer from one process, drives a headless browser through the viewer's
`?bakeEnv` one-shot (`&probe=` and `&envResolution=` override the authored
values) and attaches the result; `luxar env attach` writes a capture the bake
produced elsewhere. The map lives in a root-level `environment/` sidecar group
that no node listing sees, as a `(6, H, W, 4)` array of half-float bits under a
digest-derived name, and it carries the `content_hash` of the scene it was baked
from: a map whose scene has since changed is reported and ignored in favour of
the live capture. The group is excluded from the scene's own `content_hash`, so
attaching a map never invalidates a visitor's warm cache and attaching the same
map twice writes nothing.

`demo_mesh_reflections` — an emissive swirl with a chrome and a glass sphere,
`environment.source="scene"` — is the showcase and the bake target. Baked and
live agree at SSIM 0.9985 (WebGL) and 0.9989 (WebGPU) on the same backend; the
two backends agree at 1.000 on a baked map and 0.986 on live capture. House
materials never read the environment, so scenes without a physical mesh render
exactly as before.

#### Mesh physical materials, Phase 3: `refract_data`, glass that refracts the data

A physical glass mesh can now refract the points, lines and splats behind it:
`add_mesh(..., material="physical", transmission=1.0, refract_data=True)`. Until now
glass refracted the background and other meshes only, and Luxar's emissive data drew
on top of it, crisp and unrefracted. With the flag the glass draws after the data it
refracts — and the data IN FRONT of the glass still lands crisp on top of it, because
the frame is partitioned by depth rather than by draw order. Absent means false, and
scenes with no physical glass render exactly as before.

The mechanism is a scene-pass split owned by the post-processing pipeline, on both
backends. The refracting glass's front faces are first rendered depth-only into one
shared depth texture; the scene is then drawn with every data material in a "behind
the glass" mode, in which each fragment compares its own depth with the glass depth at
its pixel and keeps itself only when it is behind the glass or under no glass at all;
the glass draws next (on WebGL with a screen-space quad textured with a copy of the
first pass, since three's transmission target there holds only the opaque list); and
the data is drawn once more in the complementary "in front" mode, so every data
fragment is drawn exactly once and the glass paints over nothing nearer than itself.
Emissive layers still write no depth — the classification lives in their fragment
shaders, points, lines, splats and the house mesh, GLSL and TSL alike — and picking
sees all the data as before. A refracting glass also ranks last in its `layer_order`
band, and the containment hoist no longer lifts a lens above the cluster it encloses.
Every piece of renderer state the split borrows is restored inside the same render
call, the transmission target runs at half resolution for the glass pass only on
WebGL, and an EXR capture refracts too. The frame cost is paid only while a refracting
glass is visible and is carried by the glass pass itself; the partition adds nothing
measurable on the showcase.

Building it surfaced a defect the spec had not anticipated: three copies the alpha of
what a glass samples into the glass fragment's alpha, and Luxar's HDR framebuffer alpha
is an overdraw count (8 to 18 behind a point cloud), not coverage — so a glass drawn
after the data came out thousands of times too bright, or negative, on both backends.
The house already treated that channel as undefined (the mega shader reads RGB only;
the EXR export forces alpha to 1), so the physical family now refuses it as well: the
transmitted alpha is pinned to 1 in both wrappers, a pixel no-op for Phase 2 glass and
the reason `refract_data` composites correctly. One visible consequence: an
`opaque`-mode house layer or a cutout mesh seen through glass now follows the same
rule instead of alpha-blending with its own coverage. A second finding shaped the
split: both renderers force a clear at the start of every render whose scene has a
colour background, whatever `autoClear` says, so the passes after the first run with
the background taken away.

The Layers panel gains a live "Refract data" switch on physical glass, inert with a
reason until Transmission is above 0, and the per-row Reset now restores the physical
knobs too. The showcase is an example, not a demo: `mesh_glass_lens_example.py` puts a
refracting lens, the Phase 2 default and a tinted bubble in front of a faint point
lattice — orbit behind the spheres to see the rows in front of the lens stay sharp over
it. The two physical demos moved to `packages/luxar/examples/` as
`mesh_physical_materials_example.py` and `mesh_reflections_example.py`, the latter
still the `luxar env bake` target. A Playwright spec pins both halves of the contract
on both renderers: the lens refracts the lattice behind it, and the lattice points in
front of it read the same with the lens shown or hidden.

#### ESM Protein Stories: soap-bubble cluster shells, bubble framing, Biohub mark

The `esm3_protein_stories` kiosk demo now wraps each story's cluster in a
soap-bubble shell: the marker spheres use the physical mesh material (full
transmission, water IOR, iridescence and a little dispersion) lit by a
scene-captured environment, so the bubble reflects the map around it and bends
the map seen through it. Each story waypoint frames the bubble at the height of
the story panel, and a sparse cluster with a long tail is framed on its core
instead so the camera comes closer. The title is now just "ESM Protein Stories",
the dataset/model/license credit closes the Overview panel, and the generic
bottom-right caption gives way to the Biohub mark — a white-on-transparent PNG
bundled inside the package so the built store stays self-contained, blended with
`difference` so it reads on any background.

`Scene.add_image` accepts a `None` height (`size=(width, None)`), letting the
viewer size the image from its own aspect ratio, as `add_video` already did.

#### Round SDR colour quantization to the nearest byte (#2578)

SDR float colours now round to the nearest stored byte in semantic encoding and
mesh imports, removing the systematic half-LSB darkening while preserving CUSTOM
encoding's historical truncation. Regenerating affected stores may change their
``content_hash`` because the corrected colour bytes are intentionally different.

#### Viewer: shared input-capabilities profile, with iPhone and iPad recognised explicitly

The viewer now derives one memoised input profile (`utils/input-capabilities`)
that every touch adaptation reads: whether the primary pointer is coarse,
whether any pointer can hover, the touch-point count, the device class used for
memory budgets, and explicit iPhone / iPad / Android flags. iPadOS Safari
reports a Macintosh user agent by default; the profile unmasks it from a `Mac`
platform combined with a multi-touch screen, and an iPad with a trackpad keeps
its hover affordances while a bare iPad does not. The cache-pool device class
now comes from the same profile. A JS-only `?input=touch|mouse` URL parameter
forces the profile for testing and support. This is the foundation for the
touch-navigation, tap-to-pick, coarse-pointer layout and mobile-budget changes
that follow; on a mouse-and-keyboard machine nothing changes.

#### Viewer: phone and tablet layout — nothing off-screen, safe areas respected

On a phone the control rail was taller than a landscape viewport with no way
to scroll it, the help overlay, data monitor and debug console were fixed
desktop widths that ran off the screen, and panel heights ignored iOS Safari's
dynamic toolbar. All touch-layout adaptation now lives in one stylesheet,
`components/coarse-pointer.css`, whose rules apply only under the
`(pointer: coarse)` and `(hover: none)` media features, so a mouse-and-keyboard
machine receives byte-identical styling. Fixed panel widths clamp to the
viewport, `vh` heights become `dvh`, the rail gutter and every bottom-anchored
surface honour the device's safe-area insets (the page declares
`viewport-fit=cover`), buttons opt out of the double-tap-zoom delay, and the
rail no longer idle-dims where nothing can hover. The rail's item buttons move
into a wrapper that is layout-transparent on a fine pointer and becomes a
scroll box on a coarse one, so a landscape phone reaches every button while the
rail's popovers stay unclipped.

#### Bloom matches between the WebGL and WebGPU renderers again

On three's WebGL2 fallback backend — `?renderer=webgpu` when no WebGPU adapter or
device is available, and the `?webgpuForceWebgl` diagnostic flag — the bloom
pyramid's first frame after each build came out wrong along Y: a vertical gradient
in the glow lost most of its slope, while a radially symmetric one looked right. A
real WebGPU session was never affected: the render-target Y-flip uniform this rides
on is only created when `builder.isFlipY()` is true, which `GLSLNodeBuilder` returns
and `WGSLNodeBuilder` does not. The parity harness measured the composed
three-level pyramid at 16.4 mean absolute levels of difference (per covered pixel)
on a vertical ramp and 0.000 on a Gaussian blob, with the ramp's fitted gradient
falling from 4.95 to 1.25 levels per row.

The bloom TSL factories bind one texture node per pass and re-point it at a different
mip between passes. Each of the four box-filter taps is a _clone_ of that node, and
each clone derives its own render-target Y-flip from the bound texture — three.js's way
of presenting WebGPU's top-down framebuffer convention on its WebGL fallback backend.
The re-point was happening inside the node-update phase, so the taps that were already
updated derived their flip from the _previous_ texture: one tap sampled the mip
un-mirrored while the other three sampled it mirrored, and the box average collapsed to
half the vertical gradient about its own mean. That signature — a shrunken slope with
the mean untouched — is why a frame-average check never noticed. Binding the texture in
`updateBefore` instead, which the renderer runs for the whole graph ahead of any update,
makes every tap agree.

The mismatch needs the previous texture to differ from the new one in
`isRenderTargetTexture`, which in practice means the _first_ frame of each bloom
session: from the second frame on, every tap already agrees. A resize does not start
a new session — it only reallocates the mip targets, leaving the three materials and
their bound nodes in place — so the builds that pay for it are enabling bloom from a
disabled state (including the first enable) and a WebGL context restore. That is still
worth fixing, since every session that shows bloom pays it once, and it is why the
identical binding in the FXAA pass, whose host also swaps a `null`
placeholder for a render target on its first render, was moved to `updateBefore` too.
Both now share one `bindLiveTexture` helper that carries the reasoning with it.

The composed-pyramid parity case now runs twice, on the Gaussian and on a vertical
ramp. The ramp case is the one with the spatial teeth: it asserts per-row means and
a fitted gradient — including its sign and its magnitude — rather than only the frame
average the Gaussian case still checks. It also feeds the chain a render-target texture the way
production does, instead of a raw `DataTexture` plus a row flip on the way out — a raw
data texture is the one input the two backends genuinely disagree about, and flipping
the result afterwards would have hidden any real mirror regression along with the
artificial one.

#### Viewer: touch gestures reach the camera controls, and the orbit touch model is complete

On a phone or tablet a two-finger pinch over the canvas used to be taken by the
browser as page zoom, so the viewer's own pinch handler never ran and the whole
page ended up zoomed. The viewer now owns every touch gesture over its canvas:
the standalone page declares `touch-action: none` on the canvas and the app
stamps the same on an embedder-supplied canvas (only when the embedder has not
chosen otherwise), Safari's proprietary pinch events are cancelled on touch
devices, and a touch press no longer produces the synthetic mouse events that
would double-drive mouse-only code. The orbit controls' touch vocabulary is
finished: lifting one finger out of a pinch continues as a one-finger rotate
from the surviving finger's current position instead of freezing the camera, a
two-finger twist rolls the view around the viewing axis, and an Apple Pencil (or
any pen on a touch-first device) behaves like a finger for the primary tip while
its barrel button keeps the secondary action. Mouse and trackpad behaviour is
unchanged.

#### Viewer: phones and tablets get device-aware rendering and memory budgets

On a phone or tablet the viewer used to start at desktop settings and then
struggle: a scene authored for high-DPR rendering opened at the panel's full
pixel ratio (nine times the fragment work of CSS resolution on a DPR-3 phone),
the GPU geometry budget fell back to a 512 MB desktop default because WebKit
exposes no memory signal, a single node could allocate a gigabyte-scale element
texture, the adaptive-resolution floor dropped to a sixth of the panel's linear
resolution, and a 120 Hz iPad's learned refresh rate made a steady 60 fps look
like distress. The runtime now recognises the mobile device class: "allow high
DPR" caps at 2 (explicit pins are untouched), the adaptive floor is 0.75 with
thresholds capped at 60 Hz, the GPU byte budget takes the mobile cache pool's
share (128 MiB) as a peer minimum, per-node element textures are bounded to
256 MiB, the data-worker pool is capped at three, and the blend-variant shader
warm-up is skipped. Laptops and desktops resolve every one of these exactly as
before.

#### Viewer: tap, press-and-hold and double-tap reach everything right-click and hover used to own

On a touch device nothing could be selected: picking was armed only by mouse
movement, a normal tap drifted past the mouse click tolerance and read as a
camera drag, the element menu needed a right button, and the rail's Home,
Navigation and Performance popovers, the animation settings and the layer
visibility verbs were right-click only, which iOS Safari never produces for a
long press. A finger now has a route to all of it: a tap picks the element
under it (the tooltip appears as it would on hover) and then acts on it, a
press-and-hold opens the same menu a right-click would on the canvas, on rail
buttons, on the play button and on layer rows, and a double-tap re-frames the
scene. The long-press helper is the single opener on every platform, so an
Android device never shows two menus and the button's primary action never
fires under the menu that just opened. Mouse and trackpad behaviour is
unchanged.

The help overlay's Touch section lists all three alongside the camera gestures,
so the only surfaces a finger can reach are also the ones it can discover.

#### Viewer: fly mode works by touch

Fly mode listened only to mouse events, so on a phone or tablet one of the
three camera modes did nothing at all. It now understands the same fingers the
orbit mode does: one finger looks around, two fingers dragged together strafe,
a pinch flies forward or back along the view direction (pinch-in exactly undoes
pinch-out), and a two-finger twist rolls. The gestures drive the same
velocity and orientation state as the mouse, so inertia and damping feel
identical, and a touch press no longer produces the synthetic mouse events that
would have dragged the camera sideways under every tap. Mouse behaviour is
unchanged.

#### Gallery auto-exposure can use the viewer's full dimming range

The gallery capture policy now lowers exposure as far as -10 EV, matching the
viewer validation range instead of stopping at a stale -6 EV floor. Very bright
additive scenes can therefore continue the clip/background guard until the
frame satisfies its limits or the viewer's actual lower bound is reached.

#### Unified view-axis roll direction

Orbit and fly controls now use one shared direction convention for two-finger twist and Shift+wheel roll, so the same gesture rotates the view consistently in both modes.

#### Viewer: a drag that starts after a pause no longer moves nothing

Press the mouse or a finger on the canvas, hold still for a couple of seconds,
then drag, and the camera stayed frozen for the whole drag. The render loop
pauses itself after the idle timeout, and the controls only apply what a drag
accumulates on the next frame, so a gesture that began before the pause fed
input into a loop that was no longer running. A gesture in progress now keeps
the loop awake until the button or finger lifts, on desktop and touch alike.

#### Viewer: the help overlay explains the touch gestures on touch devices

On a phone or tablet the help overlay now carries a "Touch" section: one-finger
drag to orbit, pinch to zoom, two-finger drag to pan, and two-finger twist to
roll, with the ortho-mode pan/no-roll exception called out explicitly. It
appears only when the device reports touch points, so the desktop help text is
unchanged. Alongside it, the viewer gains a Playwright suite that runs under
iPhone, iPad and Pixel emulation and drives the gestures through the browser's
touch protocol, which is what caught the three touch bugs fixed in the same
series.

#### Viewer: report failed background UI actions

Dataset navigation, cache clearing, screenshots, video startup, and asynchronous
pick-result callbacks now contain and report failures instead of leaving rejected
promises unobserved. Debug-console fallback formatting also safely handles hostile
or null-prototype values.

#### Viewer: controls sized for fingers on phones and tablets

On a touch device the rail buttons, chips and panel close buttons are now 44 px,
the slider thumbs and checkboxes a fingertip wide, and every text field in a
panel is 16 px so iOS Safari no longer zooms the page into a focused field.
Where nothing can hover, a tap shows a press highlight instead of a stuck hover
state, and the first-run hint says "tap" and "hold" rather than "hover". The
rail gains a Hide panels button that always closes the open surfaces. Opening
the help or the data monitor closes the docked panels, so a phone shows one
surface at a time, and the Fullscreen chip is left out where the browser has no
fullscreen (iPhone Safari). Each dimension slider gains step buttons and a
tappable name that selects it for the bracket keys. A mouse-and-keyboard
machine sees none of this; its styling is byte-identical.

#### Neuromast demo ships a tuned two-channel appearance

The 4D two-channel neuromast demo now composites both layers volumetrically with a
near-transparent optical depth (absorption 0.02), so the nuclei read inside the
membrane shell instead of both channels flattening additively, and each channel
carries its own display window and gamma (membranes 0.007–0.242 at gamma 1.67 and
half opacity; nuclei 0.025–0.719 at gamma 2.82), while the scene lowers exposure
by 3.4 stops so the rosette core does not clip to white under both volumetric
layers. The windows are authored as intensity/offset, which the viewer maps back
to the window on a colormapped node. Rebuilding the demo store is a scene compile
only; no refit is involved.

#### Partition parts re-entering view no longer reload every LOD level

On a scene whose spatial partition parts are themselves LOD groups (the 44-part
h2afva time-lapse, every `--recipe adaptive` store, the tiled ocean-current and
galaxy layers), rotating the camera made every group drop to its coarsest level
and re-stream, over and over, even when the fine levels were already resident.
The frustum gate introduced with off-screen partition culling re-ran the view
update whenever a part came back on screen, and that re-run advanced the global
view version although the view itself had not changed. Fine levels of LOD groups
load outside the update sweep and are never re-stamped by it, so one tile
crossing the screen edge read every fine level in the scene as stale.

The view version now advances only when a query determinant of the view actually
changes (display axes, slice position, tolerance, or the dimensions signature).
A re-entering part triggers a resync of exactly that part's loaders under the
unchanged version, and the depth-sort re-commit paths that reuse the same door
are bump-free too, so resident LOD levels stay on screen through camera motion.
Parts also re-slice as soon as they return to view instead of waiting for every
progressive ladder to finish streaming, which can take minutes on a slow link.

A related latent defect in the same reload path is closed too: an `overview`
scene whose fine branch (a deferred partition or nested LOD group) was on screen
across a slice change could have that whole branch loaded a second time, doubling
its geometry on screen. The registry now reloads only leaf levels for staleness,
and a deferred group branch activates at most once.

#### Partition frustum checks reuse committed geometry bounds (#2605)

Partition frustum selection now caches committed geometry footprints and reuses
transformed bounding boxes, removing steady-state subtree walks and short-lived
allocations while still refreshing after geometry or scene-transform changes.

#### Story overlays can wait for the camera to land

A waypoint can now be authored `reveal="on_arrival"`: its dimension-bound
overlays (panels, captions, turntable videos) appear when the flight resolves
rather than the instant the hidden dimension changes, so the text arrives with
the camera. The gate keys on the waypoint driver's arrival event, not a timer:
a snap, a camera-less waypoint and a flight the visitor cancels all count as
arrival, a flight a newer waypoint supersedes never reveals, departing overlays
hide at once, and overlays without a `visible_range` are untouched. Narration
already starts on the same event, so text and voice land together. The default,
`"immediate"`, is the previous behaviour; the ESM Protein Stories demo opts in on
every waypoint.

#### Transparent video overlays that survive Safari and the exported app

A video overlay's transparency no longer depends on the codec's alpha plane,
which Safari and every WKWebView (the `luxar export --native` app) decode and
silently drop, leaving the clip on a black square. `Scene.add_video(...,
alpha_matte="stacked")` marks a clip authored as one opaque frame twice as tall,
the colour on top and the alpha channel as a grey matte below; the viewer
recombines the halves in a small shader onto a canvas, so the clip is
transparent in every browser. The protein-stories turntables are encoded this
way (their render cache re-generates once), and a clip the compositor cannot
read falls back to the raw video rather than a blank.

The stories demo also drops its per-cluster "hums" — a low spatial drone per
story on the `effects` bus that read as noise under the narration. The ambient
bed and the narration are its whole soundtrack; `attach_to` sound placement
stays available to other scenes.

Its turning protein structures are now lit by the scene's own baked
environment on top of the studio lights: the same cube map the soap bubbles
reflect is prefiltered into a small irradiance cube (a clear hemispheric tint)
and a sharper glossy cube (a strong Fresnel-weighted reflection at the limb). The
environment's digest is part of the turntable cache key, so the first build
after `luxar env bake` re-renders them lit and a build without a bake keeps the
plain studio look.

#### Auto-size embedded GPU geometry budgets

Direct `LuxarApp` and `LuxarLayer` embeds now auto-size the shared GPU geometry
budget instead of retaining the no-signal fallback for the whole session. Both
entry points also accept explicit pin and disable options matching the standalone
viewer.

#### Separate browser and Node TypeScript scopes

Browser source now typechecks without Node globals, while tests and tooling use
an explicit Node-enabled project. The published viewer package also mirrors
Vite 8's supported Node range and smoke-imports its Node 22 build on Node 20.19.

#### Network fetch failures no longer render as valid geometry

Exhausted chunk fetches and non-404 HTTP errors now fail the affected loader
instead of being decoded and cached as fill-valued geometry. Per-update aborts
reach the underlying fetch, transient failures retry automatically with a
bounded delay while the browser remains online, and LOD diagnostics direct
network failures to the monitor Retry action rather than stale-cache advice.

#### Wait for partition resyncs during offline capture

Offline turntable capture now waits for `kind=partition` frustum re-entry resyncs and visible parts' committed progressive ladders before exporting a frame, preventing stale, blank, or chunk-1 parts from being baked into the sequence. Laddered leaves outside an `lod_group` or partition remain outside the capture drain.

#### Background loading respects partition culling and hidden layers (#2635)

Progressive refinement now re-checks each loader's live partition and layer
visibility before every rung, and predictive slice prefetch skips the same
culled or hidden paths. User-controlled layer visibility is tracked separately
from the per-level Three.js visibility used by LOD selection, so undisplayed
resident levels remain eligible to refine. Refinement failure backoff is also
kept for the lifetime of each loader, preventing a returning partition part
from restarting retries and repeated failure notifications. Exhausted ladders
are reopened when connectivity returns, hidden layers resync when revealed,
and cached prefetch shadows are disposed as soon as their path becomes culled.

#### Depth-sort render ordering reuses steady-frame geometry state

Cross-layer depth ordering no longer rebuilds every partition's BSP traversal and rank map on every rendered frame. A wrapper now retains its numeric order until the camera crosses one of its stored split planes or the displayed dimensions change. The containment pass likewise reuses flat numeric sphere and graph scratch, allocating adjacency lists only when a real containment override exists.

#### Silent accelerator probes report failures without losing fallbacks

Slurm and CUDA environment probes still fall back when optional tools or metadata are absent, but an available probe that breaks now emits one warning with the exception type and message instead of failing into silence. The defect-rule lint ratchet now also covers Ruff's BLE rules, so new blind exception handlers cannot reintroduce the same failure mode while existing debt remains explicitly baselined.

#### Slow streaming chunks no longer escape the shared fetch bound (#2642)

HTTP chunk responses now keep their shared fetch-gate slot until the body is
consumed or cancelled, so a congested connection cannot accumulate an
unbounded set of streaming bodies behind the nominal 64-request limit. Header
waits and body no-progress stalls retain separate retry windows, while an
absolute body deadline derived from `Content-Length` at a 16 KiB/s floor (or
eight stall windows without a usable length) prevents a trickling response from
pinning a slot forever.

The stricter bound means metadata and validation requests share the same FIFO
queue with full chunk bodies and can wait longer under saturation. Caller abort
reasons remain intact on browsers without `AbortSignal.any`, unread bodies are
cancelled before release, and a response body can only be consumed once.

#### ESM Protein Universe — twelve stories across 7.7 million protein clusters

A new demo, `esm_protein_universe`, is the big-map sibling of the Swiss-Prot stories tour: every point is one of 7.7 million clusters of proteins from the ESM Atlas (Candido et al., bioRxiv 2026) — 6.8 billion sequences, most read straight out of environmental DNA, grouped by the features a protein language model sees in them and laid out by 3D UMAP. Every dataset statement was checked against the preprint and every map-specific line against the annotation table. It reuses the tour's story dimension, arrival-gated waypoints, soap bubbles, PDB turntables, panels and narration, and takes two hand-delivered parquet files (`local_data="manual-file"`) that the first run folds into a per-cluster cache.

Twelve stops. Seven Swiss-Prot stories carry over with their vetted facts (hemoglobin, photosystem II, Hsp70, the coronavirus spike, ATP synthase, RuBisCO, RecA), now selected by dominant Pfam family and framed on the densest, purity-weighted knot, because this map is coherent at a hundredth of a unit and a family forms several small knots rather than one blob. Three whole-map stories that only this data can tell — the ABC-transporter spur flung off the cloud, the dark proteome (one cluster in four has no characterised member) and the phage universe — light every member with no bubble, drawing a fixed 300K-point sample so the highlight fits under the viewer's residency ceiling beside the 7.7M-point backdrop. Two families whose knots are sharp here, beta-lactamases and CRISPR-Cas9, complete the tour. The backdrop is coloured by domain of life and dims the uncharacterised clusters, so the dark proteome reads as geography before its story is told.

The backdrop itself is 64 BSP tiles, each a two-level ladder whose coarse level is a 1-in-4 subsample of the tile's own points (light conserved), so the overview and the whole-map stops draw about 1.9M points and only the handful of tiles nearest a knot swap to full detail; Gaussian coarse levels were tried and rejected, since from inside the cloud they overlap on every pixel and drew the view toward the centre at 6 fps against 69 fps for points.

The stories module gains three backward-compatible knobs — the panel's count unit, the overview narration, and the bubble's minimum radius — so both tours share one implementation. Three deliberate changes reach the Swiss-Prot tour as well: every story bubble is centred on its members' bounding box and encloses the farthest member (a median centre left an asymmetric knot hanging out of one side of its bubble), the ATP synthase turntable is the whole Bacillus F1Fo machine (6N2Y) rather than the F1 head, and structures RCSB serves only as mmCIF are fetched as such.

#### Gallery generation now audits built scenes

Gallery dataset generation now runs the built-scene auditors after generation
and reports the complete local inventory on every run. Missing or inconsistent
scene credits in newly generated stores fail the build; the full-inventory pass
and LOD-ladder findings remain report-only while the existing demo corpus is
laddered, so established neighbouring stores do not block gallery capture.
Auditor subprocesses are bounded and their diagnostics are flushed in execution
order.

The static aggregate already runs both auditors without arguments, so
`make check-all` can independently report or fail on locally built unladdered
stores even without this gallery-generation path; checkout-only CI has no built
demo stores to inspect.

#### Keep partition resyncs inside the wide settle window

The environment bake, adaptive-DPR sampler, and performance settle probe now remain busy while a visible partition rising edge is waiting to be handed to the loader. This prevents a perf sample or settled-frame count from observing a re-entering part before its targeted resync begins, without widening the narrower public loading state.

#### Prepare gallery streaming ladders

The remaining oversized synthetic and atlas point/line nodes now carry bounded
additive ladders. The built-scene auditor also reads sliced Lines metadata and
rejects stale exact exemptions, and now gates newly generated gallery scenes
for a corpus-wide enforcement pass.

#### Oversized gallery scenes now stream in bounded commits

The remaining large point and line leaves in the gallery demos now carry explicit additive ladders, including slice-aware opening rungs for animated and categorical scenes. The ladder audit now measures an unladdered sliced leaf by its busiest resident coordinate tuple instead of its declared all-slices total, so the 44-million-point 4D fractal keeps its single volumetric leaf while preserving the existing 150,000-point per-plane sampling cap. Regenerated scenes paint progressively rather than asking the browser to decode and commit hundreds of thousands to millions of resident elements at once; published archives retain their previous layout until the gallery corpus is rebuilt, which also refreshes their `content_hash` values.

#### Per-node ladder decisions for the last three gallery demo leaves

Laddering the gallery corpus left three leaves that `scripts/check_demo_ladders.py`
still fails, each for a different reason, and each needing an authored answer
rather than a corpus-wide sweep.

`exotic_surfaces` has two family nodes on a hidden two-stop categorical axis, and
each node carries only its own coordinate — so `hidden_axis_stops` reports 1,
`stream_ladder` skips its sliced share floor, and rung 0 stays at the unsliced
39,062-element download budget: 4.56% of `Minimal surfaces` (857,226 points) and
8.42% of `Algebraic surfaces` (464,073), both under the gate's 10% rung-0 share
floor. Nothing is *divided* on a one-stop node, but the reset the share contract
exists for is real — stepping `family` swaps the whole wall and the incoming node
restarts at rung 0 — so the demo now applies the `n/8` share floor itself, in a
`family_ladder` helper, and keeps the **unrelaxed** 900,000-element commit
ceiling. Rung 0 becomes 107,154 and 58,010 points at 12.50% each, with largest
increments of 428,610 and 232,033, inside both the 0.6 degeneracy bound and the
1,000,000 absolute commit cap. The floor is applied through
`sliced_ladder_first_chunk`, not through `stream_ladder(slices=2)`, because the
latter also reads `slices` as a divisor for the commit ceiling, and a node with
no second slice should not get the doubled 1,800,000 ceiling: inert at the authored
`RESOLUTION = 112`, but counts scale about as `resolution**2` (measured: 2,023,609
points at 172) and the relaxed ceiling authors a 1,011,801-element increment
there, over the gate's cap, where the unrelaxed one stops at 900,000. The cost of
the share floor is accepted rather than hidden: first paint on `Minimal surfaces`
goes from 39,062 to 107,154 points, i.e. from the policy's 200 ms budget to 549 ms
at its own 25 Mbps and 16 B/element assumptions (Algebraic: 200 -> 297 ms). What
it buys is the framing after a `family` step — 12.5% of the incoming wall rather
than 4.56%.

`galaxy_simulation` fails the other arm. Its five age-bin layers are wildly
uneven — 110 / 966 / 12,455 / 44,569 / 41,900 stars, each present in all 241
frames — and a share-sized rung is the wrong currency for the thin ones. At
232,806 rows, `Disc 50-300 Myr` is only 16% over the 200,000 threshold at which a
ladder becomes mandatory, so its rung stayed at the 39,062 budget and spread to a
measured 144 rows at the sparsest 5th-percentile frame, under the 250-element
absolute first-paint floor. Every played layer now floors rung 0 at a per-FRAME
budget of 300 rows as well (300 rather than 250 because the seeded random prefix
is a multinomial over frames, whose p05 frame lands ~8-11% below the mean —
measured 144 against a 162 mean), re-resolving the same capped schedule around
whichever rung 0 is larger. `Disc 50-300 Myr` becomes three rungs of 72,300 /
72,300 / 88,206 with a measured p05 frame of 275, and every other node of the
default build is byte-for-byte unchanged, because its `n/8` share rung already
wins the `max()`. The floor is passed on the HII and bulge layers too even though
it does not bind there at the authored star count (p05 frames of 343 and 2,423),
because both populations are derived from `--stars`: HII is the youngest 3% of the
disc, so `--stars 50000` leaves 361,500 rows whose share rung spreads to a
measured p05 frame of 166 and fails the gate, against 274 with the floor. The
floor is also clamped to the gate's own 0.6 degeneracy bound on any node above its
200,000-row audit threshold, because an absolute per-frame budget is a share of
`stars_in_bin` rather than of the node: at `--stars 250000 --frames 900` the
242-star `< 50 Myr` layer would take a 270,000-row floor over 217,800 rows and
resolve to a flat leaf, and at `--stars 40000 --frames 600` the 405-star
`50-300 Myr` layer would put 74% of the node in rung 0. Merging the thin bins was
rejected: the five-way age split is the comparison the demo exists for, and the
merged 1,076 stars would still need ~28% of the node in rung 0.

The 4D fractal exposed a different accounting bug: its 44,469,233 declared
points span two hidden dimensions, but one `(fractal, w)` coordinate already
contains at most 150,000 sampled points. The no-ladder audit previously used the
declared total even for a sliced leaf and therefore treated a bounded resident
slice as one giant commit. Its chunk-bounds reduction now handles any number of
hidden dimensions conservatively, while malformed, unsliced and `extend_to_all`
leaves still fall back to the declared node total.

#### SSAA respects framebuffer limits during adaptive DPR changes

Post-processing now derives the canvas and every off-screen attachment from one
aspect-preserving, capability-clamped size. Oversized SSAA requests fall back to
the largest supported even-sized framebuffer with a transition-only warning,
while fractional DPR changes use Three.js's exact rounding and update attachments
before the observable canvas resize, avoiding incomplete framebuffers and subtle
viewport drift.

SSAA also suspends MSAA renderbuffer allocation while supersampling above 1x,
avoiding the oversized multisample allocation path; returning to 1x or disabling
SSAA restores the configured MSAA mode.

Changing the SSAA resolution multiplier now reasserts the camera projection from
the logical display size after each render-target reallocation, preserving the
viewport projection while the renderer switches supersampled allocations.

#### Same-type coarse levels for Points

`add_points(substitutive_lod=...)` now accepts `coarse="points"`, producing spatially stratified Points levels with blending-aware brightness compensation while preserving the existing Gaussian-lift default. The new path authors global overview levels; per-part same-type ladders remain separate follow-up work.

#### Gsplat adders share the scene-structure controls

Gaussian splats added from arrays can now use `substitutive_lod=` and
`additive_lod=` directly, matching the other geometry adders. File loading also
exposes partition and LOD controls, with `flatten=True` to collapse an existing
stored tree before rebuilding its authoring-time structure; the historical
`lod_group=` spelling remains available as an alias.

#### Fix CUDA kernels on non-default GPUs

Gaussian splatting and CUDA NLM denoising now launch on the device that owns
their input tensors, so explicit devices such as `cuda:1` work even when a
different GPU is current. Gaussian splatting also rejects mixed-device inputs
with a clear error instead of allowing an illegal memory access.

#### Right-click orbits the camera again in an exported native app

Right-dragging inside a `luxar export --native macos` bundle popped the system "Copy Image / Share Image…" sheet instead of turning the scene. Both controls implementations do suppress the native menu, but only on the canvas they listen to — which is enough in Chromium, where the scene overlays floating above the canvas are `pointer-events: none` and the hit test walks past them to the canvas. WebKit resolves the context-menu target geometrically instead, so inside a WKWebView the target is whichever overlay sits under the cursor: a turntable's matte canvas, its video, a logo image. None of those is the canvas, so nothing suppressed the menu and the camera never moved.

The viewer now claims the secondary click across every surface it mounts, through one delegated listener on the viewer container rather than a handler per overlay. Measured in a shipped bundle, this closes the leak on the scene overlays (text, HTML, image and video), the turntable mattes, the data monitor, the dimension sliders and the GUI panel; the canvas, control rail and layers panel were already covered. Text fields keep their native menu, since it is the only way to paste, and an embedder's own DOM is untouched — suppression applies to the canvas and to elements carrying a `luxar-` class, not to everything sharing the container.

#### Equal-energy additive ladders (`equi-energy:<n>`), and a batch of demo re-tunes

Additive ladders could be cut by equal count, by a bandwidth-derived geometric
schedule, or at explicit energy fractions. The new `equi-energy:<n>` breakpoints
vocabulary cuts `n` rungs at equal shares of cumulative perceptual energy along
the ladder's own contribution ordering, so the first rung is the few heaviest
elements and each later rung is fatter in count for the same light: first paint
is fast, and the rungs that take longest to arrive are the ones whose absence
shows least. Any increment above the shared 900K commit cap is split, so no
single commit blocks the main thread. GSplats resolve it against their
self-energy, Points against `luminance × radius³`, Lines against per-polyline
tube energy with the cap counted in vertices; the CLI accepts it wherever
`--breakpoints` is taken.

The same PR re-tunes several hosted demos from a review pass (cosmic web,
FlyWire, CELLxGENE, Tribolium, CT TotalSegmentator), gives the bird plumage demo
an explainer, re-ladders the CMU-1 pathology parts for a ~200 ms first paint,
and replaces the tractography demo's lifted-Gaussian coarse levels with
subsampled streamlines that carry labels on every level.

#### Hosted gsplat loads tolerate multiplexed slow links again (#2678)

This refines #2644 while keeping its lease-through-body semantics: the
response-body watchdog now follows aggregate fetch progress instead of aborting
each quiet HTTP/2 stream independently. A separate absolute deadline still
bounds responses that deliver no body bytes and true trickles.

Chunk-body concurrency is reduced from 64 to 24, and zarr metadata plus cache
validation use a separate four-request lane. On multiplexed transports, small
`zarr.json` and `.zattrs` probes therefore do not wait behind a full wave of
large chunk bodies.

#### Lines can stay lines through substitutive LOD

Same-type coarse Lines levels now use whole-polyline salience sampling, preserve
hidden-slice topology, and conserve additive light without inflating fibers into
wide ribbons, while retaining lifted GSplats as the default.

#### Existing LOD stores can be re-anchored without rebuilding

`luxar restamp-lod --anchor <fraction>` now explicitly re-derives whole-object
`screen-area` ladders that the migration-only command previously skipped as
already current, and sets the same requested anchor on legacy whole-object
ladders migrated in that pass. Thresholds are rebuilt from the stored level
count, the per-group old→new audit prints the numeric anchor, the
`--dry-run`/`--group` controls remain intact, and partition-bound ladders keep
their fills-screen `1.0` anchor. Repeating an anchor that is already stored
remains a true no-op, including `content_hash`.

#### Animated slices prefetch their next chunk boundary

Predictive flat spatial-index Points, Lines, and Gaussian-splat loads now use
the arrays' actual first-axis chunk shapes and the spatial index's hidden-axis
bounds to warm the nearest next chunk boundary during playback. Large hosted
chunks therefore start loading while the preceding frames are still playing
instead of only one frame before the boundary; reverse playback follows the
corresponding prior boundary. Progressive and laddered loaders retain their own
prefetch paths.

Loaders without usable chunk metadata keep the previous one-step prefetch, and
multi-axis scrubs deliberately avoid speculative fan-out.

`luxar optimize` now also reports a per-node warning when the planned layout
would put more than two actively played frames in each of multiple chunks on an
un-laddered spatial-index node. The diagnostic derives frame span from the
stored index bounds, stays silent for keypress-only axes and ladders, and treats
a whole array in one chunk as benign.

#### Add an opt-in replacement-LOD bias

The viewer now accepts `?lodBias=<positive number>` and matching app/layer
options for A/B testing finer or coarser replacement-LOD selection without
rewriting stored thresholds. The value is defined in screen-area units: `2`
advances one occupancy-halved level, while legacy diagonal-coverage ladders
receive its square root so both selector types move by the same area factor.

The neutral default remains `1`. Finite screen-area coverage tops out at `1`,
so a value below `1` makes a partition-anchored finest level unreachable and a
value below `0.5` does the same for a whole-object finest level; near-plane
saturation still selects the finest level.

#### Measure sliced additive commits at the resident slice

The built-demo ladder gate now applies its absolute commit cap to the
conservative largest per-coordinate fetch of a barrier-ordered level, using a
weighted overlap sweep over the stored chunk bounds rather than decoding every
coordinate row. Boundary chunks that straddle two slice values count toward
both, matching the viewer's fetch. Unsliced leaves, leaves without proven
one-axis slice ordering, and `extend_to_all` nodes keep the node-level cap.

The demo `stream_ladder` policy uses the matching slice-scaled authoring ceiling,
so large time-sliced nodes can keep the required first-rung share instead of
being forced into partitions solely by a whole-node commit count the viewer
never loads at once.

#### Both ESM protein tours now breathe

Under the existing turntable, the camera in `esm_protein_universe` and
`esm3_protein_stories` slowly dollies in and out over about a minute. Both maps
read as a volume rather than a flat cloud, and the near extreme brings the knots
close enough to read without anyone touching the controls. It rides with the
turntable, so `--no-auto-rotate` still gives a completely still camera.

The stories kiosk keeps the tuned ±95% swing. The universe tour uses a gentler
20% amplitude in its hosted/laptop build and restores 95% with `--high-quality`:
that scene has selectable LOD groups, so the near extreme can load finer levels,
while the stories scene's additive stream ladders keep their elements resident.

#### Remote control: a viewer can now be driven from outside the page

A Luxar viewer on a big display can be driven by something else — a kiosk touch
panel, a script, an agent. `luxar serve --control` mounts a WebSocket relay at
`/control` on the viewer app, a viewer loaded with `?control` attaches to it,
and `luxar.control.Viewer` is the other end:

```python
from luxar.control import Viewer

with Viewer("ws://kiosk.local:5173/control") as viewer:
    story = viewer.dimension_index("story")
    viewer.set_dimension_value(story, 3)
```

That last call is the whole operation for a guided tour: moving the story
dimension is all a controller does, and the authored waypoints already fly the
camera, swap the dimension-bound overlays and cue the narration.

There is no second API to learn. The wire surface is the `LuxarApp` embedder
API — every public method except `dispose` and the handful that take callbacks,
plus `subscribe` / `unsubscribe` — and a lock test fails the build if a new
embedder method lands outside that policy. `dispose` is withheld because it
tears the viewer down in one frame with no way back, which on an exhibit means a
blank screen until someone power-cycles it.

`?control` is a bare flag: the hub rides on the app that served the page, so the
socket address is derived rather than typed, which keeps it working behind an
origin-rooted reverse proxy and under `luxar export`. A path-prefixed proxy uses
an explicit same-origin path such as `?control=/exhibit/control`. An explicit
`?control=<url>` is accepted for a split origin but is same-origin only unless
`?controlAllowCrossOrigin` says otherwise — a crafted link would otherwise hand
a stranger both the display and its dataset URL. Without `--control-token`, browser sockets must be
same-host while non-browser clients remain open to anything that can reach the
hub. A valid token permits split-origin and reverse-proxied deployments and is
required on an untrusted network.

Two things were wrong on the way past and are now fixed: `switchDataset`
validated its URL not at all (the controller path now runs it through the same
validator `?src` gets), and the viewer only provisions picking when a
`selection` listener exists at load time, so a controller that subscribed later
would have received those events never and heard nothing about it.

#### Played time partitions keep a recognizable first rung

Per-timepoint partitions now author equal-count ladders whose first rung carries
at least one eighth of each played frame while every increment remains under the
per-part commit cap. The demo-ladder gate measures the same contract against the
worst partition part instead of an aggregate mean that can hide a thin frame.

#### Correct the neuromast demo's Z anisotropy factor

The two-channel neuromast rebuild recipe now scales Z by the measured MetaMorph
voxel anisotropy, `0.25 / 0.1083 = 2.3084`, instead of the historical `2.5`,
which stretched the organ 8.3 % along the axial direction.

The archives pinned in the demo manifest were built with `2.5` and still carry
that stretch, so the scene the demo downloads is unchanged. The corrected
rebuild is complete, but still needs uploading and repinning in the manifest;
it is 7.7 % shorter in Z than the pinned pair, which already differs from it in
splat count (the 2026-09 removal of the post-fit cull).

#### A touch panel for the kiosk, with no authoring required

`control.html` is a second page in the viewer bundle, meant for a tablet beside
a big display: a full-screen grid of chapter tiles, and tapping one jumps the
display to that stop of the tour. `luxar serve --control` prints both URLs.

It needs nothing added to a scene. A labelled dimension —
`Dimension(categories=[...])` — already carries the stop names, so the page asks
the viewer what dimensions it has and reads the labels that are there. Tours
built long before this page existed get a working menu against their existing
stores. Where a scene has no chapter dimension, or the page was opened with no
hub to talk to, it says so in words instead of drawing an empty grid.

The page is deliberately light: no renderer, no codecs, its own small
stylesheet. The build now checks that per page rather than globally — the viewer
may ship `three` as long as the WebGPU path stays lazy, while the panel may
reach neither, which is not something a source-level lint can see.

Two things an author can rely on. The tile classes, `data-*` state hooks and
`--luxar-control-*` custom properties are a styling contract, pinned by a test
from both the DOM and the stylesheet side, so a rename cannot quietly break a
scene's own CSS. And `?panel=<module>` loads an alternative panel, handed an
already-connected socket, for the exhibit that outgrows CSS — same-origin only,
since that module is executed.

#### A kiosk you can hand to an audience

The touch panel is now a full-page matrix of glass tiles that fits any screen
without scrolling, the scene can say how it reads, an unattended display can be
locked down, and an exported native app can host the relay itself.

The panel measures its own container and picks a grid, so ten to twelve
chapters land in a steady 4x3 on a landscape tablet and 3x4 in portrait —
checked at twelve sizes from 320x480 to 4K with no overflow in either axis.
Tiles are translucent over a slow aurora, and a partial final row sits centred
rather than trailing a hole. Labels size themselves against their own tile
rather than the viewport, because the cell shrinks as chapters are added.

`viewer_config.control_panel` adds a heading, per-chapter second lines, a pinned
column count, an idle reset and author CSS. Everything optional: a scene with no
block at all still gets the whole panel, derived from a discrete dimension's
`categories`. Both ESM protein tours are wired as the reference scenes, taking
their tile subtitles from the same `Story` table the waypoints are built from,
so the panel cannot drift from the tour. Author CSS is treated as hostile on the
`overlay_html` precedent: capped, injected as text, and stripped of `@import`
and remote `url()` — every remote URL in a stylesheet is also a beacon
reporting the kiosk's address to whoever hosts it.

`ui.kiosk` and `?kiosk` lock a display for public use: no panels, no keyboard,
no camera dragging, and optionally a watchdog that reloads only if WebGL
recovery has already had its chance. The URL flag can lock a store that predates
the block but deliberately cannot unlock one.

`luxar serve --host 0.0.0.0` also works properly now. It used to print
`http://0.0.0.0:5173` — a bind address no tablet can dial — and its data server
refused the viewer's own LAN origin, so the kiosk showed a blank screen with a
console full of CORS errors while `curl` read the data happily.

Demos keep remote control **off** unless asked: `luxar demo run <demo> --
--control [--control-token … --host 0.0.0.0]`.

#### An exported folder runs the kiosk too

`luxar export` has always copied the touch-panel page along with the viewer,
because both pages live in the same bundle — but the folder's generated
`serve.py` bound loopback, spoke no WebSocket and ran one request at a time, so
the *file* rode along while the *feature* did not. It does now:

    python serve.py --control --host 0.0.0.0 --control-token SECRET

Off by default, because a folder you double-click should not start listening
for anything that wants to drive it. The script prints a display URL and a
tablet URL, resolving a wildcard bind to a concrete address first — `0.0.0.0`
is a bind address, not a destination, and a URL containing it is one no tablet
can dial.

It is also threaded now, which is not a detail: a WebSocket occupies its thread
for as long as the kiosk runs, so on the old single-threaded server the first
attached panel would have blocked every later request, including the scene's
own chunks. A display that never finished loading would have been the visible
symptom.

The relay is the fourth implementation of one protocol, after the Python hub,
the viewer's client and the Go launcher's — and the only one that ships as a
copied file into artifacts nobody rebuilds, so it carries a copy of the
generated wire contract with a test pinning it to the source. It lives in
`luxar/cli/_export_serve_template.py` as a real module rather than a string
inside the exporter: ruff, mypy and the test suite all see it, and writing 600
lines of RFC 6455 framing inside an f-string (where every brace has to be
doubled) is not reviewable.

The folder's README now documents kiosk mode, says plainly that the token
travels in the URL and is therefore visible in the tablet's address bar, and
warns about `file://` for **both** pages rather than only `index.html` — the
touch panel is the more tempting one to double-click and fails the same way.

A mistyped token on the tablet now says so. The hub has always refused a bad
token, an unknown role or a foreign origin by accepting the handshake and then
closing it with a policy-violation code — precisely so the panel could tell
"no hub here" from "your token is wrong" — but the panel ignored the code: it
reported every refusal as "waiting for the display" and retried forever against
a hub that would refuse every attempt for the same reason. Found by opening the
page with a wrong token rather than by a test, and the first fix did not show
either, because the refused call's rejection painted over the message a
microtask later. The panel also no longer claims "connected, but no viewer has
attached yet" for failures that never said anything of the kind.

#### Guard the manifest attribution against the published record text

A dataset's provenance is stated twice: in `data_manifest.json`'s `attribution`
field, and in the record description published on Zenodo and captured under
`scripts/zenodo_record_text/`. Nothing compared the two, and they had already
drifted. The manifest says of the Drosophila timelapse that "the imaging itself
is unpublished; for the SiMView instrument see Royer et al., Nat. Biotechnol.
34, 1267-1278 (2016)", while the live record says "Imaging described in Royer et
al., ..." and, at record level, "The imaging is described in ... Users of this
record should cite that publication in addition to this record." That reads as a
data publication. The imaging was never separately deposited or published; the
2016 paper describes the instrument it was acquired with. The drift was caught
by eye, once, which is not a mechanism.

`scripts/check_record_attribution.py` is now that mechanism. For every hosted
dataset whose imaging is said to be unpublished, it locates that dataset's
bullet in the captured record text and reports any claim that a publication
describes, documents or publishes *the imaging*. The subject is the whole
question, in both directions. A publication describing the *instrument* or the
*method* is the correct framing, so "the imaging instrument is described in
Royer et al.", "Imaging method: Royer, ...", "Imaging was carried out as
described in Royer et al.", "Imaging was performed as previously described in
Royer et al." and "published as a single 4D archive" all stay clean, as does any
denial ("the imaging has not been published in any article"); a claim is only
raised when the imaging itself is what the publication covers, within one
sentence of it. The guards are kept narrow on purpose, because a guard that
reaches past its purpose is pure false-negative surface: only a replacement
*head* noun clears a claim (an artefact noun in that gap is usually a modifier
of the imaging, as in "the imaging in this archive is described in ..."), and
only "not" and "never" read as a denial ("with no post-processing" does not).
Block-closing tags terminate a sentence, so a `<h3>` heading or a `<td>` cell —
both live in these records — cannot merge into the paragraph after it and
manufacture a claim neither block makes. Quotes keep the citation whole rather
than stopping at the period in "et al." or "Nat. Biotechnol.", because the
reference is what makes the report actionable. The recall bounds are documented
rather than implied: a gap longer than 80 characters, or crossing a full stop or
a semicolon, is not seen.

Either side may raise the unpublished claim — the manifest attribution or the
record's own bullet — so rewording one of them cannot quietly drop a dataset out
of the audit, and the inverse drift (a record claiming unpublished imaging while
the manifest cites a publication) is examined too. Record-level prose names no
dataset: it is attributed to one only when every dataset on that record makes
the same claim, and is otherwise reported as a record-scoped `[HUMAN]` line
naming the record and quoting the sentence, for a person to attribute. `make
check-record-attribution` runs it, and it joins `make check-external-references`
as the first leg of that aggregator needing no network. That runner grades this
leg by exit status, not by its markers, so the command exits non-zero for a
human check as well as for drift; only a missing or unreadable input grades
ERROR.

Scope is resolved before any `[CONFIG]`, so adding a manifest entry and
capturing its record later — an ordinary sequence — is silent rather than a
broken input that would escalate the whole leg to ERROR and relabel real drift
elsewhere as "could not run". A `[CONFIG]` means an input that was genuinely
needed is missing or unreadable, or that nothing at all was in scope.

It is deliberately report-only rather than a test, and that extends to the
tests. The live record text is authored on Zenodo by the maintainer, so the
finding above stands in this repo until that edit lands and
`scripts/zenodo_record_text/capture.py` re-captures it; a hard gate would just
be red. `scripts/tests` runs inside the required `python-tests` job, so the
one test that exercises the live files asserts only properties this repository
controls — that the audit runs, reports documented levels, and blames nothing
that is not a manifest dataset. It does not assert a count, a level or the
absence of a finding, because a single sentence added on Zenodo raises a
`[HUMAN]` line, and a test asserting otherwise would redden a required check on
the very re-capture PR that fixes the drift. Its docstring says so. The failure
message names the remedy, because the obvious wrong fix — regenerating the
snapshot from `gen_zenodo_records.py` — would destroy hand-maintained prose the
generator never produced.

#### Respect GSplat dimension order when coarsening

Computed GSplat LOD ladders now map displayed and named scene dimensions back
to the input center columns before coarsening. This preserves non-displayed
categorical barriers when ``dim_order`` places them at a different column.

#### Store the neuromast rebuild in physical microns

The two-channel neuromast rebuild recipe now scales `(Z, Y, X)` by the measured
MetaMorph voxel size `(0.25, 0.1083, 0.1083)` µm instead of applying only the
Z-to-lateral anisotropy ratio. Rebuilt axis readouts and measured distances now
match the `µm` labels; scene dimensions also cover the union of both channels'
quantized bounds. This supersedes the anisotropy-only recipe correction recorded
separately for the pending archive repin.

The archives currently pinned in the demo manifest are unchanged and still use
the historical Z-only transform. Their coordinates remain in lateral-pixel
units, with the separate 8.3 % Z stretch tracked by the pending archive repin.

#### Playback detail: pin the ladder depth for smooth, consistent time-lapse playback

Dimension playback streamed each frame under a per-tick time budget: a frame showed
whatever additive-ladder rungs were resident within its tick and the background prefetch
deepened the next frame by roughly one rung per tick. On a heavy time-lapse -- millions
of splats per timepoint -- most frames therefore landed at their first one or two rungs
and quality flickered from frame to frame. The dimension context menu gains a **Detail**
section that pins the ladder depth: every frame is drawn at exactly that many rungs, cold
or not, and the tick waits for the data, so quality stays constant and the frame rate
adapts instead. The default, **Auto**, lets each ladder pick its depth from its own
`energy_fraction_cum` build stamps (the first rung at or above a 0.9 energy fraction);
a rung count or **All** pins it explicitly, and **Fast** keeps the old time-budgeted
streaming. Scrubbing is pinned the same way, with an unpinned refine once the scrub is
quiet. Scenes can author the default with `ViewerConfig(playback_lod_depth=...)`
(`int`, `"all"`, `"auto"` or `"fast"`), stored as `viewer_config.playback_lod_depth`. The
pin rides the same per-pass directive path as the frame budget (`ViewState.ladderDepth`),
reaches the t+1 shadow prefetch, and is available programmatically as
`play(dim, { ladderDepth })` / `setLadderDepth` / `setDefaultLadderDepth`. Applies to all
four geometry loaders.

#### Bounded and observable OPFS cache reads

Deep progressive passes now share a configurable page-wide OPFS read cap, and
the cache monitor reports active, queued, and canceled reads. Queueing stays
outside each filesystem-operation timeout so healthy backpressure is not
mistaken for a stalled browser backend while the original stall diagnosis
remains measurable rather than assumed.

#### Neuromast opens from above with validated channel windows

The two-channel neuromast demo now uses the amplitude windows validated against
the pinned hosted archives instead of mistaking the Layers-panel slider bounds
for display maxima. Its opening camera is derived from the amplitude-weighted
middle frame, looking down from the low-depth side at the rosette rather than
fitting the mostly empty acquisition box side-on; the data-derived pose scales
with the corrected archive geometry instead of baking world coordinates.

#### Correct the neuromast demo's Z anisotropy

The two-channel neuromast demo now fetches the Z-corrected Gaussian-splat pair,
using the measured 2.3084 axial-to-lateral voxel ratio instead of the historical
2.5 transform that stretched Z by 8.3%. The corrected archives are checksum-
verified from their dataset-specific mirror while retaining the published
`cc-by` Zenodo record as their provenance identity.

#### Changelog fragments fail fast in the documentation gate

Pending changelog fragments are now validated for UTF-8 encoding and the
documented heading-and-prose format before release preparation. The required
documentation check reports every malformed fragment separately, and these
hard failures cannot be hidden by updating the documentation-debt baseline.

#### Persist relocation scale diagnostics with fitted splats

Gaussian-splat fits now retain the dynamic-operations relocation event count,
the number of distinct relocated splats, and the initialization-scale populations
needed to interpret them. The diagnostics distinguish a configured fallback scale
from precomputed seed covariances, summarize genuinely per-splat initialization
scales, and are stored with fitting metadata rather than pipeline provenance.

#### Bound automatic local Gaussian-splat worker concurrency

`gsplat fit -j auto` and `gsplat batch-fit run --jobs-per-gpu auto` now account
for fixed CUDA-process overhead and apply host RAM, affinity-aware CPU-thread,
and configurable host caps instead of dividing VRAM by tile bytes alone.
Multi-GPU runs preserve every selected card while sharing the host-wide budget,
and both commands report the resource that limited the resolved worker count.
Set `LUXAR_AUTO_WORKER_HARD_CAP` to override the default eight-worker cap.

#### Local batch workers stay on the selected CUDA devices

`batch-fit run` now maps each parent-visible CUDA index back through the
parent's `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES` list before pinning a worker. Restricted runs no
longer jump to the same-numbered physical card, UUID and MIG tokens pass through
unchanged, and `--gpus cpu` hides CUDA while explicitly forcing the child fit to
CPU so Apple MPS cannot be selected implicitly.

Startup output reports each visible-index-to-token mapping with the device name.
CPU runs report that CUDA is hidden and CPU execution is forced. Missing
selected-device benchmark profiles are also reported before tile auto-sizing is
disabled.
Local planning also selects benchmark metadata from the GPUs that will execute
the tasks, so a nonzero `--gpus` selection no longer records GPU 0's name and
timing estimate in the manifest. On heterogeneous selections, the smallest
profiled card supplies the conservative tile and throughput profile while the
manifest records every selected model.

#### Bound packed Slurm fit allocations

`batch-fit submit --parallel` now accounts for CUDA-process overhead and target-node CPU/RAM capacity, scales the Slurm allocation from the per-task resource flags, and isolates each packed worker's GPU, thread pool, and quality budget.

#### Keep authored touch captions clear of the control rail

On phones and tablets, left-edge overlays now move beside the wider touch rail
instead of painting underneath it. Explicitly sized, left-anchored text keeps a
readable 18-character measure while staying inside the viewport, including when
its authored position is near the right edge; center- and right-anchored overlays
keep their authored horizontal origin and width.

#### Preserve fit provenance through flattening and record generation

`luxar gsplat flatten` now replaces partition-slot provenance with one honest
summary instead of dropping the subtree, retaining the part count and only
complete source and timing figures without multiplying shared source sizes by
the partition count. The Zenodo record generator also
reads source metadata nested under `part_provenance`, including legacy explicit
frame counts and newer time-first source shapes, so published descriptions no
longer omit measurements already present in the archive.

#### Preserve fit provenance through gsplat merge

`luxar gsplat merge` now replaces its inputs' component coordinates with one
summary provenance entry instead of dropping the subtree. The summary records
the input count, complete source-size and fitting-time totals, and unanimous
source shape and dtype across concatenating, stacked-dimension, and
channel-colour merges.

#### Match gsplat amplitude bits to source dtype

- Standalone gsplat writers now accept `amplitude_bits="auto"`, using 8-bit
  geometric-log amplitude codes for 8-bit integer sources recorded by the
  fitter while retaining the existing AUTO policy for unknown, floating-point,
  and wider source dtypes. Direct saves remain unchanged by default, while CLI
  fit outputs opt into source matching. Other gsplat rewrite tools and the scene
  compiler retain the 16-bit default pending #2783.

#### Same-type merged point and line LOD levels

`coarse="points"` and `coarse="lines"` now accept `method="merge"` alongside the existing `subsample` mode. Merged levels preserve the authored node type, derive representative position and initial scalar radius or width from light-weighted combined second moments, and rescale extent or colour as needed to conserve additive light without materialising Gaussian-splat children.

#### Measured quality for Points and Lines LOD

Points and Lines substitutive levels now carry measured mixture-quality stamps.
Same-type Points stamps measure geometric subsampling, while Lines stamps also
measure width compensation; color gains are not part of this metric. Authors can
disable the added measurement cost with `quality_stamps=False`. Legacy levels
