endpoint instead of its own crop minimum — see changelog.d/1616.md.) The uniform tiled path was never
affected in practice, since it subtracts the level from the raw tile *before* apodization,
whose window drives each tile's minimum to ~0.

`batch-fit` settles the open design question explicitly in favour of **one global
level for the whole timelapse**, and makes that one level safe for the dimmest
**sampled** slice by construction. It is the **minimum** of the levels resolved on a
bounded, deterministic set of at most 16 evenly spaced `(t, c)` slices spanning the
store's **full** extent: up to 4 timepoints x up to 4 channel-like coordinates,
capped *independently* so neither axis can starve the other. Concretely, `T > 1`
always samples at least two timepoints **including the endpoints `t=0` and
`t=T-1`**, and `C > 1` at least two channel-like coordinates (endpoints included).
The endpoints are what make the reduction sound: under a monotone pedestal drift
(sensor warm-up, bleaching) the run's dimmest pedestal sits at one end, so a minimum
that includes both ends is a true lower bound for the whole run. Allocating the
budget to channels *first* — a first cut of this change — made a store with 5 or more
channel-like coordinates sample exactly one timepoint, which reinstated the erase bug
in the time direction; hence time is allocated first now. The per-slice read budget
is the whole-volume budget divided by the sample count (2M voxels at the 16-slice
cap), so total voxels read stay at the single-slice budget. A minimum because the two
errors are not symmetric: under `clip(V - level, 0)` a too-LOW level is a recoverable
under-subtraction, while a too-HIGH one destroys signal — the tile worker applies the
forwarded number unguarded (by design, so no tile disagrees), so a level above some
`(t, c)`'s maximum clips that whole sub-volume to zero, which the worker legitimately
reports as an empty tile: the slice would go silently missing from the merge while
`batch-fit status` reported success. Sampling the full extent rather than the
`--timepoints`/`--channels` selection also makes the level a property of the *store*,
so a first pass over `0:50` and a resumed pass over `0:100` subtract the same
pedestal. If any sampled slice resolves to "subtract nothing" (a zero level, or the
"would erase all signal" guard refusing it), suppression is downgraded to `none` for
the whole run, loudly; each per-slice level is already guarded below its own sampled
max, so their minimum is below every sampled max and no further check is needed. It
is deliberately not resolved from the content plan's max-projection either, whose
per-voxel maximum biases the background mode upward.

**Residual risk, stated plainly:** bounded sampling can only bound the slices it
samples. A slice that is *not* sampled and dimmer than every sampled one — a
blank/bleached/bad frame between two samples of a long movie, or a channel-like
coordinate above the cap of 4 — can still be clipped to all zeros, fit 0 splats and
vanish from the merge while `status` reports success. `--floor none`, or an explicit
numeric `--floor N` low enough for the dimmest slice, is the escape hatch.

The level is recorded in the manifest as `floor_level` (documentation / inspection:
nothing reads it back) and emitted as a concrete number in every task's command.
Each sampled slice is read as a bounded sample (the whole-volume budget divided
among the samples, so plan time costs no more than before) of a **lazily** opened,
axis-pinned view, so on the normal (label-pinnable) path the floor resolution never
materializes a timepoint — not on a uniform plan, not on `submit --dry-run`, not on a
resume re-plan. (Two exceptions: the *content* box scan still materializes up to
`--plan-samples` timepoints to max-project, as before; and a store whose discovered
labels cannot be mapped onto it falls back to an eager `load_volume` per sampled
slice, announced as it happens — a correctness hedge, not the normal path.) Every
read — the floor samples and the content scan alike — pins its slice by the store's
*discovered* axis labels, so a `(T, Z, Y, X)` store **that declares its axes** (a
custom `axes` attribute or NGFF metadata) is no longer read as `CZYX` even with no
explicit `--axes`. A bare 4D zarr with no axis metadata at all still falls to the
shape heuristic, which guesses `CZYX`; pass `--axes time,z,y,x` for those. The
positional heuristic ignored `timepoint`
entirely, which made the floor measure `t=0` whatever timepoint was named *and* made
`--plan-samples` silently scan `t=0` N times instead of covering the movie. A
resumed run whose manifest predates `floor_level` keeps its recorded spec and behaves
exactly as when it was planned.

`--floor none` round-trips unchanged, and the resolved number is still subtracted
exactly once, by the same code that subtracted before — only where the number comes
from has changed. An explicit numeric `--floor 110` round-trips as that number. For
`fit --tiling content` there is one behaviour change: because the numeric now becomes
a level in the parent, which reads the volume anyway, the whole-volume "would erase
all signal" guard applies to it too, so a numeric above the sampled maximum is
reported and downgraded to `none` instead of being applied by every box. `batch-fit`
keeps forwarding a user numeric verbatim without reading anything (a numeric spec
never opens the store), exactly as before.

The complementary change is in the tile worker (`fit --tile k/M`, which is what every
uniform batch task and every `fit -j N` box subprocess runs): a *concrete numeric*
level is no longer re-guarded against the single sub-volume that worker holds. A
dim/bleached timepoint used to drop it and fall back to hard-min normalization while
every sibling task subtracted it, which is the per-timepoint pedestal difference this
change removes. **This is a behaviour change for a user numeric on that path too**:
`fit --tiling uniform --tile 3/16 --floor 110` and `fit --tiling uniform -j 4 --floor
110` (the `-j` parent forwards `--floor` verbatim) used to *warn and ignore* a level
above the volume's sampled maximum and fit anyway; they now **warn and apply** it, so
such a level windows the tile to zero and yields an empty tile. The warning is
deliberately loud and names the tile, the `(t, c)`, the level, the sampled maximum and
the consequence (0 splats, skipped by the merge), because nothing downstream of an
`.empty` marker would otherwise mention the floor. Sequential `--tiling uniform` still
guards its own single in-process resolution, as before. A volume-derived spec
(`auto`/`pNN`) is still resolved *and* guarded in the worker, since it becomes a level
for the first time there.

Bad specs (`--floor p150`, a typo, a negative `floor:` in a YAML config) are rejected
as a clean usage error *before* anything is read, on both paths (`batch-fit` at plan
time, `fit --tiling content` at the top of the content run). A *negative* resolved
level (dark-frame-corrected data) cannot be expressed as a concrete `--floor` at all,
so the SPEC is forwarded and re-resolved wherever it lands — which is not uniformly
harmless, and is not claimed to be. For `fit --tiling uniform -j N`/`--tile k/M` it is
exact: every worker re-resolves against the same whole volume with the same
deterministic sampler. For `fit --tiling content` it *degenerates to per-box
resolution*: the spec reaches `fit_gaussian_splats(crop, floor=<spec>)` per box, which
resolves it against that box crop — the same #1174 pedestal spread this change removes
elsewhere, and a violation of `fit_planned`'s own "must already be a CONCRETE level"
contract. `batch-fit` makes the same admission per task: it warns prominently that
each `(t, c)` task will resolve the spec itself (pedestals may differ across the run)
and records `floor_level=None` — "no level pinned". All three are accepted rather than
refused, because such data planned and fit fine before this change and refusing would
make it unfittable.

#### Background-floor provenance is recorded on every gsplat writer path, and `fit --cal` consumes it

The background level a fit subtracts is the only way to interpret the amplitudes
it stores — they are background-relative, never restored — yet almost nothing
persisted it under a name a reader could find. The flat non-tiled fit recorded
it as `floor`; a flat tiled merge recorded the same fact under a different name
(`applied_floor`); a `kind=partition` merge stamped that name onto a node `meta`
key the tree writer discarded; a `--tiling content` fit, a `--progressive` fit
and a `batch-fit merge` recorded nothing at all; and `GSplatData.concatenate`
built a fresh stats dict that dropped every tile's block on the way to the
merge. The format spec claimed otherwise.

There is now one key name (`floor`, alongside `image_min` / `image_max` /
`intensity_range`) in one location (the store's `pipeline/` group), written by
every fitting path: a tree carries the block on its root node's `meta` and
`write_gsplats_tree` promotes it, so a partition and a flat leaf answer the same
question the same way; the parallel `fit -j` merge reloads its worker tiles WITH
their stats and recovers the level from them; and `batch-fit merge` takes the
one level its plan pinned off the manifest. The values are in the input volume's
own units — a tiled or progressive path removes the pedestal outside the fitter
and then fits with `floor="none"`, so it shifts its inner bounds back by the
applied level rather than recording a post-subtraction minimum that means
something different from every other path's. A progressive fit goes one step
further and records the shifted `image_min` as its `floor`, not the level
requested up front: it has no shared normalization range, so pass 0 removes
whatever pedestal is left on top and a `--floor 5` on a volume whose minimum is
98.2 has really taken out 98.2 — which is what a plain fit records for the same
volume, and what the progressive one now records too. Merging is unanimous-or-silent:
`concatenate` carries a key only when every input that records it agrees,
because two independently fitted volumes have two different pedestals and
promoting the first input's would mislabel the rest. A path that cannot name one
honest level writes no key at all, because `floor: null` asserts that no
pedestal was removed. `gsplat info` now lists the block — on its node-tree
report as well as its flat one — instead of burying it in the generic metadata
dump.

`gsplat cal` recorded the floor it subtracted in `fit_config.floor_subtracted`
and nothing read it, so a `cal --floor p20` followed by
`fit --tiling content --cal cal.json` measured the density's `feature_threshold`
at `p20` but scanned and fitted at `auto` — a silent scale mismatch. `fit` now
adopts the calibration's level when the user said nothing about `--floor`,
announcing where the floor came from. Only under `--tiling content`, the one
mode that honours `--cal` at all. An explicit `--floor` (including
`--floor auto`) still wins, as does a `floor:` in a YAML `--config`. A recorded
`null` is NOT adopted: `cal` writes it both when the user asked for `none` and
when its own too-high guard refused the level, and the file cannot tell the two
apart. The adopted level is absolute, so reusing one `cal.json` across a
timelapse applies the calibrated timepoint's pedestal to every other one — said
so in the `--cal` help.

#### GSplat floor specifications now resolve consistently across fitting paths

Percentile floors now ignore exact-zero padding like the default histogram-mode
estimator, and the public floor estimator materializes array-like inputs before
filtering them. For per-array normalization, the non-tiled erase-all guard now
uses the data maximum, matching tiled, progressive, and calibration fits; when
a configured `norm_percentile` high endpoint lies below a valid floor,
normalization expands to that maximum rather than silently refusing the floor.
A re-plan of an existing padded `batch-fit` output can therefore resolve a
different `floor_level` than the one recorded for its already-fitted tiles.
A supplied whole-volume `norm_range` remains authoritative across every tile.
CLI help and the pipeline guide now spell out the intentional `--floor 0` alias
for `none`, the percentile low-end clamp, zero-padding treatment, and
negative-level behavior.

#### `--denoise` no longer removes a different background floor under tiling

`luxar gsplat fit --denoise` resolved the background floor from different data
depending on the tiling path. A non-tiled fit denoises the whole volume up front
and then estimates `--floor` from that denoised array, while a uniform tiled fit
(`--tiling uniform`, `--tile k/M`, `-j N`) resolved one global level from the
**raw** volume and subtracted it from tiles that had already been denoised.
Denoising collapses the noise tail and shifts the histogram mode, so the same
input, the same `--floor auto` and the same `h` removed measurably different
pedestals — a couple of intensity units on skewed-noise backgrounds, which is where
the floor matters most. Output amplitudes are background-relative, so that
difference lands directly in the fitted splats.

Estimating on denoised data is the better default: the mode estimator is more
reliable once the noise tail is collapsed. The tiled paths now resolve their
level on the denoised basis via `resolve_volume_floor_denoised`, which keeps the
whole-volume basis intact — one global level for the whole run, the invariant
#1174 established — and applies the denoise-induced *correction* measured on a
small bounded probe: a few evenly spaced, roughly cubic, contiguous crops
totalling at most `DENOISE_PROBE_BUDGET_VOXELS` (2M) voxels, denoised with the
tiles' exact parameters. The level moves by the shift the same estimator sees
between the raw and denoised probe. When the volume fits the probe budget the
probe *is* the whole volume, so the corrected level equals the
denoised-whole-volume estimate exactly and the two paths agree bit for bit.

Above the budget the probe is a crop of the middle of the volume, and whether its
shift can be believed depends on which estimator measured it. Measured on
synthetic stacks with a known pedestal — six background families (flat Gaussian,
Poisson, gamma-skewed, an axial gradient, a vignette, a masked middle) against the
level `--tiling none` computes — a percentile floor lands 1.4 intensity units from
the non-tiled estimate on average where the uncorrected level averaged 4.4 units
off and was as much as 11.7 off, it is closer on 28 of the 36 volumes, and it
keeps improving as the probe grows (on a 12-volume subset: 1.03, 0.98, 0.59, 0.38
units at 2.3, 4.7, 18.8, 37.5% of the volume). The `auto` histogram-mode shift does neither: it
helped on the two families whose true shift was large and hurt on the four whose
true shift was small, it ended up closer on only 21 of 36 volumes, and growing the
probe from 2% of the volume to 37% did not improve it at all (0.91, 0.75, 0.72,
0.90 — and its worst case got worse). A real light-sheet stack is nearer 0.03%
than to anything measured here. So above the probe budget the
correction is applied for a `pNN` floor and **not** for `auto`: the default keeps
its raw-basis level — exactly the previous behaviour for that volume — and prints
one note saying so and pointing at `--floor pNN` or a non-tiled fit. No probe is
denoised in that case, so the skip costs nothing rather than an NLM pass. This
replaces a first attempt at judging the shift by whether the probe agreed with the
whole volume about the *raw* level, which was backwards: it grew more permissive
the larger the proposed shift, and it refused percentile corrections that were
large, correct improvements.

The probe is a pure function of the volume's shape and the budget, so a
`--tile k/M` subprocess, a `-j N` worker and the sequential path all reach the
same level without coordinating, as they already did for the raw level and the
shared normalization range — provided they share a denoise backend as well as
`h`. `--denoise-backend auto` picks skimage on a CPU-only host and the torch
kernel on a GPU one, and the two are measurably different: on synthetic pedestals
their outputs differed by a mean of ~0.4 and by tens of intensity units at
individual voxels, and the resolved `auto` level came out different in every
configuration tried (by 0.001–0.043 units here, and up to 0.085 on a reviewer's
data). Pin `--denoise-backend` for a fleet spanning heterogeneous hosts. Where
there is a probe at all it costs one extra denoise pass, bounded by the probe
budget, per *resolution*: once for a sequential tiled fit,
but once per worker on the parallel paths, and for a volume within the probe
budget that means one whole-volume denoise pass per worker. Nothing changes with
`--denoise` off — including the log surface — and a numeric or `none` `--floor` is
a user absolute that is never corrected. An unreadable probe, an unavailable NLM
backend, any raising denoiser, and a probe that emits non-finite values all print
a note and keep the raw-basis level rather than failing the fit or handing the
tiles a NaN level.

The "would erase all signal" guard is re-applied to the corrected level against
the same bounded raw sample the uncorrected level is judged on, not against the
probe. Not because the probe would catch less — NLM shrinks the range, so the
probe's denoised max is a *tighter* bound and would veto more — but because a
centre-cropped, smoothed probe can legitimately see no signal at all (a masked or
zero-padded middle), and vetoing there drops floor suppression for a whole run.
The cost of that choice is a gap: a level between the denoised and the raw maximum
is not caught. A background-mode level does not land there in practice.

`--tiling content` still ignores `--denoise` altogether (warned about at
startup). `batch-fit` under `--denoise` keeps a raw-basis level in both of its
modes — the plan resolves it from the raw input before the denoise job runs, and
the on-the-fly mode hands the tasks that number — which is out of scope here and
tracked separately.

#### LOD ladders and `gsplat info` read the dataset's own truncation radius

Gaussian splats carry the σ support they were fitted at and are rendered at
(`truncation_radius`, canonically 2.75), but the LOD path kept a parallel knob
that never consulted the data: `compute_additive_order`, `make_additive_lod`,
`make_lod_pyramid` and `RecipeParams` all defaulted `truncation_sigmas` to a
hardcoded 3.0, so the sparse-Gram pruning that decides which splat pairs
interact was computed at a support the dataset never had. Those defaults are now
`None`, meaning "the dataset's own `truncation_radius`", resolved through a
single shared helper from the object actually being pruned — for
`make_additive_lod` that is the selected substitutive level, not the finest leaf,
since per-level radii round-trip independently. An explicit value still
overrides, and is checked locally against what this σ actually is (a finite
positive CPU pruning cutoff, deliberately *not* the render pipeline's float32
bounds), so a degenerate `--truncation-sigmas 0` fails loudly instead of quietly
poisoning every per-splat truncation radius the pair search is built from, while
a tiny-but-real `1e-5` still runs — it just yields a diagonal-only Gram, which
degrades the greedy ordering toward the score-only one. The two
private helpers that consume the number (`_truncation_radii`,
`_build_sparse_gram`) require it as a keyword with no default, so the old bug
cannot be re-introduced by a new caller forgetting to pass it.

`luxar gsplat info` had the same literal in its volume report: it measured every
splat's extent at 3σ and labelled the table `VOLUME ANALYSIS (3-Sigma)`
regardless of the file. It now measures and labels at the dataset's radius —
`(3/2.75)³ ≈ 1.3`, so a canonically-fitted 3D dataset's reported volumes were
30% too large. The volume formula itself is unchanged.

A dataset fitted at 3.0 sees no change. One fitted at anything else gets a
ladder pruned (and a report measured) at its real support, so ordering and
energy-fraction cutpoints can shift slightly — for the better, since they now
match what the viewer draws.

The wider direction costs time, and that is the price of the accuracy. Under the
truncation convention a pair whose supports do not overlap is *exactly* zero, so
pruning a 6σ store at 3σ was discarding genuinely non-zero pairs; honouring the
data restores them, and there are a lot of them. On 3000 uniformly scattered 3D
splats the sparse Gram grows from 181k non-zeros at 3σ to 1.13M at 6σ and 3.68M
at 10σ — roughly the cubic growth of the support volume — and an end-to-end
`make_additive_lod(method="greedy")` on the same data goes from 4.2 s at 3σ to
20.0 s at 6σ. The value is deliberately not clamped: a cap would simply reinstate
the accuracy bug for exactly the wide-support datasets that need the wider Gram.

`luxar gsplat decimate` inherits the change too, and it is worth calling out
because nothing in its own signature mentions σ: the `prefix` family calls
`compute_additive_order` with no knob of its own, so on non-3.0 data the exact
set of splats it keeps and discards moves with the ordering. The drift measured
small — on 400 dense splats at 2.75σ vs 3.0σ the two greedy permutations agree
for the first several dozen ranks and most prefixes keep the same set — but it is
not nil, so a re-run of `decimate` on such a dataset will not be bit-identical to
one from before this change.

#### A hidden gsplat dimension no longer fetches chunks that cannot render (#1183)

`computeTolerance('gsplats', …)` gave a hidden CONTINUOUS dimension a query
tolerance of `step × 3.0`, and every doc that described it — the module header,
both loader READMEs, `MESH_NODE_SPEC.md` — called it "3 σ". It was neither: the
number multiplied the dimension's _navigation step_ and had nothing to do with the
splat covariance or the node's `truncation_radius`.

The reach it added was also unreachable by design. `compute_chunk_bounds_gsplats`
already expands each continuous dimension of a chunk's AABB by
`sqrt(covariance[d, d]) × coverage_sigma`, hidden dimensions included, with
`coverage_sigma` set to the node's own `truncation_radius` — and the read side's
cutoff is that same radius. Which code enforces it matters, and the first version of
these docs named the wrong one: for a hidden dimension it is the CPU/WASM projection
kernel's shifted-Gaussian attenuation, `(e^{-m²/2} − c)/(1 − c)` clamped at 0 in
`project_gsplats_nd_to_3d`, exactly 0 at `m = truncation_radius`. The shader's
`uTruncate`/`uTruncateSq` discard is the DISPLAYED-dimension counterpart and never
sees a hidden dimension. So a chunk that fails a zero-tolerance intersection test
holds _only_ splats the projection attenuates to nothing: widening the query could
never make a visible splat appear, only download chunks that render nothing. (For
gsplats this array is a chunk-FETCH reach and nothing else; per-splat hidden-dim
visibility comes from that projection math, which does not read it.)

The continuous arm is now a float-safety epsilon, `max(1e-3 × step, 2.75e-5)`, with
one term per reason it cannot be a literal `0`:

- `1e-3 × step` — a continuous dimension along which the splats have ZERO variance
  (a stacked axis declared continuous rather than discrete) gets no σ expansion,
  and the write side epsilon-pads _discrete_ dims only, so its stored bound is the
  axis value itself. The dominant perturbation is that the bound is stored as
  **float32** (`chunk_bounds` is `dtype=np.float32`) while the query position is a
  float64 — ≈1.9e-7 of disagreement at a coordinate of 5.3; the `start + k × step`
  arithmetic drift is real but secondary (≈9e-16 there). At tolerance `0` membership
  would degenerate to an exact float comparison and could silently select nothing.
  At a unit step this is exactly the write side's `_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS = 1e-3`, whose
  reader-side mirror it is — pinned from the Python side by a test that parses the
  TypeScript declaration, so the two cannot desync silently.
- `2.75e-5` — the read side does not use a raw zero variance either.
  `computeMarginalCholesky` REGULARIZES a degenerate pivot, floored at
  `sqrt(CHOLESKY_EPSILON) = 1e-5` for an all-zero hidden block, so such a splat
  still renders out to `truncation_radius × 1e-5`. Term 1 alone falls below that for
  any `step < 2.75e-2` — a 10 ms-frame axis at `step = 0.01` gave a 1e-5 fetch
  window against a 2.75e-5 render band, dropping splats the kernel renders at up to
  ~60% of full brightness (the attenuation one σ out).

That band is ABSOLUTE, in the dimension's own units, because the floor behind it is
an absolute variance floor rather than a step-relative one. It therefore spans many
CELLS on a micro-step axis — ≈27.5 at `step = 1e-6` — and a cap at a fraction of a
cell, which an earlier cut of this change carried, is the wrong answer: a
`0.25 × step` ceiling gives 2.5e-7 at `step = 1e-6` while the renderer shows content
out to 2.75e-5, so a splat ten navigation steps away renders at ~60% brightness with
its chunk never fetched — narrower than the `step × 3` rule this replaces. The
quarter-cell rationale belongs to the DISCRETE arm, where over-reach bleeds a
neighbouring CATEGORY; a continuous axis has none, so window width there is a
bandwidth question (and mesh already gets a FULL cell for a continuous hidden dim).
What holds at every step is the property that matters: the epsilon is never smaller
than the band a degenerate axis can render in, so the query cannot miss renderable
content. That bounds the DISTANCE and not the fraction of a node fetched: where the
dimension's real σ is micro-scale as well (`step = σ = 1e-9`, a metre-declared axis
carrying nanometre structure) the window the data needs is `T · σ = 2.75e-9`, so the
epsilon over-fetches by ~1e4 and can pull the whole node — the one regime in which
this is worse than the `step × 3` it replaces. Narrow _and_ complete needs a
scale-aware regularization floor in the kernel, or the splats' actual per-dimension
σ plumbed into the query — not a different constant.

Three limits are documented rather than papered over, all of them "the axis is
mis-declared": coordinates far from the origin (an expansion below half a float32
ULP rounds away entirely, so with `T = 2.75` _any_ `σ_d ≲ (1.1–2.2)e-8 × |coord|`
behaves like zero variance); a degenerate dimension beside another hidden dimension
of very large σ, where the regularizer's floor is RELATIVE (`σ_max × 1e-6`) and the
rendered band `T × σ_max × 1e-6` exceeds the epsilon once
`σ_max > max(1e-3 × step / (T × 1e-6), 10)` — `≈363.6 × step` or the absolute 10,
the two branches agreeing exactly at the crossover; and a node stamping a
`truncation_radius` well above
the default, which scales the band linearly while this call site — handed only a
`DimensionInfo` — must use the default.

The "bounds already carry the extent" premise is stated with its PRECONDITION:
`compute_chunk_bounds_gsplats` expands the dims NOT in its `slice_dims` argument and
gives the ones that ARE only the tight barrier pad, so it holds while the write
side's barrier set equals the set the reader treats as `discrete`. It does for a
scene that declares its dimensions (`geometry_writers/gsplats.py` uses
`discrete and not display`); with `scene_dimensions` absent the writer falls back to
the value-based `detect_barrier_dims`, whose own docstring calls a false positive a
correctness bug. That disagreement predates this change, but the old rule MASKED it
— a bare `3.0` covered a mis-detected barrier dim's tight bounds, and `1e-3 × step`
does not. The robust fix is plumbing: the writer already publishes the set it used
as the ordering `slice_dims` attr and the tolerance computer does not read it.

The cross-language constant the band derives from now lives in the viewer's
mirrored-constant home, `config/constants.ts`, beside
`GSPLAT_DEFAULT_TRUNCATION_RADIUS`, and the TypeScript reference kernel now IMPORTS
it rather than keeping a third copy — so only `wasm/rust/src/common.rs`, the backend
that actually runs, still owns an independent literal, named in a `MIRROR:` comment
and pinned by a test that parses that one declaration. The loaders layer still does
not import a kernel module (whose top-level workspace allocations rode along).

`ToleranceOptions.gsplatsDefaultTolerance` is gone with the reach it scaled —
gsplats has no continuous-dimension knob now, because the data carries the extent.
`meshSlabTolerance` stays: a mesh has no per-element extent, so its slab thickness
genuinely has to be invented.

#### The `?debug` query log no longer prints an epsilon as `0.00`

`SpatialQueryBuilder` formatted every tolerance with `toFixed(2)`, so the whole
gsplats epsilon range (1e-3 … 1e-5) printed `0.00` — indistinguishable from Lines'
true `0`, from a zeroed array, or from a NaN, on the one surface (`?debug` /
`pnpm agent:debug`) that would reveal an "empty node because nothing matched" bug.
Sub-0.01 values now print in exponential form; the common case (`0.25`, `1.00`,
`∞`) is unchanged. The points loader's sibling `Query tolerance (with discrete
awareness)` line used `toFixed(3)` and had the same blind spot one decade lower
(`2.75e-5` → `0.000`); it now shares the same `formatTolerance` helper.

#### The points fallback query reach ignores the ViewState ride-along (#1183)

`fallbackQueryTolerance` (the points query path when a node has no
`EffectiveRadiusConfig`) read `viewState.tolerance[d] ?? maxRadius` for
spatial/continuous dims, letting a scene/config constant decide a node's fetch
reach. It now always uses `maxRadius`, which at that call site is
`attrs.max_radius ?? config.dataLoading.spatial.defaultMaxRadius` — the node's own
attr where it declares one (and otherwise the same config default the ride-along
carried, where the flip is a no-op), the quantity `io/_ordering/points.py` expanded its chunk bounds
by, and what its sibling `calculateSpatialQueryTolerance` already says in as many
words ("ALWAYS use maxRadius for spatial dimensions, ignore tolerance array"). The
cost is stated plainly: where the ride-along was the `0.1` default and a node's
`max_radius` is larger, the query now FETCHES MORE — up to that node's own radius
reach — and a differing value can also cost a duplicate SliceCache entry. Neither is
a stale serve, and a scene-wide constant cannot know a node's extent. The
`extend_to_all` sentinel branch stays ahead of it and still wins.

That closes the reconciliation #1183 asked for between the two ViewState tolerance
producers (`dims-to-view-state.ts` → `maxRadius`, `view-state-manager.ts` →
`config.dataLoading.spatial.defaultTolerance`): no QUERY path reads the continuous
ride-along any more. Its magnitude is still read for a continuous dimension by two
non-query consumers, and the docs now say so rather than claiming the remaining
readers do not care: `buildSliceViewSig` keys the SliceCache on the raw value and
`viewStatesEqual` compares it (both collapse the ride-along only for a _discrete_
non-spatial dim). The two producers are inert today only because they agree
NUMERICALLY — `scene.userData.maxRadius` is never set in production, so both resolve
to `0.1`; a future divergence would cost cache misses and progressive resets, not
wrong data.

Also corrected, without changing behaviour: the Points arm's rationale, which held
for only one of the two write-side branches. With radii PRESENT (per-point or
scalar) the bound builder expands by the full radius, and there the reader-side
`maxRadius` is exactly the pure over-fetch the gsplats arm just removed. With radii
ABSENT it uses a `max(1% of range, 0.01)` margin, which under-expands against the
default radius the renderer applies, and the reader-side expansion is what keeps
those points from being dropped at a chunk edge. The tolerance computer is handed no
radii-presence flag, which is the honest reason points cannot simply copy the
gsplats fix; the Python under-expansion is the thing that should eventually change.

#### In-repo gsplat benchmarks now pin `floor="none"` instead of inheriting `auto`

The three in-repo fitting benchmarks — `scripts/benchmark_progressive_psnr.py`,
`scripts/benchmarks/benchmark_fitting_pareto.py` and
`scripts/benchmarks/benchmark_progressive_pareto.py` — called the fitters without a
`floor=` argument and so inherited the shipped default `floor="auto"`, a
histogram-mode background pedestal estimate that is subtracted from the volume
before fitting. All three then scored PSNR/SSIM of the reconstruction against the
*raw, un-floored* volume. That is a mixed basis: the fit is penalised for correctly
dropping a pedestal the reference still carries, and the reported number moves
silently whenever the floor estimator changes. How large that penalty is depends
strongly on the dataset: the 2026-07-12 measurement recorded in
`docs/guides/developer/BENCHMARK_FLOOR_DECISION.md` found −5.86 dB on kidney_dapi
(31.77 → 25.91) but +0.01 dB on blastocyst — near zero where
there is little pedestal to remove. All three print a `METRIC=` line for
autoresearch extraction, and the two Pareto harnesses additionally return their
dominance verdict as an exit code; every one of those signals was exposed to the
drift. Every fit call in those harnesses — including the progressive Pareto
warm-up, so it exercises
the same code path as the fits it warms up for — now pins `floor="none"`, matching
the repo/manuscript convention for a benchmark scored against a raw reference.

No baseline is invalidated *in the repo* — neither Pareto baseline file is
committed — but a machine that has run either Pareto benchmark before still holds
one on disk, measured under `floor="auto"`. Both harnesses demand that every axis
be at least as good as the baseline, so comparing a `floor="none"` run against it
can print `PARETO: NOT DOMINANT` and exit 1 for a change that regressed nothing.
Delete any local `scripts/benchmarks/data/*baseline*.json` once after this change;
the next run has no baseline and becomes the new one.

The shipped default is unchanged and deliberately so — `gsplat fit`/`cal` keep
`--floor auto`, which is the right behaviour for real use, since a constant
background pedestal is not signal. A new source guard,
`packages/luxar/src/luxar/tests/test_benchmark_floor_pin.py`, keeps the two apart:
it parses every `*.py` under `scripts/` with `ast` and requires each call to a
module-level gsplat fitting function to declare its floor at the call site. The
public `fit_tiled_gaussian_splats` alias is listed alongside `fit_tiled`, and
local `import ... as` aliases are resolved within the file, so neither spelling
nor renaming on import evades the rule (a fitter passed around as a *value* —
`functools.partial` and friends — still would; that would need dataflow analysis
the guard deliberately does not have). Declaring means a `floor=` keyword, or a
kwargs dict carrying the key that is visible at the call site — an inline
`**{"floor": ...}` or a module-level `FIT_KWARGS = dict(..., floor=...)`, the
idiom the luxar-paper harnesses pin with — while an opaque `**kwargs` forward is
still an offender. Also listed are the two worker-argv builders,
`build_worker_cmd` and `_default_worker_cmd_builder`: each omits `--floor` from
the tile worker's argv when it is `None`, leaving the worker on `auto`, so a
future harness tile-fitting through them would be this same bug. It asks for a
*declared* basis rather than a particular value, so a harness that genuinely wants
the shipped suppression writes `floor="auto"` and passes. `fit_tiled_parallel`
itself stays unlisted for the opposite reason: it has no `floor` parameter at all,
so demanding one there would order an author to write a `TypeError` (same for
`fit_planned_parallel`). `fit_planned` *is* listed: it collects `**fit_kwargs` and
forwards them to a per-box `fit_gaussian_splats`, so a `floor=` at its call site
is both visible to the gate and honoured at fit time — and it needs the
declaration more than most, since an unpinned `auto` there is re-estimated
against every box crop separately. There is
deliberately no file allow-list: the
requirement is satisfiable entirely within the file that adds the call, so a
harness written on one branch can never redden the guard after merging with an
unrelated branch — and for that same cross-branch reason an unparseable file
becomes a finding that says the floor pin is not what is broken, rather than a
traceback out of the gate. Separately, it parses the raw bytes so that Python's
own source-encoding rules apply (a BOM or a PEP 263 encoding cookie is handled,
as in `scripts/check_documentation.py`). The gate's own docstring records what an
AST call-name check cannot see — `GaussianSplatFitter.fit`, argv-driven fits such
as `luxar gsplat cal` (self-consistent, so it needs no pin, and it takes its spec
inside a `fit_kwargs` *dict argument* a keyword check cannot read either), a floor
passed positionally (deliberately
still reported: "declared" means a reader can see which argument it is), and the
demos outside `scripts/` whose printed PSNR nothing gates on.

#### Capsule lines: packed joint state and one less varying

The capsule line primitive's per-segment joint state now rides packed
half-precision varyings — 12 flat floats down to 9 — with the bisector-cut
normals deliberately left at full precision, since halves there would
re-introduce the #1502 hairpin banding (each leg quantizes in its own
frame, so the error does not cancel between two planes that must be exact
complements). The WebGL shaders also derive perspective correction from
`gl_FragCoord.w` rather than carrying a dedicated `1/w` varying and
dividing per fragment: the two are the same number by spec identity.

Together these cut the worst-case (10 M hairline segments) overhead over
the legacy quad from ~1.32× to ~1.23×; fill-bound wide-line scenes are
unchanged. No joint, cap or profile behaviour changes at any width: the
two backends stay in value parity across the capsule parity fixtures, and
the only numeric difference is the endpoint radii rounding to half
precision (≤0.2% of profile, invisible).

#### The volumetric line primitive is deleted

`?linePrimitive=volumetric` — the closed-form segment-⊛-Gaussian line model
that shipped during the #1352 campaign (exact in its core ray integral and
bisector-cut algebra, with documented bounded approximations at chain
ends, near-clip, and sharp bends) — is gone, together with its GLSL and TSL
shader pairs, the pick pair, the quadrature-validated CPU reference, the
Abel-transform sharpness LUT, and the `ray-integral` shared-math module
(about 4,600 lines plus 21 parity fixtures). Since the capsule became the
default, an A/B on the QA grid found the capsule matching or beating it
visually — including near-axial, the case the volumetric model existed to
fix — at several times less frame cost, so there is no scene left that
benefits from carrying a third primitive through every cross-cutting
material change. `linePrimitive` now accepts `capsule` (default) and
`screen-space`; an explicit `?linePrimitive=volumetric` is treated like any
other unrecognised value and falls back to the default. The full
implementation remains in git history at the deletion's branch point.

#### The line primitive sizes itself to the scene

A new `Settings → Advanced → Line primitive` policy (`Auto` / `Capsule` /
`Quad`, default `Auto`) decides which primitive a lines node builds. Auto
keeps the capsule default but builds the cheaper screen-space quad for
nodes whose effective segment load — authored count scaled by an
extent-normalized width factor — reaches two million, where the capsule's
measured extra GPU cost starts eating a meaningful slice of the frame
budget on discrete GPUs (~1.5× the quad on thin lines at every count,
over 3× on wide lines). The visual and picking materials resolve through
one seam so they always agree, the decision is made once per node at
material build and never re-runs, and `?linePrimitive=` remains the
session's strongest word.

The line perf bench gains the matching measurement axis:
`LUXAR_PERF_SYNTHETIC_COUNTS` sweeps the synthetic scenarios across
segment counts, and synthetic scenes now carry the authored-count
metadata production scenes always had.

#### Mesh LOD colour fidelity is pinned by value, not by flag

The ladder's colour test asserted only `has_colors`, so a coarse level that came
back black, clipped, or cast to another dtype set the flag exactly like a correct
one — every row of the `#1355` table would have passed. It now reads the colours
back through `LuxarScene` per level and checks the dtype, one RGB triple per
vertex, and the values, across `uint8`, `uint16`, and float32 in both SDR and HDR
ranges. (The scalars ladder was already pinned by value.)

The gradient matters as much as the readback: the previous test coloured every
vertex the same, so cluster-averaging ran but nothing it could get wrong was
visible in the result — and the writer then stored that constant as a single
`(1, 3)` broadcast row, which cannot show a per-vertex error either. The three
channels now carry different values too, so a dropped or swapped channel cannot
pass, and the per-vertex count is asserted so a level whose broadcast row was
never expanded to its own vertex count cannot pass as one colour. A `(1, 3)`
broadcast row — the other shape the issue measured — now has its own ladder test.

#### `luxar mesh lod` names what it leaves behind (#1357)

The command reads a scene, picks one mesh node, and writes a BRAND-NEW scene
holding only that node's ladder — so everything else in the source is gone, and
until now it went without a word. A scene of one mesh plus a points cloud came
back as the ladder alone; the mesh's own per-vertex `labels` / `image_labels`
disappeared too (`MeshData` has no field for them, so the round trip cannot read
what it would have to write); and a mesh nested under a group with a transform on
it landed somewhere else entirely, because only the LEAF's attrs are forwarded
while the group's are inherited in the source and absent in the output.

The nodes still cannot be carried — there is nowhere in a single-ladder output
scene for them to go — but they are now REPORTED, by name, before anything is
written. Four categories: every other node (points / lines / gsplats / meshes /
groups, and user-authored overlays), each ancestor group whose inherited
placement or compositing is genuinely lost, the picked mesh's label channels, and
nothing else. Refusing outright was the alternative and is worse: it would leave a
multi-node scene with no way to build a ladder at all.

"Genuinely lost" is the load-bearing word in the ancestor line. Gating on mere
presence of a compositing key fires on the command's own output — every mesh leaf
carries `opacity` / `gamma` / `intensity` / `absorption` at 1.0 and `offset` at
0.0, and the ladder wrapper inherits those neutral values — so re-laddering a
level of an existing ladder would warn about five keys while losing none. A key is
reported only when it can actually change the picture: a non-neutral scalar, a
non-identity `transform` / `nd_transform`, a `blending_mode` neither the leaf nor a
nearer group already overrides (nearest setter wins), or a `layer` / `visible` away
from its own default. `join` never counts, since `add_mesh` refuses it in the first
place.

The warnings sit after every validator that can still abort the run and before
the destructive rewrite of the output path — announcing a drop and then erroring
out was its own small lie. A large partition collapses to one counted line per
parent rather than one line per sibling; the count is always the full one, never
a silent truncation.

#### LOD coverage metric no longer drifts with viewport aspect ratio

The auto-selecting `kind=lod` group picked a coarser level than intended on a
wide monitor, reproducing #1361's opening-framing blur at aspect ratios beyond
roughly 16:9. The cause: `calculateCameraDistance` fits the camera to the
VERTICAL field of view for any viewport aspect >= 1 (so the framing distance is
independent of width), while the coverage metric normalised the projected bbox
diagonal by the viewport's DIAGONAL — which keeps growing with width regardless.
So the framing did not widen with the canvas but the metric's denominator did,
and a shape's raw coverage ratio fell as `raw(aspect) = raw(1)·√2 / hypot(aspect,
1)`. Measured before the fix: a cube's opening-framing metric fell from 3.43 at
1:1 to 1.31 at 32:9, and thinner shapes (a flat pancake, a cloud elongated in the
image plane) dropped below the finest-level threshold entirely on an ultrawide
canvas.

The fix normalises by the viewport's **fitted screen axis**
(`min(viewport.width, viewport.height)`) instead of its diagonal — exactly the
extent `calculateCameraDistance` fits in both aspect regimes (the vertical
extent for aspect >= 1, the horizontal one for aspect < 1). This is provably
exact for aspect >= 1: camera distance there has no aspect dependence at all, so
the projected pixel diagonal is EXACTLY proportional to the viewport height,
independent of both aspect and absolute viewport size (verified to 12
significant digits). The viewer's `FILL_FACTOR` anchor moves from `0.25` to
`0.5` in the same change, chosen so the metric's VALUE is preserved (within
~2%, measured) at the mainstream 16:9 reference — every existing
`coverage_fraction` threshold, hysteresis band, and cross-fade band keeps its
meaning. Python's `MAX_COVERAGE_FRACTION` stays `4.0`, re-expressed as the new
`SCREEN_FILL_DIAGONAL_RATIO / FILL_FACTOR` (a screen-filling object's projected
diagonal is no longer exactly the fitted axis, but `~2`x it at the 16:9
reference the constant is anchored at — `1.41`x at 1:1 and `2.57`x at a 21:9
panel, hence the trade-off below).

Trade-off, deliberately accepted: `MAX_COVERAGE_FRACTION` is now aspect-EXACT
only near aspect ratio √3 ≈ 1.73 (it was aspect-exact everywhere under the old
diagonal normalisation). A partition-bound ladder's finest level — the
fills-screen anchor used by tiled layers (`adaptive`, `overview`) — therefore
needs a somewhat larger projected size to reach it at square-ish/portrait-ish
aspect ratios than before this fix (measured: `x1.41` at 1:1, `x1.20` at 4:3,
`x1.06` at 16:10, `~x1.0` at 16:9) and a somewhat smaller one at ultrawide
ratios (`x0.78` at a real 21:9 panel, `x0.54` at 32:9). This is the intentional flip side of
making the WHOLE-OBJECT anchor (`coverage_fractions`, reached by a normal
full-frame view) aspect-exact instead — that anchor is what #1410's blur
actually hit, while a tiled layer's per-tile anchor was already a coarse
heuristic.

Also known and unchanged here: `updateCameraAspect` never re-fits the camera
distance on a window resize (it only preserves the vertical fov / ortho
extent), so with height held fixed, narrowing a viewport is not symmetric
with widening one: the new metric only overtakes the old past a crossover
around aspect ~0.56 (506x900 for a 1600x900 baseline) — down to that point
the new normalisation is actually LESS inflated than the old one (1600x900 ->
500x900, aspect 0.56: `x1.80` new vs `x1.78` old, already a near-wash), and
only below it does narrowing inflate the metric faster than before
(1600x900 -> 200x900, aspect 0.22: `x4.50` new vs `x1.99` old). Widening a
viewport — the actual #1410 symptom — is exactly stable under the fix (proven
above); narrowing one past that crossover without a re-fit is a pre-existing,
separate limitation this fix does not address.

Not fixed here: a cloud elongated along the VIEW axis (e.g. `1×1×100`) still
measures a near-zero metric, because `calculateCameraDistance` sizes the
distance from the largest dimension even when that dimension barely
contributes to the projected AABB — a camera-framing issue, not a
normalisation one.

#### The demos' `Neutral` tone-mapping pins are now chosen by range

Seven files in the demo package set `tone_mapping="Neutral"` on a
`ViewerConfig` when #1459 was filed, most with some version of the same
comment: colour here is an
exact encoding, and ACES shifts hues. (Two argued differently —
`demo_flywire_connectome` said ACES "blew the 300K-line luminous connection glow
out into a white wash", and `_interop_common` said the imported RGB is already
display-referred.) Five demos are swept here; the shared
`_interop_common` helper is treated separately below, and
`demo_flywire_connectome`'s own flip to a re-tuned ACES was PR #1527's half of
#1459 and has already landed, so it needs no exception row here.
The premise is right; the conclusion only follows over range. `Neutral`
(Khronos PBR Neutral) is not a passthrough — it subtracts an offset taken from
the channel *minimum* (0.04 once that minimum reaches 0.08, `x - 6.25*x*x` below
that, which crushes near-black hardest), so anything but a fully saturated
colour moves even well inside gamut, and then, from peak 0.76 up, it compresses
the peak and mixes toward the achromatic value *equal to that compressed peak*,
with weight
`g = 1 - 1/(0.15*(peak - newPeak) + 1)`. Running the three.js formula:
`(1, 0, 0)` leaves it at `(0.880, 0.016, 0.016)`, `(0.5, 0.5, 0.5)` — well
inside gamut — at `(0.46, 0.46, 0.46)`, `(8, 0.5, 8)` at
`(0.992, 0.535, 0.992)` (g = 0.51) and `(100, 0, 0)` at
`(0.999, 0.936, 0.936)` (g = 0.94), very nearly white. For a scene whose colours
already fit inside [0, 1], the pin was dulling exactly the encoding its comment
set out to protect.

Over range, what Neutral costs is **chroma, not hue**. Its compress-and-mix is
"scale every channel, then add the same amount to all", which preserves the HSV
hue angle exactly: `(100, 0, 0)` stays at hue 0° and drops to saturation 0.06.
A hard clamp is not the clean mirror image it looks like: `(100, 0, 0)` clamps
to `(1, 0, 0)` at full saturation, but only because its darkest channel is
already 0 — `(2, 0.5, 0.5)` clamps to `(1, 0.5, 0.5)` and drops from saturation
0.75 to 0.5 — while `(2, 1, 0)` clamps to `(1, 1, 0)` and moves from hue 30° to
hue 60°, and every structure above 1.0 goes flat; ACES shifts hue by design. So
nothing is faithful over range, and the choice is which distortion you can live
with — where colour is a hue encoding, Neutral is the one that keeps the hue.

`"None"` is the exact choice inside [0, 1]: the viewer maps it to
`THREE.NoToneMapping`, which the mega-shader aliases to its Linear (clamp) mode,
and exposure, offset and gamma still apply because they run *before* the
tone-mapping switch. Two demos moved there on that reasoning —
`demo_ocean_currents_earth` (Blue Marble texture plus a blue→white speed LUT,
both in [0, 1], normal blending at intensity 1.0) and
`demo_gsplats_recipes_tribolium` (an hsv-derived hue/shade palette over six
volumetric gsplat nodes, one per `RECIPES` entry, each of whose emitted radiance
works out to `color * (1 - exp(-tau)) / absorption` with `tau = absorption *
opacity * intensity`. `opacity` does not drop out of that: the
`opacity * intensity` ray mass cancels against the `tau` under the S(tau)
self-screening factor, and what survives, `1 - exp(-tau)`, is below 1 for *any*
`tau >= 0` — so the per-node in-gamut bound comes from `absorption=1.0` and
holds whatever `opacity` and `intensity` are. Their `One`/`OneMinusSrcAlpha`
composition of bounded premultiplied sources keeps the sum bounded too, and the
demo's `add_text` labels are DOM overlays outside the HDR pass entirely. A
viewer who drags the Layers panel's live κ slider below 1 raises that bound to
1/κ and can push a node over range again).

The remaining three keep `Neutral`, and their comments now say why rather than
merely that they always have. All three run over range, and for the first two
colour is a hue encoding — `demo_nd_transforms` (a deliberately HDR lit palette
running to 2.4, where a red R must read as red) and
`demo_biodiversity_planetary_scale` (`GLOBE_INTENSITY` 4.88,
`OCCURRENCE_INTENSITY` 100.0 over a categorical taxonomic palette) — so Neutral
is exactly the right operator there: it is the hue-exact one over range, and it
sheds the chroma of the brightest peaks to get that. `demo_gsplats_3d_tribolium_embryo`
(`exposure=1.97`) keeps its own reason: the pin
was verified against that volume, and Neutral rolls its peaks off instead of
clipping them flat. Re-pointing any of them at ACES or at `"None"` trades hue
fidelity for chroma, so it needs a live A/B render rather than a blind flip. The
shared `_interop_common.build_interop_scene`
default keeps `"Neutral"` for a narrower reason: the imported captures carry
per-splat RGB clipped to [0, 1], but `demo_gsplats_interop_sog_matrixcity` builds
`recipe="overview"`, whose substitutive merge emits amplitudes with no bound of
1 that the gsplat `normal` shader feeds straight into RGB — so that one needs a
render check before it can claim to be in gamut.

A new AST guard, `demos/tests/test_demos_tone_mapping_policy.py`, pins the
policy: every statically known `tone_mapping` in the demo package — literal,
signature default, or string constant resolved in the scope it is used in —
must be `"ACES"` unless its module carries a row (with a reason) in the test's
exception table, and a row covers one site per value — a second copy of the same
non-ACES pin in that module fails, which is the copy-paste being guarded
against. The house
rule in `CLAUDE.md` and `HDR_GUIDE.md`, `gsplat convert`'s own `--help` and
docstring, the compiler's LUT notice, `ViewerConfig.tone_mapping` and the
viewer's tone-mapping tooltip were all saying "reach for Neutral when you need
exact colour"; they now say to pick by range — `None` inside [0, 1], and over
range come back into range, accept ACES's rolloff, or keep Neutral where hue
matters more than the chroma of the peaks.

#### The Gaia demo is now `gaia_milky_way`, and names the stars it marks

The demo's key was `galaxy`, which said nothing about Gaia and collided as a
substring with the two `spiral_galaxy` demos in every list and filter. It is now
`gaia_milky_way` — `luxar demo run gaia_milky_way`, output
`datasets/demos/gaia_milky_way.luxar.zarr`, and the same id in the gallery
manifest.

The three reference markers (Sun, Betelgeuse, Rigel) carry hover labels, and a
legend in the bottom-left corner names them with a colour swatch read from each
marker's own RGB, so the orientation cues are readable without hunting for a
tooltip. The star cloud's volumetric appearance was retuned as one set — opacity
0.5, absorption 0.12, intensity 0.175 — which keeps the disc translucent front to
back instead of hiding the far side of the bulge behind the near side.

#### A written ground truth for the viewer's visual design

The viewer's design language — the "quiet instrument" — lived in people's heads
and in a handful of exemplary files (the control rail, the data-loading
monitor's end-of-file "Refinement layer" block). Everything else was
reconstructed by reading whichever panel happened to be nearby, which is how a
green scrollbar and a solid-green "interactive" slider became precedent.

`docs/guides/developer/UI_DESIGN_GUIDE.md` writes it down and declares itself
authoritative: the 87 design tokens and their traps (the spacing key is *half*
the pixel value; `--luxar-blur-*` values are complete `blur()` functions; there
is no `--luxar-radius-xs`), what differs between the four themes, the
glass-surface system and the five hard constraints that break a theme when
violated, color semantics (`highlight` is interactive, green is *healthy*), the
surface/header/scroll recipes, typography, the two icon contracts, motion,
placement, interaction states and a11y, naming, and a checklist for a new
surface.

Sections 15.1–15.5 are a verified inventory of the code that still contradicts
the guide, so nobody mistakes debt for a pattern. The five modernization
tranches they cataloged have since landed — a11y hardening (#1476),
emoji→stroke icons (#1479), the dataset browser (#1472), the accent migration
plus the shared panel-header/close recipes (#1480) and token hygiene (#1478) —
leaving a shorter but not merely cosmetic list.

Two surfaces still mix raw values into their chrome: the recording
start-confirm dialog and the scene-identity banner. A parallel
`config.ui.zIndex` scale in TypeScript interleaves with the z-index tokens, so
the guide tabulates the two side by side and says which one actually decides
what paints over what. The rest is the raw `rgba()` and `color: white` the
token sweep did not reach, two hand-rolled copies of the shared header and
close recipes that have since drifted from their originals, seven focus rings
spelled without the mandatory fallback, the resolution indicator's opacity ramp
on a glass root, sub-AA contrast on the glass themes' micro-label ranks, and one
modal that doesn't yet trap focus.

§15.6 is the opposite list. It registers the deliberate exceptions —
sanctioned literals, the three `!important` categories, the off-tier `calc()`
z-indexes — so nobody migrates one away and deletes the record with it.

#### Two glass surfaces that fought their own theme

Two panels violated the glass-surface constraints the UI design guide spells
out in §5.1, and both showed it only under liquid-glass. The toast faded
`opacity` on its own glass root, so the refraction and tint layers rode the
fade out with the badge instead of staying behind it. The dimension-sliders
panel scrolled on its glass root, and a scroll container clips the very layers
that paint at `inset: 0` behind it.

The toast is no longer a glass surface at all. A two-second badge whose dismiss
animation *is* an opacity fade belongs with the REC pill and the cursor context
menus — framed with the badge tier of the panel recipe, but not glassed — so the
fade is now legal rather than tolerated, and liquid-glass paints it the same
dark tint those siblings already get (that theme's `--luxar-bg-secondary` is a
translucent white, which would leave white text on a bright render). The
dimension sliders delegate scrolling to an inner `__scroll` wrapper like every
other panel, keep their glass root at `overflow: visible`, and move from the
baseline in-canvas layer to the dropdown tier their placement implies.

One surface in this class is still open and is now named as such in the guide's
debt inventory: the resolution indicator ramps `opacity` on its own glass root
via its fade-in/fade-out keyframes, and wants the same treatment — an inner
wrapper, or the toast's route out of the glass system.

#### Capsule joint stencil reach is now something the tests can see

A capsule joint reserves the full disc at a cut end whenever a deficit packet
exists: the deficit term renders `max(mine − partner, 0)`, so the leg's own
profile bounds it and any shorter reach lets the rasterizer chop the light the
deficit rule adds back. That reach shipped correct but unmeasured — the CPU
composition model evaluated the profile over the whole plane, so the clip that
turns a shortfall into a chopped disc rather than a dim one was absent from
the one sweep that could have caught it.

The model now mirrors that reach, width gate included, and clips each leg by
its own footprint; a negative-control test injects the pre-fix half-disc rule
and requires the sweep to chop, which it does at −0.41 of peak against a 2 px
partner. The short-partner bounds sit at (−0.01, 0.005), which a half-disc
revert now breaches on four of the five rows — at a 40 px partner the light
the shorter reach removes (0.0045 of peak) stays just under that row's own
AA-ramp deviation (0.0046), so it scores the same either way; a source
pin checks the packet branch of all four vertex surfaces, and a new
`line-capsule-joint-taper` parity fixture gives the joint alternating vertex
widths so the branch runs on both backends. Note that the e2e layer is not
part of the mobile-only `e2e-tests` job; the dedicated `tsl-parity` CI job
exercises it alongside the unit coverage.

#### An unwritable colour dtype no longer strands a partial node

A `colors` array whose dtype the writer cannot store was refused by the encoder,
not by the pre-write validator sweep — so the refusal landed mid-write, after
part of the node was already on disk. `np.array([[255, 0, 0]])` is `int64` on
Linux, which makes this the easy mistake to make. Measured residue, each of it
surviving `finalize()`: a flat write left the node holding its geometry arrays
and nothing else (`positions` for Points; `vertices`/`segments`/`widths` for
Lines; `centers`/`amplitudes`/`cholesky_*` for GSplats; `vertices`/`faces` for
Mesh); a `partition=` that really split left a `kind=partition` wrapper holding a
partial `part_0`; `additive_lod=` left an `additive_0` child (measured for
Points and for Lines); a Mesh
`substitutive_lod=` left a `kind=lod` group holding a partial `child_0`; and the
GSplats substitutive door, `add_gsplats_from_data(..., lod_group=…)`, left a
`kind=lod` group holding a partial `child_0` — or, when only the finest level's
colours were bad, a COMPLETE `child_0` beside a partial `child_1`, a half-written
ladder. Only Points and Lines under `substitutive_lod=` were clean, because the
gsplat lift carries its own copy of the rule.

`validate_colors_for_writing` now enforces the dtype rule itself, through a new
`validate_color_dtype` helper: a COLOR array must be floating point (any width)
or integer `uint8`/`uint16`. That validator is what every geometry type's
pre-split gate runs against the SOURCE arrays before a `partition=` /
`additive_lod=` / `substitutive_lod=` decomposition, and the gsplats
`lod_group=` gate now walks every rung of every substitutive level with the same
validator before its wrapper group is created. Measured across the 17 doors that
exist — Points and Lines flat / `partition=` / `additive_lod=` /
`substitutive_lod=`, GSplats flat / `partition=`, Mesh flat / `partition=` /
`substitutive_lod=`, and `add_gsplats_from_data` flat / `additive_lod=` /
`partition=` / `lod_group=` — an unwritable colour now leaves the store
completely untouched, and the wrapped path reports the same COLOURS verdict as
the flat one, byte for byte. (Only the colours verdict: a call that also trips a
Cholesky fault still reports colours under a wrapper where the flat path reports
Cholesky, which is the pre-existing pre-split-gate precedence asymmetry the
`labels` gate already has.) The rule is
also spelled as a whitelist rather than an integer special case, which closes the
same stranding for a `complex` array: complex is numeric enough to pass the
finiteness check, so it used to reach the per-channel encoder and die there with
`color_mode required for float COLOR arrays`, positions already written.

The check runs last inside `validate_colors_for_writing`, matching the
precedence of the encoder rule it mirrors: a negative integer array still
reports negativity, and an empty array still passes through with no dtype
opinion at all (the encoder writes empties ahead of its own validation). Two
things that used to write now do not, both deliberately: a `complex` colour
array whose values happen to be uniform used to reach the broadcast encoding and
land on disk as a `complex64` zarr array the viewer cannot decode, and the
standalone `.gsplats.zarr` writer inherits the same refusal. Everything else is
untouched — floating point colours of any width including `longdouble` (still
accepted, still quantized to uint8 by AUTO), `uint8`/`uint16`, a uniform RGB(A)
list or tuple (which takes the broadcast door, becomes float32 and never meets
the rule), and a bool array, which keeps its existing non-numeric refusal.

#### `image_labels` on a `substitutive_lod=` wrapper is checked before anything writes (#1491)

`scene.add_points("p", positions, image_labels=[...], substitutive_lod=True)` with
a wrong-length `image_labels` used to be refused only from deep inside the finest
child's own write — after every coarse gsplat level, and after that same child's
positions, colors, radii, sharpness, scalars and text labels, were already on
disk. The result was not a childless or truncated ladder: it was a complete,
fully loadable `kind=lod` group at every level, silently missing only the image
labels the caller actually asked for — harder to notice than a missing level, not
easier, since nothing about the store looked wrong. `image_labels` never fit the
per-part slicer the rest of this gate (#1437/#1446) relies on, since it is
forwarded only to the finest child, so it needed its own check. The length
(dense list) / index-bounds (sparse dict) validation is now hoisted out of
`write_image_labels_csr` into a standalone, pure function that both the
Points/Lines `substitutive_lod=` pre-split gate and every flat writer
(`write_points`, `write_lines`, `write_mesh`, `write_gsplats`) run before the
group is created. Mesh gained the same fix for the same reason on its own
decimation ladder.

A right-length list with one wrong-typed entry (an `int` where an image was
expected) strands identically, so the TYPE dispatch that used to live only in
the blob-encoding step was split out too and is now checked pre-write alongside
the length/index gate — one implementation, shared by both callers. That
dispatch also validates an `ndarray` entry's shape (`(H,W)` / `(H,W,3)` /
`(H,W,4)`) eagerly, since that costs nothing a type check does not already
cost; a mis-shaped array used to strand the same way a mistyped entry did.

Two narrower cases of the same strand went with it. A sparse key that is in
range but not a real integer index (`{1.5: blob}`, or a `np.float64` from an
arithmetic slip) used to clear the bounds check and then fail on the writer's
own list subscript, post-write; keys are now checked for integer-index
semantics (numpy integers still pass) alongside their bounds. And a dense
`image_labels` that can only be iterated ONCE is now refused up front with a
pointer to `list(...)`: a pre-write gate has to walk it to validate it, so
accepting one would leave the writer an exhausted iterator and stamp an
all-empty image CSR.

Separately, a `partition=` / `substitutive_lod=` split that recurses into the
same adder for a synthesised child (`part_0`, a decimated mesh `child_3`) used to
report a doubly-nested message naming that internal node — `Could not add points
'p': Could not add points 'child_3': ...` — rather than the node the caller
passed. The four adders now un-nest a same-geometry inner failure before
re-raising, so the message matches what the flat write would say for the same
input. A cross-geometry inner failure (the Points/Lines ladder's coarse children
are lifted `gsplats` nodes) is left alone on purpose, since collapsing it would
misattribute a different geometry's fault — including attributes the outer
geometry does not even recognise — to the wrong one.

#### Lines render with the capsule primitive by default (#1352)

`DEFAULT_LINE_PRIMITIVE` flipped from `screen-space` to `capsule` after the
re-gate passed on both axes: ≤1.09× the quad's frame cost on the
10M-segment worst case (parity at vsync on fill-bound scenes, 1.04× on the
4.4M-segment zebrahub streamlines) and a visual sign-off on the QA grid at
arbitrary zoom. Three joint-composition decisions came with the flip:
the bisector cut, found by the tightened line-join gate, is a 1 px AA ramp
rather than a hard step (each leg evaluates the plane in its own local
frame, so hard-step boundary pixels flipped independently — black and
double-bright speckles at every joint vertex); the cut normal is left
unquantised (an interim 1/1024 snap was dropped pre-release, #1502 —
each leg rounds in its OWN local basis, so the rounding never cancels);
and the zigzag flux floor in `line-join-artifact.spec.ts` is re-baselined
to the round-join geometry (0.895 measured vs the quad miter's 0.985 and
the unmitred pathology's 0.780 — the capsule's joins are round, like the
volumetric reference's). The quad (`?linePrimitive=screen-space`) and
volumetric (`?linePrimitive=volumetric`) primitives remain selectable
until their scheduled deletion.

#### Thin capsule lines keep their whole leg at a sharp bend (#1495)

The joint deficit packet — the term that fills in the light a plain bisector
cut would chop when the partner leg cannot cover my foreign side — was skipped
below a 4 px stencil half-width, on the rationale that a deficit at a hairline
joint is sub-pixel. It is not, once the bend is sharp: past 120° of turn the
bisector tilts toward the leg's own axis and cuts its rod LENGTHWISE, so a
short or hairpin partner left part of a leg unrendered anywhere along it.
Measured on the CPU joint model with a short partner (`ql = 0.4 r`), the plain
cut deviates −0.28 of peak at 135° and −0.53 at 160° at r = 1.5 px, and −0.35 /
−0.72 at r = 3.5 px, against −0.11/−0.12 and −0.05/−0.05 for a congruent joint
at the same angle and radius. Thin polylines with sharp direction changes now
render whole.

The width gate itself stays, so nothing changes for the common case, and the
exception to it is doubly narrow: the turn must be sharper than 120° — the same
axis-dot test the packet gate's own sharp clause uses, rather than a second
threshold — and BOTH of the segment's raw radii must reach the 1.5 px AA
radius floor. Below that floor the fragment's thin-width energy compensation
dims a leg while the deficit still cancels the partner's unscaled profile, so a
pair at different scales OVER-brightens (+0.14…+0.16 of peak measured at 175°
with one end sub-floor) — a bead, which is the artifact class this primitive
exists to remove. That is a real trade, not a free win: a drawable sub-floor
taper would compose better WITH a packet (−0.05…−0.07 against −0.33…−0.79
gated), and we take the dim gap over the bright bead. Nor does the floor make
the deficit under-fill-only: the near-fade term can still differ between two
legs sharing a vertex, a pre-existing hole this change does not close.

The cost is fragment work, not stencil area: a live packet makes every
foreign-side fragment evaluate the partner rod instead of discarding, and past
120° that region runs lengthwise along the rod — 18.3% of a leg's own covered
footprint at 121°, 27.5% at 150°, 56.8% at 175° (r = 2 px), against 12–15% at a
gentle joint. The thin-line fill arm was not re-run, and the perf benches are
not obviously immune: their random-walk generator draws each step
independently, so 24.9% of their joints turn past 120°.

Three residuals are accepted deliberately, all pinned by the unit sweep: a
joint at or below 120° still hard-cuts (−0.19 of peak at `ql = 0.4 r`, growing
to −0.39 as the partner shortens); the angle threshold is hard, so a projected
bend sweeping through it pops (−0.175 → 0.000 across 119.5° → 120.5°); and the
radius floor is a harder pop still (−0.21 → 0.000 at 125°, −0.72 → 0.000 at
175°, across raw 1.4999 → 1.5 px) that a plain zoom sweeps through. All four
vertex surfaces — both material backends, both picking backends — carry the
same condition, so the pick shape still tracks the drawn pixels.

#### An explicit `None` in `add_gsplats_from_data`'s `**attrs` now means "absent"

Everything that is not a named parameter of `Group.add_gsplats_from_data` arrives
in `**attrs` and is forwarded verbatim to the children of whatever wrapper the
call produces, where `validate_render_attrs` rejects an unknown key **by name**
and never looks at its value. A present-but-`None` key was therefore not the same
thing as an absent one, even though most of these keys are named parameters of
the leaf `Group.add_gsplats` defaulting to `None` one level down. #1471 fixed that
for `labels` / `image_labels`; the rest of the family was still live, in three
different severities.

The loudest: `add_gsplats_from_data("g", data, lod_group=True,
additive_lod={"n_lods": 2}, partition=None)` — the idiomatic
`partition=maybe_partition` spelling, and the combination stock `gsplat lod
--recipe levels` output takes, its per-level stream ladders being on by default —
raised `Could not add gsplats 'child_0': Unknown node attribute 'partition'. Did
you mean 'absorption'?` **after** `add_gsplats_as_lod_group_impl` had already
created the wrapper, leaving `g` on disk as a childless `kind=lod` group that
survived `finalize()`: a scene the viewer loads and finds empty. The
route-dependence is what made it easy to miss — the same key was fine on
`lod_group=True` alone and on the bare flat route, and merely refused (nothing
written) on a flat ladder.

The merely-wrong: `colors=None` was refused on every route, as a raw `TypeError`
("got multiple values for keyword argument 'colors'") on the flat one and as the
misleading `Unknown node attribute 'colors'. Did you mean 'colormap'?` on the
other three. `truncation_radius=None` — a key this adder *injects* from
`result.truncation_radius` — suppressed that injection and then failed the
render-attr float conversion with `Truncation radius must be convertible to
float, got NoneType`.

The silent, and the worst of the three because nothing complained:
`colormap=None` was **accepted** and wrote a broken node. `validate_render_attrs`
guards its colormap check on `is not None`, so the `None` survives to
`compositing.sync_custom_colormap_attr`, which rewrites it to `'custom'` (a
`None` is not a str in `BUILTIN_COLORMAP_NAMES`) and writes no `colormap_lut`
beside it. Measured on uncoloured data: `colormap='custom'` where omitting the
key writes `colormap='gray'`. The viewer (`build-scene-graph.ts`) sees
`colormap === 'custom'`, cannot find the LUT, warns, and falls back to
**viridis** — so `colormap=maybe_colormap` silently rendered the node in viridis
instead of the intended gray. `demos/_interop_common.py` already hand-guards
`if colormap is not None:` before splatting into `add_gsplats_from_file`, which is
in-repo evidence that authors were working around this. `coverage_fraction=None`
was the same shape one attr over: a literal `coverage_fraction: null` selector
threshold on disk on the flat route, and on the multi-substitutive route the
`coverage_fraction must not be passed …` refusal for a caller who effectively
passed nothing.

The strip `strip_absent_label_kwargs` performed for the two label channels is now
`strip_absent_attr_kwargs` over `ABSENT_WHEN_NONE_ATTRS` — `labels`,
`image_labels`, `partition`, `colors`, `truncation_radius`, `colormap`,
`coverage_fraction` — and runs at the entry of `add_gsplats_from_data_impl`, of
`add_gsplats_from_file_impl`, and of `graft_gsplat_node`, above every route and
above every wrapper. A `None` for any of them is now indistinguishable from
omitting it, asserted against an omitted-key control store: the wrapper writes its
children, the data's own colours reach disk, the data's own truncation radius
applies (an explicit non-`None` radius is still a legitimate override and still
wins), the colormap is `'gray'`, and no null threshold is written. The set is
*derived* from `GATE_FORWARDED_LEAF_PARAMS`, the node-attrs gate's own exclusion
tuple, so the two cannot drift; it is deliberately wider, because the four keys
beyond that tuple must stay out of it — a non-`None` value of each still has to be
judged.

Every OTHER render attr is deliberately left refusing a `None`, because each
refuses loudly on its own and reading it as "absent" would only mask typos.
Measured, one call each: `opacity` / `gamma` / `intensity` / `absorption` answer
"must be convertible to float, got NoneType"; `blending_mode` "must be a string,
got NoneType"; `layer` / `visible` "must be a boolean, got NoneType" — their value
validators run unconditionally, unlike the colormap one. `scalars=None` refuses
too, for a different reason worth keeping straight: GSplats has no scalars channel
at all, so it is an `Unknown node attribute` regardless of value.

A `colors` key with a value, or a `centers` / `amplitudes` / `cholesky_factors`
key **at all**, is judged as what it actually is: a collision.
`add_gsplats_from_data_impl` passes all four positionally off the `GSplatData`
(`centers=result.centers`, `colors=result.colors`, …), and on a split route they
could not be sliced per child anyway — a coarser substitutive level holds merged
representatives and an additive rung holds a prefix, each with its own element
count, the same argument the `labels` refusal already makes. All four are now
refused at the entry of the adder, the file door and the graft door, before any
route is chosen and before anything is written, as a `ValueError` (the flat route
used to leak Python's raw `TypeError`, escaping a caller's `except ValueError`)
whose message names the collision and says where the value comes from, instead of
advising a switch to `colormap=` that would silently change what was asked for.
`colors` is asked first, then `centers`, `amplitudes`, `cholesky_factors`, so a
call passing several is answered deterministically.

Note the asymmetry, spelled out because it is easy to state wrongly: the refusal
tests for the KEY, not the value, so `amplitudes=None` and
`cholesky_factors=None` are refused too — those three are required positional
parameters of the leaf adder with no `None` default, so there is no "absent"
reading available for them, and `amplitudes=maybe_amps` is **not** a safe call
form. Only `colors` has one, because it alone has a `None` default at the leaf.

`centers` mattered most of the four: on the `from_data` routes nothing was ever
written for any of them, but at the graft door
`scene.add_gsplats_from_file("g", <nested partition store>, centers=…)` raised the
raw `TypeError` **and** left `g` behind as a childless `kind=partition` surviving
`finalize()`.

One verdict gets QUIETER rather than louder, and it is worth naming rather than
leaving to be discovered: `colors=None` used to raise (a `TypeError` on the flat
route, `Unknown node attribute 'colors'` on the others) and is now accepted and
ignored, with the `GSplatData`'s own colours reaching disk. That is the intended
reading of the rule, and it makes `colors` the one key in this family where
neither spelling does what a naive caller might expect — a `None` is silently
ignored, a value is refused. The refusal message for `colors` therefore says so
explicitly, since its own opening clause ("`colors` cannot be passed as a keyword
here") is not literally true of the one value it accepts.

Two precedence consequences, both deliberate and both now pinned with negative
controls. The collision refusal sits at the adder entry, so it outranks
everything below it — the `dim_order` spec validators, the rank guard, the
`coverage_fraction` refusal: a channel collision means the adder cannot build the
call it is about to make at all, so there is nothing below it worth reporting
first. And the pair runs once at the top of `add_gsplats_from_file_impl` rather
than being left to that method's two branches, because with it left to the
branches they disagreed: measured with a 4-column store into a 3-dimension scene
plus `colors=<arr>`, the matrix-shaped file answered the collision while the
partition file answered `Dimension mismatch for 'g': centers array has 4 columns
…` — one public method, one mistake, a verdict decided by a structural property of
the file. That is exactly what `from_io`'s own comment on the stored-column-count
check says must not happen.

While in there, the multi-substitutive `coverage_fraction must not be passed …`
refusal gained the `Could not add gsplats '<name>': ` prefix every sibling refusal
in that module applies by hand; it was the only one without it, so the same fault
was worded two ways depending on which check caught it.

Known residual, unchanged here: the LEAF adders keep both holes. `add_gsplats`,
`add_points`, `add_lines` and `add_mesh` all write `colormap='custom'` for
