`colormap=None` (measured on each — it is not a gsplats quirk), and the leaf
gsplats door likewise still writes a literal `coverage_fraction: null`. Only the
`add_gsplats_from_data` / `add_gsplats_from_file` / graft doors are fixed, since
those are the ones that forward `**attrs` through wrappers; the leaf half is the
same rule applied to four adders' own attrs handling, which is a wider change than
this one and is tracked in #1574. The two doors therefore disagree in the
meantime: `add_gsplats_from_data(colormap=None)` writes `'gray'` and the
`add_gsplats(colormap=None)` it delegates to writes `'custom'`. Also unchanged:
an invalid `partition` **spec value** still refuses from inside `child_0` (the
spec check lives one level below the gate, tracked in #1550), and a
right-length `labels` plus a decomposition kwarg on a grafted exempt leaf remains
the #1505-era residual it was.

#### The LOD method flags are named symmetrically: `--add-method` / `--subst-method` (#1498)

`gsplat lod` took `-m/--method` for the **additive** ordering but
`--substitutive-method` for the level-replacing reduction — one qualified, one
bare — so the unqualified name silently meant "additive" across every gsplat
surface. Meanwhile `luxar mesh lod` used that same bare `--method` for its
**decimation** algorithm. Two commands, one flag name, two different mechanisms,
and no way to tell from the name which one you were setting.

Both halves are now qualified and neither is bare: `-m/--add-method` and
`--subst-method`, with `--merge-add-method` / `--merge-subst-method` on the
`batch-fit` merge. `mesh lod`'s decimation knob becomes `--subst-method` (it
selects the substitutive reduction, as on `gsplat lod`, even though the
algorithms differ) and gives up its `-m` to the additive ordering, which claims
it when mesh gains its own ladder. Old spellings are refused with a
pointer naming the replacement and carrying your value, rather than silently
falling back to a flag's default and doing different work than you asked for.

Batch manifests written before the rename keep working. They persist these knobs
under dash-less keys, which looks like a vocabulary independent of the flags —
but the sbatch generator turns each stored key straight into a flag, so a
pre-rename manifest would have emitted `--substitutive-method` into its merge
command and every resumed Slurm merge job would have died on an unknown option.
The translation is applied at both ends: when a stored plan is read, and when the
merge command is emitted.

#### Mesh gets an additive ladder, and it is a reveal (#1503)

`add_mesh(additive_lod=…)` now writes `additive_<i>/` levels inside the leaf,
each holding one concentric shell of **faces**, innermost first — so a large
surface grows outward from its centre as it streams instead of appearing
all-at-once. Mesh was the one geometry type with no additive axis, refused on
the grounds that a prefix of an index buffer is a surface with *holes* rather
than a coarser one. That argument is true of an **arbitrary** order and only of
an arbitrary order: a spatially coherent reveal has a contiguous partial
surface at every prefix. So the refusal narrowed rather than lifted —
`MESH_ADDITIVE_METHODS` is `{"radial"}`, and `random` / `salience` / the two
element samplers are still refused with the holes argument, as are
`salience_kind` (a triangle has no independent energy) and `seed` (a reveal is
deterministic). `substitutive_lod=` remains the way to make a surface genuinely
coarser.

Two consequences fall out of the restriction, which is what marks it as the
right cut rather than a convenient one. **No energy stamps, by construction**:
`additive_level_stats` already suppresses `energy_fraction_cum` /
`reference_energy` for every reveal method, so the viewer's `1/e(k)` brightness
compensation — gated on the blending mode and never on geometry type — cannot
reach a mesh ladder and blow out its innermost shell before dimming it as the
surface completes. The adder's existing energy-stamp guard is unchanged and
still refuses *hand-supplied* `level_stats` / `lod_stats`; only its message
needed correcting. **Vertex duplication stays modest**: each level re-indexes
its own vertices (`luxar.mesh.split.split_mesh_by_faces`), and a connected patch
has one boundary curve, so the cost scales with that curve — measured at 4
levels, reveal vs a random order of the same faces: 1.66x vs 2.95x on a
288-face plane, 2.67x vs 3.31x on a 320-face icosphere, 1.69x vs 3.25x at 1280.

The ordering grows **best-first through face adjacency**, keyed on radius from
the reveal centre, rather than sorting by radius. That distinction is the
feature: a radius sort keeps a prefix connected on a convex blob and fails on a
closed surface — the isosurfaces and segmentation boundaries this geometry type
targets — because every face centroid sits at nearly the same radius, so the
order is decided by noise spread over the whole shell. A 1280-face icosphere
came out as 20 disconnected patches at both 25% and 50% loaded: lace over the
whole sphere, which is the failure mode the reveal-only restriction exists to
avoid. Growing through shared edges makes contiguity structural on any topology,
and it is what earns the duplication numbers above — under the radius sort the
same spheres measured 2.81x and 2.17x, close to random.

The reveal seeds **every** connected component up front rather than opening one
when the frontier runs dry. On a *stacked* mesh — several timepoints held in one
vertex array — the components ARE the timepoints, so draining one before opening
the next sequenced the ladder by time: two stacked spheres with `n_lods=4` gave
160/0, 160/0, 0/160, 0/160 faces per level, and a viewer parked on the last
timepoint rendered nothing until the final level landed. It also defeated the
machinery built to prevent exactly that, since `spatial_dims` already keeps the
stacked column out of the *score* and connectivity reintroduced the effect. One
heap over all components interleaves them by radius while each still grows only
through shared edges, so every level now carries faces at every timepoint and
every prefix is still exactly one patch per component (#1514).

The ladder's parent group carries the same DESCRIPTIVE attrs a flat mesh write
stamps — `ndim`, `has_normals` / `normal_dims`, `has_colors`, `has_scalars`,
`shading`, `double_sided`, `ordering`, and the colour/scalar window as a union
over the levels — not merely the totals and `n_additive_sublods`. The parent IS
the node (the `additive_<i>` subgroups are pruned from the scene graph), and a
reader fixes a mesh's vertex-attribute set once, from those flags. Found by
rendering an authored ladder rather than by reading the store: without
`has_normals` on the parent the levels' normals could never reach the GPU, and
the surface drew faceted and forced double-sided beside an identical unladdered
mesh that drew smooth.

The new writer `write_mesh_multi_lod` is the one place the four ladders differ
in kind: it writes **no union label CSR** and refuses a level carrying
`labels`. Its three siblings put one CSR on the parent spanning the levels,
which works because their elements are independent rows; a mesh level
re-indexes, so one source vertex maps to slots in several levels and that union
index space is ill-defined. `additive_lod=` alongside `labels` or
`image_labels` therefore degrades to a plain leaf with a `UserWarning` — the
data is kept, the ladder is not — and labels ride the `substitutive_lod=` and
`partition=` paths intact. `additive_lod=` also cannot yet be combined with
`substitutive_lod=` or `partition=`; both pairings are refused by name with the
mesh-side obstacle spelled out, where Points and Lines compose both.

The viewer half ships alongside this, as #1515: until it landed,
`data/scene-loader/loaders/loader-factory.ts` REFUSED a mesh node declaring
`n_additive_sublods > 1` — deliberately, so a store could not quietly render
only its coarsest shell — which is why the two are coupled and merge together.

#### `labels=` on a multi-child gsplats wrapper is refused, not stranded (#1471)

`add_gsplats_from_data("g", two_level_pyramid, lod_group=True, labels=[…8…])`
raised `Could not add gsplats 'child_0': labels: Labels length (8) must match
element count (2)` and left `g` in the store as a childless `kind=lod` group that
survived `finalize()` — the same shape as #1422 / #1437 / #1446, a wrapper missing
one door of its pre-split gate. Neither `labels` nor `image_labels` is a named
kwarg of `add_gsplats_from_data`: both travel in `**attrs` and rode into every
child through `child_attrs`, unsliced.

This one is not a hoist. Every substitutive level is its own set of merged
representative splats with its own count, so no single list has a per-element
correspondence to carry — slicing would pair entries with the wrong splats, and
passing it whole only ever fits whichever level happened to match. Both are now
REFUSED up front, naming the caller's node, with nothing written. Label a
single-level node instead (`lod_group=False` collapses to the finest level), or
build the `kind=lod` group yourself with `add_lod_group()` and give each
`add_gsplats()` child its own labels. An `additive_lod=` ladder is not an
alternative for gsplats: `write_gsplat_leaf_subtree` has no labels channel at all
(the ladder-union CSR labels of #1422 are Points/Lines only).

The refusal is LAST in the `_reject_before_wrapper` gate, and deliberately so:
unlike every other check there it has no flat-path counterpart — the flat path
ACCEPTS `labels` and validates it last of all, in the writer sweep — so ranking it
higher would let it outrank a fault the flat path reports first, silently changing
what #1446's parity assertions mean. A call passing both hears about `labels`
(the leaf adder's signature order).

Two more doors into the same strand, closed with the same template. An explicit
`labels=None` — the idiomatic `labels=maybe_labels` — was read correctly as "no
labels" by the gate, but the KEY stayed in `**attrs` and rode into `child_attrs`,
where `validate_render_attrs` rejects an unknown key by NAME without looking at
its value: any child taking the additive-ladder writer then raised `Unknown node
attribute 'labels'` with the wrapper already on disk, which stock `gsplat lod
--recipe levels` output triggers on its own (its per-level stream ladders are on
by default). Both keys are now dropped when None. And `graft_gsplat_node` — the
door for every non-matrix-shaped file (`--recipe tiles|overview|adaptive`,
`gsplat partition`, a `batch-fit merge` `kind=partition`) — builds its wrappers by
calling `add_lod_group` / `add_partition_group` directly and so never met the gate
at all. It had the worse of the two failure modes: a list whose length happened to
equal a part's own count raised nothing and was written onto EVERY part. It now
refuses up front unless the grafted subtree is exactly ONE LEAF WITH ONE
ADDITIVE SUB-LOD — the only shape that can actually carry labels. Leaf count, not
node type: a one-part `kind=partition` of a flat leaf still has an exact
per-element correspondence and keeps labelling normally. A one-part partition of
a LADDERED leaf is refused as well, but for its own reason and in its own words:
`write_gsplat_leaf_subtree` has no labels channel at all, so exempting it would
merely move the refusal down into `part_0` with the wrapper already on disk —
and since `--recipe tiles` carries a stream ladder by default, that is an
ordinary call. (Its answer therefore changes: from `Unknown node attribute
'labels'` blaming `part_0`, to a prefixed refusal naming the caller's node with
nothing written. The `additive_lod=` door is untouched — it writes once, so it
strands nothing, and still answers as before.) Multi-leaf cannot be sliced here at all, because a stored
`GSplatPartition` carries no per-part index arrays (unlike `add_gsplats(partition=…)`,
which slices the BSP `parts` it just computed); the only definable mapping would
be implicit leaf-concatenation order, which is the storage-order coupling this
gate exists to remove. `gsplat flatten` is the named remedy for exactly that
reason — it emits that order, so the list a caller would have had to guess is the
list that works on the flattened file.

Points and Lines were already correct for `labels`: their substitutive wrappers
check it against the SOURCE element count and hand it only to the finest child,
which carries the full element set. NOT so for `image_labels` — their pre-split
gates take no such parameter, so the same class of strand is live there
(measured: a 4-level Points wrapper with a half-length `image_labels` refuses from
inside `child_3` with all four children on disk). Tracked separately in #1491.

Scope: this closes the strand for `labels` and `image_labels` only. The same
shape for `colors=` (a raw `TypeError` and a childless wrapper, on both doors),
`partition=None` and `truncation_radius=None` is tracked in #1496 and deliberately
left alone here.

#### The one-flat-leaf graft exemption now checks LENGTH, not just shape (#1505)

`#1471` exempted exactly one shape from the graft door's labels gate
(`_reject_labels_on_a_grafted_wrapper`): a grafted subtree that resolves to a
single leaf with a single additive sub-LOD, because that leaf holds every
splat and so has an exact per-element correspondence for `labels` /
`image_labels`. What it did not check on that exempt branch was whether the
list was the right LENGTH for that leaf. Measured on `main`: grafting a
5-splat leaf under a one-part `kind=partition` with an 8-long `labels` sailed
straight through the exemption and refused one level down instead, from
inside `part_0`'s own leaf write — `Could not add gsplats 'part_0': labels:
Labels length (8) must match element count (5)` — with the childless
`kind=partition` named by the caller already on disk, surviving `finalize()`.
`image_labels` stranded identically (`Image labels length (8) must match
element count (5)`), and the flat control — the same three arrays via
`scene.add_gsplats(...)` — refused with the byte-identical message and wrote
nothing at all.

The exempt branch now validates whichever channel(s) are present, in the flat
writer's own order (`labels` then `image_labels`, `write_gsplats` steps 0d
then 0e), reusing the same validators the flat writer runs rather than
reimplementing either rule:
`core.group.compositing.validate_labels_before_split` for `labels`, and
`io._compiler.labels.image_labels.validate_image_labels_for_writing` for
`image_labels` (guarded on `is not None`, since that validator has no
built-in no-op). Both are caught as `(ValueError, TypeError)` and re-raised
with the same hand-applied `Could not add gsplats '<name>': ` prefix the
gate's other refusals already use, `from e` — `TypeError` matters here too,
since some malformed `image_labels` inputs (a non-integer dict key, a
one-shot iterable, a wrongly-typed entry) raise that rather than
`ValueError`, and the leaf adders' own `except (ValueError,
TypeError)` funnel converts it on the flat path, so skipping it here would
have made the two paths diverge in exception TYPE as well as message. The
leaf's own `n_splats` is unambiguous at this call site: `GSplatLeaf.n_splats`
sums over every additive sub-LOD, but the exempt branch is only ever reached
after the caller has already ruled out more than one, so the sum degenerates
to that one sub-LOD's own count.

Placement matters: the length check lives strictly below the multi-leaf and
laddered-leaf refusals, so a wrong-length channel on a shape that is ALSO
structurally disqualified (a multi-leaf graft, or a one-part partition of a
LADDERED leaf) still gets that shape's own structural message, not a length
one — those faults keep precedence, as everywhere else in this gate.

The verdict is now byte-identical to the flattened control's, both channels,
on every one-leaf shape the exemption covers — a direct one-part
`kind=partition`, a bare-leaf graft, and a nest that still resolves to a
single leaf two wrappers deep — for a single-fault call. The new check is the
first statement of `graft_gsplat_node`, so a call that ALSO trips an unrelated
fault (an unknown attr, a bad node name, a duplicate sibling name, NaN
centers) now hears the label fault here, where the flat path answers the
other fault first; both refuse and neither writes. That is not a new problem:
it is the same documented trade
`compositing.validate_points_channels_before_split` already names for "a NaN
position, an unknown attr", and `from_data._reject_before_wrapper` already
makes it on the `lod_group=` door, so the placement is unchanged — only this
note is new.

#### Layers panel interaction depth: right-click menus, type-to-filter, and shared panel motion

The Layers panel gains right-click context menus, built on a new shared
menu widget (`ui/overlay-widgets/context-menu.ts`) with full menu ARIA,
roving keyboard focus, one side-flyout submenu level, and viewport
containment in both position and height. Rows offer Solo (toggle-restore:
re-Solo brings back the exact pre-solo visibility set), frame-camera-on-layer,
per-layer reset to authored state, copy-path, and Colormap/Blending radio
submenus plus apply-appearance-to-all; the eye button and panel header carry
visibility-verb menus. Shift+F10 / the ContextMenu key open the same menus
from the keyboard.

Layer-heavy scenes (more than eight layers) get a live name filter above the
list, and the help overlay gains shortcut search — both on a shared
`.luxar-panel-filter` recipe whose keystrokes never leak to viewer shortcuts.
Every floating surface now enters with the dataset browser's transform-only
scale-settle pop (shared `.luxar-panel-pop`, glass-safe), and the dataset
dialog contains Tab within itself while open, releasing the trap on hide and
close.

The control rail also moves above the three left-docked panels rather than
below them: its fractional resting opacity makes the rail a single stacking
context, so a docked panel stacked over it buried the hover tooltips that
reach rightward across it. It still sits below the modal tier, so dialogs
keep dimming it.

#### Glass theme text clears WCAG AA over a bright scene

`frosted-glass` (the default theme) and `liquid-glass` both paint UI text over
a translucent dark panel tint, so the panel's actual on-screen color depends
on whatever scene the user has loaded behind it. Composited over the worst
case a scene can produce — pure white — frosted-glass's panel tint composited
to `#6b6d71`, giving primary/secondary/muted 4.88:1 / 3.73:1 / 2.56:1
(secondary and muted below WCAG AA's 4.5:1 floor for normal text, and muted
also below the 3:1 non-text floor for a meaning-bearing icon). Liquid-glass's
`::after` tint layer additionally carried a stray `opacity: 0.7` on top of its
own alpha, so its effective tint composited to `rgb(157)` and gave
primary/secondary/muted 2.61:1 / 2.19:1 / 1.73:1 — all three below AA, not
just secondary/muted.

Frosted-glass's panel tint (`background.secondary`) is raised from 0.65 to
0.75 alpha, and both themes' `text.secondary` (0.75 → 0.85) and `text.muted`
(0.5 → 0.72) alphas are raised alongside it — the panel tint and the text
alphas are independent knobs and both needed to move. Liquid-glass's panel
tint now lives in one place, a `--luxar-glass-tint` CSS custom property in
`liquid-glass.css` (raised 0.55 → 0.68), shared by the glass surface tint, the
recording indicator, the cursor-anchored context menus, the control-rail
tooltips, the control-rail first-run hint bubble, the recording confirmation
dialog, and the offline capture overlay (which all paint the same dark tint
for the same white-on-white — or, for the two modal surfaces, a too-light —
reason); the stray `opacity: 0.7`
multiplier on the `::after` layer is deleted so this alpha is the one
actually painted. Measured over the worst-case pure-white composite, both
themes now clear AA on all three text ranks: frosted-glass 6.8:1 / 5.8:1 /
4.7:1, liquid-glass 7.3:1 / 6.2:1 / 5.0:1 (primary / secondary / muted). The
dark-scene direction — already comfortable — is documented alongside these
numbers, though it isn't independently pinned: for white-ish text the
bright-scene case above is always the stricter one. A new unit test,
`tests/unit/themes/glass-contrast.test.ts`, pins these six numbers plus the
bright-scene rank ordering — and, for liquid-glass, the effective alpha
itself — so a future change to either theme's tint, text alphas, or a
reintroduced opacity multiplier cannot silently regress below AA again.

#### The viewer loads a mesh reveal ladder (#1515)

`data/scene-loader/loaders/loader-factory.ts` used to REFUSE a mesh node
declaring `n_additive_sublods > 1`. It now builds one — `MeshProgressiveLoader`
over the `additive_<i>` subgroups — so a mesh authored with `additive_lod=`
loads, and the surface grows as its levels arrive instead of appearing whole.

What changed is the claim, not the principle. Mesh still has no additive LEVEL
OF DETAIL and never will: a prefix of an arbitrary index buffer is a holed
surface, not a coarser one. What it has is a REVEAL, and the writer earns that
word — it admits only orderings whose every prefix is one connected patch, so
what streams in is a growing surface.

**The loader is half the size of its three siblings, and the reason is
structural.** They are per-slice streaming ladders whose sub-loaders answer a
range query, so a slice move genuinely changes what each level holds; that
forces a view-state equality check, a reset generation, a departure-store /
restore against the `SliceCache`, and a per-view concat. A mesh level is
whole-node resident, so the ladder is **view-independent**: only the level count
decides what is loaded, and the cull decides what is drawn exactly as for an
unladdered mesh. So there is no `SliceCache` entry (each sub-loader's decode IS
the cache, for the node's lifetime), and the concat memo keys on the level count
alone — which means a slice move returns the same object, and with it the same
loader-owned projection scratch. Had the ladder reset per view like its
siblings, every scrub frame would have reallocated and re-uploaded the whole
vertex buffer (#1245).

**Faces are offset, not copied.** Each level's indices are local to its own
vertex table, so the concat adds the running vertex count — the same value-adding
loop `concatenateLinesData` uses for segments, and the reason faces cannot go
through `concatRequiredField`. Getting this wrong does not crash: it draws a
plausible surface stitched from the wrong vertices, which is why the tests assert
index VALUES and that every index addresses a real vertex of the merged buffer.

**`committedEnergyFraction` exists and returns `null`, and both halves matter.**
Absent, `stampLadderComplete` takes the non-progressive branch and stamps a
half-revealed mesh as carrying all its energy; numeric, `energyCompensation`
brightens it by `1/e(k)` — right for a coarse prefix of an emissive cloud,
exactly wrong for a partial object at full brightness (`MESH_NODE_SPEC.md`
§9.1). Returning `null` makes the stamp ABSENT, which the display gate reads as
unstamped and answers with committed-count crossover. Three latches hold it: the
writer refuses the energy keys, the factory reads no energy table, and this
getter. The unit test asserts the consequence through `stampLadderComplete`
rather than the getter, with a control pinning the other branch.

Mesh also joins the refinement gate as a fourth phase (`queue-next.ts`,
`lifecycle/load-scene.ts`, `data/mesh/lod-refinement.ts`), and
`commit-mesh-geometry.ts` now calls `stampLadderComplete` — without it the
never-downgrade display gate reads a half-revealed mesh as complete.

Verified in a browser against a store written by the Python half, not only in
unit tests: a 4-level icosphere ladder streams to 4/4 (3,607 vertices / 5,120
faces), every face index addresses a real vertex, the energy stamp is absent on
the laddered node and `1` on an identical unladdered one beside it, and the two
render the same surface. That comparison is also what found a writer bug — the
ladder's parent group was missing the attrs that describe the surface, so the
laddered copy drew faceted and forced double-sided (fixed on the authoring side).

Two further defects turned up reviewing the branch, both silent. A laddered mesh
used as a lazy `kind=lod` LEVEL would have frozen at its first patch:
`load-lod-group-node.ts` passed no `hasMoreLODs` probe for mesh, on the grounds
that a surface could not have an additive ladder, and a lazy level is kept out of
the per-slice sweep precisely so the registry drives it — so nothing would have
advanced the reveal. And `MAX_MESH_VERTICES`, which bounds the pick vote-key
stride, was charged per LEVEL: four levels of 40M each pass their own preflight
while composing a 160M ladder whose vote keys alias. The cap is now charged
against the ladder's total, before a single subgroup is opened.

A third, found the same way: a reveal ladder is the first thing in the viewer
that makes a mesh's vertex and face counts GROW between commits, and
`rendering/mesh-geometry.ts` is built on the opposite assumption — its
allocate-once-and-`drawRange` design exists precisely because three frees a
replaced attribute's GL buffer from nowhere (not on replacement, and not on
dispose either: only what is still bound is freed). Sizing the buffers from the
committed prefix therefore rebound `position`, `color`, `normal`, `aScalar` and
the index on every level, orphaning the previous level's buffers for the session
— roughly 150 MB for a 4-level 2M-vertex surface with normals and colours, near a
gigabyte at 10M. They are now sized and dtype-chosen from the node's LIFETIME
totals, which `write_mesh_multi_lod` stamps on the ladder's parent, so the
allocate-once invariant is restored rather than weakened and the index dtype
cannot flip Uint16 → Uint32 mid-reveal on an already-drawn geometry. Unladdered
meshes pass no capacity and are byte-identical, zero-copy colour path included
(#1521).

Two more, from the closing review. The parent's declared totals are now
CROSS-CHECKED against what its levels declare before the ladder is built: those
totals are what the capacity above is taken from, the parent group has no
`vertices`/`faces` array for a preflight to check them against, and `n_faces`
has no cap of its own — so a store pairing a tiny `additive_0` with an enormous
parent `n_faces` would have had the first commit allocate an index buffer sized
to the declaration, failing as an uncatchable `RangeError` instead of a
node-scoped load error. `write_mesh_multi_lod` stamps those totals FROM the
levels, so a store it wrote passes untouched. And the monitor's Scene-Graph tab
now sees the mesh loader map: the tree already stamped `LOD x/N` on a laddered
mesh parent, but with no loader behind it every revealing mesh read `LOD –/N`,
"not streaming", for the whole reveal.

#### A mesh reveal ladder's byte budget no longer multiplies per level (#1517)

`preflightMesh` refuses a mesh node whose declared arrays would account for more
than `MESH_DECODE_BUDGET_BYTES` (512 MiB, stored bytes + decoded bytes + the
largest single chunk buffer), before a single chunk is fetched. The mesh reveal
ladder (#1515) builds one `MeshWholeNodeLoader` per `additive_<i>` subgroup and
runs that same preflight independently for each level — so a ladder's real
ceiling had quietly become `n_levels x budget` rather than the budget itself. A
surface written as four levels of ~300 MiB each passes every level's individual
gate while accounting for roughly 1.2 GiB in aggregate and reliably kills the
tab; the same surface written as a plain leaf is refused up front with an
actionable message.

`MeshProgressiveLoader` now charges the ladder's aggregate byte budget on its
own first load — the same point at which a leaf's own budget is enforced
(inside `MeshWholeNodeLoader.fetch()`), and still strictly before any level's
chunks are fetched. It awaits every level's metadata-only preflight in
parallel, sums the levels' accounted bytes, and refuses the ladder as a whole
when the total exceeds the same per-node ceiling. A mesh ladder concatenates
its levels into one committed buffer and keeps all of them resident, so
charging the sum once against one budget is the right quantity — and it is
exactly what turns N budgets back into one.

The first load is also the only place the check can live without losing
something. Run at ladder-construction time there is no node yet to attach a
failure record to, so a level's own transient preflight failure has nowhere
safe to go: propagating it loses the whole node with no retry entry, and
swallowing it lets that level's bytes go uncounted — defeating the check it
sits inside. At first `updateView` the refusal lands in the same contained
path a leaf's fetch already uses, so a level's rejection is recorded, retried
and reported like any other load failure, and the ladder is never latched as
admitted until every level has actually been accounted for.

The aggregate refusal is latched rather than re-derived, and that matters
because the new check is itself the hazard: a ladder it refuses never loads a
level, so its loaded-level count never grows, `hasMoreLODs` keeps reporting
`true`, and every slice scrub re-fires refinement on a node that can never
succeed — burning its failure budget and toasting "showing a partial surface"
for a surface of which not one triangle was ever committed. The sum is
deterministic once every level's metadata has opened, since nothing is left to
vary, so it is computed once, cached, rethrown as the same error object with no
further preflight calls, and read directly by `hasMoreLODs` so the node leaves
the refinement loop instead of being re-failed forever.

A level's own preflight rejection is not latched: it propagates as itself, and a
later attempt genuinely re-preflights, because the ladder is never marked
admitted until every level has been accounted for and a failed metadata open
caches nothing. A `dispose()` racing the gate — which reaches it as a rejection
from the torn-down sub-loaders — resolves quietly with the ladder's empty
payload instead of being recorded as a load failure. Gating on every level's
metadata before level 0 paints also has a cost on a store without consolidated
metadata (a serialized round of `.zarray`/`.zattrs` opens per level); for a
Luxar-written store, which always carries `.zmetadata`, that cost is close to
zero.

#### Cap numpy below 2.5 to keep the mypy gate green

numpy 2.5.0 rewrote its type stubs to use PEP 695 `type` statements (62 of them in
`numpy/__init__.pyi`). mypy checks third-party stubs against the configured target
(`python_version = "3.10"`), where a `type` statement is a syntax error — so a fresh
CI environment that resolved numpy 2.5.x aborted the type-check step ("Type statement
is only supported in Python 3.12 and greater") and turned `main` and every open PR red.
numpy is capped to `>=2.0,<2.5` (the newest clean stubs are 2.4.6) until the mypy target
moves to 3.12 or numpy and mypy reconcile.

#### One step quantum per dimension: a Step override, and wheel stepping on the sliders

The animation context menu itself was redesigned from a tall radio list
(three stacked sections, ~1000 px) into a compact chip card (~250×185 px):
each section is a micro-header row over one wrapping row of selectable
chips — FPS presets as mono numerals with the unit riding the header,
loop modes as three equal segments, step presets as ×-multiplier chips
with their computed values in tooltips and the active quantum as a muted
header readout. The FPS presets also widen at both ends: 1/2 (one frame
every 2 s, shown as a fraction) through 120 (the per-tick floor drops to
8 ms, reachable on ≥120 Hz displays).

Animating a continuous dimension used to ignore its authored step entirely —
the play button advanced by a tenth-of-the-range-per-second pace scaled by
FPS (the 4D hypersphere's W stepped 0.3 while `[`/`]` moved 0.5 and a slider
notch 0.03). The per-dimension right-click menu now has a Step section
alongside Speed and Loop Mode: Auto (the historical behavior), preset
multipliers of the dimension's base step with their computed values, and a
custom field. The chosen step drives both the animation tick and the `[`/`]`
keys, so the playback quantum is decoupled from the playback rate — FPS only
decides how often a step lands. On a discrete dimension the override is
quantized to the authored grid (one cell minimum), so a sub-cell quantum can
never freeze playback against the value snap, and the preset list offers only
whole-cell multipliers there.

The sliders also gain mouse-wheel stepping: one base step per notch
(the authored step, else 1% of the range), Shift for fine tenth-steps,
Ctrl for coarse ×10 jumps, and Ctrl+Shift for extra-fine hundredth-steps,
clamped at the range ends.
The wheel deliberately ignores the animation override — hand stepping stays
on the dimension's own grid — and slider dragging is unchanged. Wheel
stepping reads whichever scroll axis carries the motion, so Shift+wheel on
a standard mouse (which browsers deliver as a horizontal scroll) steps in
the scrolled direction instead of always stepping down; the Layers panel's
range sliders and the GUI number sliders (rendering controls) get the same
axis fix. The GUI number sliders also drop their inverted modifier
convention (Shift used to mean coarse there): relative to their
1/10th-step base, Shift is now finer, Ctrl coarse, Ctrl+Shift finest —
matching every other slider, and they stop the event so the new coarse
tier no longer yanks the camera FOV on its way to the window-level
Ctrl+wheel zoom. And a discrete dimension's value snap is now
range-aware, so an off-grid range end can no longer snap the playhead
outside the data, and the t+1 prefetch predicts exactly the snapped value
a loop wrap lands on.

#### A mesh reveal ladder's vertex buffers now track the committed prefix (#1522)

`#1521` sized a mesh's `position`/`color`/`normal`/`aScalar`/index buffers from the
node's LIFETIME totals rather than the committed prefix, so a reveal ladder's
levels write INTO the same capacity-sized buffers instead of rebinding (and
orphaning) them on every level. That capacity change left every one of those
vertex attributes needing an in-place UPDATE path of its own, and two of them
did not get one.

**`color` first.** Its guard kept comparing counts — and once the buffer is
bound at the node's full capacity, every level of a ladder binds at that SAME
count, so the guard could never tell "just installed" apart from "still holding
an earlier level's prefix". Every vertex a later level revealed kept the
zero-filled slot it was born with, which zeroes alpha for a padded RGB or any
RGBA mesh — invisible, not merely wrong-coloured, since `vAlpha` is a mesh's
entire coverage term — and leaves a `float32` RGB mesh black-but-opaque.

**`normal`/`aScalar` have the identical bug.** `replaceVertexAttribute`
gated its in-place copy on `existing.array !== data`, comparing the BOUND
buffer's identity against the caller's array — but once that buffer is a
capacity-sized copy `atCapacity` made at the first rebind, it is never
identity-equal to the caller's array again, including on the very level that
produced it. So a laddered mesh with normals or scalars re-uploaded the ENTIRE
capacity buffer (`V·12` bytes for normals, `V·4` for scalars) on every slice
move, with no update ranges, at every level — real bandwidth at the 2^27-vertex
cap, not merely a missed optimization.

Both are fixed the same way now: `isAttributeCurrent`/`stampAttributeCurrency`
track currency by the SOURCE array's own identity plus the committed vertex
count, stamped on `geometry.userData`, instead of comparing against the bound
buffer. `color`, `normal` and `aScalar` share one helper rather than three
near-copies of the same two lines. The in-place writes are also now bounded to
the prefix actually rewritten via `clearUpdateRanges`/`addUpdateRange`, mirroring
`applyMeshIndices` — before, both `color`'s pad-loop write and `normal`/`aScalar`'s
copy dirtied the WHOLE capacity buffer on the classic WebGL backend, which
honours update ranges. A shared `padRgbIntoRgba` helper replaces the RGB→RGBA pad
loop that used to live twice (once per fresh-buffer build, once per in-place
refresh), so the `uint8`/`uint16` opaque-alpha constant cannot diverge between
them.

**A second, unrelated defect surfaced the same way: `position` could go stale
across an aborted ladder commit.** `updateMeshGeometry`'s position upload is
gated on `positionChanged || keyChanged`, both derived from the projection's
`displayDims` key — but neither one can see a LEVEL change. A superseded commit
(an ordinary scrub landing mid-fetch) lets `projectMeshTo3D` stamp the
loader-owned scratch's `displayDimsKey` and memoize the level's data without the
geometry ever receiving it; the next sweep then re-projects the same memoized
level with `positionChanged === false` and an unchanged key, while the index and
draw range advance anyway. Every vertex that level revealed kept the zero fill
`atCapacity` gave it, so the newly revealed triangles drew as a fan collapsed at
the display-space origin — and stayed wrong until the next `displayDims` change.
Fixed the same way `keyChanged` repairs a key gap: `geometry.userData.
meshUploadedVertexCount`, stamped only where the upload actually runs, adds a
`countChanged` term to the gate so a commit whose prefix the geometry never
uploaded gets uploaded on the very next sweep.

Belt-and-braces alongside these: the default-white colour rebind now clears the
authored-colour currency stamps instead of leaving them stale (not reachable
today — colour presence is a per-node constant — but a stale stamp there could
otherwise make a later authored commit a permanent no-op).

#### FlyWire connectome: luminous neurons, ACES tone mapping, and the exception retired (#1459)

`demo_flywire_connectome` now bakes the hand-tuned neuron appearance — every
`Neurons — …` layer at `opacity=0.79` with `blending_mode="luminous"` (was 0.95 and
the default `additive`) — and moves the scene from `Neutral` to the house `ACES`.
That retires the one `Neutral` exception that was written as a *condition* rather
than a reason — its comment said to move only alongside a re-tuned exposure and an
actual A/B render, and this is that render. The remaining `Neutral` pins stand on
their own standing rationale and are untouched: a categorical or otherwise exact
colour encoding that ACES's hue shift would blur (`demo_biodiversity_planetary_scale`,
`demo_nd_transforms`, `demo_ocean_currents_earth`, the `build_interop_scene` default)
and `demo_gsplats_3d_tribolium_embryo`'s verified pairing with `exposure=1.97`.
ACES costs about half a stop on this scene: captured
through the gallery harness at the shipped -1.0 stops the still goes from 1.9% of its
lit pixels blown (`Neutral`) to 5.4%, just past the harness's own 5% clip guard. So
the demo's gallery exposure override moves to -1.5 stops, where the still is back to
0.9% blown with a 0.50 histogram spread — the `Neutral` still's profile — and keeps
its structure and its super-class palette.

The connections keep `opacity=0.08`. #1459 asked for 0.79 on those layers too, to
match the neurons, and the render is what refused it: 300 000 luminous segments at
0.79 blow 78% of the frame's lit pixels to white and the fly brain becomes a
featureless blob — exactly the wash the old comment described. It is not an exposure
problem: given 2.5 extra stops of headroom (the harness's own auto-exposure lands at
-3.45 rather than -0.91) 17% is still blown and the blue optic lobes, orange central
brain and green sensory clusters have all gone achromatic; even 0.24 pales the optic
lobes. A brighter connective glow needs fewer edges or a per-layer intensity
rebalance, not a slider.

#### The node-attrs gate now runs once, at the adder entry, ahead of every split path

`add_points` / `add_lines` forward the caller's `**attrs` unchanged into three
structurally different split paths — `substitutive_lod=` (synthesised gsplat
coarse levels under a `kind=lod` group), `partition=` (a `kind=partition`
group of BSP parts), and `additive_lod=` (a progressive `additive_<i>`
ladder) — before ever reaching the flat writer's own node-attrs validator
(`validate_render_attrs`). All three paths could strand bad output or report
the wrong verdict. A bad node attr on `substitutive_lod=` — e.g.
`amplitude_range=`, which `GSPLATS_RESERVED_ATTRS` reserves but
`POINTS_RESERVED_ATTRS`/`LINES_RESERVED_ATTRS` do not — was refused only from
inside the synthesised gsplat `child_0`; by then the `kind=lod` wrapper group
itself was already on disk, childless (`child_0` is the FIRST coarse level,
so nothing else had been written yet). The same was true of `partition=`:
`add_points("p", pos, partition={"max_elements": 100}, blending="max")`
raised the right message but left a childless `kind=partition` node for
`"p"` on disk, and that node survived `finalize()`. `additive_lod=` was
worse: the multi-LOD writer calls the validator with no reserved-attrs set at
all, so a genuinely points/lines-RESERVED key like `ordering=` or
`max_radius=`/`max_width=` was reported as an *unknown attribute* instead of
the correct #1221 *reserved* verdict (the `LuxarZarrCompiler(ordering_method=...)`
hint fires only for `ordering=`) — nothing was written either way; and
a caller-supplied `position_bounds=` alongside `additive_lod=` didn't raise
at all (it isn't reserved from the multi-LOD writer's point of view) — real
ladder data was written and the writer's own stamp clobbered, and
`finalize()` then failed later with an unrelated `ValueError: Could not
finalize Zarr store: list indices must be integers or slices, not str`.

Both adders now run the flat writer's own gate once, on the un-split caller
attrs, at the adder entry — above every structural branch, so nothing is
written before it runs. The split paths now refuse byte-identically to the
flat path (same message, same exception type, same reserved-vs-unknown
verdict) with nothing written; the flat path itself simply validates twice
(idempotent — the function only inspects `attrs`), which also means a
multi-fault flat call now reports the attrs fault where it used to report an
`extend_to_all` fault (attrs now validate first, matching the writer's own
step 0a). This mirrors the #1446 dimension-count gate, which already sits at
this same adder-entry point; the nearest precedent for the validator itself
is mesh's own `_maybe_add_mesh_substitutive_lod` (`mesh.py:401-403`), the
substitutive branch's dispatcher, which already calls it before ever handing
off to the wrapper. It does **not** mirror the
#1437 channel gate, which deliberately stays at the top of each wrapper
(per-element channels are only sliceable once a split has been decided) — the
new attrs gate, sitting above the wrapper, now outranks it, matching the flat
writer's own order (`validate_render_attrs` before the channel sweep). A
compositing attr (`opacity=`, `blending_mode=`) was already refused before
this fix, with nothing written, via a separate wrapper-level check; the fix
also makes those compositing-value refusals byte-identical to the flat
message, which they were not before. Mesh and GSplats did not gain this
gate here — their own `partition=` paths still stranded a childless
`kind=partition` node; #1534 closes that, see the entry below.

#### The mesh index-buffer reuse guard now survives WebGPU's own in-place substitution

`applyMeshIndices` allocates a mesh node's index buffer once, at its full
face-count capacity, and draws the visible prefix via `setDrawRange` — because
three never frees an index buffer when `geometry.index` is *replaced*
(`WebGLAttributes.remove()` only runs on geometry disposal), so a per-epoch
`setIndex` would orphan one GPU buffer per slice move. Reuse depended on a
dtype check comparing the existing buffer's array type against whatever
`createMeshIndexAttribute` would allocate for the node — but on the native
WebGPU backend, `WebGPUAttributeUtils.createAttribute` rewrites any non-normalized
Uint16Array (or Uint8Array) index attribute to Uint32Array IN PLACE the first
time it uploads it, mutating `bufferAttribute.array` directly. After the first
WebGPU upload of any mesh under 65,536 vertices, the existing buffer's array was
already a Uint32Array even though it was allocated as a Uint16Array, so the
"matches what I would allocate" comparison failed on every subsequent epoch —
forcing a `setIndex` (and the leak this function exists to prevent) on every
slice move, on the native WebGPU backend only (the WebGL2 fallback keeps the
buffer at its allocated width, so its reuse never broke).

The guard now asks the right question: can the existing buffer *carry* the
indices about to be written, not whether it is the exact dtype the node would
be allocated fresh. A Uint32Array always can; a Uint16Array can only when the
node itself fits under 65,536 vertices. The genuine widening direction — a
node whose existing buffer is a Uint16Array but which now needs 32-bit indices
— still falls through to `setIndex` and rebinds, since a Uint16Array cannot
represent an index past 65,535 no matter what mutated it.

#### Mesh and GSplats now run the node-attrs gate at the adder entry too

`add_mesh(..., partition={...}, blending="max")` and `add_gsplats(..., partition={...},
blending="max")` raised the right message but still left a childless
`kind=partition` node on disk, and that node survived `finalize()` — the same
stranding #1529 fixed for Points/Lines, one geometry type over. Neither adder
validated the caller's node attrs before dispatching into its `partition=`
wrapper: the bad attr was only caught from inside the first synthesised part
(`part_0`), by which point `add_partition_group` had already created the
wrapper group.

Mesh's `substitutive_lod=` branch already ran the same validator
(`validate_render_attrs`, with the correct `MESH_RESERVED_ATTRS` set) before
this fix, so it never stranded anything — but it ran the check *after*
resolving its own `extend_to_all`, the opposite of the order Points/Lines
settled on in #1529. Mesh's `additive_lod=` reveal ladder had no attrs check
of its own at all: it fell straight through to the multi-LOD writer's
unreserved validator, matching the shape of the #1529 additive bug with BOTH
of its symptoms, not just the milder one. A genuinely mesh-reserved key that
is not also a generically-allowed one (`ordering=`) came back as an *unknown
attribute* instead of the correct *reserved* verdict — still refused, nothing
written. `position_bounds=` — reserved for mesh, but also a generically
allowed node attr — didn't raise at all: a real reveal ladder was written,
and the returned `Mesh` node's own construction then re-persisted the
caller's stale `position_bounds` value right back over the writer's own
correct stamp, breaking `finalize()` later with an unrelated `ValueError`
far from the actual cause — byte-for-byte the symptom this same changelog
entry's #1529 predecessor documented for Points/Lines.

Both adders now run `validate_render_attrs` once, on the un-split caller
attrs, at the top of the adder — above every structural branch (`partition=`
for both; `substitutive_lod=` and `additive_lod=` for Mesh too) and above
`extend_to_all` resolution, so nothing is written before it runs and every
split path refuses byte-identically to the flat one. GSplats' only structural
door on `add_gsplats` is `partition=`; its `lod_group=`/`additive_lod=` doors
live on the separate `add_gsplats_from_data` adder and carried the same
`lod_group=` stranding one level up (a bad attr was refused correctly, but
only from inside `child_0`, after `add_lod_group` had already created the
`kind=lod` wrapper) — now closed the same way, before that wrapper is built.
`additive_lod=` on that adder needed no change: its writer
(`write_gsplat_leaf_subtree`) already ran `validate_render_attrs` with the
correct `GSPLATS_RESERVED_ATTRS` before creating any group.

Unlike the four leaf adders, the `lod_group=` gate on `add_gsplats_from_data`
cannot hand its caller's `**attrs` to `validate_render_attrs` unfiltered:
`labels` / `image_labels` are named parameters of the LEAF `Group.add_gsplats`
but not of `add_gsplats_from_data_impl`, so on this one door they arrive inside
`**attrs` and need their own dedicated (and more informative) refusal instead
of being misreported as an unknown attribute — see #1471/#1504. `partition`
is excluded for the same reason and sits in the exact same position: a
leaf-only named parameter, forwarded structurally into each substitutive
child, where it drives that child's own BSP split. So
`add_gsplats_from_data(..., lod_group=<...>, partition={"max_elements": N})`
keeps working and still builds a partitioned child per level; the gate only
sees the keys that genuinely belong to it.

Some verdicts on this door genuinely change, and are called out here rather
than left implicit: a bad attr NAME/reserved-KEY collision on `lod_group=` now
refuses immediately, naming the caller's own node, before the `kind=lod`
wrapper is created — previously the same fault fired from inside `child_0`,
after the wrapper was already on disk (and it survived `finalize()`). And
because this gate's value validators (colormap, opacity, ...) now run on this
door too, a bad `colormap`/`opacity` VALUE outranks the dedicated
`labels`/`image_labels` refusal below it — matching the flat path's own
precedence between its attrs gate and its labels handling.

What this closes on that door is the stranding for every attr key OTHER than
the three excluded ones — `labels`/`image_labels` were closed earlier by #1471
and #1504, and a valid `partition=` never stranded in the first place. Two
neighbours stay open and are worth naming rather than implying away. A
present-but-conflicting `colors=` or `truncation_radius=None` in the same
`**attrs` is #1496, whose design question — what `colors=` should MEAN on a path
that already forwards the data's own colours — this gate leaves untouched (#1496
went on to answer it: an explicit `colors=None` now means "absent" and is
accepted, so do not read the gate as refusing it). And an invalid partition SPEC, as
opposed to an unknown attr key — `partition="nonsense"`, `partition={"max_
elements": 0}` — is still refused only from inside `child_0`, leaving the
childless `kind=lod` wrapper on disk: the spec check lives in the leaf adder,
which is one level below this gate, so hoisting it is a separate change.

#### Two shapes of doc drift: a CLI flag that never existed, and mesh's reveal ladder (#1536)

`docs/guides/user/CLI_REFERENCE.md` told readers to run `luxar mesh lod -o out`,
but the command's output is a positional argument, not a `-o` option — copying
the example got Click's "No such option: -o". A new drift-guard test now
checks every option spelling named INLINE within a per-command section of the
CLI reference against the live Typer app's declared options — a leaf section
strictly, a group section against the union of its subcommands' — not just the
command paths the existing guard already covered. A fenced example block's
catalog lines are a separate, deliberately unchecked surface: they legitimately
cross-reference another command's flags, and the guard does not follow them.

Several other passages — the mesh spec, this package's mesh README, the
front-page README, the architecture concept doc, `CHANGELOG.md`, `CLAUDE.md`,
the viewer's `data/README.md`, and the Zarr writer/protocol docstrings — still
asserted mesh has no additive ladder at all, or no progressive loading, which
stopped being true once mesh gained a *reveal* ladder
(`add_mesh(additive_lod={"method": "radial"})`, #1503/#1515): a growing
surface, not a coarsening one, so a prefix of the index buffer stays valid the
way a prefix of an arbitrarily-ordered one never could. Each passage is
corrected to say a reveal ladder exists and substitutive LOD (decimation)
ships, while an additive ladder over an *arbitrary* order and `volumetric`
blending are still refused — the distinction, and the reason for it, are
unchanged.

#### Camera fitting follows projected scene bounds

Perspective and orthographic auto-framing now size the opening view from the
scene's screen-plane extent rather than whichever bounding-box axis is longest.
View-axis-elongated datasets therefore open at the intended level of detail, and
degenerate depth-aligned lines receive a safe fallback extent instead of placing
the camera on the geometry. This supersedes the closing "not fixed here" note in
the unreleased #1410 entry. Under the default screen-area ladder, some ordinary
window shapes may consequently open one rung coarser than before. The fit still
uses the axis-aligned bounds; sparse clouds with outlying depth tails may need an
authored percentile-based camera and an ``overview`` LOD topology.

#### An invalid `partition=` spec on the gsplats wrapper doors no longer strands a wrapper

`add_gsplats_from_data(..., lod_group=True, partition="nonsense")` raised
`Could not add gsplats 'child_0': partition must be None, True, or dict; got
str` and left `g` on disk as a childless `kind=lod` group that survived
`finalize()` — so it reached the viewer. The same held for `partition=3`,
`partition={"max_elements": 0}` and `partition={"rule": "bogus"}`: the two
faults #1529/#1534 closed elsewhere, a stranded wrapper and a message blaming
an internal `child_0` for the caller's own kwarg.

#1534 hoisted `validate_render_attrs` into the pre-wrapper gate on this door,
which closed the bad-attr-KEY half. The spec half stayed open because
`partition` is one of the three keys that gate deliberately excludes — it is a
named parameter of the leaf adder and must ride through to drive each child's
BSP split — so its VALUE was still judged one level down, inside `child_0`,
after `add_lod_group` had created the group. The fix is not a wider exclusion:
excluding the key is exactly what lets a valid spec through.

The leaf adders' partition-spec validation is now one function,
`core/group/partition.py::resolve_partition_spec`, replacing four byte-identical
inline copies (Points, Lines, GSplats, and Mesh's private
`_resolve_mesh_partition`). The gsplats `lod_group=` gate calls it in the slot
right after the node-attrs gate, for its verdict alone. Messages and exception
types are unchanged and now byte-identical to the flat `add_gsplats(...,
partition=<same bad value>)` call, prefix included, with nothing written on a
refusal. Precedence parity with the flat path is pinned in both directions now
— the node-attrs gate above the check still wins, the labels refusal below it
still loses — because the slot, not the check, is the design claim here.

The GRAFT door had the identical bug and is closed the same way.
`scene.add_gsplats_from_file("g", <nested .gsplats.zarr>, partition="nonsense")`
answered `Could not add gsplats 'part_0': …` and left the `kind=partition`
wrapper on disk through `finalize()`, because `graft_gsplat_node` builds its
wrapper from the stored tree before the first leaf write; one call in the slot
that already holds that door's `strip_absent_attr_kwargs` /
`reject_data_owned_channels` pair fixes it, with the same message parity.

Two values are deliberately NOT judged, at either door, because the leaf does
not judge them either. `partition=False` is vocabulary, not a bad spec — it is
the explicit no-partition bypass, and the only way to opt a `lod_group=` ladder
out of a compiler-level `auto_partition_max_elements` (which would drop
`coverage_fraction` and break the LOD selector). And below 2 spatial dimensions
the leaf DROPS the request with a warning before it ever resolves the spec, so a
1-dimension scene accepts even a nonsense spec on the flat path; the gates skip
silently there rather than emit a second warning.

A VALID-spec strand of the same shape is closed alongside it, at both doors.
`add_gsplats_from_data(..., additive_lod={…}, partition={"max_elements": 2})`
answered `Could not add gsplats 'child_0': Unknown node attribute 'partition'`
and stranded the `kind=lod` wrapper, because the multi-LOD child writer has no
`partition` parameter. `add_gsplats_from_file("g", <partition of laddered
leaves>, partition={"max_elements": 4})` did the same from inside `part_0`,
leaving a childless `kind=partition` — and that is the most commonly produced
store shape in the whole gsplat pipeline, since `gsplat lod --recipe
tiles|overview|adaptive` and `batch-fit merge --recipe stream` all emit it with
stream ladders on by default. Both are now refused up front, the data door above
its route branch so the two routes say the same thing, the file door in the slot
that already holds its other pre-wrapper gates. Partitioning a ladder is a
feature, not a wording fix.

The refusal names the STRUCTURE and gives each door its own remedy, through one
shared reason builder — the convention `labels_on_wrapper_reason` /
`GRAFT_REMEDY` already keep in the same module. On the `additive_lod=` door it
still says "drop one of the two"; on the file door it names the stored ladder and
points at `gsplat flatten`, because there is no `additive_lod=` in an
`add_gsplats_from_file` call and nothing there to drop.

`partition=False` on those same routes stranded the identical wrappers, from
`Unknown node attribute 'partition'` rather than from a conflict. It is now
DELETED instead, and the calls succeed: `False` is the no-partition bypass, and
writing no partition is exactly what the multi-LOD writer does. The deletion is
scoped to that destination only — `resolve_auto_partition` reads `user_partition
is False` to bypass a compiler-level `auto_partition_max_elements`, so stripping
the key at the adder entry (the way an explicit `None` is stripped, #1496) would
silently re-enable auto-partitioning everywhere else. A multi-substitutive call
keeps the key and hands it to each child, where the same question is asked per
level.

The file door's half of that gate reads the ladder off the STORE, so it also has
to honour the kwarg that empties the store's ladder: an `additive_lod=False` in
the same call is the documented "collapse the ladder" spelling, and
`resolve_additive_axis_gsplats` flattens every level to a single sub-LOD before
the data door asks the same question. Both `add_gsplats_from_file("g", <laddered
leaf>, partition={"max_elements": 4}, additive_lod=False)` and its nested
`kind=partition` twin split into real parts, so the gate skips that spelling
rather than refusing them. Only that spelling: telling a `{"n_lods": 1,
"recompute": True}` that resolves to one rung apart from a `{"n_lods": 2}` needs
the resolved rung count instead of the spec — the same missing query as the graft
residual below.

`core/group/partition.py::is_requested` is the fifth thing this PR de-duplicates:
the `partition is None or partition is False` predicate the new gates need, which
`adders/mesh.py::_requested` already spelled (with the `partition=0` / `0 ==
False` hazard it documents). One predicate rather than two more copies, in a
change whose thesis is that the copies were the bug.

Known and NOT closed: the ladder conflict is checked ABOVE the route branch, so
it outranks the node-attrs gate, the `dim_order` spec check and the
colours/colormap exclusion, where the same call without `additive_lod=` reports
the other fault. Every combination still refuses with an empty store, so only the
naming differs. It is a deliberate trade — the two routes must answer
identically, and only one of them has a pre-wrapper gate to sit in — stated in
the helper's docstring and pinned by
`TestTheLadderConflictOutranksTheOtherPreWrapperFaults`.

Also not closed: one graft shape still strands. The graft gate reads the ladder
off the STORE (`iter_leaves`), so an unladdered nested file grafted with
`partition=` *and* `additive_lod=` — where the ladder is built per part, after
the wrapper — is still refused from inside `part_0` with the childless
`kind=partition` left behind. Closing it needs the resolved rung count, not the
kwarg's presence: `additive_lod={"n_lods": 1}` resolves to a single rung and
takes the flat route, where `partition=` is perfectly legitimate, so a
presence-only check would refuse a valid call. That is a design question of its
own rather than another line in this slot.

The sibling `substitutive_lod=` doors on Points, Lines and Mesh were checked
for the same shape and do not have it: all three refuse `partition=` together
with `substitutive_lod=` outright ("partition-of-substitutive is not
implemented"), before any wrapper exists, so an invalid spec can never be
forwarded into a ladder child there. They do not agree on the `False` spelling —
`add_points`/`add_lines` guard on `substitutive_lod is not None`, so
`substitutive_lod=False` beside a `partition=` is refused there and accepted on
Mesh, which uses the shared `is_requested`. Pre-existing, left alone here rather
than changed as a drive-by: adopting the shared predicate at those two sites
relaxes a user-facing refusal and wants its own tests. That survey covered the
gsplats `lod_group=`/graft doors and those three; it is not a claim about every
adder kwarg that rides into a child.

#### Partitions carry, keep, and transform their split planes

A `kind=partition` gsplat node can record the split planes of the decomposition that produced its parts (`bsp_tree`), and the viewer traverses them to order parts back-to-front exactly — correct for any camera pose, including inside the volume. Without that record it falls back to sorting parts by their content centroid, which is not a valid painter's order: it flips discretely as the camera moves, so an order-dependent blending mode (`normal` or `volumetric`) pops at the seams between parts on every orbit.

Three separate defects meant that record was usually missing. **It was never produced by a tiled fit:** the content planner has always *been* a recursive BSP, but it discarded its own split planes and kept only the flat box list, so `fit --tiling content|uniform` and every `batch-fit` merge emitted a partition that could not say how its parts stacked up. **It was silently dropped on rebuild:** `GSplatPartition.bsp_tree` defaults to `None` and both generic tree-rebuild helpers omitted the field, so a `tiles`/`adaptive` dataset lost exact ordering the moment it passed through `gsplat transform` — including for intensity-only transforms that move no centers at all — or through `gsplat additive`, whose documented contract is that partition parts keep their shape. **And nothing mapped it when centers moved:** `split` is a coordinate in the centers' own space, so preserving a tree verbatim across a geometry transform would have been worse than dropping it, since a stale plane still yields a plausible-looking part order and the ordering would degrade with no sign that anything was wrong.

All three are fixed. The planner keeps its recursion and hands it to the fitted partition; the tiled, content-tiled and batch-merge paths all carry it through; and `gsplat transform` now maps the planes through the same affine it applies to the centers — translations, per-axis scales and quarter-turn rotations map exactly (a reflection also swaps each node's halves), while an arbitrary rotation shears the cells out of axis-alignment, which the format cannot express, so that tree is dropped and the ordering downgrade is announced rather than left to be discovered in the viewer.

The subtle part throughout is numbering. Every tiled producer plans more regions than it writes — a box whose budget rounds to zero, a tile that fits no splats, a part emptied by a cull, a batch slot empty at every timepoint — and parts are numbered over the *survivors*. A tree still labelled with pre-drop indices would point at the wrong parts while remaining a perfectly valid permutation, so a single shared helper prunes and renumbers leaves against the surviving set, and a tree that cannot be reconciled with the parts is discarded rather than half-applied.

Uniform tiling is the one approximate case, and is documented as such: its apodized tiles keep their overlap band, so neighbouring parts genuinely share space and no exact order exists. The cuts are placed at the midplane of each shared band, which confines any misordering to that band instead of letting whole tiles swap.

On the viewer side, the within-group comparator no longer mixes BSP ranks with centroid depth. That mix is non-transitive whenever a stored tree names only some of a wrapper's parts, and `Array.sort` may then return an order satisfying neither key; the group now falls back to depth wholesale, which is approximate but well defined.

#### An integer `--seeds` is a whole-volume budget a tiled fit divides

A default `luxar gsplat cal` reports a whole-volume K*, and the documented
pipeline is `cal` → `fit --seeds K*`. But when tiling engaged — `--tiling auto`
on a large stack, an explicit `--tiling uniform`, a `--tile k/M` worker, or a
uniform-mode `batch-fit` task — the same `--seeds K` was handed to *every* tile,
so the realized total was roughly K × n_tiles. A 108×1352×532 stack fitted with
`--seeds 256000` auto-tiled into 21 tiles and produced 2,449,962 splats in
17.4 min instead of ~256,000 in 1.9 min, with nothing to warn that the number
asked for was not the number being fitted.

An integer `--seeds K` is now read as a whole-volume budget: a fit split into N
tiles seeds each tile with `ceil(K / N)` — divided across the tiles instead of
multiplied by them — and prints the budget, the per-tile count and the tile
count as it does so. That notice is emitted wherever the tile count is first
known, so it survives the paths that capture worker output: the parent of a
parallel `-j` run prints it, and `batch-fit run` / `submit` print it at plan time
(visible under `--dry-run`). It is a budget, not an exact count: the split is
equal per non-empty tile rather than occupancy-weighted, so uneven grids can
misallocate the budget between busy and barely occupied tiles, and a K smaller
than the non-empty tile count gives one seed per tile. A
non-positive `--seeds` is left untouched so the fitter still rejects it, as it
does on the whole-volume path.

The division happens once, in the single-tile worker and the in-process
sequential tiled path, so a parallel `-j` run (whose workers each re-enter
`fit --tile i/M`) and a `batch-fit` task (likewise a `--tile k/M` invocation, per
(t, c) volume) inherit it without double-dividing. A *ratio* `--seeds` (a float
in `(0, 1]`) is left untouched: a ratio is a fraction of whatever voxels it is
applied to, so it already means the same density per tile as whole-volume.
`--tiling content` is unaffected — it already ignores `--seeds` and sizes its
boxes from the density plan. The library entry points `fit_tiled` / `fit_tile`
keep their per-tile `seeds` semantics, now documented as such.

One caveat comes with it: `cal --auto-region` calibrates on a content-rich
sub-volume, so *its* K* is region-scoped rather than whole-volume and does not
belong on `--seeds`. `cal` now says so where it matters — the
`★ Recommended K*` headline is marked region-scoped whenever a real crop was
used, pointing at `fit --tiling content --cal` (the `splat_density` transfer)
instead of `--seeds`. A volume small enough that the region short-circuits to
the whole array is correctly left unflagged. The tutorial documents both, plus
the rough uniform-tiling alternative of scaling a region-scoped K* by the tile
count.

#### LOD selection switches to screen-area occupancy (`selector: "screen-area"`)

Derived LOD ladders now switch levels by the portion of the screen the node
actually occupies. Every auto-derived `kind=lod` ladder stamps the new
`selector: "screen-area"`, under which each child's `coverage_fraction` is a
literal screen-area fraction (the node's projected bounding rect over the
viewport area): the finest level holds while the node covers at least half the
screen, and each halving of occupied area steps one level coarser
(`[0, …, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2]`; a partition tile anchors at 1.0 — the tile alone
filling the screen). This replaces the projected-diagonal metric for derived
ladders, which held the most expensive level across nearly the whole usable
zoom range on dense sub-pixel data — no single diagonal anchor can serve both
the opening-framing guarantee and prompt zoom-out coarsening, while the two
separate cleanly in area. The metric is built from NDC fractions, so selection
is identical on any monitor.

Existing stores and explicitly authored `coverage_fractions=[...]` lists keep
the legacy `selector: "coverage"` diagonal semantics and render unchanged; the
viewer supports both, and round-trips preserve the selector together with the
thresholds it describes. The standalone `.gsplats.zarr` format version moves
to v3.4 for the new selector vocabulary (every v3.3 store is also a valid v3.4
store); `gsplat migrate-format` and `gsplat transform`'s re-derivation emit
the new selector. The zebrahub velocity-streamlines demo gains a
`--streamline-lod` flag that authors its streamlines as a 4-level ladder
(three gaussian-impression levels under the full lines set) to exercise the
new selection end to end.

#### The capsule joint's bounded partner rod is now pinned by tests, not just by code

The capsule line primitive's joint deficit rule rebuilds the partner leg from a
packed packet — a radius gradient in `cut.z`, the partner's projected length in
`cut.w` — and renders `max(mine − partner, 0)` on the partner's side of the
bisector. #1490 was that the reconstruction ignored `cut.w` on the profile side:
an unbounded rod, with no far cap, subtracted far past where the partner
actually ends. That defect is already fixed in all four capsule shader surfaces
(the GLSL visual and pick fragments, and their two TSL twins) and in the CPU
mirror; this change adds no behaviour, it closes the hole that let the fix be
deleted again in silence. Deleting the far cap's overshoot term from the four
shaders while leaving the mirror alone keeps every other test in the viewer
unit suite green.

Two pieces of coverage close it. A source lock
(`tests/unit/rendering/materials/line/capsule-joint-packet-source-lock.test.ts`)
pins, across all four shader surfaces, the bounded reconstruction, both packet
lanes and the packing that transports them, the partner call and its per-end
operands, and the four packet-gate clauses (#1495 / #1501); it also checks that
the CPU mirror carries the same bounded rod, and that no fifth surface has
appeared unlocked. Everything matches on comment-stripped text, so prose can
never satisfy a pin. A parity fixture pair
(`line-capsule-joint-short-partner` and its pick twin) renders a joint whose
partner ends well inside the joint disc — the regime the far cap exists for,
which no previous capsule fixture reached — so both backends actually execute
the term.

Adding the pair also turned up a latent false green next door: the existing
`line-capsule-pick-joint` fixture rendered with the depth test off on the WebGL
side while its WebGPU twin had it on, so the two backends could resolve
different pick winners and still land under the parity bound. It now opts into
the harness's `depthCompete` flag like the new pick entry.

The source lock is the unit-test half; the parity harness runs in the dedicated
`tsl-parity` CI job, where the fixture pair remains the only thing that can catch
a divergence in just one backend.

#### Preserve integer seed budgets on sparse uniform grids

Uniform tiled fits now divide an integer whole-volume `--seeds K` budget by
the tiles that survive floor subtraction and Hann windowing, rather than by
the full geometric grid. Sparse volumes no longer lose most of their requested
budget merely because empty tiles are skipped. The remaining split is equal per
non-empty tile, so uneven occupancy can still misallocate the budget between
busy and barely occupied tiles; `--tiling content` remains the
density-proportional option. Parallel and batch planning notices now report a
conservative per-non-empty-tile lower bound until each worker resolves the exact
surviving count.

#### An explicit `None` render attr now means "absent" at the leaf adders too

#1496 settled the rule — a present-but-`None` key whose absent case has a working
default means *absent*, and the fix is to drop the key before anything looks at it
— on the three `**attrs`-forwarding gsplats doors, and deliberately left the leaf
adders alone as a wider change. Two render attrs were therefore still mishandled
one level down, inside `add_points` / `add_lines` / `add_mesh` / `add_gsplats`
themselves.

The silent one: `colormap=None` wrote `colormap='custom'`. `validate_render_attrs`
guards its colormap check on `is not None`, so the key passes, and
`compositing.sync_custom_colormap_attr` then rewrites the `None` to `'custom'` (a
`None` is not a str in `BUILTIN_COLORMAP_NAMES`) without writing any
`colormap_lut` beside it. The viewer's `build-scene-graph.ts` answers a
`'custom'` with no LUT by warning and falling back to **viridis** — so the
idiomatic `colormap=maybe_colormap` shipped a node rendered in viridis where
omitting the key gives gray, on all four geometry types and not just gsplats. The
quieter one: `coverage_fraction=None` persisted a literal `coverage_fraction:
null` LOD selector threshold into the node's zarr attrs.

Both are now dropped at the top of each leaf adder, above every consumer — the
colours gate, the entry attrs gate, each adder's `sync_custom_colormap_attr` call
sites (two per module, one in `gsplats.py`), and every structural branch — so no
route can see the raw `None`. Being above the structural branches is the part
that matters in practice: `add_points(partition={'max_elements': 150},
colormap=None)` used to stamp the LUT-less `'custom'` on *every part*, and a
partitioned scene is exactly the one nobody inspects node by node. The
rule lives in exactly one place: `compositing.strip_absent_attr_kwargs` with the
key set as a required argument, and the gsplats pipeline's wider
`ABSENT_WHEN_NONE_ATTRS` is now *derived* from the same
`ABSENT_WHEN_NONE_RENDER_ATTRS` tuple the leaves pass rather than restating it.
The set is a required argument on purpose: the pipeline door additionally reads a
`None` `labels` / `image_labels` / `partition` / `colors` / `truncation_radius` as
absent, and neither door should be able to inherit the other's set by accident.

This closes the asymmetry #1496 left behind and named: `add_gsplats_from_data(colormap=None)`
wrote `'gray'` while the `add_gsplats(colormap=None)` it delegates to wrote
`'custom'`. Both now write `'gray'`, asserted against each other and against an
omitted-key control read back from the store.

A Points/Lines `substitutive_lod=` ladder gains a second, visible fix from the
same line. The `None` never reached the coarse levels there — they are gsplat
*lift* targets and were written `'gray'` — so, measured, only the finest child
(the Points/Lines leaf itself) came out `'custom'`: an internally inconsistent
ladder, gray at every coarse level and viridis at the finest, i.e. a colour pop
at every LOD switch. Every level now agrees.

Every other render attr is still left refusing a `None` loudly, and the leaf set is
narrower than the pipeline's for exactly that reason: `opacity` / `gamma` /
`intensity` / `absorption` / `truncation_radius` answer "must be convertible to
float, got NoneType", `blending_mode` "must be a string", `layer` / `visible`
"must be a boolean". Reading those as "absent" would only mask typos, so a leaf
strip reusing the pipeline's set unchanged would have been a regression rather
than a fix.

#### Gaia demo can build its catalog locally

The Gaia Milky Way demo now offers an explicit `--build-catalog` first-run path
that queries ESA Gaia DR3, prints the ESA/Gaia/DPAC acknowledgement, caches the
raw table for resume, and atomically promotes the correctly named zip archive.
`--recompute` replaces a cached catalog, and `astroquery` is now included in the
`demos` extra and `luxar demo deps` dependency table.

#### Volume re-fit works on tiled and stacked data, at every entry point

`--refine volume` was the highest-fidelity rung of the coarse-LOD ladder but was
reachable only when nothing was partitioned and nothing was a barrier — which
excluded every timelapse, since a stacked time axis must be a barrier or
coarsening would blend timepoints. Two guards refused those combinations, both
because a re-fit was handed the whole volume when its seed only explained part of
it.

Both now hand each re-fit the sub-volume it is actually responsible for. That is
one mechanism, not two: a barrier group owns one index along the barrier axes, a
BSP tile owns a box of the spatial axes, and they compose — which is exactly what
a tiled timelapse needs.

The barrier axis is sliced out of the fit rather than held still, because it
cannot be held still: the fitting stack has no freeze mechanism, so a 4D re-fit
would drag splats off their timepoint and widen them along time whatever penalty
it was given. Slicing makes that unrepresentable; the barrier coordinate and
covariance rows come back verbatim from the seed, recombined in factor space so
positive-definiteness is structural. A per-tile re-fit that moves a centre more
than one splat sigma out of its own cell is discarded in favour of the merge,
since the never-worse MSE guard is blind to a splat leaving its tile while the
viewer frustum-culls by part bounds.

Available from all three entry points: `gsplat lod` (with `--target-axes` for a
stacked target), `gsplat fit --recipe levels --refine volume` (no `--target` — the
volume being fitted is already in hand), and `batch-fit merge --recipe levels
--refine volume`, which re-opens the source the manifest recorded and crops it per
tile as that tile streams. The volume is only ever sliced, never read whole, so a
lazy zarr target stays lazy: a 253-timepoint 407x2048x2048 uint16 timelapse is
431 GB while one timepoint is 3.4 GB.

A re-opened batch source is the FULL array, so it still carries the axes the fit
selected a single index of — a channel, and the time axis itself when only one
timepoint was fitted. Those are pinned lazily to the index the fit used, so the
canonical `(t, c, z, y, x)` OME-Zarr shape works rather than having to be reduced
to `(t, z, y, x)` first. What cannot be mapped — several selected channels, a
channel index folded over more than one axis, a missing `--axes` — is refused at
PLAN time, before any tile has been fitted.

Measured +7.7 dB mean on coarse levels of a stacked 3-timepoint fit that
previously could not be refined at all.

#### A hand-placed demo input is no longer treated as a clearable cache

The Gaia Milky Way demo is the first whose *input* is a file the user puts under the
demo cache root by hand: the Gaia DR3 catalog is CC BY-NC, so it is not shipped,
and recovering a deleted copy means a ~90-minute ESA TAP re-query. Every piece of
tooling that walks `~/.cache/luxar/` assumed everything there was a
re-downloadable derivative, and neither possible `DEMO_META` state protected it —
with `"caches": []` the inventory called `milky_way_gaia_3m/` an *orphan* and
`luxar demo cache clear --orphans` deleted it, while declaring the name in
`caches` quieted the orphan report but then made `clear <key>` and `clear --all`
delete it as if it were a download.

There is now a third classification, `luxar.demos.registry.PROTECTED_INPUT_DIRS`,
in the spirit of the existing `NON_CACHE_DIRS` guard. Such a directory is still
inventoried — the bytes are real and the user should see them — but it is claimed
