every task rescales back to it, so the splats never leave the grid's frame.
Recording it changed no split plane and falsely refused `--merge-refine volume`.

#### `inspect_gsplats_zarr()` now works on a compressed archive, and stops inventing a compression ratio (#1625)

`save_gsplats(..., compress="zip")` nests the store one directory deep inside
the archive (`a.gsplats.zarr/.zgroup`, …), but the inspector handed the archive
path straight to `open_group`, so inspecting an archive Luxar wrote itself died
with `GroupNotFoundError`. It now resolves the store root through the same
helper `load_gsplat_node` uses — extract to a temp directory, open the resolved
store, remove the temp directory in a `finally` — and gives the same clear
`ValueError` as the loader for a regular file that is not a `.zip`/`.tar.gz`.

The other archive shape is the *flat* one, whose store sits at the archive root
(`zip -r x.gsplats.zarr.zip .` from inside a store, or a zarr-native `ZipStore`
write). Zarr opens that shape in place, so the inspector always could read one —
and did, which is where the size bug below was measured. Sharing the resolver
must not quietly break that, so the resolver recognises the flat shape from the
zip index (a group document at depth 0 and nothing under a top-level
`*.gsplats.zarr/` directory) and hands the archive itself to `open_group`
instead of extracting it. That path is opt-in (`flat_zip_in_place=True`) and
only the inspector opts in: `load_gsplat_node` never accepted a flat zip and
still does not, because the appearance peek and the `gsplat info` CLI resolution
do not handle that shape either. A `.tar.gz` is still always extracted; zarr has
no tar store, so a flat one was never openable.

The size was wrong too. The storage walk only summed a directory's files and
scored anything else as `0`, so a single-file archive reported `storage_bytes:
0` and the compression ratio then fell onto its `total_bytes > 0 else 1.0`
guard — `format_gsplats_info()` printed "0.0 MB, 1.0x" for a real dataset. A
non-directory path is now sized by its own `st_size`, measured on the path the
caller supplied (the archive's bytes, not the extracted copy, which is what
"how big is this on disk" means). When the size genuinely cannot be measured,
`compression_ratio` is `None` rather than a fabricated `1.0`, and the formatter
prints the size line without a compression figure.

#### A `.gsplats.zarr` archive whose store sits at its root is now a readable dataset

A "flat" archive holds the zarr store at the archive ROOT — `zarr.json` (or
`.zgroup`) and `centers/…` at depth 0 — which is what `zip -r x.gsplats.zarr.zip .`
from inside a store, or a zarr-native `ZipStore` write, produces.
`save_gsplats(..., compress=…)` never writes one, but they exist in the wild, and
until now only `luxar gsplat info`'s metadata peek handled the shape: it opens a
flat zip in place as a `ZipStore`, so it never had to resolve a store root at all.
Everything else did, and resolved it wrongly. `extract_compressed_zarr` defined
the store as a top-level DIRECTORY, so for a flat archive its "sole top-level
directory" fallback picked whichever child `iterdir()` yielded first — one of the
store's own arrays.

The two failures that cost real work: `luxar gsplat lod flat.gsplats.zarr.zip out/`
wrote `absorption 1.0, blending None, opacity 1.0` over a source that authored
`0.7 / volumetric / 0.5`, because the appearance peek refused a depth-0 attrs
document by design and `{}` is indistinguishable from "this dataset authored no
appearance"; and `luxar gsplat info` on a flat-zipped 4-part partition resolved to
one of the store's own child groups instead of its root, picked by `iterdir()`
order. Measured on this code that is exit 1 with `Invalid format_type: None`, and it
can be nothing else: every child a `gsplat partition` writes (`fitting`,
`part_0`…`part_3`) lacks that key, which only the store root carries. The issue was
filed with `Root kind: leaf` and a quarter of the splats at exit 0 — a line printed
only once the node load has SUCCEEDED, so that report came from a store shaped
differently from a `gsplat partition` output. Same root cause, and either answer is
wrong. `load_gsplats` / `load_gsplat_node` raised `ContainsArrayError: An array
already exists in store …/amplitudes`.

Store-root resolution now has three tiers instead of two: a top-level
`*.gsplats.zarr` directory, as `_compress_zarr` writes; then the archive root
itself when a zarr GROUP document sits at depth 0; then the first top-level
directory, whatever it is called. The order matters — the named directory keeps
winning even in the odd archive carrying both shapes, because that is what the
flat-zip classifier already decides and the two must not disagree. An extracted
flat tree is moved one level down under a store-shaped name, so the returned
path's parent stays a temp directory the caller may remove, which is the contract
every caller relies on. `.tar.gz` gets the shape for free, and for tar this is the
only possible route (zarr has no tar store).

One shape is reversed by that order, deliberately. An archive carrying a depth-0
group document *and* the real store one level down under a non-`*.gsplats.zarr`
name — `zip -r x.gsplats.zarr.zip .` run from inside a parent zarr group that
merely contains the store — used to fall through to the directory and load; it now
resolves to the wrapper and fails loudly with `Invalid format_type: None`. Nothing
in an archive distinguishes "a store whose root has one child group" from "a wrapper
around a store", and gating the flat tier on "the sole child is not itself a group"
would break the flat partition that is this issue's own repro. Re-archive the inner
directory on its own to read such a wrapper.

A zip's symlink members are now rejected the way a tar's already were.
`extractall` writes one out as a regular file holding the target path, which
escapes nothing — but it is a way to hand the extractor a depth-0 `.zgroup` that
the index-only resolvers skip, so a crafted archive could make the loader and the
appearance peek read different nodes.

The appearance peek grew the matching middle tier, gated on the same condition the
classifier uses: a depth-0 attrs document is the store's root only when a depth-0
GROUP document is there with it. A loose `.zattrs` with no `.zgroup` beside it is
still a stray and still loses to a real store one directory down. The sole-directory
tier is refused outright once the archive is flat, so a flat store that authored no
root attrs carries nothing rather than handing back `centers/.zattrs` as the
dataset's appearance.

`luxar gsplat view` and the tree branch of `luxar gsplat info` now resolve through
`resolve_store_path` — the same call the loader makes — rather than reaching for the
extractor directly. That matters most for `info`, which uses the loader purely as a
gate and then re-resolves: the two could previously disagree about which node an
archive holds, which is precisely how a partition came out as a leaf.

`luxar gsplat view` also leaked its own extraction, which this fixes on the way
past. Cleanup lived only in the `KeyboardInterrupt` and the generic `except`
arms, so a NORMAL return from the viewer — and the `typer.Exit` a failed
`pick_port` raises after the archive has already been extracted — left a full
uncompressed copy of the dataset behind in `/tmp/luxar_gsplat_*`. It is now
removed once, in a `finally`. The leak is pre-existing and never had anything to
do with the flat shape (a nested archive leaked exactly the same way); what makes
it worth fixing here is that `view` serves flat archives too now, so it reaches
the extractor on a wider set of inputs than before.

`flat_zip_in_place` stays, and the metadata inspector keeps opting in, but its
justification has changed: both routes work now, so the flag is about temp space
rather than capability. Reading a flat zip in place costs none, where extraction
costs the dataset's full uncompressed size — a poor trade for a call whose whole
purpose is a cheap metadata peek. Readers that touch array data still resolve to a
directory store.

#### One intensity scale for every tile of a tiled fit

A tiled fit normalized each tile by its **own** min/max, so every tile was
stretched to fill `[0, 1]` by a different factor. Output amplitudes are rescaled
by that same factor, so the physical amplitude of a linear fit largely cancels —
but everything the optimiser states as an absolute quantity in the normalized
range does not: the convergence tolerance (`max_abs_error`, 1% of it by
default), the seeding and culling thresholds, `amp_max`. A dim tile was
therefore resolved to a far finer physical accuracy than a bright one, and
neighbouring tiles' splats were not mutually comparable.

`resolve_volume_norm_range` mirrors `resolve_volume_floor`: same bounded
sampler, same 32M-voxel budget, same determinism guarantee, so every worker
fitting one array — `--tile k/M`, `-j N`, or a uniform-tiled `batch-fit` task —
resolves the same range without coordinating. `fit_tiled` resolves it once and
hands it to every tile; `fit_tile` resolves it itself when called standalone.
A `batch-fit` task's array is one `(t, c)`, so the range is shared across that
timepoint's tiles rather than across the whole timelapse — unlike the floor,
which the planner pins globally.

Three measurements carry no usable scale, and each makes the tiles fall back to
their own with a printed note rather than share it: a non-finite top; a top with
no positive extent, where the bounded sample landed entirely in empty or masked
space (sharing a zero range fills every tile with a uniform 0.5 and fits a
fabricated flat field; a negative one inverts the sign); and a top the applied
floor reaches, which leaves nothing but the epsilon the shift manufactures. That
last one is reachable through the single-tile worker, which applies a numeric
`--floor` unguarded on purpose, and normalizing by that epsilon would have made
real signal ~1e12 times too dark. A volume that is honestly dim is none of these
and keeps its shared scale.

`image_min` is pinned at zero for tiles — that is where the array a tile fitter
sees starts, since the floor subtraction clips at 0 and the Hann window tapers
every overlapped face to 0. A positive `image_min` would subtract a constant
from both sides of an overlap and clip the taper away, re-introducing the seam.
A supplied full-range scale carries no ceiling either: it is estimated from a
bounded sample, so a voxel above it is real signal rather than an outlier to
clip. A `norm_percentile > 0` range asked for outlier clipping and keeps its
ceiling. The auto `amp_max` follows that peak rather than capping at 1.0: the
cap is a `clamp` with no gradient above it, so a hard 1.0 would pin the
brightest splats and flatten the very peak the unclipped scale exists to
preserve — it stays exactly 1.0 whenever the range came from the array itself.
A supplied range must be finite with `image_max > image_min`; a reversed or
empty one used to fit "successfully" on nonsense (an empty range lands in the
near-uniform branch, which replaces the array with 0.5). Residual passes of a
progressive fit keep their own per-pass scale; only pass 0 shares the
whole-volume one.

Whole-volume fits are unaffected. One behaviour change worth knowing for tiled
fits: a tile far dimmer than the volume maximum is now held to the same
*absolute* tolerance as the rest of the volume, so it converges earlier instead
of resolving its own noise at full contrast — which is the whole-volume fit's
behaviour a tiled fit is meant to approximate. `--tiling content` boxes still
normalize against their own crop (see #1616).

#### Grafting a partition beside an `additive_lod=` ladder no longer strands a childless wrapper

`scene.add_gsplats_from_file("g", <unladdered nested .gsplats.zarr>,
partition={"max_elements": 4}, additive_lod={"n_lods": 2})` answered `Could not
add gsplats 'part_0': partition= is not supported alongside an additive_lod=
ladder …` and left `g` on disk as a childless `kind=partition` that survived
`finalize()` — the last strand of this family left open by #1550.

`partition=` and a multi-rung ladder are mutually exclusive (the multi-LOD
writer has no `partition` parameter), and the data door already judges that
correctly, because it reads the resolved `GSplatData`. The file/graft door read
the ladder off the STORE instead, and `additive_lod=` is not a parameter of
`graft_gsplat_node` at all — it rides in `**attrs` down to each part's own
`add_gsplats_from_data_impl`, which BUILDS the ladder there, one level below the
wrapper the graft has already written. So the conflict surfaced after the damage.

The gate now asks one question per leaf: would a ladder still be there once the
kwarg is applied? Checking the kwarg's mere PRESENCE would be wrong — `{"n_lods":
1}` resolves to a single rung and partitions perfectly well, while `{"method":
"radial"}` carries no `n_lods` to read and takes the `n_lods=4` default, four
rungs on any leaf of at least 4 splats — so the answer comes from a new
`gsplats.lod.additive.additive_rung_count(n, n_lods, breakpoints)`, pure
arithmetic over the SAME cut resolver `make_additive_lod` uses. Sharing that
resolver is what makes equal-count, `stream:<c>` and explicit counts exact:
they are counted off the very cuts the build would consume, never re-derived.
(The query also mirrors the build loop's `if end <= prev: continue`
de-duplication, but as a mirror against a future cut resolver that emits a
duplicate — the resolver returns strictly-increasing positive cuts on every
non-energy path today, so the branch is unreachable in both loops.) Parity with
the builder itself is pinned per breakpoint kind. A new
`core.group.lod.gsplats.resolve_additive_rungs` applies the `additive_lod=`
vocabulary to one leaf on top of it, mirroring `resolve_additive_axis_gsplats`
key for key — the two are one contract stated twice, down to judging an explicit
`counts:` list in the resolver's own order: strict `validate_counts_breakpoints`
first and `clamp_counts_breakpoints` only after, because a single grafted leaf IS
the `substitutive_levels[0]` that validator measures against and the clamp is
there for the coarser levels of a pyramid. Clamping first answered a confident
wrong count exactly where the resolver raises — `{"recompute": True,
"breakpoints": [100]}` on a laddered 12-splat leaf clamped to `[12]`, counted one
rung, and stranded the wrapper anyway.

That closes the mirror-image half too. A laddered store plus
`additive_lod={"n_lods": 1, "recompute": True}` collapses to a single rung, takes
the flat route and splits fine, but the store-only test refused it; only the
`additive_lod=False` spelling had been skipped by hand.

Which remedy the refusal names is now decided per call, by the OFFENDING leaf's
store alone. If that leaf's store carries a ladder the message is unchanged — it
names the store and points at `gsplat flatten` — which is also the right answer
when the call ALSO rebuilds that ladder, since a stored ladder is the obstacle
that survives dropping the kwarg and "drop one of the two" would only buy a
second refusal. When the ladder exists only because `additive_lod=` builds it,
the refusal names `additive_lod=` and says to drop one of the two. "Offending",
not "anywhere in the tree": on a mixed store where the kwarg collapses the
laddered leaf and ladders the flat one, the blocking leaf is the flat one, so the
message names `additive_lod=` while a stored ladder sits untouched next door —
correctly, since `gsplat flatten` would rewrite a ladder that is not in the way.

The reason BODY of the kwarg-built refusal is byte-identical to what the data
door says for the same call one step later (they share
`partition_beside_a_ladder_reason`). The whole message matches on the
matrix-shaped branch; on the graft branch it deliberately names `'g'` where the
data door would have named `part_0`, which is the whole point. And even the body
matches only for a call whose only fault is this conflict. The gate runs
above the data door's `lod_group=` resolution, so
`add_gsplats_from_file(..., lod_group="bogus", partition={…}, additive_lod={"n_lods": 2})`
answers the conflict where `add_gsplats_from_data` with the same effective
arguments answers `TypeError: lod_group must be …`. Both refuse and write
nothing, so the divergence is in naming only.

An unknown count falls back to the store. An energy-fraction `breakpoints` list
cannot be counted without the ordering and the energy curve — the expensive half
the query exists to avoid — and neither can a malformed or junk spec, but `None`
there is a statement about the KWARG, not about the store: the store's own ladder
still stands, and refusing on it is exactly what the pre-#1632 gate did. Skipping
the leaf instead re-stranded the very wrapper this change closes. The cost is one
over-refusal in the conservative direction, `{"recompute": True, "breakpoints":
[1.0]}` on a laddered store, which pre-#1632 also refused.

That fallback leaves two cases to be reported from inside a child on an
UNLADDERED store. First, an INVALID call: `additive_lod=True` there is one rung,
skips the gate, and still fails from inside `part_0` with "additive_lod=True
requires every substitutive level to already carry an additive ladder", and a
malformed spec does the same with its own message. Both fail identically without
`partition=` at all, so the fault is the call's and the report is the builder's —
"a query must not pre-empt the builder's own fault report", preserved where it
belongs. The transaction added in #1763 removes any partial graft. Second, a VALID
energy-fraction spec:
`partition={"max_elements": 4}, additive_lod={"breakpoints": [0.5, 1.0]}` on an
unladdered store counts UNKNOWN, falls back to a stored one rung, skips — and
then hits this very conflict refusal from inside `part_0`. The transactional
graft added in #1763 removes the wrapper and descendants before re-raising.
Nothing is malformed there; the builder really does make
two rungs from that spec, and the count is unknowable only because energy cuts
need the ordering and the energy curve. Refusing on UNKNOWN instead was rejected
deliberately: `{"breakpoints": [1.0]}` resolves to a single rung and partitions
fine, so a gate refusing every uncountable spec would refuse what the flat path
accepts — its own regression. One further trade, in the other
direction: a fault the count cannot see (a bad `method`, a stray
`substitutive_level` key) is now masked by this refusal rather than reported by
the builder — acceptable, the conflict being the more fundamental fault and
nothing being written either way.

#### The test suites are fast enough to run in the loop again

Both suites were slow for configuration reasons, not because the tests are heavy.
The TypeScript unit suite burned 468 s of CPU to run 38 s of test bodies, and the
Python suite ran locally without the two settings CI had already applied to
itself. `hatch run test` now takes 13 min 54 s instead of 79 min 19 s, and
`pnpm test --run` 22.5 s instead of 165 s, with identical or better pass counts —
nothing was deleted, skipped, or relaxed.

`ci.yml` had pinned `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and friends to one thread and passed
`-n 4` since the self-hosted runner landed, recording 45.5 min → 15.8 min for
the same tests and the same coverage. None of it reached `hatch run test`,
the documented pre-push gate, because `pyproject.toml` carried no `env-vars`
block and no script passed `-n`. Both are set now. `--dist loadfile` is
mandatory rather than incidental: plain `--dist load` rebuilds module-scoped
fixtures once per worker, which would undo the sharing that
`gsplats/tests/conftest.py` credits with taking that directory from ~14 min to
~1 min. Pinning also *fixed* eight subprocess-fitting tests that had been
failing on self-inflicted CPU oversubscription — Python failures went 11 to 3.
The pin is environment-wide, so it reaches real work run through hatch too — a
`--device cpu` fit, a demo, a benchmark. An explicitly exported value therefore
wins over it: `OMP_NUM_THREADS=16 MKL_NUM_THREADS=16 hatch run ...` runs at full
width, while a bare `hatch run` stays pinned.

On the TypeScript side `environment: 'jsdom'` applied to all 559 unit files
even though only 124 touch a document, and constructing one costs ~1.8 s of CPU
per file. `node` is the default now and the files that need a browser global
carry a `// @vitest-environment jsdom` docblock, derived empirically rather than
guessed — a slightly larger set than those 124, because a handful were pinned
for other browser globals rather than for a document. A missing docblock fails
loudly with `ReferenceError` instead of silently running in the wrong
environment, and the two arrangements were proved equivalent: on the same tree,
node-default and jsdom-everywhere produce identical test-ID sets with zero
status differences across 11,521 tests. Exactly one deliberate exception has
been added since that audit, so a re-run is no longer clean: the #1642 test
`initWasm URL resolution without a DOM` asserts `typeof self` and
`typeof location` are `undefined` as a non-vacuity precondition, which makes it
environment-sensitive on purpose and red under `--environment jsdom` by design
(`src/tests/unit/wasm/`: 310 passed under `node`, 309 passed / 1 failed when
forced to jsdom, that one test being the whole difference). It is not a phantom
to chase.

Fixture staleness moved from mtime to a content digest. The old check compared
every fixture against the newest `.py` under `encoding/` and `io/` — including
the 52 test files there — so editing an unrelated Python test, rebasing, or
switching worktrees forced a full regeneration before a single TypeScript test
ran. Expectations remain coupled to fixture rebuilds, because
`generate_test_data.py` is not byte-reproducible and a rebuild from unchanged
inputs still invalidates them.

Two test bugs that blocked the parallelism are fixed along the way:
`available_port` scanned deterministically upward from 8000, so concurrent
workers collided, and the `test_server` fixture never shut its server down,
leaking a listening socket per test.

E2E screenshots, video and traces were being recorded for every passing test and
then discarded; they are failure-only now, and tests within a file run in
parallel with the resource-bound specs opting out. Finally, the documented
pre-commit checklist ran both suites twice — `check-static` and `check:static`
are test-free gates so `make test-all` is the only place tests execute, and
`make test-fast` is a new inner loop (~35 s scoped).

#### A content-planned fit keeps the truncation radius it was fitted with

`gsplat fit --tiling content` stored the wrong support for its own splats. With
`truncate: 3.5` in a `--config`, a uniform tiled fit of the same volume and the
same config recorded `truncation_radius: 3.5`, while every box of the content fit
recorded the 2.75 default — the fit ran at 3.5 and the store then claimed 2.75,
so the renderer evaluates each Gaussian over a smaller support than it was
optimised for. `--plan-box K` (which is also what every array task of a content
`batch-fit run`/`submit` invokes), the sequential boxes and the `-j N` parallel
merge were all affected; a partition and a `--flat` leaf alike.

The user-visible consequence was worse than a wrong attribute, because
`GSplatData.concatenate` **requires** its inputs to agree on the radius: a
content result no longer composed with a uniform-tiled one produced from the same
config, failing with "Truncation radius mismatch". Merging a content fit of one
channel with a uniform fit of another was simply impossible.

The cause was a lossy internal hand-off. The per-box fitter returned bare
`(centers, amplitudes, cholesky_factors)` arrays, so all four consumers rebuilt a
`GSplatData` from those three arrays alone — and a rebuilt dataset takes the
default radius. It now returns the fitted dataset itself, and the two flat merges
go through `GSplatData.concatenate` (what the uniform tiled path already used),
which carries the shared radius through. A box with a zero budget fits nothing but
still answers with the radius its config asked for rather than the default.

The `-j N` path had a second, independent copy of the same bug: the box workers
were handed only `--preset`, and `truncate:` is settable *only* through a YAML
`--config` (no preset sets it, and there is no `--truncate` flag), so every box of
a parallel run fitted and stamped the default no matter what the config said. The
`--preset` they were handed made it worse: an absent `--preset` was substituted
with `standard`, whose 5000 iterations and `cull_retention: 0.999` a sequential
`-j 1` run never applies (it resolves 1000 / 0.95), so `-j N` fitted with different
parameters than `-j 1` even without a config. The run's fit configuration
(`--preset`, `--config`, `--iters`, `--loss`, `--lr`, `--cull-retention`) is now
forwarded verbatim to each box worker — an absent flag stays absent — mirroring the
uniform-tiled sibling, so both paths resolve the same fit config. `--seeds` is
deliberately not forwarded: a content box's budget comes from the plan.

Per-box fit stats (`psnr_db`, `final_loss`, `iterations`, the normalization
metadata) ride along with the radius, reaching each part of a bare-leaf
`kind=partition` result instead of being dropped at the box boundary. (With
`--recipe stream|levels` the ladder builder writes its own per-sub-LOD stats, and
on `--flat` `concatenate` replaces them with its merge summary, so the per-box
values are visible only on a bare-leaf partition.) Part of the set is re-scoped to
what the part actually holds: a box is fitted on a halo-padded crop and then
core-masked, so the crop's region stamps — the whole `source_shape` /
`source_voxels` / `source_bytes` / `fitted_shape` / `fitted_voxels` / `occupancy` /
`voxels_per_splat` group a `--bbox` crop already drops — go whenever the padded
crop is larger than the box or the mask removed splats, and `n_splats` is
restamped to the kept count. The remaining figures (`psnr_db` / `ssim` / `mse`,
the `final_*` losses, the cull provenance `n_original` / `n_culled` /
`amplitude_retention`) are the box's own fit provenance — measured on the padded
crop with the pre-mask splat set, the same provenance a uniform tile-part carries
— not part-scoped fidelity. A non-finite figure is dropped rather than persisted:
a signal-free crop fits to `psnr_db = inf`, the leaf writer stamps `lod_stats`
raw, and zarr would emit a bare `Infinity` token that a strict JSON parser (the
viewer's) refuses. The flat merged leaf's
stats keep every `planned_fit` / `n_boxes` / `n_boxes_fit` / `overlap` /
`volume_shape` key it had before, now beside `concatenate`'s own
`concatenated_from` / `splats_per_source` summary — with `time_seconds`
overwritten by true wall clock, as the uniform tiled merge already does.

One caveat for a content `batch-fit` run that is already in flight: its finished
tiles carry the old radius, and a resume only fits the missing ones. Mixed radii
either stop the merge (`concatenate` refuses them when it stacks a spatial slot
across timepoints or channels) or, for a single-`(t, c)` streaming merge, pass
silently with each part rendering at its own support. Re-fit the tiles of such a
run — `batch-fit validate` checks store integrity, not the stamped radius.

#### The debug snapshot reports a real `isLoading`, so the E2E data waits gate on something

`window.__luxarDebug.getState()` never carried a loading flag, and the E2E
helpers in `src/tests/e2e/helpers.ts` have always read `state.isLoading` — in
eight places (`waitForDataLoaded`, `waitForDimensionNavigation`,
`waitForSpatialQuery`, `waitForSpatialQueryOrThrow`,
`waitForNavigationComplete`, `waitForNavigationCompleteOrThrow`, and the
state-based fallbacks inside `waitForRenderStable` and `waitForNextRender`),
plus `real-dataset-loading.spec.ts` and the two capture specs under
`src/tests/screenshots/`. `!undefined` is `true`, so `waitForDataLoaded`,
`waitForDimensionNavigation` and both spatial-query waits resolved the instant
`getState()` returned an object: they waited for the debug interface to exist
and for nothing else. `waitForNavigationComplete` first waits for
`typeof isLoading === 'boolean'`, which could never become true, so it took its
catch branch and degraded to a fixed 300 ms sleep on every call — the silent
variant several specs deliberately prefer, blaming flaky keyboard events.
`waitForNavigationCompleteOrThrow` requires `isLoading === false` strictly and
could therefore only ever time out, which is why it has no callers.

The snapshot now carries `isLoading`, sourced from
`SceneLoaderManager.isAnyLoadPassInProgress()` — true while a sweep for the
requested view is outstanding on *any* registered loader rather than only the
default one, because the manager's contract admits several and the default is
merely one elected entry. It is read inside the `getState` closure, per snapshot,
so a load that starts after the debug interface was installed is visible.
`computeDebugState` takes it as a parameter alongside `isAnimating` and
`initialized`, keeping that helper free of singleton lookups.

"Outstanding" is the running `updateView` sweep (fetch/decode/upload) up to its
geometry commit, minus the progressive-LOD refinement drain, plus a view-state
that is queued and has not started loading yet. The refinement subtraction comes
first: that drain does not take the serialization lock, it inherits it — the
update tail and the post-load kick hand `_updateInProgress` straight to the
refinement orchestrator, whose last phase releases it once every additive ladder
has emptied. Folding it in would make the flag report full-ladder latency
instead of first-commit latency, the same distinction
`update-view/queue-next.ts` already draws where it settles its pass waiters at
refinement entry. `SceneLoader` tracks that stretch in a `_refining` flag and
exposes `isLoadPassInProgress()` alongside the existing `isUpdateInProgress()`,
which keeps its broader "the lock is held at all" meaning for the adaptive-DPR
manager and the init pipeline.

Subtracting the drain alone would have left a hole exactly where the E2E waits
live. On any laddered dataset the steady state right after a commit is "lock
held, refining"; a keyboard nav arriving then takes `updateView`'s supersede
branch, which parks the state with `viewStateQueue.setPending` and returns
without touching either flag. Both would still describe the refinement that
preceded the request, so the flag would read idle while the slice the user asked
for had not begun loading — every poller would settle on its first poll and
assert against the previous slice, which is the vacuity this change exists to
remove. `isLoadPassInProgress()` therefore also reports the queued slot. It
cannot latch: the slot is cleared by `takePending()` at the moment the next pass
starts, whether that is `queueNext` re-entering `updateView`, the refinement
loop's loop-top cancellation check handing off, or `finalReleaseLock` draining.
`kickRefinementIfIdle` counts a live refinement as busy for the same reason —
the final phase opens the lock while `_refining` is still set (it is cleared one
level up, in the orchestrator's `finally`), and a continuation landing in that
gap would otherwise start a second refinement run whose drain the first run's
`finally` would then mis-report as a load pass.

`dispose()` clears the lock, the refinement flag and any queued view-state, as
defence in depth rather than a fix for an observable bug: only the lock can
genuinely latch (an early update phase bailing before its release runs), and no
production caller can see it, since every `SceneLoaderManager` disposal path
detaches the loader from its map before disposing it — the only self-dispose that
stays in the map is `lifecycle/load-scene.ts`'s, on the loader-reuse path the
class documents as unsupported. That is the manager's ordering hiding a
torn-down loader's state, not the loader being consistent on its own, so teardown
now clears it outright.

One real latch did turn up, in the post-load refinement kick in
`lifecycle/load-scene.ts`. Its rejection handler released the lock but left the
queued view-state alone, unlike its two siblings — `update-view/queue-next.ts`
and `kickRefinementIfIdle` — which drain the slot into a fresh `updateView` and
then settle the parked pass waiters. That slot is routinely occupied in exactly
this window: the kick fires from inside `loadScene`, before it returns, so the
init pipeline's first `updateAllNDNodes` → `updateView` lands while the kick
holds the lock, takes the supersede branch and parks its state. A rejection
escaping outside the refinement loops' own `finally`s — a double fault, not an
expected path — therefore stranded the user's initial slice, and with the queued
slot now counted would also latch `isLoadPassInProgress()` true for good, so
every polling helper would burn its full timeout. The handler is now symmetric
with its siblings: release, drain, resolve.

Two things the flag does not cover, documented rather than fixed here: the
initial `loadScene` (it only touches the lock at its very end, to hand it to the
post-load kick — and an in-page dataset switch therefore reads `isLoading:
false` throughout its load, with `initialized` staying true as well), and lazy
substitutive-LOD / deferred-partition `ensureLoaded` promotions, which run
outside any `updateView` cycle.

No helper CODE changed and no spec was touched — only one
`waitForNavigationComplete` docstring, which claimed a cached path "may never
toggle it true at all". A same-task keyboard nav always does toggle it true
(`updateView` takes the lock before its first await); the honest statement is
that a fully cache-served pass may never be OBSERVED true, because polling is
discrete and such a pass can start and finish between two polls. Nine call sites
do get faster:
`waitForNavigationComplete` used to burn its full 10 s first-phase timeout on
every call, and its six callers in `spatial-index-accuracy.spec.ts`, two in
`dimension-animation.spec.ts` and one in `keyboard-input-system.spec.ts` now
settle as soon as the loader is idle.

#### The E2E render waits stop hanging on a starved page

Tests in `webgl-errors.spec.ts` started failing on a Linux/NVIDIA workstation
without catching anything: they died on `Test timeout exceeded` while still
waiting for frames, having seen no `GL_INVALID*` and no "Vertex buffer is not
big enough" at all. The cause is in the shared helper. `page.evaluate` is
dispatched with no timeout of its own — neither `actionTimeout` nor
`setDefaultTimeout` bounds it, only the test budget does — and the frame-counter
read and the `renderOnce()` kick in `waitForNextRender` were both unbounded
evaluates. Every other wait in that helper is capped and swallowed, so on a page
too starved to answer (the app drops from ~30 FPS to ~4 under load here) the
helper blew past its own fallback instead of taking it. Both evaluates are now
raced against `Math.min(timeout, 3000)`: an unanswered read yields `null`, which
already routes to the state-based fallback, and the kick is best-effort.
`waitForRenderStable` carried the same two unbounded evaluates verbatim and gets
the same treatment, so the fix reaches all thirty-five specs that pace
themselves on a render. Falling back promptly is not the same as having
rendered, though, so both helpers now warn once naming which branch they took,
and `waitForNextRender` returns `false` instead of reporting nothing; all 263
existing call sites ignore the return value and are unaffected. The warning
matters most in `waitForRenderStable`, whose callers are almost entirely
screenshot comparisons: bounding its frame read means a starved page now returns
from the fallback in a few hundred milliseconds where it used to hang, so
without the warning a capture taken before the paint it was pacing on would be
diffed against the baseline with nothing in the log to say so.

The spec file also opts back out of `fullyParallel` with
`test.describe.configure({ mode: 'default', timeout: 120000 })`. It is
resource-bound — ten tests performing ~14 scene loads over one dataset server,
OPFS and the GPU — and it used to run sequentially against a two-worker pool, so
the ambient load from three other workers is worse than what this restores; the
raised budget is headroom on a loaded machine, not the cure. `default` rather
than `serial` keeps all ten detectors reporting. Finally, a file-level
`afterEach` prints whether any WebGL-error text was observed whenever a test
ends unexpectedly (skips excluded, since a skipped test observed nothing by
construction), because a timed-out test never reaches its own `expect` or its
dumps and the shared fixture skips teardown for `timedOut`.

#### The WASM loader no longer needs a browser to resolve its own URL (#1642)

`initWasm()`'s dev-server branch resolved the shim against `self.location.origin`.
`self` does not exist in Node, so a **dev build** running in a DOM-less host — a
plain `node` test environment being exactly that — threw
`ReferenceError: self is not defined` before it ever reached the dynamic import,
and the `catch` flattened that into the documented "no WASM build" TypeScript
fallback. The dereference sat inside the `import.meta.env.DEV` branch and Vite
folds that constant to `false` in the production and library builds, so a host
consuming the published bundle never reached it. The fallback is the right answer
for a missing artifact and the wrong answer for a loader that assumed a browser,
and because the TypeScript reference implementation is a real production backend
(it is the >16-dimension path), the degradation was silent.

The origin branch now reads the bare `location` global — present in both window
and dedicated-worker scopes — and reads it through `typeof`, so a dev build in a
host that merely lacks the global falls through to the
`import.meta.url`-relative candidates (#1649): there is no dev-server origin to
resolve against in Node, so the bundle-relative URLs are the only resolution that
could mean anything there. The fallback warning also names the candidates it
RESOLVED, in order (or says resolution failed before the import), since "the
artifact isn't there" and "the loader never computed a URL" read identically
otherwise — precisely how this stayed invisible. It stops short of claiming each
one was fetched and rejected, because the same `catch` also covers a failure
after a candidate loaded fine, and it doubles any `%` in the URLs: the message is
`console.warn`'s first argument, so an unescaped percent-escape in a path would
consume the swallowed `error` as a substitution and drop it from the warning.

What this does *not* do is hand a DOM-less host compiled kernels. `initWasm` is
not part of the package's public exports, and `LuxarApp.init` refuses a caller
with no `window`/`document` outright, so such a host only reaches the loader by
deep-importing internals; even then Node cannot load the artifact through it,
because the wasm-bindgen shim's async `default()` fetches a `file://` URL and
Node rejects that with `TypeError: fetch failed`. The change is that the loader
stops dying on a missing browser global and starts reporting which URLs it
resolved, which is what makes this class of downgrade visible in the first place.

The seven test files pinned to jsdom to supply `self` are back on `node`. They
were not buying compiled-kernel coverage: `initWasm`'s success path cannot run
under vitest in *any* environment, because its
`new Function('url', 'return import(url)')` indirection is not serviceable by
vitest's VM module runner. jsdom only changed which error the `catch` swallowed.
Tests that want the real kernels load the built artifact through
`src/tests/helpers/wasm-artifact.ts`, and the comments in the two `wasm/` test
files that credited jsdom for the limitation now say so.

#### The L2 OPFS cache gets a circuit breaker, and `?noOpfs` skips it outright (#1645)

A systemically stalled OPFS backend — the norm under automated Chromium —
used to cost the full ten-second operation timeout on every chunk,
serially, inflating scene readiness by half a minute and starving
downstream initialization (the E2E known-failing baseline traced to
this). The store now counts consecutive OPFS timeouts and, at
`cache.opfsTimeoutTripThreshold` (default 3) in a row with no settlement
between, disables the L2 tier for the session through the same
degradation path as an init failure: later operations are instant
no-ops, the in-memory tiers keep serving, and the data monitor shows the
existing `opfs-unavailable` badge. Any success or fast rejection resets
the count — the breaker targets stalls, not error rate. The store's
teardown metadata flush is now deadline-bounded too: a backend that
stalled just before teardown used to leave `dispose()` unresolved
indefinitely, hanging the dataset switch waiting behind it.

For environments that know their OPFS is hostile, the new `?noOpfs` URL
parameter skips the tier at construction (the deterministic sibling of
the breaker, mirroring `?noSliceCache`); a deliberate disable does not
raise the badge. The E2E suites that never assert L2 now pin it, which
un-stalls the long-standing known-failing families.

#### The first blend-mode switch no longer links its shader on the click path (#1648)

Switching a layer's blending mode flips shader defines (`max`, `volumetric`,
gsplat `normal`, mesh `opaque` cutout), so the first click onto each variant was
the first time its program existed — and the link is synchronous. On a real
driver that is a hitch; on headless Chromium, which runs WebGL through
SwiftShader and exposes no `KHR_parallel_shader_compile`, it monopolized the main
thread for tens of seconds and starved every queued interaction behind it.

The viewer now pre-links each *distinct* reachable variant after a dataset load,
one compile per post-frame idle opportunity so visible rendering and input each
get a turn in between, and keeps the programs pinned with isolated keeper
materials until the source material is replaced or disposed. Variants are deduped
against an approximation of Three's own program cache key, so a mode that lands
on a program another mode already produced costs nothing, and a material whose
compile-time state moves for an unrelated reason (colormap enablement, the
element-texture width define, the mesh flat-normal variant) has its keepers
rebuilt rather than pinning programs that no longer match. The set is rebuilt
across scene replacement, material disposal, and WebGL context loss/restore.

Warming is WebGL-only — WebGPU/TSL sessions never configure it — and
`?noBlendWarmup` turns it off.

A dataset load waits for the warm-up before reporting readiness, so an
interaction cannot race the initial queue, but it waits on a *budget* rather than
on the queue emptying. The queue is not a finite set: every geometry commit
schedules the node it just populated, so a progressively-loading partition keeps
handing the drain new work for as long as it streams, and gating readiness on
"nothing left" would hold `window.__luxarDebug`, the `dataset-loaded` event and
`switchDataset`'s promise for the whole load. The same wait never returns at all
in a background tab, where `requestAnimationFrame` is not serviced and no turn
ever comes. After five seconds readiness is released and the remaining variants
keep warming behind it.

#### Adaptive DPR now acts in the regime it was built for

Adaptive resolution was structurally inert below about 2.9 fps — exactly the regime a
software rasterizer (headless Chromium's SwiftShader, a machine without a usable GPU)
puts a heavy gsplat scene into. Two mechanisms conspired. The frame-gap reset, meant to
throw away a one-off stall (a GC pause, a synchronous decode, an idle resume) before it
poisons an otherwise-healthy window, fired on _every_ frame once every interval exceeded
its 350 ms threshold, clearing the sample window and pushing the evaluation clock forward
so the control loop never ran at all. And the 1-second sliding window dropped the previous
frame as too old before the next one arrived, leaving a single sample and an undefined
frame rate. A measured 116-second episode at 0.48 fps rendered at full native pixel ratio
from beginning to end.

A long interval is now classified by comparison rather than by an absolute threshold: it
is dead time only if it clears the 350 ms floor _and_ is strictly more than four times the
median of the four intervals that preceded it. A 5-second gap in a 60 fps stream is a 300×
outlier and is still thrown away; a 2-second interval in a stream whose recent intervals
are all around 2 seconds is simply the frame rate, and its samples are kept so the manager
scales down. The interval being judged is deliberately not part of the median it is judged
against — mixing it in makes the test partly self-referential, and after a session boundary
that decided the verdict: with a two-sample memory the candidate was half of it, so a
5-second shader-compile stall one frame into a session measured as "the frame rate" and the
manager reduced the pixel ratio and armed a probe on a window holding nothing but dead
time. That is the ordinary startup and idle-resume path.

The cadence memory survives the reset it triggers, which is what makes it converge — a
scene that genuinely slows down costs one or two misread intervals before adaptation
resumes — and is cleared only where the frame stream itself breaks (display change, pause,
disable, dispose). A scene-content change is deliberately not one of those: frames keep
arriving at the rate they were arriving at, and a cold memory falls back to the absolute
threshold alone, which misreads the very next ordinary interval of a slow loop as dead
time — which in turn threw the freshly restarted window away a second time and voided the
probe in flight.

The evaluation clock is no longer pushed forward by a dead-time reset at all. What keeps
dead time from counting as progress toward the next evaluation is instead the tick's own
return value: a tick that found no samples — the window having just been cleared — is not
an evaluation and does not consume the interval budget. Pinned to the stalling frame's own
timestamp, an outlier hitch recurring more often than the 500 ms evaluation interval
re-pinned the clock before it could ever mature and the loop never evaluated: measured over
43 seconds, a repeating 16.7/16.7/400 ms cadence (about 6.9 frames a second as perceived)
produced zero evaluations with a frame rate to judge, and so did 8×16.7+360 ms; they now
produce about fifty and eighty. Clamping the pin to one interval before the frame was tried
as well and measured inert — evaluations, pixel ratio, floor and applied-ratio counts came
out identical on six cadences, because a clamped pin leaves the gate satisfied on every
subsequent frame anyway — so it was dropped rather than kept as decoration. What those
evaluations can _see_ is a separate limit, described at the end.

With per-frame LOD churn at half a frame per second the pixel ratio walked unratified from
2.0 all the way down to the floor of 0.5, and no probe ever produced a verdict of any kind
to learn from. A content change no longer voids an in-flight probe when the loop is too slow
to run a replacement experiment (below roughly two frames per probe window, every armed
probe was voided before it could ever be judged), and the verdict such a probe finally
produces is treated as _confounded_: its baseline was measured on the old content and its
settle sample on the new one, so it says nothing about what the pixel-ratio change did. A
per-frame swap to a finer, heavier level reads as a rejection, and acting on that would push
the pixel ratio back _up_ — adding pixels to a scene that just got heavier — and pin a
30-second floor that blocks all scale-down; a swap to a coarser level reads as an acceptance
and would credit the coarsening to the pixel-ratio step, wiping the rejection-backoff
streak. So a confounded probe teaches nothing at all: the reduction stands, because fewer
pixels never hurt a stuttering loop, and there is no revert, no floor and no backoff
movement.

Under sustained churn the pixel ratio therefore still walks down unratified toward the
minimum — a probe whose window spans a content change cannot ratify anything, so a reduction
with no verdict is all the loop has, and that is the right distress response: it is bounded
by `minDPR` and lifts again through the normal scale-up hysteresis once content settles. What
discarding the verdict buys is the absence of _thrash_. Measured over twenty minutes of
per-frame churn at a third of a frame per second on a native 2.0 display, acting on those
verdicts produces 100 reductions and 98 reverts back up — 202 pixel-ratio applications, each
one a render-target reallocation — while discarding them produces 13 monotone reductions and
not one revert. A previous revision instead held the walk while a churn clock ran; that
mechanism was measured to invert its own goal and has been removed. Its window was the same
5-second constant the notifications coalesce on, so churn arriving just slower than the window
was fully acted upon and completely invisible to the hold: at a content change every 4.5 to 6
seconds the ratio walked to the 0.5 minimum where not having the hold stopped it at 1.62 with
a measured floor, and under per-frame churn it pinned a 0.33 fps scene at 1.62 indefinitely —
2.6× the pixel work of ratio 1.0 on a scene rendering a third of a frame per second. The FPS
window's retention floor keeps two samples regardless of age, so the estimate stays defined
slower than the window itself.

Behaviour at healthy frame rates is unchanged, and an isolated long stall — one, or up to
two in a row — is still discarded outright. By the third in a row half the cadence memory
is dead time, so it is absorbed as the frame rate; there is no way to tell the two apart
from timestamps alone, since three five-second gaps in a row genuinely is a fifth of a
frame per second for fifteen seconds. A cadence that has only just been reclassified is
therefore untrusted for a couple of intervals: the reduction still applies, because fewer
pixels never hurt a stuttering loop, but nothing is learned from a window that may hold
nothing but dead time. The protection is bounded on purpose and counted in _intervals_, and
intervals is the only form the guarantee takes — what it buys in wall clock depends on how
long they are (four five-second gaps is twenty seconds, four 400 ms hitches is 1.6) and on
how much of its own 1.5-second window and representative span a probe can still gather
afterwards, so it has to be measured per cadence rather than stated as a single number. For
consecutive 400 ms hitches inside a 60 fps session, measured with the production step, the
turnover is at nine: eight of them (3.2 seconds) leave the floor untouched and the pixel
ratio lifts again, nine (3.6 seconds) pin a floor — at which point the "burst" is a slow
regime the manager should be free to learn from.

One regime this does not cover, measured and left alone: on a _hitch-heavy_ cadence the walk
can still reach the minimum with no probe ever ratifying it, because every hitch is a
dead-time reset and a dead-time reset voids the probe in flight. At native 2.0 over 400
frames of 30 ms with a 1.2-second hitch every 40 (about 17 frames a second as perceived, 33
between the hitches — genuinely below the scale-down threshold), thirteen reductions reach
0.508 and not one probe produces a verdict. Rate-limiting the unprobed reduction was tried:
capping it at one step per untrusted episode is inert here, because the loop already takes at
most one, and a latch cleared only by a settled probe cannot clear at all while hitches keep
destroying probes — measured, that froze a neighbouring 400 ms-hitch cadence at a single step
for fifty seconds, which is the structural inertness this whole entry is about. The walk stays
bounded by the minimum and lifts at the normal hysteresis rate (sixteen scale-ups in the
minute after the hitches stop, exactly as many as from a shallower start).

The rule sees only inter-frame intervals, so two patterns still escape it. A dead period
alternating one-for-one with a single fast frame lands the median between the two phases,
so the dead time is kept as the frame rate and the FPS window mixes it with real render
cost; the manager still adapts there (measured on a 2000/100 ms stream at native 2, the
only rates it ever reports are 0, 10 and 0.5 — all far below the down threshold — and the
pixel ratio does come down), but the rate it reports is not the rate the user perceives.
Two or more fast frames between dead periods fail the other way: the median stays fast, the
dead time is correctly discarded every cycle, and the window accumulates nothing but those
few fast frames — so the 16.7/16.7/400 ms cadence above now evaluates, and reads a healthy
60 fps at about 6.9 perceived.

The Performance panel's FPS row no longer rounds a sub-1 fps rate to `0`, which is its
sentinel for "not rendering at all"; below one frame a second it shows a decimal. The rail's
performance gauge now shares that formatter, so the two readouts can no longer disagree about
the same rate — the gauge used to render a real 0.4 fps as `0` in exactly the
software-rasterizer regime this entry is about.

#### The library build's entry chunk can find its WASM shim (#1649)

`initWasm` resolved the wasm-bindgen JS shim with a single bundle-relative
literal, `new URL('../wasm/luxar_wasm.js', import.meta.url)`. Six chunks carry
the loader, and that literal is correct for five of them and wrong for the
sixth. The compiled artifact always lands in a `wasm/` directory at the output
root, while the chunk carrying the loader sits at one of two depths: the app
build emits `dist/assets/index-*.js` alongside `dist/assets/data-worker-*.js`
and `dist/assets/sort-worker-*.js`, and the library build emits
`dist/lib/assets/data-worker-*.js` and `dist/lib/assets/sort-worker-*.js` — all
five one level below their build's `wasm/` — but the library build emits its
ENTRY chunk at `dist/lib/luxar-viewer.js`, the output root itself, where
`../wasm/…` climbs out of `dist/lib/` and lands on a `dist/wasm/` that does not
exist.

The consequence was invisible rather than loud. An embedder consuming the
published package unbundled (a CDN, or a served `node_modules`) without passing
`LuxarAppOptions.wasmPath` got compiled kernels in the data and sort workers,
whose chunks resolve correctly, and a silent `TypeScriptFallback` on the main
thread — which since the in-process Points projection landed is a path that
matters. `module-overrides.ts` only applies `wasmPath` when it is truthy, so
nothing downstream corrected the default.

One literal cannot serve both depths, so the loader now tries an ordered list:
`../wasm/luxar_wasm.js` first, then `./wasm/luxar_wasm.js`. The order is the
point — every hot path resolves on the first entry, so the app build and all
four worker chunks still cost exactly one request and only the library entry
chunk pays a failed import before finding its shim. The resolved list is
deduplicated, so it is not always two: `new URL()` clamps at the URL root, and a
chunk served there (`dist/lib/*` copied to a site root) resolves both specifiers
to the same href — keeping the duplicate would have cost nothing on the success
path but made a genuine failure report `tried, in order: X, X`. A candidate only
counts as a hit if it exposes a callable `default`: a 200 with an empty body, or
a JavaScript stub/redirect module served in place of the absent artifact,
imports fine and then throws on `default()`, which would reproduce the original
symptom on that host class. (An HTML error page is a different failure and was
already covered — HTML does not parse as an ES module, so the import itself
rejects.) The shape check reads a property and instantiates nothing, so the
commit-to-the-winner rule stands: once a candidate wins, initialization and the
staleness check run against that module alone, because re-running them elsewhere
risks instantiating the binary twice and would mask a genuinely stale artifact
behind the next candidate's 404. Failures are attributed per candidate — a
single-URL attempt (an explicit `wasmPath`, or the dev server) rethrows its own
error untouched, while a multi-candidate walk throws an `AggregateError` naming
every URL in order, so a real failure on candidate 1 (shim served as
`text/plain`, blocked by CSP, corrupt) is no longer reported as a 404 on a
phantom `dist/assets/wasm/` directory that exists in no layout.

Both halves are exported and unit-tested: `wasmShimCandidateUrls` pins the two
real depths, ordering included, plus the root-served collapse to one candidate,
and `importFirstWasmShim` takes the dynamic importer as a parameter so the
candidate walk itself — try order, short-circuit, fall-through on a rejection,
on a `default`-less module and on a non-callable `default`, and the error
attribution, including the mixed walk where a shape rejection and an import
rejection must both reach the `AggregateError` — is exercised with a stub. That
injection is what makes the loop
testable at all: `import.meta.env.DEV` is true under vitest, so every in-suite
`initWasm()` takes the single-candidate dev-server branch and never reaches the
list. `check-lib-exports` gains a built-layout assertion in the same spirit: it
walks every `.js` under `dist/lib`, and for any chunk that spells out a
bundle-relative shim specifier it requires at least one of them to resolve, from
that chunk's own directory, to a file that exists inside the published tree. It
strips comments before scanning and accepts only quoted string literals, since
the unminified library bundle ships every loader comment verbatim and one that
named the path in quotes would otherwise satisfy a naive grep — and because that
makes it a text-level check that could quietly self-disable, the build as a whole is
additionally required to name at least one specifier somewhere (a whole-build
total, not a named chunk: which chunk carries the loader is a code-splitting
detail, and every placement is still verified by the per-chunk check). The
ordinary
typescript-tests job does not build the library; `build:lib` runs in the
`release-readiness` job (and in `publish-npm.yml` on a tag), and this script is
the only thing that inspects the shipped layout there.

#### A bare `page.evaluate` in an E2E test can no longer eat the whole test budget

`page.evaluate` carries no timeout of its own — neither `actionTimeout` nor
`setDefaultTimeout` reaches it — so an evaluate the page never answers can only
be stopped by the whole Playwright test budget. On a software-rendering Linux
workstation that is not hypothetical: a run of `webgl-errors.spec.ts` sat for the
entire per-test budget inside the console-buffer probe in
`getConsoleMessages`, which at the time the shared fixture's
`assertNoConsoleErrors` teardown ran for every spec that imports `test` from
`./fixtures` (59 of the 67; the other 8 import `@playwright/test` directly and
get no fixture teardown). That fixture call is gone (#1760); the call sites the
bound now protects are the specs that gate on the in-page buffer from their own
`test.afterEach`, which get the same After-Hooks slot, plus the mid-test callers,
which share the test body's budget. Playwright reported it as
`Tearing down "page" exceeded the test timeout` pending
on that one line. The issue report saw the same wedge burn the two-minute budget
its own run allowed, and noted there that the page stayed alive throughout — the
viewer's own adaptive-DPR probe kept logging — it simply never got around to
running the injected function.

Instrumenting that wedge on the sharpness-showcase scene answers the other half
of the issue, which asked why it happens at all. On an otherwise idle box a
trivial `page.evaluate(() => 'ok')` went unanswered for its 5 s deadline twelve
times in a row, about 78 s of wall clock, while the page kept rendering. The
rendering evidence comes from two counter samples 28.0 s apart (t = 7315 ms and
t = 35338 ms) — a window _inside_ that stall, not a measurement across the whole
of it: over those 28 s `requestAnimationFrame` ticked 123 times and the
renderer's own `info.render.frame` counter advanced 246, i.e. ~4.4 rAF/s and
almost exactly the two `renderer.render()` calls per animation frame the default
two-pass pipeline issues. `visibilityState` stayed `visible` and the WebGL
context was never lost. An in-page `setInterval(…, 1000)` sampler over the same
28 s window fired twice.

So this is main-thread task starvation, not a stuck GL command buffer and not one
unlucky probe: a saturated software-rendering rAF loop schedules frames back to
back at ~230 ms apiece and the lower-priority task sources — in-page timers and
Playwright's `Runtime.callFunctionOn` round trip — starve for tens of seconds
while rendering continues. Whether that is task-source priority alone or sheer
queue depth is not settled here, and the arithmetic points at depth: under pure
priority the event loop still runs one task per turn, so at ~4.4 rendering
turns/s a `setInterval(…, 1000)` should still fire about once a second, and two
fires in 28 s is ~14x slower than that. That fits a deep backlog of
already-queued work better than priority does. The `OPFS timeout: set(...)
exceeded 10000ms` warnings arrive in the same window, and a flooded OPFS write
queue is a canonical producer of exactly such a backlog — which that single
instrumented run could not tell apart from a symptom, but a before-and-after can.

It largely was the cause, and saying so plainly is what keeps this change from
claiming more than it does. With #1647 — the OPFS circuit breaker and `?noOpfs`
kill switch, now on dev — merged in, the whole spec passed 10 of 10 in 58.8 s,
with two `OPFS timeout` lines in the run. Current dev _without_ this change fails
3 and passes 7, twice in a row, with 10 to 12 of those lines: one run's three
failures are the unbounded-evaluate signature (`page.evaluate: Test ended` after
the budget, plus `page.waitForFunction: Test timeout of 60000ms exceeded`), the
other's are a `Target page, context or browser has been closed` cascade. At the
pre-#1647 dev the same file failed 4 of 10 in 2.1 min with 9 such lines, and four
runs of this branch on that base failed 5, 5, 2 and 4 — the pass count varies run
to run on this box and the wedge moves from one test to another, so no single run
is a measurement. The OPFS write path is where this file's failures largely came
from, and #1647 is what removes most of them. What the bounds added here
contribute is narrower and orthogonal: when the page does starve, the failure now
arrives in seconds and names the probe that went unanswered, instead of consuming
the whole budget and then reporting nothing about where it went. This change is
not claimed to fix the spec's failures.

Three things follow for the tests. Bounding the evaluates is the right test-side
fix, since nothing the test does can make the page's own render loop yield. The
deadlines have to be generous, because the stall is environmental and outlasts
any bound that still fits inside a per-test budget — which also means any bound
can cut short a stall that would have ended, so the bound is a trade rather than
a free win. And zero observed render ticks is not by itself a failure: the
counter demonstrably advances during the stall, so what is starved is the
observation, and the only version of that worth a red test is a page that answers
promptly and a renderer that still is not drawing.

`getConsoleMessages` and the three bare evaluates in `webgl-errors.spec.ts` are
now bounded by the same `raceEvaluate` helper #1640 introduced for the
render-pacing waits: a race between the already-started evaluation and an
explicit deadline, resolving with a sentinel the in-page function can never
return so the call site can tell a real answer from a missed one. What a missed deadline _means_ is decided per call site.
`getConsoleMessages` throws after 45 s saying the page never answered the probe
and that the console-error check therefore could not run — deliberately not empty
buckets, which would have turned that gate into a vacuous pass for every spec
that calls it. 45 s rather than the whole budget because Playwright gives the
After Hooks phase a _fresh_ timeout slot equal to the per-test timeout (the
config's 60 s, or more in a file that raises its own), so an `afterEach` gate
always has that full slot no matter how much the body used: 45 s lands inside it, which is what makes the failure attributable to this
probe by name, while still leaving a wide margin for a page that recovers late. The
same default bounds the mid-test call sites, where the probe shares the body's
budget instead. The two detectors in the spec (the `gl.getError()` drain and the
geometry-buffer traversal) keep a 15 s bound and throw likewise, naming what went
unverified — their answers are what the tests assert on, so cutting them short
buys nothing — as does a page that answers but exposes no numeric frame counter
at all, since there is then nothing to confirm a render tick against. An
_unanswered_ counter probe is the starvation case instead, and is reported rather
than thrown. The per-tick kick is the one deliberately best-effort part: it is
counted, not asserted.

The same spec also stopped asking the render-pacing helper for frames it does not
guarantee. `waitForNextRender` is documented as best-effort and its fallback is
silent, so a detector could not tell a confirmed flush from a fallback, and a GL
error that only appears on the tenth draw might never get logged. A new
`tests/e2e/render-ticks.ts` module now kicks and confirms each tick in turn
against the renderer's own counter, with a 3 s per-tick bound _and_ a 10 s
aggregate budget for the whole flush — the per-tick bound alone was paid twice per
iteration and up to `ticks` times, so a ten-tick flush could have spent a whole
60 s per-test budget and reproduced the very timeout being fixed. Each wait is
clamped to whatever is left of the budget, and the report says when the budget is
what ended the loop — including the case where the wait that timed out was one the
remaining budget had clamped, which otherwise reports as an ordinary per-tick miss
and never mentions the budget at all. The aggregate bound is per CALL, so the one
test that loops over all five datasets in a single body passes a smaller one; the
comment there does the arithmetic and admits what it cannot fix, since five scene
loads in one test can exhaust that test's budget whatever the flush is bounded to.
A tick count that is not a positive integer is rejected outright instead of
producing a phantom zero-tick flush on a healthy page. The counter is
`info.render.frame`, which counts `renderer.render()` calls — about two per
animation frame with the default WebGL pipeline — and it is the same counter the
previous helper watched, so the numbers the detectors ask for are unchanged; only
the confirmation is new. (`WebGPURenderer` has no `info.render.frame`, so there
the probe falls to `info.frame`, which THREE advances from its own animation loop
whether or not anything was drawn; a confirmed tick is weaker on that backend, and
the module says so rather than pretending otherwise.) Living in its own module
rather than at the foot of the spec is what makes all of this unit-testable
against a fake page — `src/tests/unit/tests/e2e-render-ticks.test.ts` covers the
counting loop, the targets, the budget (both the clamped-wait case and the
per-tick miss that must _not_ blame it), the error re-throw rule and every verdict
branch, and executes the two injected in-page closures for real against a stubbed
`window` so that the baseline probe's wrapped answer and the `>= target` predicate
are not merely assumed.

A _partial_ flush is reported rather than failed (a strict version is reported in
#1652 to turn the healthy case red on a box rendering at the ~4.4 rAF/s measured
above) and the assertions still run
against whatever landed. A flush that confirmed nothing at all gets a verdict,
taken after the detector's own dump and assertion so a real GL error stays the
error you see, and taken from evidence rather than from the tick count: one
bounded probe re-reads the counter, the context-lost flag and
`document.visibilityState` in a single round trip, and the run only goes red when
the page answered that probe, the context is not reported lost, the flush had a
baseline, the counter still reads exactly that baseline, the page reports itself
`visible`, _and_ at least one kick was actually answered. That last condition
matters because the animation loop
auto-pauses after ~2 s of idleness: with no answered kick, nothing is confirmed to
have asked the renderer to draw and a frozen counter needs no renderer defect to
explain it. Everything else is a single warning naming which case it was — the
observation channel starved, so nothing can be said either way and the detector's
`page.on('console')` capture was unaffected regardless; or the counter did
advance, so only the per-tick confirmation was starved; or the counter came back
_below_ the baseline, which a monotonic counter cannot do and which means the
renderer was re-created, leaving nothing comparable; or the page is not visible, so
it is getting no animation-frame callbacks at all; or no kick was answered; or the
WebGL context reports itself lost, which `fixtures.ts` already allow-lists
as environmental and which freezes the counter by construction, THREE skipping
`renderer.render()` entirely while the context is gone. Where no WebGL context can
be read at all — `canvas.getContext('webgl2')` returns `null` on a canvas already
in `webgpu` context mode — the message says context loss is _unknown_ rather than
claiming it is false.

#### GSplats and lines chunk bounds no longer lose their extent at large coordinates

`chunk_bounds` is a float32 array while every pad the geometry builders add to it
is a small ABSOLUTE quantity — a gsplat's `coverage_sigma · σ`, a line segment's
full endpoint width, and the `_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS = 1e-3` float-boundary pad on a
categorical axis. Past `|x| ~ 2**23` a float32 ULP exceeds 1, so accumulating
`center ± extent` in float32 and storing it round-to-nearest lands straight back
on the unpadded coordinate: the stored bound comes out TIGHTER than the ellipsoid
or ribbon the renderer draws, and a query at an element's own edge simply does not
fetch its chunk. Nothing reports it — the element is missing, not wrong.

Points were fixed this way in #1658; the same treatment now covers the three
sibling builders. `compute_chunk_bounds_gsplats`, `compute_vertex_chunk_bounds`
and `compute_segment_chunk_bounds` accumulate their intervals in float64 and
narrow them to the float32 store with OUTWARD rounding — a bound is stepped one
ULP away from the interval, but only when the cast moved it the wrong way, so a
padless spatial vertex dimension still stores exactly its own coordinates. The
`_store_outward_f32` helper moved from `points.py` into the shared
`io/_ordering/bounds.py` alongside a vectorised `(d,)` form, and the four builders
now share one `slice_dims` sanitiser that raises on an index outside `[0, ndim)`
rather than each ignoring or crashing on it in its own way (an unresolvable
barrier index would silently cost that categorical axis its tight bounds).
`sort_splats_spatial` runs the same check, so a bad index fails before any splat
is reordered. A negative index in particular is a sort-side bug in its own right
(it lands in the barrier set AND in `ordering_dims`) and would be persisted raw
into the store's `slice_dims` attr, which the viewer then rejects wholesale.

Two consequences worth knowing. First, the effective barrier pad is now
`max(1e-3, one float32 ULP at |x|)`, so a unit-step categorical axis with large
absolute values — a millisecond timestamp, an acquisition index offset into an
experiment — over-fetches a whole neighbouring category above `|x| ≈ 2**23`. That
is the deliberate trade (over-fetching a neighbour beats dropping the chunk at its
own category value); re-base such an axis near the origin if the extra traffic
matters. Second, this can change the stored BYTES of a gsplats or lines spatial
index, so a rebuilt store may get a fresh `content_hash` and warm viewer caches
invalidate on their own. Not every array moves: a padless `vertex_chunk_bounds`
with no barrier dim at near-origin coordinates comes out byte-identical, because
the outward store is a no-op when the cast did not move the bound (the branch's
own test pins that). (Superseded for COMPILED stores by the quantisation pad
added in the same release: the compiler now also widens every bound by the
encoder's per-axis uint16 round-trip slack, which is nonzero on any non-gridded
axis, so a compiled `vertex_chunk_bounds` generally does move. The
byte-identical claim still holds for a direct call to the builder, which passes
no `coord_slack`.) `segment_chunk_bounds` and the gsplats `chunk_bounds` carry
a pad on every spatial axis, so those generally do change (near the origin, on
exactly-representable data, even a padded array can come out byte-identical). Existing stores are not
rewritten and keep their old, occasionally-too-tight bounds.

The write side is also where the reader-side documentation had drifted: the
gsplats tolerance computer's "coordinates far from the origin" limit described the
expansion being rounded away as a live hazard. It is now the stored coordinate
alone — a genuinely zero-variance dimension still yields a zero-width bound — and
the note says so.

#### Points and lines chunk bounds now contain the DECODED coordinates, not just the authored ones

A `chunk_bounds` interval is a promise to the reader: if a slice query does not
intersect it, that chunk is never fetched. The points and lines bound builders
computed the interval from the coordinates the writer was handed, but under the
default AUTO encoding those coordinates are then stored as per-axis uint16 fixed
point — so what the reader actually compares its query against is a coordinate
that can have moved half a quantum, `extent/131070`. On a 1000-unit axis that is
7.6e-3, some 125x the float32 ULP the outward-rounding store was added to
preserve, and far more than the `_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS = 1e-3` a categorical axis
gets. A chunk whose own extremum drifted outward is simply not fetched at that
edge, and nothing reports it: the geometry is missing, not wrong. Measured on
real compiles at an axis extent of 1000, 6 of 6 points chunks, 15 of 15 vertex
chunks and 5 of 5 segment chunks stored a bound their own decoded coordinates
escaped.

The encoder now answers the question directly.
`ArrayEncoder.coordinate_round_trip_slack(data, mode, *, allow_lut=True)` returns
the per-axis distance a COORDINATE write can move a value — `None` when the write
is exact on every axis — by replaying `_encode_coordinate`'s own exits without
writing anything and without repeating its warnings. PRECISION, an empty array
and an extent at or above the 2^16 float32 fallback are exact; per axis, a
constant axis is exact and so is a gridded one (the grid snap makes it round-trip
bit-exactly, and `gridded_axis_step` proves it by replaying the encode and the
decode); anything else gets the conservative half-quantum. A non-2D array
answers `None` because it is not the `(N, d)` shape the per-axis answer is
defined for — NOT because it is exact (a 1-D COORDINATE array is quantised like
any other), and the bound builders all require `(N, d)`. Non-finite input
answers `None` rather than a NaN entry that the bound validator would reject
with a message pointing at the wrong culprit. Keeping the predicate immediately
next to the encoder it mirrors is the point — the two cannot drift apart in
separate files.

`allow_lut` is the one exit the CALLER has to declare, and it mirrors
`ArrayEncoder.encode`'s parameter of the same name. A LUT stores values verbatim,
so a LUT-eligible array is exact — but only where the write is allowed to reach
for a LUT. The lines writer encodes `vertices` with `allow_lut=False` (the
spatial-index loader reads that array as raw chunked zarr), so a lines vertices
array with ≤256 distinct values is quantised on disk while looking eligible; the
lines glue passes `allow_lut=False` to match, and the points glue keeps the
default because `write_positions` does not block LUT and such a points node
genuinely stores `lut_uint8`. Measured on a 4D lines compile with a 250-value
irregular palette (60,000 segments / 120,000 vertices): treating eligibility as
exactness left 30 of 44 vertex chunks (8,203 rows) and 7 of 15 segment chunks
(487 endpoints) outside their own bound; declaring `allow_lut=False` takes all
four counts to zero. Those counts are that fixture's — the segment half in
particular depends on how the polylines are wired, and a connectivity that keeps
every endpoint interior shows the vertex half alone. The zero after the fix is
what holds regardless.

Because the predicate is asked on every compile, its cost is part of the fix.
The LUT probe is a whole-array `np.unique` and the dominant term whenever it
runs, so it is now gated twice. It is asked LAST — after the cheap exits and the
per-axis grid loop, and only when some axis came out with nonzero slack, since
otherwise the answer is `None` regardless — and it is asked only when no single
AXIS already holds more distinct values than a scalar-mode LUT can address
(`LUT_SCALAR_MAX_DISTINCT`, 256; a COORDINATE array is never the ≤4-channel 2-D
COLOR shape that reaches the uint16 ROW-mode tier). One column above that cap
proves the whole array cannot LUT-encode, because a column's distinct values are
a subset of the array's — and the count is free, since the grid loop's own
`np.unique` supplies it. On 1M×3 float32 continuous coordinates — the common
points path, which previously paid the probe in full — the predicate drops from
467 ms to 120 ms, and at 5M×3 from 3.41 s to 0.79 s, i.e. down to what the
`allow_lut=False` lines path always cost. An all-gridded array is 64 ms. The
irreducible case is an array with ≤256 distinct values per axis but more than
256 overall; only a whole-array pass can settle that one.

`compute_chunk_bounds_points`, `compute_vertex_chunk_bounds` and
`compute_segment_chunk_bounds` take a new keyword-only `coord_slack` vector and
add it outward on EVERY dimension, in float64 before the outward float32 store:
on top of the radius or width footprint on a spatial axis, and on top of
`_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS` on a barrier axis, because the epsilon is float-boundary
safety while the slack is a real displacement and the two add. The compiler fills
it in from the encoder for both geometries — for lines, one vector shared by both
bound sets, since they are both in D-space over the same vertices array. It
defaults to `None` (zero everywhere), so a direct caller of a builder still gets
authored-coordinate bounds byte for byte. A shared `_normalise_coord_slack`
validator rejects a wrong-length, negative or non-finite pad, the first because
the entries are positional per-axis quantities and the second because a negative
pad tightens the very bound it was meant to widen.

Because the slack is per-axis, an ordinary stacked integer time or channel axis
is untouched: it is grid-snapped, so it round-trips exactly, gets slack zero, and
keeps the tight barrier bound that stops a single-timepoint query pulling in its
neighbour. Only axes the encoder genuinely cannot store exactly pay anything. One
