consequence worth knowing: a rebuilt points or lines store generally gets
different `chunk_bounds` bytes and therefore a fresh `content_hash`, so warm
viewer caches invalidate on their own. Existing stores are not rewritten.

Keeping the two models in step is now a mechanism rather than a comment. The
writer carries a SECOND, independent model of what the encoder does — four
replayed exits — and this change's own history shows that is easy to get wrong
(the LUT exit was wrong for lines on the first attempt). A parametrised corpus
in `encoding/tests/test_coordinate_quant.py` therefore asks the predicate AND
performs a real encode/decode of the same array, for every mode × `allow_lut`,
and requires per-AXIS agreement in both directions: an axis the predicate calls
exact must be bit-exact on disk, and an axis it pads must not move further than
the pad (plus half a float32 ULP, the decode contract). Dropping the `allow_lut`
gate, dropping the grid snap, or giving `_encode_coordinate` a lossier tier each
turn it red.

GSplats close the corresponding decoded-center gap in the companion
`1870-gsplat-barrier-bound-slack` entry by applying the same encoder-reported
coordinate slack to their chunk bounds. The scalar half of points/lines
footprints is addressed by the companion entry on decoded radii and widths.

#### The gsplats reader now reads the barrier set the writer published, instead of re-deriving it (#1655 items 2 and 3)

`compute_chunk_bounds_gsplats` expands a chunk's bounds by `truncation_radius · σ`
on every dimension _except_ the ones it was told are barriers (time, channel), which
get only a tight `_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS` float-boundary pad. The viewer's chunk-fetch
tolerance depends on that split in opposite directions — a σ-expanded dimension wants
a near-zero float-safety epsilon (anything wider is pure over-fetch), a barrier-padded
one wants the quarter-cell reach — and the reader was deciding which was which on its
own, from `dimensions[d].discrete`.

The two agree whenever the scene declares its dimensions, because
`geometry_writers/gsplats.py::scene_barrier_dims` uses exactly `discrete and not
display`. They need not agree otherwise: with `scene_dimensions` absent (a standalone
`.gsplats.zarr` grafted into a scene) the writer falls back to the value-based
`detect_barrier_dims`, whose own docstring calls a false positive a correctness bug.
A really-spatial axis with integer, low-cardinality values then gets barrier-tight
bounds while the reader, seeing it as continuous, queries with a ~1e-3 epsilon — and
a spatially extended splat near a chunk edge is simply never fetched. The old
`step × 3.0` tolerance was wide enough to mask that; the epsilon that replaced it in
#1183 is not, which turned a latent disagreement into a documented precondition.

The writer already publishes the exact set it used, as the `slice_dims` group attr,
on every ordered gsplats leaf and every lightweight `additive_<i>` sub-LOD alike. The
loader now reads it and hands it to the tolerance computer as the authoritative
barrier set, so barrier-ness is settled by the party that made the decision rather
than inferred twice. An empty list is a real answer ("I ordered purely spatially,
nothing is a barrier") and is honoured as one. Barrier-ness is resolved in one shared
place, `isBarrierDim`, which honours the published set for GSPLATS ONLY. That scoping
is deliberate rather than an accident of who calls it: reading the set picks the rule
matching the chunk BOUNDS, which can narrow a window the renderer still draws, so each
arm owes its own floor first and only the gsplats arm has one. Lines' continuous arm is
a literal `0` (while its projection path keeps clipping against a half-cell slab) and
both of mesh's arms are membership gates, where narrowing changes what the user sees;
wiring either up is therefore a deliberate edit that has to add that floor. Points
classify from their own `spatialExtendDims` and are untouched.

Reading the published set decides which rule matches the chunk BOUNDS, and that is
all it decides. The per-splat gate for a hidden dimension is still built from the
scene's `discrete` flag (`data-processor-gsplats.ts` → the projection kernel's
`|Δ| ≤ step × 0.5` test), and a dimension in that set is routed to the binary
half-cell gate _only_ — `classifyHiddenDims` keeps it out of the continuous group, so
the Gaussian attenuation never runs on it. A dimension the writer OMITTED while the
scene declares it discrete therefore gets the half-cell as its FETCH window too, the
one place where a membership window and a chunk-fetch window have to be the same
number. Not the quarter-cell reach the barrier arm uses: that fraction is `0.25`
rather than `0.5` only because legacy stores pad barrier bounds by ±0.5 step and pad
plus reach must stay under a full step, and a dimension the writer never
barrier-padded has no such pad — a quarter would still have missed splats sitting 0.3
off a `step: 1` grid (what `gsplat merge --as-dimension --values 0.3,1.3,2.3` writes),
which are inside the render gate and outside a 0.25-cell window. The BARRIER arm keeps
that `(0.25, 0.5]` gap, deliberately: the pad budget is real there, and off-grid values
on a scene-declared discrete axis are a write-time authoring fault the compiler already
reports (`io/_compiler/finalize/validation.py::validate_discrete_dimension_ranges`
warns when such an axis's declared range sits more than a quarter step outside its
data).

Without that case, the dimension's fetch reach would have narrowed ~500× at `step = 1`
while the renderer still drew a half cell, and most of the node would have
disappeared — not all of it: with `slice_dims: []` the compound sort is a pure
spatial curve over every center column, so a chunk straddling two adjacent stacked
values still spans the query and matches, and what is lost is every chunk sitting
entirely inside one value. It also needs the scene's declared grid to be misaligned
with the stored values, since the query snaps to a multiple of the step while the
splats sit where they were written; an axis whose values are multiples of its step has
offset 0 and matches even on the bare epsilon.

The path that actually reaches the arm is the STANDALONE OPEN, not a graft. Serving a
`.gsplats.zarr` directly (`?src=….gsplats.zarr`, which the writer enables by stamping
`layer` on the root) leaves the scene with no `scene_dimensions`, so
`load-scene.ts::synthesizeSceneDimensionsFromNode` marks every axis ≥ 3
`discrete: true, step: 1` regardless of the stored values, while the store publishes
whatever its own value-based `detect_barrier_dims` found — `[]` for a stacked axis whose
values are not near-integers. Scene-discrete, writer-omitted: demote. GRAFTING such a
store into a scene does not reach it, because `add_gsplats_from_file_impl` routes
through `add_gsplats_from_data_impl` / `graft_gsplat_node`, both of which write through
the scene gsplats writer, which re-sorts and RE-STAMPS `slice_dims` from
`scene_barrier_dims` (`discrete and not display`) — so an axis the scene declares
discrete and non-displayed comes back inside the set and lands on the barrier arm.

The promote direction needs no such window, and not because it only widens: it
replaces `max(1e-3 × step, T × 1e-5)` with `0.25 × step`, which is narrower whenever
`step < 4e-5 × T` (≈1.1e-4 at the default radius — a 110× narrowing at
`step = 1e-6`). It is safe because `_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS = 1e-3` is an ABSOLUTE pad, not
a step fraction: the writer, having listed the dimension, already extended its bounds
by 1e-3 either side, which dwarfs the `T × 1e-5` band the renderer can draw there for
any `T < 100`, so even a zero tolerance would match. Being absolute is also why that
argument cannot be ported to a geometry whose bounds are not barrier-padded.

Be precise about what this fixes. The writer can still pick the _wrong_ barrier set —
that is a write-side bug and it still produces bounds tighter than the splats' true
extent. What is gone is the reader independently disagreeing with whatever the writer
chose, which is the half that was silent and unfixable from either side alone. A
legacy store that publishes no `slice_dims` still falls back to `discrete`, and the
attr is validated all-or-nothing: anything that is not an array of integers in
`[0, ndim)` is discarded whole. Filtering it element-wise would drop a genuine barrier
dimension and _narrow_ the fetch window — the exact failure the plumbing exists to
prevent — whereas falling all the way back reproduces the previous behaviour exactly,
so no store ends up worse off than before the attr was read.

The same call site closes the second, smaller gap. The tolerance's degenerate-band
term is `truncation_radius × 1e-5`: the read side regularizes an all-zero hidden
covariance block to a pivot of `sqrt(CHOLESKY_EPSILON)`, so such a splat still renders
out to that distance, and the fetch window has to cover it. The term was pinned to the
default radius of 2.75 because the computer only ever saw a `DimensionInfo`, leaving
`(2.75e-5, T × 1e-5]` uncovered for a node stamping a larger `T` — little visible was
lost in practice (the old window edge sits at 2.75 σ of the regularized pivot, where
attenuation is ≈2.3%), but the limit was real. The node's
own radius now travels with the query, sanitized through the same
`clampTruncationRadius` the material path uses, so the band the query covers is by
construction the band the renderer draws rather than a second, independently-derived
number. That clamp gained a non-number branch to make the identity hold for an attr
that is not a number at all: `truncation_radius: "6"` passes every numeric test in it
by coercion (`"6" * "6" === 36`), so the string used to be handed straight to the
`uTruncate` uniform — a 6σ material band against a 2.75σ fetch band, the very gap
being closed. A non-number now falls back to the default on both paths.

Tying the band to the node's radius also gives it no ceiling, and that is documented
rather than capped. A node stamping `truncation_radius: 1e18` — finite, and a legal
authored value on both sides of the contract, since `clampTruncationRadius` and the
write-side `MAX_TRUNCATION_RADIUS_FLOAT32` share the same `sqrt(float32.max)` ≈ 1.84e19
bound — yields a fetch window of ~1e13, i.e. the whole node. Capping it would be the
wrong fix, because the material draws that same band: a cap would re-create exactly the
fetch-narrower-than-render under-fetch this change removes. The remedy is not to author
such a node.

#### A points chunk written without radii is now bounded by the radius it is actually drawn with

`compute_chunk_bounds_points` expands each chunk's spatial bounds by the point
radius, which makes `[min - r, max + r]` exactly the set of query positions for
which some point in the chunk can still be visible — right in both directions,
not merely wide enough. That held only when the node carried a `radii` array.
With `radii=None` the bound was padded by an unrelated fudge instead — 1% of the
chunk's own coordinate range, floored at 0.01 — which bears no relation to the
0.5 the renderer falls back to: tighter than the footprint for any chunk
spanning less than 50 units, looser than it above that, and different for the
same scene authored in micrometres and in millimetres.

The tight case really did drop points, on a hidden continuous spatial dimension
— displayed dims and `extend_to_all` dims query with a tolerance of `1e10`
(`data/points/effective-radius-calculator.ts`), so the pad is inert there, and a
discrete axis never got radius extent on either the old or the new path. On such
a dimension a node with no `radii` array carries no `max_radius` attribute either
— the writer stamps that only alongside radii — so the viewer's spatial-index
query falls back to `defaultMaxRadius = 0.1`. A total reach of
`0.01 + 0.1 = 0.11` against a 0.5 disc leaves a point near a chunk boundary
genuinely unfetched, with nothing to notice it had gone.

Absent radii now simply mean the default radius: the no-radii case reuses the
scalar-radius path with `DEFAULT_POINT_RADIUS`, and the two produce identical
bounds. Barrier/discrete axes are unaffected — they still get only the tiny
`_BARRIER_BOUND_EPS` float-boundary pad on every path, because a categorical
axis has no footprint to cover.

The writer path that sees `radii=None` is `write_points_multi_lod`, reached
whenever `add_points` builds an additive ladder before the authoring default is
materialized — via `additive_lod=`, via the default stream ladder that
`substitutive_lod=` composes for its finest child, or via `partition=` parts that
carry a ladder of their own. `LuxarZarrCompiler.write_points(..., radii=None)` is
the low-level door. A plain `add_points` (and a bare `partition=`, whose parts
recurse back through it) fills in `DEFAULT_POINT_RADIUS` first, so those write a
uniform radius rather than none.

A second, independent hole is closed along the way, and this one affects nodes
that *do* carry radii. `chunk_bounds` is a float32 array while the pad added to
it is a small absolute quantity, so past `|x| ~ 2**23` a round-to-nearest store
drops the pad entirely and the stored bound comes out tighter than the footprint
— a 0.5 radius, an authored 0.05 one, and the removed 1%-of-range fudge alike
(1% of a 10-unit chunk is 0.1 against a half-ULP of 1.0 at `|x| = 2e7`). Each
interval is now accumulated in float64 and narrowed to the store with outward
rounding, which restores "never tighter than the footprint" at any coordinate
magnitude, on every radius path. A points node authored in nm over a ~10 mm
field sits exactly in this range.

The 0.5 itself is now owned by `luxar.typing_utils.constants` instead of being
restated at each site. `add_points` (which materializes it when a caller
supplies no radii), the chunk-bounds writer and the viewer sites that stand in
for a missing radii array all read one constant per language, with the usual
mirror note and tests on both sides naming each other.

Only the write side changes here. For a radii-less node the reader still runs no
per-point effective-radius cull and still queries with the 0.1 tolerance
fallback, so an honest (wider) bound means more chunks fetched AND drawn — the
right trade against the old under-fetch. Shrinking the reader's tolerance to a
float-safety epsilon now that the bounds are honest is tracked as items 2 and 3
of issue #1655; those will have to account for stores written before this
change, which keep the old tight bounds and carry no version stamp to tell them
apart, so the reader cannot simply assume every bound already includes the
footprint.

#### A fit now records how well it reconstructed the signal, not just the volume

Global PSNR is a poor summary of a sparse fit. On a synthetic volume that is
99.9% empty — the shape a light-sheet stack has — a reconstruction that discards
nine tenths of the signal still scores 37 dB, because most of what it got right
was the emptiness. Every fit
now also records `foreground_psnr_db` — the same PSNR, averaged over
`target > otsu(target)` instead of over everything — which scores that same
reconstruction at 0.9 dB.

Alongside it go `foreground_threshold` and `foreground_fraction`, because a dB
figure taken over 0.01% of a volume means something quite different from one
taken over 40%, and a reader cannot tell which they are looking at otherwise.
`gsplat info` and `gsplat compare` print all three; the trio lands in
`fitting/` beside the global figure.

A metric that comes out undefined is now omitted from the store rather than
written. A volume with no foreground at all (a constant tile, a signal-free
crop) gives a `nan` foreground PSNR, and zarr serializes that as a bare `NaN`
token — which is not JSON, and which cost a strict reader the whole metadata
document, not just the one number. The same already applied to the `+inf`
global PSNR of an exact reconstruction. `foreground_fraction: 0.0` stays, so
the store still says why the dB figure is absent.

Foreground is defined on the *target*, so a fit that hallucinates structure is
still scored where the signal actually is, and `data_range` is taken from the
whole volume rather than from the foreground's own narrower span — matching
`held_out_psnr_foreground`, and avoiding an inflation that would otherwise be
invisible.

Otsu's threshold is computed in `luxar.gsplats.metrics` rather than delegated
to scikit-image. That library lives in the `demos` extra, and the existing
calibration helper quietly falls back to `V.min()` when the import fails —
tolerable for a seeding heuristic, not for a number that gets published, since
the *definition* of foreground would then depend on which extras happened to be
installed. The reimplementation is pinned against `skimage.filters.threshold_otsu`
to the exact histogram bin.

#### The demo records cannot be published by accident, and cannot mis-state a license

A Zenodo record carries one license field, so the demo datasets are grouped
into records by license family while each keeps its own true license alongside.
That model was documented and correct but unenforced, and the failure it admits
is quiet: a ShareAlike dataset filed under the CC-BY record would be offered
under terms its source does not allow, and nothing would say so until someone
downloaded it.

A gate now checks that every hosted dataset names a real record, that its
license is one the record's family can actually offer (public-domain
dedications qualify — a record's license is a floor, not a claim), that nothing
marked non-redistributable or carrying NonCommercial terms or an unresolved
license is hosted at all, and that every hosted dataset credits its source.
`gsplats_tribolium`, whose license is recorded as an outright authority
conflict, and `milky_way_gaia_3m`, which is CC BY-NC, are the live cases this
keeps out.

It also pins `published: false` on all three records. Whether the drafts go
public is the maintainer's decision, taken by hand on Zenodo; a change that
flipped it here would now land in a test first.

#### Datasets say what they were fitted from, at the level where the comparison is honest

The compression figure on a Zenodo record has two halves: against the raw
voxels of the source grid, and against that source *as stored*. The first is
stamped per archive at fit time. The second cannot be, because a dataset is
often several archives — one per channel — fitted from a single file, and only
the dataset as a whole is comparable to the acquisition as a whole.

So the manifest now carries a dataset-level `acquisition` block: what the
source actually is, and either its stored size or the reason no honest ratio
exists. Four datasets take the second route, each for a different mechanism:
`cmu1_pathology` reads one level of a multi-level slide pyramid and resizes it,
`ct_totalsegmentator` repacks a multi-scan subset, `visible_human_head`
converts colour photographs to a greyscale volume, and `nexrad_supercell`
re-grids one moment out of polar sweeps carrying several. In each case the
stored size measures something other than compression, and quoting it would
repeat an error already corrected once.

A gate enforces it: every Zenodo-hosted gsplat dataset either declares an
acquisition or appears on a shrinking list, a `comparable: true` promise must
produce a positive `stored_bytes`, and an incomparable one must argue its case
and must not carry a denominator that could get quoted anyway. The selector
works by bucket rather than by name, so a dataset promoted from
`local-compute` to `zenodo` joins the hosted set and fails the gate on its own.

#### A demo's LOD topology is now chosen, not inherited from its fitter

Whether a cached demo artifact shipped a streaming ladder used to depend on
which fitter the demo called. `GSplatData` carries `additive_sublods`, the
progressive fitter returns several as a by-product of its passes, and
`fit_gaussian_splats` returns exactly one — so the five shipped archives with no
ladder were precisely the joint-fitted ones. None of the twenty-one carried a
substitutive level at all.

`luxar.demos._lod_policy` makes the choice explicit and shares the per-recipe
parameters, so two demos asking for the same topology cannot drift apart. Six
demos now route their cache write through it: `cryoem_virus` and `milky_way_dust`
take coarse→fine `levels`, being large single objects that get orbited;
`cmu1_pathology` takes `adaptive` spatial tiles, being a 33000×46000 slide that
gets panned and zoomed; `nexrad_supercell`, `ct_totalsegmentator` and
`visible_human_head` take a plain `stream` ladder. The choice applies from the
next refit onwards: the hosted archives keep whatever topology they were written
with until they are refitted and reuploaded, since the manifest pins their
checksums.

Being a large orbited object is necessary but not sufficient for `levels` —
`ct_totalsegmentator` and `visible_human_head` are both that and both take
`stream`, because a topology only reaches the scene through
`add_gsplats_from_data` (handed the whole `GSplatData`, whose matrix form holds
the levels) or `add_gsplats_from_file` (grafted node-for-node). Those two rebuild
their scene from loose `centers=`/`amplitudes=` arrays instead — the atlas masks
per tissue supergroup, the head carries a per-splat colours sidecar — and plain
`add_gsplats` writes a flat leaf, measured: no `kind`, no child groups, whether
the archive was written `stream` or `levels`. `levels` there would have bought
nothing and cost the +38% below. `stream` is the floor rather than "no ladder"
because a prefix ladder is the same splats regrouped, so it is essentially free
and still honoured by `luxar gsplat view` on the archive itself.

Choosing `adaptive` changes how a demo READS its own cache, which is the part
that does not announce itself: a `kind=partition` store has no flat matrix form,
so `GSplatData.load` — and `load_dataset_gsplats`, which ends in that same call —
refuses it. cmu1 now fetches paths and grafts each channel with
`add_gsplats_from_file`. Two incidental things go with it. The scene keeps slide
pixel coordinates instead of re-centring on a shared centroid (the three channels
are fits of the same image on the same grid, so they were never out of alignment,
and the viewer frames on the bounding-box centre either way), and the old
per-channel `scale_intensity(0.1)` is dropped as the no-op it was — a colormapped
gsplat layer is windowed by its own `amplitude_data_range`, so a global amplitude
scale cancels. `load_dataset_gsplats` now says all of this when handed a
partition, instead of surfacing a bare "node is not matrix-shaped".

Substitutive levels cost bytes, and the honest figure is worth stating: on
ct_atlas (660,934 splats) `levels` takes 9,635 KB where `stream` takes 6,966 KB,
so +38%. The same comparison on a 743-splat fit reads 3.6×, which is
per-zarr-group overhead rather than data — a difference recorded next to the
policy, since the misleading number is the easier one to measure.

#### The Zenodo record descriptions are generated from the data

The three demo records describe several dozen files between them, each with a
splat count, a compression figure, a reconstruction quality and a licence. Typed
by hand those drift from the data within one refit, and a record is the one place
where a stale number is published rather than merely wrong.

`scripts/gen_zenodo_records.py` derives the text instead: disposition and
licensing from the manifest, per-file characteristics from each archive's own
`fitting/` stamps, with anything unstamped printed as absent rather than guessed.
`--check` turns the same read into a work list of rows that would publish
incomplete. The script never contacts Zenodo — it writes markdown for a human to
paste, and publication remains a manual act.

A timelapse bundle — an outer zip of per-frame stores — is described whole: the
splat counts and source bytes are summed over every frame and the reconstruction
quality is quoted as the range across them. Reading the first frame alone put
`celegans_s1` at 15,721 splats instead of 5,485,103 and quoted its best frame's
PSNR as the archive's. Datasets that list their archives under size `variants`
(the h2afva timelapse, whose record is the whole point) are resolved through
those variants rather than rendering as "no files uploaded yet".

Two further claims it would otherwise have made falsely are now impossible. An
`.npz` is also a zip and a point-cloud `.luxar.zarr` is also a zarr store, so
both parsed as splat stores and came back defaulted — one dataset was described
as having "single level" detail when it holds no splats at all. The reader
identifies the format before describing it, and datasets that are not fits get a
plain file list rather than a table of dashes implying unmeasured figures. The
mirror image also holds: a declared fit whose archive is not on this machine (an
unpulled LFS file, a demo never fetched) keeps its place in the splat table with
its figures absent, and `--check` says how many rows it could not read instead of
reporting a clean bill of health having read nothing.

#### A fit in physical coordinates still gets a PSNR

`output_space="real"` is the default, so a fit handed a `voxel_size` returned
splats in physical coordinates — and the post-fit quality metrics were skipped
outright, because those coordinates no longer matched `config.V`'s grid. Ten
demos pass a `voxel_size`, so ten cached archives were being written with no
`psnr_db` at all and, since the foreground metric landed, no
`foreground_psnr_db` either.

The conversion is a pure per-axis rescale of centers and Cholesky rows with
amplitudes untouched, so the pre-conversion arrays describe the same mixture on
the fitted grid. They are kept and scored; the caller still receives physical
coordinates. It costs one round-trip render — the same one the voxel-space path
has always paid, but genuinely new work on a real-space fit, which did none
before, and once per tile on a real-space tiled fit.

A test asserted the old behaviour — that the metrics were skipped — which had
quietly turned the defect into a contract. It now asserts the metrics are
present, and that the returned centers are still physical so the scoring copy
cannot leak back. A new equivalence test scores the same fit through both output
spaces and requires the same PSNR, under a deliberately anisotropic voxel size:
an isotropic one would hide a per-axis bug in the row-by-row Cholesky scaling.

`fit_tiled` remains without a merged-volume PSNR of its own — the tiles overlap
and are apodized, so per-tile errors do not compose into the merged one.

#### A tiled fit scores the archive it actually ships

Every tile of a tiled fit scores itself, but the tiles overlap and are
Hann-apodized, so their errors do not compose into the merged one — and the
merged result is what gets written. A tiled archive therefore carried no
`psnr_db` and no `foreground_psnr_db` at all, which is precisely what a
published dataset is asked to state.

`fit_tiled` now renders the merged reconstruction once against the whole volume
it still has in hand and stamps the metrics. When the fit returned physical
coordinates the merged splats are first mapped back onto the tile grid: the two
frames differ by one per-axis factor that scales centers directly and Cholesky
row `i` by `scale[i]`, so dividing both inverts it exactly. That inverse is the
part worth testing, and it is: the same fit scored with and without the
conversion must agree, which a mutation collapses from 46 dB to 25 dB.

Scoring is capped because it runs *before* the archive is written, so an
over-budget score does not cost a metric — it costs the whole fit. The default
budget is half the memory actually free, held under a 24 GiB ceiling, so a fit on
a laptop is not licensed by a constant that describes a workstation;
`LUXAR_TILED_QUALITY_MAX_GB` overrides both (`0` declines scoring outright, and a
value that cannot be read falls back with a note rather than taking the run
down). The cap is measured against the real peak, which sits inside SSIM rather
than at the render: the reconstruction, the reference, and the convolution
intermediates SSIM keeps live, whose own tiled fallback engages on CUDA only.
When the cap declines, or the score fails,
it says so out loud even under `--quiet` — an archive that silently carries no
PSNR is the failure this exists to end. Two cases are deliberately left unscored
and say why, printing under `--quiet` for the same reason: a `kind=partition`
merge, whose tree node has no fit-stats dict to stamp and which this path saves
without threading any through, and the parallel worker path, which is handed only
the tile grid's shape and not the volume. `luxar gsplat compare` is the recourse
for both, and it reads the written archive whatever its shape — a
`kind=partition` included. Content-adaptive tiling (`--tiling content`) goes
through the planner and is untouched here; it still stamps no merged metric.

#### Per-splat sidecars are written in the store's own splat order (#1670)

Two demos ship a per-splat payload as a separate `.npz` sidecar indexed
positionally against a cached `.gsplats.zarr` fit — the organ label per splat in
`demo_gsplats_3d_ct_totalsegmentator` (which drives the colors, the per-tissue
toggle layers *and* the hover tooltips) and the sampled RGB per splat in
`demo_gsplats_3d_visible_human_head`. Both sampled that payload at the in-memory
fit's centers *before* writing it. But the write (`save_with_lod`, which ends in
`GSplatData.save`) applies a spatial ordering (`ordering="hilbert"` by default),
so `GSplatData.load()` hands the splats back under a different permutation:
measured on a fresh 1606-splat fit, 1605 of 1606 rows move. `payload[i]` then
describes some other splat entirely, and nothing anywhere raises — the demo
renders plausible nonsense.

Both demos now save the fit FIRST, reload it, and sample the payload at the
RELOADED centers, then return that reloaded fit alongside the sidecar. The pair
is aligned by construction under any writer ordering (hilbert, morton, none, or
the streaming LOD ladder these demos now write), and the `--recompute` path now
returns exactly what the cached path will load on the next run — not only the
sidecar's uint8 quantization but the `EncodingMode.MEMORY` fit itself. That mode
quantizes everything it stores: centers to a per-axis uint16 fixed-point code,
amplitudes and Cholesky factors to a uint8/uint16 tier chosen from their own
distribution. Centers included — a fresh off-lattice fit round-trips with an
error up to half a uint16 step, and the shipped fits look exact only because
they have already been through that code once. Which strengthens the point
rather than weakening it: there is no attribute for which "the in-memory fit"
and "what the next run loads" are the same array, so returning the reloaded
store is the only way the two paths agree — they now read the same stored bytes.

Alignment is also now CHECKED on load rather than assumed, by
`luxar.demos.voxel_sampled_payload_agreement`. Both payloads come from
nearest-voxel sampling, which gives an exact O(N log N) invariant: two splats
whose centers round to the same voxel must carry the same payload row. Correct
data scores exactly 1.000, and the 0.99 threshold is deliberately TIGHT rather
than generous: a full shuffle only falls to the payload's own chance level
`Σ p²` — which is payload-dependent (0.027 for the CT's 117 organ labels,
1.4e-05 for the Visible Human's sampled uint8 RGB) — but the failures worth
catching are NEAR MISSES, and those land just under the gate. Measured on the
shipped CT pair (660,934 splats), permuting its aligned sidecar the way each
mistake would have written it: a different space-filling curve (the writer's own
morton order instead of hilbert) scores 0.901, a roll-by-one 0.955, an
adjacent-pair swap 0.962. Do not loosen it — a test now pins the constant above
the worst of those. A cached or shipped pair that fails (or whose
lengths disagree) is reported with the two file names and the measured
agreement, and the demo falls through to its existing download-and-refit path
instead of rendering it. Where a fit is too sparse for enough splats to share a
voxel the helper returns `None` and the pair is accepted *and reported* — the
demo names it as accepted UNVERIFIED — because unverifiable is not a failure,
but it is not silent either.

`scripts/reencode_gsplat_demos.py` now REFUSES both sidecar-bearing datasets.
Its `--apply` path reorders a fit in place (`flatten` + `lod --recipe stream`)
and has never touched the `.npz` beside it, so running it was itself a way to
recreate this bug.

The invariant was measured against both originally shipped artifacts. The CT one
was already aligned (agreement 1.000 over 660,934 splats — re-sampling the
rebuilt label volume at the stored centers reproduces `ct_atlas_labels.npz`
exactly). The Visible Human one exposed the bug at agreement 0.00097 over
1,911,192 splats, against a measured full-shuffle baseline of 2.85e-05. Its fit
was sound but the sidecar order was not; the companion Visible Human changelog
entry records the regenerated sidecar and restored fast path.

#### `--floor auto` no longer crashes on a float32 volume with a large offset

`estimate_floor(..., method="mode")` — the estimator behind the default
`--floor auto` — histogrammed the sub-p95 background band in the input dtype. On a
float32 volume whose background sits at a large offset (e.g. a raw microscope
pedestal of ~30000), 512 bins across that narrow band were finer than float32 can
represent and NumPy raised `ValueError: Too many bins for data range`, aborting the
fit. The band is now histogrammed in float64, which has the dynamic range to place
the bins — including the degenerate case of a band that is one repeated value. On
data float32 could already bin the floor is the same level: the float64 edges are
only re-rounded, so the peak bin moves at most in a near-tie, by well under the
pedestal's own noise.

#### The WebGL default path stops downloading the WebGPU renderer

The production default backend is WebGL, but every session — WebGPU or not — was
fetching and parsing the entire three.js node system before first paint.
`dist/index.html` `modulepreload`ed the `three-webgpu` chunk and the entry chunk
imported it statically, so roughly a quarter of the initial JavaScript was a
renderer that only runs when someone passes `?renderer=webgpu`.

The whole TSL cone now hangs off a single `await import()` in
`rendering/tsl/load.ts`, reached only from `SceneManager.setupWebGPURenderer()`.
Measured on the production build, the eagerly-loaded JavaScript drops from
794 kB to 598 kB gzipped — **196 kB, about a quarter, off the critical path** —
with no change to what either backend renders.

Getting there meant cutting six independent static edges, not one. The
`MaterialManager` dispatch tables hold thunks instead of classes; the
`ShaderSource.webgpu` closures stay next to their GLSL twin but obtain their
factory from the registry instead of importing it; `material-sync-helpers.ts`
identifies material families by structural probe rather than `instanceof` on TSL
classes; `erfPolyTSL` moved out of `erf.ts`, whose pure-CPU `erfRef` was pulling
`three/tsl` into the GLSL gsplat material; and `createWebGPURenderer` imports the
renderer class inside the function that needs it. The nine TSL material classes
keep their ordinary `extends NodeMaterial` shape — only the module graph above
them changed, so no test needed to become async.

The last edge was not in the source at all. `three.core.js` is shared by
`three.module.js` and `three.webgpu.js`, and with no chunk group of its own it
landed such that the plain `three` chunk imported `three-webgpu` — pinning the
WebGPU system into the eager graph while every source file was already clean.
`vite.config.ts` now splits the shared core into its own `three-core` chunk.

Two gates keep it from coming back, because those two failure modes need
different instruments. An ESLint `no-restricted-imports` rule bans value imports
of `three/webgpu` and `three/tsl` outside the registry (type-only imports stay
legal). And `scripts/check-eager-chunks.mjs`, chained into `pnpm build`, asserts
against the built `dist/` that nothing statically reachable from the entry
imports the chunk — and that the chunk still exists, so deleting WebGPU support
is not a way to pass. Both were verified to fail on the real regressions before
being trusted; a dependency-cruiser rule was tried first and dropped once it
turned out it could never fire, since that config excludes `node_modules` from
its graph.

#### Offline capture stops fighting the render loop

Waking the animation loop for the duration of a smooth turntable or EXR sequence —
which is what made the camera rotate at all — had a cost nobody had looked at: every
tick ended in a full post-processing pass whose result was thrown away, because each
captured frame runs its own independent pipeline pass into an offscreen target. The
readback of that pass is asynchronous, so the loop ticked many times inside every
captured frame. For an EXR sequence it was worse than wasted work: the capture holds
global raw-HDR shader flags (effects off, no tone mapping) across the await, and the
capture overlay's scrim is translucent, so the viewport visibly flickered between the
normal image and a blown-out one for the whole sequence.

The loop now skips only its own render while an offline capture is driving the pipeline.
Controls and every per-frame callback still run each tick — the depth-sort scheduler and
the LOD group selector have to follow the orbiting camera, which is why the loop must run
in the first place. The suppression is offline-only: the real-time recording path
records the canvas the loop paints, and silencing it there would produce an empty
video. The trade-off is stated plainly: the viewport behind the translucent capture
overlay goes dark for the duration, not merely static — bringing the capture
resolution up already resized the render target, which cleared the canvas, and now
nothing repaints it. Progress is the overlay's own preview canvas, which shows each
captured frame; an EXR sequence never sets that preview, so it shows the frame counter
alone. That is what the viewport looked like before the loop was woken for a capture
at all, minus the flicker.

The capture's teardown also guarantees a repaint now. Restoring the recording state
resizes the render target back, which clears the canvas, and by that point the
keep-alive callback is gone — so a loop that was still stopped, or that the idle timer
halted in the gap right after the resize, left the viewer blank until the next mouse
move.

The confirmation dialog's promised frame count was rounded before it was multiplied,
while the capture loop and the panel's own Output field both use the unrounded
duration. At 7°/s and 30 FPS the dialog promised 1530 frames and a 51-second video
against the 1543 frames the capture actually produces; all three now agree.

Finally, the shared animation-controller test double never ran per-frame callbacks at
all — it was four bare stubs with no loop state — which made it structurally blind to
the class of bug that caused all of this: deleting the loop wake-up from the real-time
recording path failed none of the recording-panel tests. The double now models the real
stopped-loop semantics — only `startAnimation()` starts the loop, registering a
callback never does, and callbacks run only while it is running — and records the
`continuous` option, so the keep-alive that holds the loop open past the two-second
idle timer is asserted rather than assumed.

#### The pick pass no longer depends on which fragment entry point three builds first (#1683)

`colorNode` and `depthNode` are two independent fragment entry points of one
NodeMaterial, and a TSL value materialised with `.toVar()` is assigned wherever
three first BUILDS it — which entry point that is is not part of three's API. The
gsplat and mesh pick factories both share their whole fragment chain between the
two (the Mahalanobis/intensity/brightness chain on gsplats, coverage/near-fade/
brightness on mesh) and both have a BRANCHING `depthNode`, the `uSurfaceDepth`
convention selector. When the depth flow is built first, that branch becomes the
first build site: three lowers it to a real `if`/`else` and the shared assignments
land inside one arm, while every top-level reader — both `Discard` conditions and
the output vec4 — reads a variable that was never assigned, i.e. `0`. The result is
not a subtle artefact: every pick fragment discards, the pick buffer comes back
empty, and hover and click stop working entirely on the WebGPU path.

Each factory now assigns every value the two entry points share in a `'void'`-typed
`Fn` prologue invoked as the FIRST statement of both of them, so the assignments are
emitted in unconditional top-level flow whichever flow three emits first. On mesh
that includes the alpha-cutout flag, read by both the prologue's brightness select and
`colorNode`'s cutout discard. Left free-standing it was still materialised — three
gives a select's condition its own `bool` — so it was never duplicated, but its first
build site moves into the arm under the depth-first order just like the rest, and then
the top-level cutout discard reads `false` and stops discarding anything at all.
Assigning it in the prologue brings the last shared value under the guard too.
The three sibling pick factories (points, lines, capsule lines) keep their shared
brightness var: their
`depthNode` is branchless, so the assignment lands at top level either way — each
one now says so at the site, together with the note that adding a branch there needs
the same prologue treatment.

The gsplat prologue's fragcoord reconstruction and its centre delta are `.toVar()`s
too now, like every value around them, so the whole prologue is a statement list
rather than one subexpression re-expanded at each of its six uses. Same arithmetic,
shorter generated fragment (its snapshot moves accordingly).

The runtime pin does not move here — `three` stays at `~0.184.0`, whose colour-first
build order was never affected — so nothing about the shipped renderer changes with
this fix. What it removes is the blocker in front of the r185 bump, where the order
flip is what turned a latent hazard into a dead pick pass. (That bump followed
separately, and the runtime is now on r185.)

A codegen guard comes with it, over all four pick shaders that expose a named shared
var (gsplat, mesh, line, capsule line). The TSL snapshot spec now parses the generated
pick fragment's `main()` body, tracks the brace depth of every line, and asserts two
things: every assignment sits at depth 0, and the first READ comes after the first
assignment that is not the dead `NAME = 0.0;` initialiser three emits for a
`float(0.0).toVar(name)` declaration. It is keyed on the explicit `.toVar('name')`
names rather than three's generated `nodeVarN` numbering, and fails with the remedy
(compute it in the fragment prologue).

The two halves have different reach, and which one is live depends on the runtime
revision. At r184 the read-order half is the live one: dropping the
`fragmentPrologue()` call, or moving a reader above it, leaves the value holding its
declaration default and the assertion says so. The brace-depth half is the inert one
there — colour-first order builds even the pre-fix free-standing `.toVar()`s at top
level — and it is the one that goes live once the runtime moves to r185, which trades
the two around rather than arming both. Both run in the FULL E2E suite
(`make test-e2e`), not in the mobile-only `e2e-tests` job or the narrow
`tsl-parity` job, which deliberately excludes the codegen snapshot. The mesh spec's
TSL house rule grew a third clause to match.

#### Three.js runtime moves to r185, closing the one-minor type/runtime skew

`three` was held at `~0.184.0` while `@types/three` sat a minor ahead at `~0.185.1` —
a deliberate skew, because the r184 definitions reject a correct componentwise
`pow(vec3, vec3)` in the capsule-line shader and the r185 ones do not. The runtime
could not follow because r185 broke the TSL path in four measurable ways, most
starkly a gsplat pick surface that rendered zero pixels. #1697 root-caused all four
to one bug of ours — pick shaders sharing fragment values across `colorNode` and
`depthNode`, so they depended on which entry point three built first, and r185 flipped
that order — and fixed it by assigning every shared value in an unconditional prologue.

With the blocker gone, the runtime is now `~0.185.1` and both pins sit on the same
minor. The shaders still measure clean at r184 *and* r185: the fix removed the
dependency on build order rather than adapting to r185's, so `tsl-shader-parity` +
`tsl-codegen-snapshot` were 101 passed at both revisions. What the bump changes is
which revision the checked-in snapshots pin.

All 74 generated-shader snapshots were regenerated, and the diff is presentational
throughout: the `r184` header line, a new empty `structs` section, the `object` and
`render` std140 blocks swapping order with the `nodeUniformN` / `nodeVarN` renumbering
that follows, `modelViewMatrix` emitted lazily at its first use instead of at the top
of `main()`, and `(!x)` printed `( ! x )`. The one structural move is the flip itself:
in the six pick fragment shaders the whole `depthNode` flow, `gl_FragDepth` write
included, now sits above the discards. That is inert — a discarded fragment updates no
buffer, depth included — but it is the change an order-insensitive check cannot see, so
it is named rather than folded into "presentational". The rest was checked rather than
assumed: with
the generated identifiers normalized away, 58 of the 74 `main()` bodies are an
identical multiset of statements and the remaining 16 differ only by that `!` spacing.
The lazy `modelViewMatrix` emission is the same hazard class #1697 fixed, so it was
re-checked the same way: a scan for values first assigned inside a branch and later
read at top level returns the same set under both revisions.

The bump also trades around which half of the codegen guard is live. The brace-depth
half was inert while the runtime sat at r184 (colour-first order builds even a
free-standing `.toVar()` at top level) and is the live one now — r185's depth-first
order is exactly what buried the pick chain in an `else` arm. The read-order half went
the other way: with the prologue emitted at the top of `main()` by the depth flow,
nothing `colorNode` does can trip it. One consequence is called out at the site rather
than left to be rediscovered — `colorNode`'s own prologue call is verified by nothing
at r185 (removing it leaves the generated GLSL byte-identical) and is kept deliberately,
so both entry points stay self-sufficient whichever one a future three builds first.

The revision floor in `assertThreeRevision` moves to 185 to track the peer range's
minor. So does the pinned importmap URL in the `examples/embed/` sample, which reaches
for `three` over a CDN and so is not covered by the peer range at all — left at r184 it
would have thrown the guard's own error on load. And `THREE_VERSION_NOTES.md` now describes the pin that exists rather
than the one it used to block. Comments elsewhere that state what the *current* pin
does — the WebGPU compat-mode adapter workaround, which three still defaults to at
r185 exactly as it did at r184 — were updated; dated r184 measurements in the mesh and
depth-sorting specs were left as the record of what was checked and when.

One of those current-pin statements is a number rather than a name: the size of the
lazily-loaded `three-webgpu` chunk, quoted in seven places as the payload a default
WebGL session does not download. Re-measured on the same tree with `three` the only
variable, it moves from 172.5 kB gzipped at r184 to 181.8 kB at r185, so the quoted
figure goes from ~173 kB to ~182 kB. The chunk stays lazy — `check-eager-chunks.mjs`
is green on the r185 build.

#### A matrix of tracked zebrafish embryos, from the Biohub cell-tracking challenge

`luxar demo run gsplats_4d_cell_tracking_challenge` builds six crops of a
developing zebrafish embryo — the most densely annotated crops of the public
[Biohub cell-tracking competition](https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/biohub-cell-tracking-during-development)
data — into one 3x2 matrix scene. The crops go onto the most compact grid that
holds them, which is why the default is six rather than nine: the last two of the
nine ranked crops are behind Kaggle's per-account download quota, and seven tiles
fill no rectangle while six fill a 3x2 exactly. Each tile carries a full 100-timepoint
timelapse in three geometries at once: the image data as a 4D (ZYX + time)
Gaussian-splat volume, every annotated cell position as points that appear only
at the timepoint they belong to, and every tracking link as one `indexed` lines
node whose shared vertices make a cell division render as a real fork. Colour is
lineage throughout. Scrub time and the markers walk along their own tracks.

`luxar.gsplats.interop.geff` reads **GEFF** cell-lineage graphs — the tracking
interchange format used by ultrack, trackedit, tracksdata and traccuracy — into a
plain-NumPy `TrackingGraph`, with physical-unit positions, connected-component
lineage ids for colouring, division detection, and edges remapped to positional
indices so a lineage forest drops straight into `scene.add_lines`. No `geff`
package, no `networkx`; a GEFF store is a zarr v3 group, which the `zarr>=3.2`
the project now depends on reads directly.

Two authoring choices are measured rather than guessed, and both matter more than
they sound. The per-timepoint fits drop the top 5% of splats by characteristic
size: a fit of densely packed nuclei leaves a diffuse large-scale tail, and under
volumetric blending optical depth grows with path length, so that few percent
renders as opaque discs burying the nuclei underneath.

And the LOD ladder's depth is the frame budget. The `screen-area` selector
anchors its finest level at half the screen and halves per step, so a matrix
tile draws a COARSE level whatever the ladder's length — one knob therefore sets
both what the opening framing costs and how much detail it throws away. Grid
shape moves the tile's share of the screen, so it is worth re-reading
`activeLevel` after changing the layout rather than deriving it: a naive area
formula puts a 3x2 tile just over the halving threshold and predicts one level
finer, and the viewer disagrees — camera padding and viewport aspect keep it on
the coarsest. A one-level ladder drew 20,072 splats per
timepoint per crop and scrubbing time was visibly choppy. The shipped four-level
ladder draws about 4,900 per timepoint per crop — a 4.1x cut, 29,774 per frame
across the six-crop matrix, measured in the viewer — and it never even fetches
the finer levels. That costs
nothing visible: rendering the drawn level back to a volume shows quality
saturating around 5,000 splats per timepoint, while masked PSNR is useless here,
flat at 19.7-19.8 dB across a 37x range in count because merging preserves the
low-frequency envelope it scores. Zooming into one embryo still climbs to the
full four-million-splat fit.

Track lines are thin (0.35 um) and translucent (opacity 0.15): they are context
for the volume, not the subject, and at full width and opacity a matrix tile is
mostly cage. Track width and marker radius are re-derived from constants at load
rather than read back from the hosted payload — both are uniform, so storing them
would pin the demo's appearance to a 0.68 GB artifact and make retuning a
re-upload.

The splat budget comes from measurement too. `gsplat cal` puts the held-out peak
at K* = 12,126, but that is the noise-masked criterion; against a scale-invariant
PSNR over the nuclei alone the fidelity climbs ~1 dB per doubling with no plateau
(37.4 dB at 9.4k splats/timepoint, 39.3 at 42.6k, 40.3 at 83.3k), and the
difference is plain in a MIP. The default is 60,000 seeds, keeping ~43k.

Fitting the whole matrix is 600 per-timepoint fits (~24 s each on an RTX PRO
6000), cached per timepoint, so the demo is resumable and a second run is cheap.
The competition data is behind an authenticated endpoint, so the demo declares
`local_data: "kaggle-auth"`, gates the Kaggle client through `require_module`,
and backs off when Kaggle rate-limits a bulk fetch. The redistributable derived
product (per-crop 4D volumes plus track geometry, ~700 MB) is registered in
`data_manifest.json` as a `zenodo` dataset so a warm run needs neither
credentials nor a GPU.

`scripts/zenodo_upload_draft.py` adds files to an unpublished Zenodo draft and
is deliberately incapable of publishing: there is no publish call in it, a
submitted deposition aborts the run, dry run is the default, and every upload is
verified against the checksum Zenodo computes.

#### `luxar demo` reads as a catalogue instead of a wall of rows

Bare `luxar demo` printed one undifferentiated row per bundled demo, each
prefixed with arbol's `├` tree glyph, followed by four cramped lines of
commands. Nothing told you where to start, the rows would not copy-paste
cleanly, and the requirement column spelled a 29 GB download as `⬇30000MB`.

The listing is now grouped into labelled category sections, rendered through
`rich` so it carries colour and adapts to the terminal, and printed to plain
stdout so a row is exactly what you would type. Whether you already have a demo
moved into a one-character left rail — `✓` built, `•` inputs cached, blank for
neither — which both collects "what is on disk" into a single scannable stripe
and buys back the ten columns that were pushing rows past 80 and wrapping them.
Downloads are humanized (`29 GB`, `150 MB`), GPU and local-data requirements are
words rather than emoji (`GPU`, `GPU?`, `git-lfs`, `kaggle`, `manual`), and a
legend decodes both — naming the third rail state as `(blank)` rather than
inventing a dash the rows never print. The footer is six aligned lines that name
a concrete starter demo and keep the actionable half of every pair, so `--install`
still sits beside what `deps` reports and `cache clear` beside what `cache list`
measures. `luxar demo info`, `luxar demo deps`, and `luxar demo cache list` follow
the same visual key — one colour vocabulary throughout, and the same measured
section rule over `deps` and `cache list` (`info` describes a single demo, so it
is headed by that demo rather than by a rule) — so the sub-app reads as pages of
one document rather than four unrelated tables; `info` now reports build status
too, and `deps` colours its three-way ok / OUTDATED / MISSING verdict. A test
renders the whole bundled catalogue and fails if any line exceeds 80 display
columns, so a long new demo key cannot quietly wrap the table again.

#### The SortWorker starts before the data, not during it

The SortWorker was spawned lazily by the first order-dependent commit, which is
precisely when this thread and the data-worker pool are saturated decoding the
scene — and the worker's `initialize()` reply has to be dispatched on that same
busy thread. At around three million points (`demo_gaia_milky_way_3m` is exactly
this shape) the reply simply queued behind the decode: in the reproduction the
worker logged its own readiness, WASM up and answer sent, while the main thread
was still waiting for it.

The worker is now started at app init, while nothing is loading, so WASM
initialization no longer overlaps the data flood at all. The commit path still
calls `ensureWorker()` and still dedupes on the cached init promise, so an
embedder that configures late is unaffected — but it now normally finds a worker
that came up seconds earlier. The chunk and its WASM are now fetched on every
page load, including scenes with no order-dependent geometry; `?depthSort=0`
spawns nothing at all. One consequence for anyone relocating the worker bundle:
`setSortWorkerUrl` / `setSortWorkerWasmPath` must be called before
`LuxarApp.init()`, since the spawn they redirect happens during app init rather
than at the first commit. Those two are internal entry points on
`rendering/depth-sort-coordinator` — not re-exported from `src/index.ts`, and the
package's `exports` map publishes only `.` and `./styles.css` — so they are
reachable from inside the source tree (a vendored or bundled viewer), not from an
npm install.

The coordinator also stopped hand-rolling its own init race and now uses the
data-worker pool's `worker-pool/lifecycle/init-with-guard.ts`, which is how the
two startup paths stay in step. It gains the `onmessageerror` arm the private
copy never had: a worker answering with an unserializable payload used to leave
`initialize()` pending until the deadline, i.e. reported as a slow start rather
than as the broken worker it is. The deadline itself is now the configurable
`depthSort.workerInitTimeoutMs` (default 30 s, `0` disables the guard) instead of
a module constant.

Finally, giving up is no longer silent. Once the subsystem has given up for the
session AND some visible, still-committed, order-dependent node actually wants
sorting, the data-loading monitor's performance footer says `depth sort
UNAVAILABLE` — the same "does anything want sorting" predicate that gates the
retry, so the two cannot drift, and so a CSP-blocked warm-up on an all-additive
scene does not report on a subsystem that scene never uses. The note is a
one-directional proof: when it shows, visible order-dependent geometry IS being
drawn in storage order. Its absence proves nothing — a starved init that is still
retrying, `?depthSort=0`, and a single commit that could not reach an otherwise
healthy worker all draw identity order without it.

#### One colormap window per gsplat structure — LOD switches no longer re-tone or pop

Every gsplat node derived its own `amplitude_data_range` — the colormap window the
viewer maps amplitudes through — as `[min(a), p99.9(a)]` of *that node's own*
amplitudes. On a lone flat leaf that is exactly right. On anything larger it is a
per-node window over one object, and it showed. A `kind=lod` ladder's coarse level
packs the same total mass into far fewer merged representatives, so its p99.9 sits
~4.5x above the finest level's while its *typical* amplitude only grows ~1.1x: at
every LOD switch the object re-toned through the colormap and popped ~2x in
brightness. A `kind=partition` compounded it — two adjacent tiles of one object were
measured windowed at `[0.40, 4.04]` and `[0.0036, 0.0355]`, a ~100x difference across
a single seam.

Finalize now harmonizes the whole structure. For each maximal `kind=lod` /
`kind=partition` group holding gsplats, one reference window is taken from the finest
content and handed down: LOD levels get it scaled by their **mass-weighted mean
amplitude ratio**, partition parts get it **verbatim**. The two rules were picked by
measurement, not by symmetry. Scored on a rasterized orthographic proxy of the real
colormap render against the finest level, per-level windows gave luminance ratios
0.49 / 0.51 / 0.71 and chromaticity L1 0.187 / 0.183 / 0.100; the mass-weighted
scaling gives 1.04 / 1.01 / 1.00 and 0.048 / 0.028 / 0.028. That estimator also
tracked the swept optimum (1.19/1.10/1.09 predicted vs 1.22/1.06/1.06 measured) where
the p99.9 the window itself uses did not at all (4.51/3.95/2.36). For a partition the
answer is the opposite: parts are disjoint spatial pieces of one object with no
representation change between them, so there is nothing to normalize away — a dim
tile really is dim. Per-part windows scored luminance 0.62 / chroma 0.123 with a 5.6x
spread in window tops; one shared window scored 1.00 / 0.0001.

A partition's own reference is pooled from its parts: the exact union minimum for the
bottom, and the **count-weighted mean of the part tops** (weights = each part's splat
count) for the top. Both candidate rules are biased, in opposite directions, and
neither recovers the union's true p99.9. `max` over part tops drifts upward without
bound in the part count — 1.05x the union's true p99.9 at 2 parts, 1.58x at 256, 3.40x
at 5000, and ~1500x for 60 dim tiles plus one small bright one, at which point the
whole object renders black — and the batch-fit streaming merge routinely writes
thousands of parts. The count-weighted mean is biased slightly low instead, because a
part's own p99.9 already under-estimates the union's. It wins on two counts: its bias
does not grow with the part count, and its failure mode is the recoverable one —
clipping outlier-bright content, which is exactly what a p99.9 window does by design.
It is not unbiased and not a consistent estimator of what a flat store would derive;
it is the better-behaved of two biased choices.

The reference LOD child is the finest one that actually carries a *usable* window
(`hi > lo`), not necessarily the literal finest. Three shipped shapes put an
un-windowable node there: a `substitutive_lod` Points/Lines ladder, a scalar-amplitude
level, and — the one that bites hardest — a constant-amplitude level, which the writer
windows as the degenerate `[x, x]`. `gsplats/interop` gives *every* imported classical
splat file (INRIA PLY, `.splat`, SPZ, SuperSplat) `amplitudes = 1`, so
`gsplat import` → `gsplat lod --recipe levels` produced exactly that, and the pass
would then have refused every write and left the ladder on its per-level windows with
no diagnostic. A degenerate top is likewise excluded from the partition pool (its `lo`
still counts toward the union minimum): admitted at full weight, a 100 000-splat
`[1.0, 1.0]` part next to a 1 000-splat `[0.01, 50.0]` pooled to `[0.01, 1.49]`,
over-brightening the second part 34x.

To make that computable, each written splat set now carries two cheap O(N)
statistics: `amplitude_mass` (`Σ aᵢ·|Σᵢ|^½`, the integral mass this codebase already
ranks LOD ladders by) and `amplitude_mass_weighted_mean` (`Σ aᵢ²·|Σᵢ|^½ / Σ aᵢ·|Σᵢ|^½`
— total self-energy over total mass, i.e. the amplitude a unit of mass typically
carries). Both use the RAW amplitudes, since that is the scalar the window applies
to. An additive ladder's parent aggregates them over its sub-LODs. They are stamped
unconditionally — a mass-less set gets `0.0` / `0.0` — because "present and zero" and
"absent" have to stay distinguishable: absence is how the pass recognises a legacy
store. These two are format-additive: an older reader ignores them, and a store that
lacks them shares the reference window verbatim instead of being scaled. That fallback
is not provably better than the self-consistent per-level windows it replaces — it can
clip a legacy sibling — but it is the honest answer with no ratio to scale by, and it
puts the structure on one window, which is what the partition arm does anyway.

The level ratio is clamped into `[1/10, 10]`, mirroring the analogous mass rescale in
`gsplats/lod/substitutive.py`: the real ratios are ~1.1-1.2, `mwma` is a second-moment
ratio and so not robust on heavy-tailed amplitudes, and a 10x window rescale would be
a larger switch pop than the ~2x defect being fixed. Out of bounds the ratio is
clamped rather than thrown away — discarding it applies the *full* uncorrected error
(at a genuine ratio of 0.02, scale 1.0 leaves the level windowed 50x too wide and it
renders black, where clamping to 0.1 caps that at 5x) — and each harmonized structure
reports its clamps in one rolled-up line rather than one per level.

This is producer-side only: no viewer change, and the `amplitude_data_range` attr set
is unchanged — the pass only ever **overwrites** a window a writer already stamped,
never creates one, and refuses to write anything that is not a finite `lo < hi`. It
runs in `LuxarZarrCompiler.finalize()` and in both standalone `.gsplats.zarr` writers,
before the content hash is stamped — so `gsplat lod` / `fit` / `convert`, the scene
graft, and the batch-fit streaming merge all get it. One knock-on worth knowing: a
`levels` structure's reference top is a real p99.9 while an `overview` / `adaptive`
one is a pooled estimate, so the same splats can tone slightly differently depending
on the topology they were written in (measured 222.34 vs 160.50 on one dataset).

#### OME-Zarr 0.5 metadata is read instead of silently guessed

`discover_ome_zarr_shape` only understood the OME-Zarr **0.4** attribute layout,
where the NGFF block sits at the top level of a node's attributes. OME-Zarr
**0.5** — what a zarr v3 store declares, and what every crop of the Biohub
cell-tracking competition data is — nests the whole block one level down under an
`ome` key. Nothing raised: `multiscales` simply came back missing, the custom
`axes` fallback did not match either, and discovery landed on the shape heuristic
that guesses axis roles from ndim and recovers no physical voxel size. On a 4D
`TZYX` store that heuristic reads the TIME axis as a channel, so `batch-fit`
planning fanned out over the wrong axis — seven channels of one timepoint instead
of seven timepoints — while reporting an ordinary-looking result.

Both layouts now parse, resolved in one place by the new exported
`luxar.io.ome_zarr.resolve_ngff_attrs`, which every reader of NGFF attributes
should go through (the demo's local copy of the same logic now calls it). The
layout deliberately cannot be inferred from the store's zarr format version: a
zarr v3 store written by a 0.4-era tool has the v3 chunk layout with top-level
0.4 attributes, so both spellings are always tried. The nested block wins only
when it carries a NON-EMPTY `multiscales` (or when the top level declares none at
all, so "declared but unusable" is still reportable). Presence alone is not
enough, in either direction: an `ome` block holding nothing but `omero` rendering
metadata, or an empty `ome.multiscales` list, must not displace a perfectly good
top-level 0.4 pyramid — that is the same silent mis-read from the other side, and
it made the give-up notice blame an empty `multiscales` that the store did not
have.

Several adjacent wrong answers went with it. A `multiscales` block whose `axes`
count disagrees with the SELECTED array's ndim — the classic image-with-labels
store, a 5D `TCZYX` pyramid beside a 3D `labels/cells` — is not metadata about
that array; it used to be parsed anyway and `batch-fit … --array-key
labels/nuclei` died on a bare `IndexError`, where discovery now falls through to
the remaining fallbacks. For a nested `array_key`, discovery uses the
`multiscales` block of the nearest ancestor that DECLARES the selected array —
not merely the array's parent group, and only on that evidence — and matches
`datasets[].path` exactly relative to whichever group that is, so a same-named
level in an unrelated root pyramid cannot supply a confidently wrong spacing.
Exactly, but on the two spellings *normalised*: a surrounding `/` and one leading
`./` are cosmetic, so a pyramid writing its levels as `"./0"`, `"./1"` still
matches (comparing the raw strings cost such a store its voxel size outright, and
silently — a multi-level pyramid has no single-level fall-back to `datasets[0]`,
and the block parses, so no "unusable" notice fires either). A path still
carrying a `.` segment — `"."`, `"./"`, `"a/./b"` — names no level and matches
nothing, rather than collapsing into a match for whichever one was selected. An
optional `coordinateTransformations` on the multiscales entry itself is composed
on top of the per-dataset one rather than ignored. Where that composition or that
match cannot be made honestly, the answer is now no spacing rather than a
plausible one: a multiscales-level scale whose length differs from the dataset's
cannot be composed (a half-composed number was being returned as fact), and an
`array_key` that matches no entry of a multi-level pyramid means the selected
array's spacing is simply unknown. Malformed metadata degrades throughout instead
of raising a traceback out of discovery — a `datasets` that is not a list of
mappings, a `scale` carrying a `null` or a non-numeric string (numeric strings
still convert), an axis record with no `name` or a `null` `type`. And when
discovery does fall through to the heuristic on an ambiguous (≥4D) store it now
says so on the console — naming the guessed labels, the missing voxel size, and
the `axes_override` / `--axes` escape hatch — and distinguishes "nothing
declared" from "declared but unusable", quoting the reason.

`batch-fit` planning gained a guard for what it can now learn. Without an
explicit `--axes` the manifest records no axes, so every fit worker slices the
store POSITIONALLY (`luxar.io.volume._load_zarr_volume`: at 4D it can consume
exactly ONE leading axis, preferring `--channel` over `--timepoint`). Discovery
reading real labels means the planner can learn a layout that contract cannot
reproduce — a `(t, c, y, x)` store planned 5 timepoints × 3 channels while the
workers only ever read 3 distinct volumes, so the merged partition was five
duplicate timepoints and nothing raised. Planning now refuses such a layout up
front. It decides by comparing two sets rather than matching whole layouts
against a per-ndim table: the axes the loader CONSUMES for a task (axis 0 for the
timepoint, the axes that fold into the flat channel index, both read off the
loader's own branches) and the axes the plan FANS over. They have to agree axis
for axis once singleton axes are dropped from both — a size-1 axis is indexed at
0 whatever the task index says, and contributes nothing to a flat channel decode
— and what is left after the loader's indexing has to be the planned spatial
shape, squeezed, because `load_volume` squeezes its positional result. The
set comparison is what admits a 2D timelapse with a singleton channel (`t,c,y,x`
at `(5, 1, 32, 32)`, whose worker `arr[3]` IS the planned volume): the table
refused it while admitting its `T=1` sibling, so its verdict flipped on the size
of T alone. The question is asked of the decomposition discovery published —
`OMEZarrInfo` gained `time_axis` / `channel_indices` / `spatial_indices`, the
axis roles it actually used — and never of the axis LABELS: NGFF classifies by
the `type` field, so re-deriving the roles from names disagrees in both
directions. A channel axis named `stain` looks spatial to a name rule (refusing a
canonical 5D store that always worked), while an axis typed `view` is spatial to
the parser and channel-like to a name rule (waving through a plan that tiles four
dimensions the worker never sees). Layouts whose non-spatial axes are all
singletons — `t,c,y,x` at `(1,1,32,32)`, `z,y,x,c` at `(16,32,32,1)`, `t,y,x` at
`(1,64,64)` — still plan, because `load_volume` squeezes them away; 2D gsplats
are a first-class authoring path and refusing them would be a real regression.

The refusal quotes an `--axes` string only when the store is one that spec can
address, which takes two conditions rather than one. Its vocabulary is narrower
than discovery's (`volume._axis_kind` rejects `stain` and heuristic `dim0…dimN`
labels), so quoting those back prints a command that fails — and worse,
`plan_batch`'s override path is lenient enough to ACCEPT it first, folding the
unknown label into the tile grid so that every worker dies later instead. And a
recognised spec is not sufficient either: `_apply_axes_spec` pins EVERY
channel-kind axis with the same `--channel` value and never decodes the flat
channel index the batch tasks carry, so on a `camera,time,channel,z,y,x` store at
`(2, 3, 2, …)` following the quoted advice plans 4 channel tasks of which task 1
silently loads (camera 1, channel 1) and tasks 2-3 die with "--channel index 2 is
out of range for the 'camera' axis". A spec is therefore quoted only for a store
with at most one channel-like and at most one time label; otherwise the message
says which condition failed — the unrecognised labels, or the second
channel-like axis and why a flat index cannot address it — and asks for an
`--axes` spec of the user's own. (The flat-index limitation in `_apply_axes_spec`
itself is pre-existing and tracked separately; this only stops the refusal from
recommending it.) Forwarding the discovered labels automatically was deliberately
not done, for the same reasons.

Known gap, unchanged and documented on the guard: a size-1 SPATIAL axis. The
loader squeezes it away while the plan's `spatial_shape` keeps it, so a canonical
`t,c,z,y,x` store at `(3, 1, 1, 512, 512)` plans a 3-D `(1, 512, 512)` volume the
worker loads as 2-D `(512, 512)`, and the merged partition's split planes then
name center columns that do not exist. The comparison above is squeezed on both
sides precisely so this keeps planning exactly as it does today; closing it means
dropping the axis from the plan's spatial shape everywhere, which is its own
change.

A bioformats2raw-style store — root attributes `{"ome": {"version": "0.5",
"bioformats2raw.layout": 3}}` with the `multiscales` block on a CHILD image
group — auto-selects nothing at the root, because root key `0` is itself a
group. Discovery descends into that image group (see #1777, which landed
alongside this) and reads the child pyramid's axes and voxel size off the group
that declares them, so `--array-key 0/0`, `--array-key 0` and no key at all all
describe the store the same way.

Upgrade note: a `batch-fit` output directory PLANNED against a 0.5 store before
this fix will re-plan after it. The recovered T/C roles change every tile
filename, so a resume refits from scratch and the previously fitted tiles stay
in `tiles/` unreferenced — delete them, or plan into a fresh output directory.

#### The CI diff classifier now names gate inputs that carry no Python extension

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` sorts a PR diff into language domains and runs each
suite only when its domain is set, but `scripts/complexity_baseline.json` matched
none of the patterns. Since the C901 ratchet is enforced by a pytest test inside
`hatch run test-cov`, a baseline-only diff reported `python-tests (3.12)` green in
about seven seconds without ever running the check whose entire job is to assert
that the tree still matches that baseline — observed on #1678. That check is what
catches a baseline that has come loose from the code: keys dropped while still over
the limit come back as newly over-complex, values below what the tree measures come
back as worsened, and an emptied file trips a fail-closed assertion. (It does not
police a deliberately raised entry — the ratchet reads that as debt paid down
elsewhere — and #1678's own baseline was in fact a legitimate tightening. The hole
was real even though the harm did not land there.)

The classifier now also owns the other non-Python inputs read by pytest:
`scripts/gallery/manifest.json`, `docs/guides/user/CLI_REFERENCE.md`, the root
`README.md`, and `packages/luxar/src/luxar/demos/README.md`. Their guards
cross-validate the gallery manifest, live CLI, demo documentation, and exported
helper inventory; a JSON- or Markdown-only diff previously skipped those tests.
The guard table also covers the viewer fixture-generation entry points already
classified for `test_fixture_environment.py`.

A new guard, `packages/luxar/src/luxar/tests/test_ci_diff_classifier.py`, keeps the
principle the `changes` job already states in its own comment: every input of a
gated check must be classified into the domain that runs it. It extracts each
domain pattern from the workflow text and evaluates it with a real `grep -E` — the
matcher CI actually uses, rather than Python's subtly different `re` — over a table
of gate inputs that carry no Python extension. Negative controls run
against all four language domains and against the documentation gate, so a pattern
that had degenerated into a catch-all fails instead of passing everything, and the
rule that puts the workflow file itself in every domain — the only thing that
classifies it at all — is now pinned too.

#### Depth sorting recovers when worker init loses its deadline race to a busy main thread (#1694)

`ensureWorker()` in the depth-sort coordinator caches its `initPromise` and races
the Comlink `initialize` RPC against an init deadline
(`config.depthSort.workerInitTimeoutMs`, default 30 s). The deadline exists for a
real reason: a worker whose script dies during async module evaluation emits an
`error` event but never settles that RPC, and every order-dependent commit
attaches a continuation to the cached promise — closing over its centers provider,
which for points pins a whole `LoadedPointsData`. Left pending, those closures
accumulate one per commit forever, so the promise MUST settle. What did not
follow is that it must settle _permanently_: the cached rejection stood for the
session, so every later commit fell into the warn-once path and the identity
(storage) ordering was what got drawn, with nothing but one console line to say
so. At ~3M points (`demo_gaia_milky_way_3m`) the main thread is saturated long
enough during load that worker startup simply loses the race, and a condition
that would have cleared in seconds disabled depth sorting for the rest of the
session — 200k and 1M sorted correctly, 3M rendered unsorted indefinitely.

The settle contract is unchanged; the failure is now CLASSIFIED. Only the
deadline timer rejects with `WorkerInitTimeoutError`
(`workers/worker-pool/errors.ts`, shared with the data pool); a worker `error`
event, a rejected `initialize`, and a constructor throw (a CSP-blocked script)
all stay permanently fatal, because nothing about waiting longer would help them.
A missed deadline is retried at most 3 times in total (the initial attempt plus
2), with a 2 s-per-miss backoff on the monotonic `performance.now()` clock — a
window of three deadlines plus the two backoffs, ~96 s of wall clock at the
default deadline. The bound is what keeps the anti-leak property: each attempt
opens one more deadline-long window in which commits can queue continuations, so
the number of windows has to be finite — and between attempts the cached
rejection is still what every commit drains into, exactly as before.

The retry is driven from the per-frame scheduler rather than a timer, because the
frame loop is where "the main thread has room again" is observable, and it is
already gated on the conditions a retry must respect: it runs after the
`isLoadInProgress` early return (the in-flight sweep IS the starvation), and it
declines to spend an attempt during an offline capture or on a scene where no
visible, still-committed, order-dependent node actually wants sorting. Because
the render loop is on-demand and idle-pauses after `animation.idleTimeoutMs`,
arming a retry also arms exactly one wake-up `setTimeout` that requests a frame
just after the backoff expires — otherwise a static "load it and look at it"
scene, whose loop pauses at or before the first eligible instant, would never run
the scheduler again and never recover. If that wake fires when there is no
`requestRender` to call at all — before `configureDepthSort`, or while an offline
capture has deliberately nulled it — it re-arms the same delay instead of being
spent on nothing while the retry stays armed.

A late success then has to get the centers across, since the fresh worker holds no
registrations and the coordinator retains no centers by design: it invalidates
both freshness stamps on every unregistered, still-committed, order-dependent node
and requests one reprocess — the same two-line recovery the switch-to-sorted
blending-mode hook has always done, now factored into one shared helper so the two
cannot drift. Doing that for several nodes at once has two accepted transient
costs, both self-healing and both already inherent to the one-node case: a cleared
