`loadedViewVersion` marks the node stale for the LOD freshness check, so a
substitutive-LOD group visibly drops to its coarsest ready level until the
settle-gated reload climbs back; and while `committedData` is absent the node is
skipped by the per-frame pass, so it misses that frame's cross-node `renderOrder`
assignment (a transient wrong back-to-front order across parts).

Every module-scoped write past an `await` inside the init closure is guarded by an
attempt EPOCH, bumped on dispose and whenever a retry supersedes an attempt. The
deadline timer lives in that closure and nothing outside it can cancel it, so
without the epoch an orphaned attempt from a disposed app would fire one deadline
later and classify a miss against the NEXT app's perfectly healthy worker:
'starved' with a retry armed, the resolved `initPromise` dropped, a third worker
spawned over the live one (leaking that thread and its transferred centers
buffers), and — since every node still reads as registered — a new worker holding
no registrations at all, i.e. the same silent death this issue is about through a
new door. The success path is guarded symmetrically. A stale attempt still
terminates its own worker; it just writes nothing and logs nothing.

The console message no longer claims more than it knows: that catch also fires for
a throwing lazy centers provider and for a `transfer()` of an already-detached
buffer, so it reports that the commit could not reach the SortWorker and that the
identity (unsorted) order is drawn, quoting the worker's actual init state rather
than asserting one. The degrade is inspectable rather than console-only:
`getDepthSortWorkerStatus()` reports `idle` / `ready` / `starved` / `failed` plus
the deadline-miss count, and is exposed on `__luxarDebug`.

#### An offline turntable no longer bakes coarse-LOD pops into the exported sequence

Since the rAF loop began running for the whole offline capture, the depth-sort
scheduler and the LOD group selector correctly follow the orbiting camera — but
that also leaves the auto-LOD selector live for the entire sweep, and it is
frustum-aware. On a `tiles` / `adaptive` / `overview` gsplat scene, a tile whose
world bbox leaves the frustum mid-orbit is demoted to its coarsest ready level,
and the resident-byte budget may release its fine one. When it swings back into
view the fine level reloads asynchronously — but `OfflineCaptureStrategy` took
exactly one `requestAnimationFrame` per exported frame and never waited for
readiness, so those frames went into the ZIP/MP4 at the coarse level and popped
back a few frames later.

The capture loop now waits. After each frame's orbit callback is removed (the
camera pose is fixed from that point, so the extra frames only let pending loads
land — draining any earlier would keep orbiting while waiting), it spends extra
rAF ticks until every in-frame LOD group is showing its selected level at final
quality. That predicate is the new `LODGroupRegistry.isCaptureQuiescent()`: it
skips off-screen entries (held coarse on purpose, drawing nothing) and entries
that are not effectively visible (a layer toggled off, or authored
`visible=false`, anywhere up the ancestor chain — those cannot start a deferred
load at all, while the frustum-only selector still records a fine level for
them, so blocking on one would never resolve), and otherwise
requires that the displayed level equals the aspiration, that the aspiration is
ready, fresh for the current view version and done streaming its additive
ladder, and that no child is loading. "Done streaming" takes both available
signals: a lazy child's live `hasMoreLODs()` thunk, and the commit-time
`committedLadderComplete` stamp — read off a leaf directly, and folded over the
visible stamped leaves of a deferred group child (the `overview` recipe's fine
`kind=partition` branch). Neither alone covers it. A group child has no thunk,
and its part leaves are at chunk-1 the instant the branch becomes ready, so a
thunk-only check would have released the frame on exactly the recipe this issue
is about; and the thunk is only attached on the deferred path, so a stamp-less
check would have declared the eagerly-loaded default level complete while it was
still climbing its own ladder under the background refinement loop. It also
requires that the selector is not
still _wanting_ a different level — a new `LODGroupEntry.desiredChildIndex` records
what the selector picked before the ready gates get a say, which closes a real
one-frame hole: `activeChildIndex` only ever advances onto a READY level, so in
the frame where a lazy level's load lands (`ready` set, `loading` cleared) the
swap has not happened yet, and a predicate reading only ready/loading/displayed
would call that window settled and film the coarse level. A `desired` level that
has `failed` deliberately does not block, since it can never become ready this
frame.

The first of those extra ticks is mandatory rather than part of the wait, for a
per-frame-callback-ordering reason. `AnimationController.animate` runs
`controls.update()`, then every per-frame callback in Map insertion order, then
the render. The LOD selector is registered once at pipeline init while the
capture removes and re-adds its orbit callback on every iteration — so the orbit
callback is always last, and `applyOrbitRotation` moves the camera
synchronously. Inside the single frame the loop awaits for frame N, the selector
therefore evaluates pose N−1 and only afterwards does the camera advance to pose
N. Polling straight away would read state computed for the previous pose, and on
the exact frame a tile re-enters the frustum the selector has not seen the
re-entry yet — the predicate would report settled and that frame would still be
filmed coarse, one popped frame per re-entry. One more tick puts the selector on
the pose being captured. The cost is one rAF per frame even on a fully settled
scene that has LOD groups; against a full render plus an async GPU readback plus
an encode per frame, ~16 ms is noise.

A scene with no LOD at all pays nothing, not even that tick. The settle hook is
tri-state — `true` / `false` / `null` — and the provider wired at init returns
`null` when there is no scene loader, no LOD registry, or a registry with zero
registered `lod_group`s. `null` means "no `lod_group` to wait for" and skips the
drain outright, which matters because the provider is wired unconditionally:
without the third state, a plain points/lines capture would have started paying
the catch-up frame for a selector it does not have. That answer is deliberately
narrow, and narrower than "nothing here can be mid-load": a `--recipe stream`
scene (one leaf with an additive ladder, no `lod_group`) answers `null` while
its progressive refinement is still climbing the ladder, so its early frames can
still be exported at a partial prefix — the same artifact class, out of scope
here. The hook is read through a `try`/`catch` as well (the treatment
`AnimationController.pacingSuspended()` already gives its injected predicate),
so a throwing provider degrades to "do not wait" instead of being caught by the
loop's outer handler and discarding the sequence as "Recording failed".

The wait is bounded by both a 2 s deadline (on the monotonic
`performance.now()`, so an NTP/DST step cannot move it backwards) and a
120-frame cap (inclusive of that catch-up tick), whichever trips first — the
frame cap is not redundant, since under a stubbed clock (unit tests, fake
timers) the millisecond deadline alone would spin forever. After three
consecutive timeouts the loop pauses draining and warns once, so a scene that
can never settle (resident-byte thrash on an over-budget partition) cannot
silently multiply the capture's wall-clock by the timeout on every remaining
frame. That pause re-arms: a paused frame still spends a free, non-waiting probe
of the predicate (no rAF, no poll, so it costs exactly what an undrained frame
did) and resumes draining the moment the probe reports the scene settled. A
terminal pause would have made the fix inert on precisely the scenes it targets
— an over-budget `adaptive` / `overview` partition, or a Capture pressed before
the initial load finished, burns the budget on frames 0–2, pauses at frame 3,
and would export the remaining hundreds of frames with the old behaviour even
though the scene settles seconds later.

Any timeouts at all are reported at the end of the run with a warning and a
toast, so a degraded sequence is visible rather than a mystery — an exact "N of
M frames" (M = the frames the loop attempted) when waiting stayed on for the
whole run, and otherwise a statement that waiting was paused after three
consecutive timeouts and the frames captured while it was off were taken without
it. The count cannot be quoted in that second case: it only counts the frames
that waited and gave up, while everything captured with the wait off is
uncounted, so it badly understates the damage. (It is not pinned at three —
three bounds the consecutive streak, and a run alternating timeout/settle can
total more before three land in a row.) Both reports say the frames may not show
the level the selector had settled on, rather than that they are coarse: the
predicate is direction-blind, and `displayed !== active` also fires while the
never-downgrade gate legitimately holds a _finer_ previously-displayed level
over a coarser aspiration that is still streaming.

Waiting rather than forcing the finest level is the deliberate choice: a capture
visits the whole scene, so pinning finest across a tiled partition would make
peak residency the entire dataset, which is exactly what the resident-byte
budget exists to prevent. Waiting costs time, not memory. The distance-driven
coverage cross-fade is deliberately left alone — its weight is a function of
projected bbox area rather than wall-clock, so it already spreads smoothly over
consecutive exported frames, and draining it would turn a dissolve into a hard
cut.

#### The LOD-policy gate recognises a demo that names its own topology

Two changes that were each green on their own branch were red together: the gate
that requires every fitting demo to choose an LOD topology, and the cell-tracking
challenge demo. The demo does choose — `build_lod()` asks `build_recipe` for
`levels` with time as a hard coarsening barrier, and the precomputed crop it ships
is that result — but it makes the call itself rather than going through
`save_with_lod`, which was the gate's only definition of "chose".

Neither existing exemption described it: it does ship an artifact, and it does not
keep whatever topology its fitter happened to produce. So the gate gained a third,
narrow door for a demo that names the topology of its shipped artifact in its own
source with a literal `build_recipe(...)` recipe. Narrow is the point: an
AST-parsed detector demands a constant in the recipe slot, since a variable there
(the recipes gallery loops over all of them) names nothing a reviewer can read off
the source, and a new staleness test re-measures the claim every run — the member
must still fit, must still not use the helper, and must still carry that literal
call naming a recipe a builder answers to, so the exemption cannot outlive its
reason.

The door excuses a demo from *choosing* through the helper, not from the two gates
that make a costly choice worth its bytes: the topology it names in its own source
is still put through the "does this survive to the scene?" checks, so naming
`levels` yourself cannot buy the ladder and then discard it at the scene step.

#### `reencode` re-quantizes centers too, and the skills learn how to tune a fit

`luxar gsplat reencode` has been documented everywhere as changing "only the
on-disk Cholesky encoding". It does not: `write_gsplats_tree` re-encodes the
centers with the same mode, and for a coordinate column `auto` and `memory` both
mean per-axis uint16 fixed-point (float32 only once an axis spans 2**16). So a
`reencode -e memory` — the command's own default — re-quantizes positions, and
centers are bit-exact only under `precision`. That matters most on a stacked
axis, where a coordinate off by one quantization step lands ~150 sigma from its
own slice and the slice renders as nothing. The claim is corrected in the
command's help, the CLI README, the format/migration guide and the gsplat-edit
skill, and `reencode` now has a test pinning the contract: the endpoints of a
stacked column land on exact codes under every mode, but its interior value
round-trips exactly only under `-e precision`.

`batch-fit`'s `--cull-retention` help still promised "0.95 for uniform tiles,
0.999 for content boxes". Every batch task is a `fit --preset <the run's
preset>` and every preset sets 0.999, so both modes have been near-lossless for
a while; the help now says so. `fit`'s own copy of the flag called 0.95 "the
default" without saying that only a preset-less fit gets it.

`gsplat compare --shape` advertised itself as overriding the reference shape.
It cannot — the metrics need both volumes on one grid, so any value that differs
from the reference exits 1. The help says what the flag actually does.

The skills gain the fit-tuning material that was written for them but never
reached this branch: a symptom-to-knob index over the measured sections, how to
read `fit`'s stamped foreground PSNR against `compare`'s, what `--seeds`
actually proposes once the post-fit amplitude cull has disposed, the two
microscopy containers that do and do not load (`.lsm` eagerly, `.h5j` not at
all), the fixed `transform` order and its pre-rotation frame, and how a demo's
generated data manifest is meant to be regenerated rather than hand-edited.

#### Uniform tiled partitions publish merged quality metrics

The default `gsplat fit --tiling uniform` partition output now records whole-volume `psnr_db`, `ssim`, `mse`, and foreground quality metrics at the archive root. Partition scoring sums the surviving tile-part renders without flattening the splats, parallel tiled fitting scores against the parent's matching (and, when requested, downscaled) reference volume, and `gsplat info` displays the root `fitting/` block.

#### Local E2E parallelism is sized to the machine, not hardcoded at 4 (#1705)

`playwright.config.ts` ran `workers: process.env.CI ? 1 : 4` locally. Four is a
defensible CEILING — the binding resource is the GIL-bound
`python3 -m http.server 9000` dataset server, which is why
`all-examples-smoke-test.spec.ts` already carries a 120 s timeout to "absorb
HTTP-server contention" — but it is not a target. A developer workstation shared
with CI runner slots and other jobs sits at a 1-minute load average of 12–24 on
16 cores, and four more Chromium instances on top of that starve the very input
handling Playwright's action timeouts measure.

Measured on such a box: `dimension-animation.spec.ts` failed **15 of 21** tests at
the config default of 4 workers and passed **21 of 21** in 3.3 min at
`--workers=1`. Every failure was a bare wall-clock timeout with no product cause —
`page.click: Timeout 10000ms exceeded` whose own call log reports the element
visible, enabled and stable before the hit-target step never gets a turn, plus
`page.evaluate` test timeouts. At one worker the page was demonstrably responsive:
an in-page round trip measured a median of 145 ms idle and 90 ms with a dimension
animation playing — both well under a second, animation playing or not — and a
real DOM click was serviced in 869 ms / 1216 ms respectively.

The ceiling is now scaled by the box's FREE FRACTION:
`clamp(round(4 * (cpus - load1) / cpus), 1, 4)`. Because the count is rounded to
nearest, the bands are fractions of the box and hold at any size: four workers
while at least 7/8 of the box is free, three down to 5/8, two down to 3/8, one
below that. On 16 cores that is four up to a load average of 2, three up to 6, two
up to 10, and one above that. The scaling is deliberately scale-free, so an
**idle** box of any size — a 2-core laptop included — still runs at the historical
four; the count only ever backs off under load, turning a red run into a slower
one. When either half of the signal is missing the ceiling is returned unchanged,
which is what "no signal" means; Windows, whose `os.loadavg()` is a hardcoded
`[0, 0, 0]`, is detected explicitly and reported as no signal rather than mistaken
for an idle box.

The mechanism is a heuristic and worth only so much. Two counts were measured — 4
(15/21 failing) and 1 (21/21 passing), both at load 12–24 on 16 cores, so 16 cores
at load 12 → 1 is the configuration actually observed green; the intermediate 2 and
3 the formula can select are interpolation. The 1-minute load average lags by
construction and is read ONCE, at config load, so a run launched just after a burst
ends can crawl on a box that is already idle again, while one launched into a lull
can take all four workers straight into the next burst: the protection is
probabilistic, the slowdown it costs is certain. On Linux the load average also
counts uninterruptible-sleep tasks, so heavy I/O elsewhere (a fixture generation, a
`git lfs pull`) throttles the suite for contention it is not competing in.
Sampling `os.cpus()[].times` twice would give a lag-free signal instead, but it
needs a ~150 ms wait and Playwright re-evaluates the config module in every worker
process as well as the parent, so that wait would be paid N+1 times per run — the
lag is cheaper than the startup cost. The wall-clock guards in
`nd-navigation.spec.ts` (8000 ms) and `worker-wasm-integration.spec.ts` (10000 ms)
get correspondingly more headroom on a loaded box than the same box would give them
at four workers; their comments now say exactly that, and stop short of comparing
machines, because a loaded box at one worker still needed 869–1216 ms to service a
real click.

The arithmetic is a pure, unit-tested function in
`packages/luxar-viewer/tools/e2e-workers.ts`; only a thin resolver touches `os`
and the environment. The run's decision is printed as one line —
`[🧵] [E2E] parallelism: max 1 worker — 16 cpus, load1 22.2 (capacity)` — from the
E2E **global setup** rather than the config module, because Playwright applies
`--workers=N` (and `--debug`, which forces 1) only after the config has
been evaluated: stamping it at config load printed four workers for a run that went
on to use one. The stamped count is the run's CEILING (`config.workers`), which is
why it reads `max`: Playwright narrows it to
`min(workers, maxConcurrentTestGroups)` after global setup, so a single-file run of
a spec pinned to one worker is stamped `max 3` and then reports "using 1 worker".
A ceiling that differs from what was sized prints both numbers —
`(capacity sized 3, run with 1)` — and claims no cause, since `--workers=N`,
`--ui`, a connected watch session and `playwright.perf.config.ts`'s own
`workers: 1` all produce that divergence. The line goes to stderr so it cannot
corrupt `--reporter=json`. Pin the count with `LUXAR_E2E_WORKERS=N`, clamped to
`[1, cpus]` as a typo guard for `=40` on a 16-core box — a pin may still exceed the
ceiling of four, which is the point of an explicit pin — or with Playwright's own
`--workers=N`, which overrides the config outright. CI stays unconditionally
serial. `points-rendering-perf.spec.ts`, whose JSON summary exists to be diffed
between runs, now records the concurrency it measured under and the load average
at capture time.

#### The Zenodo uploader authenticates by header and fails without a URL (#1706)

`scripts/zenodo_upload_draft.py` sends its `deposit:write` credential as an
`Authorization: Bearer` header and never in a URL, so it cannot be copied into
server or proxy access logs, a TLS-terminating middlebox's records, or anything
that formats `HTTPError.url`. The header is *unredirected*: `urllib` copies
ordinary headers onto a redirect's follow-up request, whatever host `Location`
names, so this one is withheld there and a redirect fails closed instead. A bucket
PUT that is rejected, or that dies at the transport level instead of answering with
a status, exits non-zero naming the file and the status or reason — never the URL.
That includes the failures `urllib` does not wrap in `URLError`
(`RemoteDisconnected`, a read timeout, a bad status line, a short body), which are
the likely end of a multi-GB transfer: Zenodo checksums the body only after all of
it lands, so the long wait is on the response.

`ZENODO_TOKEN` is also stripped, and refused outright if a line break survives
inside the value. A CRLF-terminated token file used to work by accident — a URL
drops `\r` and `\n`, a header value does not — and the resulting `ValueError` from
`http.client` would have printed the whole credential.

The bucket URL now percent-encodes the filename, which is a path segment rather
than free text: a space in it used to be rejected as an illegal request line
before any byte went out, and a `?` or `#` truncated the key Zenodo stored the
file under — so a re-run no longer recognised it and uploaded it again.

#### Recording: correct frame edges, an honest encode script, and capture sizes an encoder accepts

The `geq` filter that re-applies the viewer's grade to an EXR sequence was sampling with
ffmpeg's default bilinear interpolation, which clamps the sample coordinate to
[0, w−2] × [0, h−2]. The rightmost column and the bottom row of every frame therefore came
out as copies of their neighbours: on an 8×2 float frame under an identity expression, a
last column of 1.0 read back as 0.6. The expressions only ever read integer X, Y, so every
`geq` in the generated script now asks for `interpolation=nearest`, which is both exact and
cheaper.

The exposure/offset/gamma block now always emits the shader's `max(…, 0)`. It used to be
emitted only when the grade carried a non-zero offset or a non-unit gamma — so the default
grade, where the whole block collapsed to a bare channel read, left a negative component in
a scene-linear EXR free to run through the tone curve the viewer never applied it to —
Reinhard maps −2 to +2, so a black pixel encoded as white. The cost warning in the script header was also
describing the wrong thing: it quoted wall-clock figures as if `geq` ran on one core, when
the filter is slice-threaded. It now gives CPU time (~2.9 s/frame at 720p, ~7.5 s at 1080p,
~35 s at 4K) alongside the measured wall clock for the 1080p chain (~0.73 s/frame on 16
threads), rather than a divide-by-your-cores rule the measurements do not support.

The header also no longer promises that "the video matches what you saw" unless the chain
really carries the viewer's curve. It used to make that promise whenever the grade was
readable, which put it six lines above the NOTE explaining that AgX has no closed form and
degrades to a plain clamp. The exposure/offset/gamma and tone-mapping lines are still
printed for AgX — they are worth reading, and they _are_ applied — under a lead-in that
only claims the grade.

When the viewer's grade cannot be read at all, the script says the frames are "only clamped
and sRGB-encoded" — and now that is actually what happens. That branch previously emitted no
`geq`, so nothing clamped the linear floats before the transfer conversion and over-range
values were clipped per channel after the RGB→YUV matrix instead: a linear (100, 0.5, 0.5)
pixel came out (255, 237, 7) where clamping first gives (254, 186, 186). No shipped code
path reaches that branch today — `PostProcessingManager` always answers
`getGradeSettings()` — so it is the defensive fallback that is now honest rather than a
user-visible failure that was fixed.

HTML overlays are composited through `XMLSerializer` rather than `outerHTML`. The markup
goes into an `image/svg+xml` data URL, which the browser parses as XML, and HTML
serialization leaves void elements unclosed — a single `<br>`, which the overlay allowlist
permits and several demos use, was a fatal well-formedness error, so the image never loaded
and the overlay was missing from every captured frame. Wrapped overlay text no longer
treats `\n` as a line break either: the overlays this path can see are laid out
`white-space: normal`, where a newline collapses to a space, so honouring it broke lines the
DOM does not and a trailing newline lifted a bottom-anchored overlay by a whole line.

Finally, capture resolution. Offline captures were truncating the target height to a
multiple of 16, so the menu entry labelled 1080p recorded 1072 lines and "Native" recorded
neither the canvas size nor anything the tooltip claimed. Multiples of 16 were never the
requirement: H.264/H.265 with yuv420p need _even_ dimensions, and encoders pad to their own
macroblock size internally. The requested height is now walked down until the PHYSICAL frame
is even — the frames on disk are the SSAA-multiplied render size, not the size asked for —
and the width is derived from the aligned height, so the framing the user set is preserved.
A 3024×1698 Native target at SSAA 1.5× captured at 4536×2547, and x265 refuses an odd height
outright ("Picture height must be an integer multiple of the specified chroma subsampling"),
writing a 0-byte file after the user had already downloaded a multi-gigabyte ZIP. Only the
product has to be even, so the walk steps by one pixel rather than two; requiring the
request to be even as well threw away half the candidates and cost far more than a factor of
two, which is how a legal 1.05× multiplier ended up shipping 1700 → an odd 1785 — six even
steps from an answer the unit walk finds in one.

That capture size is now read from `PostProcessingManager.getDisplaySize()` instead of
`renderer.getSize()`. The two are not the same number: post-processing hands the renderer the
SSAA-multiplied size and stamps the display size on the canvas CSS, while `resize()` takes a
display size and applies the multiplier itself. So under SSAA the multiplier was being
squared. "Native" on a 1512×850 canvas at DPR 2 with 2× SSAA asked for a 12096×6800 render
target — four times the pixels of the canvas the option's own tooltip promises, and ~1.3 GB
of float per EXR readback, which in practice means a lost context part-way through the
capture. The same read is what the session snapshots and restores whenever it scales the
resolution — every offline capture, and a real-time one at an explicit resolution rather than
"Native" — so such a recording used to leave the viewer at twice its size, compounding on the
next one.

#### Harden zipped-scene loading at the browser boundary

The `.luxar.zarr.zip` reader had no positive-path browser coverage because the
E2E fixture server ignored HTTP range requests. Playwright now uses the
range-capable fixture server, and the browser suite checks both STORED and
DEFLATE archives against the element counts of their directory twin.

That equivalence assertion prevents a false pass from an archive that reaches
viewer initialization while loading no geometry. ZIP64 archives beyond the
65,535-entry boundary and the producer-side `luxar serve` range contract are
covered as well.

The viewer guide now documents the hosting tradeoff: a single-file scene is
useful for distribution, but its first load costs more requests and bytes than
a directory store. Warm revisits remain cache-backed.

#### `luxar optimize` re-chunks a store that already exists, without touching a value (#1717)

Hosting the demo gallery on object storage exposed a problem that no amount of
bandwidth fixes. The demo corpus (`datasets/demos`, 80 stores) is 606,349 files
for 2.94 GB of real bytes — an average file of 5.1 KB, 97.0% of them under
16 KB and 48.6% under 4 KB, against a `TARGET_CHUNK_BYTES` of 64 KB and a
documented 16-256 KB band. Cold-loading `desi_galaxies` from Cloudflare R2 in a
real browser took 245 s over 9,390 requests as written, and 51 s over 2,348
requests once re-chunked to 64 KB, for 20 s of CPU. It was never bandwidth-bound
— 38.6 MB over 245 s is 158 KB/s — it was round trips.

`luxar optimize src.luxar.zarr out.luxar.zarr` is one structure-preserving pass
that changes zarr chunk shapes and nothing else. No refit, no source volume, no
GPU. Values are bit-identical, and `--verify` re-reads the output and compares
every array — and every payload file the pass copied — byte for byte rather
than trusting a metadata checksum, reporting how many of each it checked. dtype,
compressor, filters, serializer, `fill_value`, memory order and every group and
array attribute except the two the pass must move — the root's `content_hash`
and the `chunk_layout` summary beside it, the cache guard described below —
survive verbatim, and a v2 store stays v2 (format conversion is
`gsplat migrate-format`'s job). Codecs are reused off the SOURCE array rather
than re-derived, because an omitted compressor is not "no compressor" — zarr's
`"auto"` is Blosc/lz4 at format 2 and zstd at format 3 — and some Luxar arrays
are deliberately RAW. The plain non-zarr files a group's attrs name — an overlay
image, written straight into its group's directory and reachable through no
array or group API — are carried across byte for byte and compared by `--verify`
like everything else, so a re-chunked scene does not silently lose an overlay
the source still holds. Three kinds of name never reach the output, and none of
them quietly: one that is not a plain file name (it addresses a key outside the
group's own directory, which the hasher likewise folds in by name and never
reads) is skipped with a notice, as is an attr whose file the source no longer
has; and a name that collides case-insensitively with a zarr metadata document —
`Zarr.json` is an ordinary file on ext4 and the group's own document on macOS —
REFUSES the re-chunk outright when the source really holds those bytes, naming
the file and asking for a rename, rather than dropping the payload and shipping
an `image_file` attr pointing at nothing. A payload the source has but cannot be
read (a mode bit, an NFS hiccup) refuses the run the same way, and that is a
deliberate divergence from the compile-time hasher, which degrades an unreadable
payload to a deterministic term so a compile can still finish: a re-chunk has
nothing to gain from finishing without it. `--target-kb` /
`--target-bytes` set the budget directly,
`--profile {hosting,local,archive}` picks 256 KB / 64 KB / 1 MB, `--dry-run`
reports without writing, and `--generic` allows a plain zarr store.

This is not the writer fix (#1713) applied twice. It reaches data that already
exists, where regeneration means a GPU-days refit or a new Zenodo DOI. It sizes
from the STORED dtype, where the writer can only see the input dtype — float32
positions, before the encoder quantizes them to uint16 — which leaves its chunks
2-4x under target; on `spiral_galaxy` the writer fix bought 3.1x fewer requests
and re-chunking bought 8.6x. And authoring and serving want different targets,
which is a flag rather than a rebuild.

The hard part is what must NOT move. `chunk_size` and `chunk_bounds` are the
viewer's partition grid, so every emitted chunk is a whole multiple of the
node's atom — rounded down from the byte budget, never below one atom — and no
row-range read straddles a boundary; Lines' two atoms
(`vertex_ordering.chunk_size` for the per-vertex arrays,
`segment_ordering.chunk_size` for `segments` alone) are resolved separately, and
the bounds arrays themselves are never re-chunked. A `chunk_size` attr is
believed only when the matching bounds array is there: a gsplat leaf written
with `ordering="none"` still gets a default `chunk_size` stamped, its arrays are
not on that grid, and the stamped value is a power of two — so "the array's
chunk is already a multiple of it" is a coincidence, not proof. `array_ref`
placeholders (physical shape `(0, D)`), `(1,)` / `(1, k)` broadcasts and sharded
arrays are copied as-is, a sharded array keeping its SHARD grid rather than
having its inner chunk shape promoted; the chunk key layout (v2
`dimension_separator` / v3 `chunk_key_encoding`) survives; nothing is ever
chunked smaller than it already is; and the copy runs in chunk-aligned slabs,
never `arr[:]` on a whole array — the corpus contains a 629 MB one, and the
content-hash recompute is slab-wise for the same reason.

Cache invalidation is the part with no error to raise, so it is worth stating
which half does the work. The viewer's `MultiLevelCachingStore` validates its
persistent cache on `content_hash`, and that cache holds encoded chunks keyed by
chunk index, so a re-chunk that left the hash where it was would have chunk key
`0/0` covering a different row range while a warm client believed itself current.
Since #1719 and #1721 both hashers fold layout in themselves —
`compute_content_hashes` hashes each array's storage identity (name, shape,
dtype, chunks, shards, codec ids, own attrs) before its values, and the
`.gsplats.zarr` stamp folds the same identity terms over metadata alone — so
recomputing over the output lands on a different digest by construction. What
makes that reach the viewer is the RESTAMP: nothing else rewrites the stored
`content_hash`, and the stored one is what gets compared. The `chunk_layout`
summary attr written on the root is folded in too (attrs ARE hashed):
belt-and-braces against a layout-aware hasher, and still the whole guard for a
store carrying no `content_hash` to restamp, where the viewer falls back to a
digest of the raw root document bytes. The restamp runs for `--generic` too:
that flag describes the INPUT, and gating cache safety on it shipped
re-chunked Luxar scenes under their source's hash.

The output is all-or-nothing. It is built in a hidden sibling directory and
renamed into place only after the copy — and `--verify`, when asked for — has
succeeded, so a failure leaves neither a half-written store at the destination
nor a damaged previous one. A `.zarr.zip` destination is compressed out of that
directory rather than written into a `ZipStore`, which appends rather than
replaces: writing directly produced 211 members for 50 unique names, and under
`-W error` the duplicate-name warnings were a hard failure. Overwriting an
existing output needs `--overwrite`, which replaces an existing zarr store or an
empty directory and refuses anything else; a destination that contains the
source or lives inside it is rejected before the source is even opened; and
rewriting in place is refused outright, precisely because "republish under a new
URL prefix" is the real fix and cannot be enforced from a CLI.

`luxar info --stats` grew the matching diagnostic, computed off the same helper:
average chunk KB, the share of arrays under the 16 KB floor, and the projected
request count for a full load. The problem is now visible before you host
something and count round trips.

`--jobs` is deliberately not implemented. The pass is ~20 s of CPU on the
measured dataset and the copy is I/O bound; parallelism can come later if a
corpus-wide sweep ever wants it.

#### `content_hash` now covers storage layout and encoding, not just values (#1718)

`content_hash` is the token the viewer's `MultiLevelCachingStore` compares against
the remote to decide whether a cached dataset is still valid, and that cache holds
**encoded chunks keyed by chunk index**. What a chunk index addresses is a function
of the chunk shape — so two stores holding byte-identical values under different
chunk shapes are not interchangeable, and until now they hashed EQUAL. As reported
in #1718, re-chunking a compiled scene left its `content_hash` untouched, so a
client holding a cached copy of the original would have served those chunks for
the re-chunked store at every key. Two smaller omissions fell out of the same
loop: array NAMES were not hashed (a renamed array was invisible), and neither was
SHAPE (`tobytes()` of a `(2, 3)` and a `(3, 2)` array holding the same values is
identical, so a reshape was invisible).

Both implementations of that token now fold an array's storage identity into the
hash: `name`, `shape`, `chunks`, `dtype`, the shard shape (`None` when unsharded,
folded in unconditionally so its presence is stable) and the array's codec **ids**
in encode-pipeline order. That happens in `compute_content_hashes` (the compiler's
finalize pass, which also keeps hashing the decoded values) and in
`_stamp_content_hash` (the metadata-only variant the gsplats writers,
`gsplat annotate-quality` and `gsplat doctor --fix` use, which must never read
array data). All of it comes from metadata already in hand, so there is no extra
I/O. The two remain separate digests over different serializations and are never
compared with each other; they simply now agree that chunk/shard layout and codec
identity are part of a store's identity. Folding it into the metadata-only variant
matters less for today's callers than for tomorrow's: neither in-place re-stamper
can currently change layout (every mutation on those paths is attrs-only), but a
future in-place re-layout tool must not be able to re-stamp a store to its input's
digest — and the two digests should agree on what identity means regardless.

The codec ids are derived at **both** on-disk formats. Format 3 lists its pipeline
under one `codecs` member; format 2 holds the same information under `filters` plus
`compressor`, and folding only the format-3 spelling would have left the very
defect this entry describes standing at format 2 — where three arrays identical in
values, shape and chunks but written raw / Blosc-zstd / GZip all hashed the same.
Luxar writes format 2 on demand (`LUXAR_ZARR_FORMAT=2`) and re-finalizes legacy v2
stores, so a mixed-format tree is the normal steady state. Both formats contribute
**ids** rather than full codec settings: an id list catches a raw↔compressed switch
and a codec-family switch (blosc↔gzip), each of which changes what the stored bytes
at an unchanged chunk key mean, while a pure tuning change (a blosc `clevel`, a
gzip `level`) leaves the ids — and so the hash — alone instead of churning every
store's digest. That exclusion is sound rather than merely pragmatic: blosc/gzip/
zstd streams are self-describing (cached bytes decode correctly against metadata
announcing different settings), and the one Luxar codec whose settings *are*
load-bearing, `luxar_delta_v1`, derives its `cols`/`bits` from the array's column
count and dtype itemsize, both already hashed. Both directions are pinned by tests.

The one place the full pipeline is folded in is a SHARDED array: there a chunk key
addresses a shard, and everything that decides what its bytes mean — inner
`chunk_shape`, inner `codecs`, `index_codecs`, `index_location` — sits nested
inside the single top-level `ShardingCodec`, behind an id list that would read only
`["sharding_indexed"]`. Both implementations expand it. Nothing in Luxar emits a
sharded store today, so a test that varies only the inner compressor is what keeps
that fold honest.

Group NAMES are hashed too, for the same reason array names now are. A node's own
digest does not carry its name, and the parent used to fold in only the digests of
its children — so renaming a node while leaving its contents alone produced a store
whose root hash was identical to the original's, and a client holding a cached copy
kept serving the old tree (including the consolidated root document that enumerates
the old names). Each child now contributes its name alongside its digest.

Also closed, an adjacent blind spot of the same function found in review: each
array's **own** `attrs` were hashed by neither implementation. That is where Luxar
keeps every array's dequantization parameters — `/amplitudes` carries an
`encoding` document with the quantization `min`/`max`, `/centers` a per-channel
`col_lo`/`col_hi`, a `broadcasted` array its `n_elements` — so those attrs are what
turn the stored ints back into scientific values. Mutating a single `min` shifted
the decoded float of every splat and moved neither digest; a `broadcasted`
`n_elements` even changes the decoded *length*, which the value-hashing compiler
variant could not see either. Each array's attrs now contribute one term, sorted
and serialized the same deterministic way the group attrs already were. Nothing
writes an array attr after the stamp (finalize's back-fills touch group attrs only,
and all of them run before the hash), so the input is stable.

The accepted consequence: changing the hash inputs changes every existing store's
hash **on its next write**. A client holding an L2/OPFS cache for a dataset that
gets re-finalized will see the hash change, invalidate, and re-download once —
which is exactly the behaviour the token exists for, and it happens one time per
dataset. Nothing rewrites hashes for stores already on disk: an un-touched store
keeps the hash it was written with until something re-finalizes it, so old and new
stores coexist without a migration.

#### The content hash now covers overlay image bytes

An overlay image lives inside its zarr group as a plain file, named by the
group's `image_file` attr (`overlays/<name>/image.png`), with no chunk grid and
no zarr metadata. The finalize-time hash walk enumerated `array_keys()` and
`group_keys()`, so it never saw those bytes: two scenes compiled from the same
script and differing *only* in their overlay image received the same root
`content_hash`. That token is advertised as a content fingerprint and consumed as
one — the viewer's scene-identity watchdog, cache validation — so a rebuild whose
only change was the logo was indistinguishable from no rebuild at all. (zarr had
been telling us all along, in its own way — every compile with an image overlay
warned that `image.png` "is not recognized as a component of a Zarr hierarchy".)

`compute_content_hashes` now folds such payload files into each group's digest,
between the attrs and the child groups, reading them through the store itself via
a new `_zarr_compat.read_raw_bytes`. Which attrs name a payload is a list
(`PAYLOAD_FILE_ATTRS`, today just `image_file`); a payload that cannot be read
folds a deterministic sentinel rather than failing the compile, and the three
ways that can happen — missing, refused by name, refused by the store — stay
distinguishable from each other and from a zero-byte file.

A group naming no payload file adds no terms at all, so a payload-free store's
digest is byte-identical to what previous versions produced and existing caches
are not invalidated wholesale. For a scene that *does* carry an image overlay the
consequence is the intended one: a rebuild changing only the overlay image moves
the root hash, so a client holding that dataset in its L2/OPFS cache re-downloads
its chunks once — which is exactly what the token exists for. Scope note: this is
a compile-time fingerprint, so replacing the PNG inside an already-finalized
`.luxar.zarr` restamps nothing. The metadata-only `_stamp_content_hash` used for
`.gsplats.zarr` is deliberately untouched: those stores carry no overlays and
that variant must never read bytes.

#### A starved E2E state probe now says so, instead of spending the whole test budget

`getLuxarState` was the last of the two probes the E2E suite leans on that still
ran an unbounded `page.evaluate`. On a page whose frame loop has saturated the
main thread, that probe does not fail — it simply never answers, so the run
reported a bare `Test timeout of 120000ms exceeded` pointing at a line inside the
helper, with nothing to say which dataset or which probe was pending. It is now
deadline-bounded at 45 s like `getConsoleMessages`, and throws a diagnostic that
names the starvation and the viewer bug behind it. The sentinel it races against
is a fresh Node-side object rather than `null`, because `getState()` is an
untyped payload the viewer may reshape: a primitive sentinel would turn a
legitimate falsy answer into a bogus "main thread saturated" verdict.

The four poll loops that call it (`waitForPointsLoaded`,
`waitForDimensionNavigation`, and the two silent variants) catch a failing probe
and retry, since a missing debug interface is legitimate during initialization.
That catch was swallowing the new diagnostic whole, so the two throwing loops now
carry the last probe failure into their own timeout message — otherwise a
saturated main thread is reported as missing data. That record is cleared on
every answered probe, so the initialization-window miss that legitimately
happens on a healthy page does not get blamed for a loop that then polled fine
for the rest of its budget. They deliberately do NOT clamp
the probe to their own remaining budget: these loops succeed on any satisfying
answer, so clamping would newly fail a healthy-but-slow page across some sixty
call sites.

`performance_benchmark_example.luxar.zarr` was parked in the smoke spec's
`KNOWN_FLAKY_LARGE_DATASETS` while the underlying viewer bug was open: that
100-node scene collapsed to ~1 fps about 30 s after it loaded and starved the
control channel hard enough that a 0.5 ms `getState()` took 111 s to cross the
bridge. The frame-pacing entry in this same release removes that cause, so the
dataset is back in the all-examples run and the 100-node load path has coverage
again.

#### Frame pacing stops a slow scene from livelocking the whole main thread (#1724)

`performance_benchmark_example.luxar.zarr` (100 point-cloud nodes, 100k points,
8 MB) rendered a healthy ~59 fps for about thirty seconds while its nodes
arrived, then collapsed to ~1 fps and never recovered. It also wedged the
Playwright/CDP control channel: `getState()` costs 0.5 ms in-page but took 111 s
across the bridge, and a trivial `page.evaluate` timed out at 15 s. The dataset
was consequently parked out of the all-examples smoke test.

None of the usual suspects was responsible. Pinning `?dpr=0.25` — sixteen times
fewer pixels — left the frame at 925 ms against 940 ms, and a hundred-fold
covered-area sweep did not move it either, so this was not fill rate. Cost was
strictly linear in element count (1k points 21 ms, 100k points 1030 ms) and
100k points in _one_ node cost the same as in a hundred, so it was not draw-call
or node count. Adaptive DPR was not starved out: it ran, walked 0.99 → 0.89 →
0.80, and its U-shape probe correctly rejected further steps because there was
no fill to shed. Time inside WebGL calls was under 2 ms per frame and an
explicit `finish()` returned in 0 ms. What was busy was the GPU process (~1100 %
CPU over thirteen SwiftShader threads at nice 5), starving the renderer's main
thread while V8 sat 99.4 % idle.

The mechanism is the animation loop's scheduling. Every frame re-arms
`requestAnimationFrame` back-to-back, so at ~1 s per frame the main thread is at
a 100 % duty cycle of long tasks and _nothing_ else ever gets a slot — not
worker message delivery, not a CDP `Runtime.callFunctionOn`. That is a livelock
rather than merely a slow render: the depth-sort worker sorted each node in
0.1 ms, but its Comlink replies were dispatched at ~0.5/s (round trips climbing
from 4 ms to 60 s), and every reply that landed staged an ordering apply that
called `requestRender()`, re-arming the loop. The rendering starved the very
hand-off that would have let it stop — 200 dispatches, ~120 still outstanding
after 70 s, `animating=true` throughout.

`AnimationController` now paces itself. When a frame's own cost exceeds
`config.animation.pacing.slowFrameMs` (250 ms — 4 fps, already far past any
interactive threshold, so every healthy frame rate keeps the untouched fast path)
for _two consecutive_ frames, the next frame is scheduled after a cooldown of
`min(maxCooldownMs, 25 % of the cost)` instead of re-arming immediately. The
cooldown is a bounded _fraction_ rather than a constant because a flat gap cannot
track the cost across the band where the fraction is what decides it — 250 ms to
1 s, where a fixed 100 ms over-yields at the bottom and under-yields at the top
(9 % of wall-clock after a 1 s frame, against the fraction's 20 %). Past 1 s the
`maxCooldownMs` clamp makes the shipped behaviour flat as well, which is its job:
it bounds the added latency of an on-demand repaint. (The measured wedge, at
~1042 ms a frame, sits essentially at that clamp.)

The gap is armed from a zero-delay hop — `setTimeout(0)` →
`setTimeout(cooldown)` → `requestAnimationFrame` — and that indirection is the
whole of it. The scheduling decision is taken at the _top_ of the frame so the
loop survives an exception thrown by controls, a per-frame callback or the
render; but a slow frame spends its second on browser rendering work that runs
after the rAF callback returns and inside the same main-thread task (which is
why the `longtask` entries read ~1042 ms while V8 sits 99.4 % idle). A timer
armed at the frame's start is therefore always already overdue by the time the
thread frees: it fires immediately and inserts nothing. The hop runs at the
first event-loop turn _after_ that work, and only then is the real cooldown
armed. Both halves of the fix then hold — no animation-frame request is
outstanding while the frame is drawn, so the compositor stops driving main
frames back-to-back, and a genuine cooldown follows it.

The cost measured is the frame _period_ minus the gap we ourselves inserted: the
wedge's second is non-JS main-thread time, so a JS-body span reads ~2 ms and
would never fire, and not subtracting our own gap would make pacing latch on for
the rest of the session. The measurement resets on the stopped→running edge, so
an idle rest or a tab-hide is not read as one enormous frame. Being a _period_
also means a foreign main-thread task of that size is charged to the loop even
when the loop did not cause it: scene loading runs frames in that neighbourhood
(the repo's own `tests/e2e/render-ticks.ts` measures ~230 ms periods, just under
the threshold), so a heavier load crosses it and does pace — which is what you
want there, since the cooldown yields to the decode tasks.

That last property is why the trigger is a _streak_ rather than a single frame.
The wedge is sustained — every frame ~1042 ms, forever — so waiting for a second
consecutive slow frame delays the first cooldown by exactly one frame and gives
up nothing, while a lone outlier (a GC pause, a shader compile, one synchronous
chunk decode, a foreign task charged to the loop because the measurement is a
period) is precisely what must _not_ be paced. Pacing one of those fed adaptive
DPR a cooldown it read as a 3.75 fps frame rate off a freshly cleared two-sample
window — an unprobed 10 % DPR scale-down — and pushed a just-under-`gapResetMs`
interval just over it, inventing a stall gap-reset that had not happened. A
single fast frame drops the streak back to zero, so recovery is immediate; an
_alternating_ slow/fast cadence is deliberately never paced, because the fast
frames are proof the main thread is already getting the slots a cooldown would
have bought. Sustained foreign work — a heavy scene load — still paces, which is
the behaviour you want there: yielding to those decode tasks is the point.

Frames are delayed, never skipped: each one that runs still emits exactly one
`frame-start` / `frame-end` pair, and still calls `recordFrame()` whenever it
does GPU work of its own (that call was already gated on the context-lost and
render-skip predicates, and pacing does not change the gate) — both on the real
clock.
The achieved frame rate really is lower and neither the FPS readout nor the DPR
control loop is told otherwise — a steady paced cadence is absorbed by the stall
detector's median-based outlier test rather than read as a gap, and the
isolated-hiccup interactions above cannot arise, because an isolated slow frame
is never paced. Pacing is suspended outright for the whole
of a recording, where the loop's exact cadence belongs to someone else — the
real-time MediaRecorder path records the canvas this loop paints, and the
offline capture drives its own `await requestAnimationFrame` cadence with
one-shot per-frame orbit callbacks registered on the controller. (A plain
screenshot needs no suspension: it reads the canvas after its own awaited
frame.) A suspend predicate that throws is treated as "not suspended", because
this scheduling point is the loop's only re-arm and a lost re-arm freezes the
viewer with no way back.

With pacing in place the same scene settles (`animating=false`) at 15 s and
`page.evaluate` answers in 1–5 ms, so the benchmark example is back in
`all-examples-smoke-test.spec.ts`, joined by a focused `frame-pacing.spec.ts`
that asserts the scene really loaded, then both halves of the fix: the loop idles
within a bounded budget (stably, not just for one poll tick), and the control
channel stays responsive afterwards under individually bounded probes. Neither
the spec nor the un-parked example is in the smoke subset
(`pnpm test:e2e:smoke`), so both run only in the full E2E suite.

#### The nav, spatial-query and WebGL-error E2E waits stop returning on unread state (#1726)

Two of the E2E poll loops ended their budget by simply returning:
`waitForNavigationComplete` closed with `// Timeout is not an error - loading may
have completed` and `waitForSpatialQuery` with the same shape, and every
iteration of both swallowed a probe failure in an empty `catch`. That is right
for the case they were written for — a navigation or query that settled before
polling started, which is exactly why several call sites deliberately choose the
silent variant, their action never toggling `isLoading` at all. It is
indistinguishable, though, from a run in which every probe FAILED:
`getLuxarState` rejects on a page with no debug interface, on a destroyed
execution context, and — since it gained a deadline of its own (#1651 / #1724) —
on a page too starved to answer within 45 s; the loop swallowed each rejection
and returned after its full budget having read no viewer state at all.

What that cost at today's call sites is ATTRIBUTION, not a false pass. All nine
`waitForNavigationComplete` calls follow the wait with a page probe of their own —
`getLuxarState`, a bare `page.evaluate`, or a `getDimensionValue` that answers
`-1` and then fails its own `expect` — so a helper that read nothing produced a
FAILING test one statement later, charged to the wrong statement and reported as a
bare `Debug interface not ready` or a nonsense `-1`. Six of the nine (all in
`spatial-index-accuracy.spec.ts`) additionally sit right after
`waitForSpatialQueryOrThrow`, which cannot have succeeded unless the page answered
within the last 8 s, so on those the new throw is near-unreachable and what they
get is the attributed warn. The vacuous pass proper — confirmed nothing, and
nobody re-probes afterwards — is a hole in the CONTRACT rather than a bug in a
current caller, and it is closed here for the next caller alongside the
attribution win, which is the immediate one.

The end of the budget is now a real decision, split on one question: did any
probe ever answer? If none did, the helper throws, naming itself, its nominal
budget, the time it actually spent, how many probes went out and how many of them
yielded no usable state (a rejection, or an answer the condition could not be read
off), and the last probe failure — it never once read viewer state, so there is
nothing for the caller's assertions to stand on. If a probe answered but the
condition never settled, the helper still returns normally — the tolerated case
those nine call sites depend on — but emits exactly one `console.warn` in the
house `[⚠️] [E2E <helper>]` form, with the same counts and the carried probe
diagnostic appended in the shared `describeLastProbeError` wording the two loops
that already throw (`waitForPointsLoaded`, `waitForDimensionNavigation`) use. Both
reports are composed by one module-private helper next to it, since the two loops'
messages differ only in their names and nouns, so a single grep still finds every
carried-failure report. Both loops clear that record on an answered probe, as
those siblings do: a missing debug interface during initialization is normal and
recovers, and carrying that first failure to the end would blame it for a loop
that then polled a healthy page. The COUNTS are what survives the clearing —
without them a 15 s window in which 149 of its ~150 probes rejected and only the
last one answered would report as a clean "answered but never settled" on the
strength of that single read. Both reports also state the measured elapsed time
next to the nominal budget, because neither loop clamps its probes: that is
deliberate — these loops succeed on ANY satisfying answer, so a clamp would fail a
healthy-but-slow page — but it means a `waitForNavigationComplete(page, 15000)`
whose preliminary wait spends 10 s and whose probe then burns its own 45 s
deadline runs for ~55 s, and reporting that as "15000ms" would send the reader
after the wrong problem. A non-positive budget needs no special case: it never
enters `waitForSpatialQuery`'s loop, and the counts then report "0 probe(s)
attempted" rather than implying probes that were tried and came back empty. The
healthy path is unchanged and stays silent: those call sites succeed on their
first probe, `isLoading` already being false when they poll.

`waitForNavigationComplete` also had a second silent exit. Its preliminary
`page.waitForFunction` for `typeof isLoading === 'boolean'` used to `catch`, sleep
300 ms and return, on the stated reasoning that "navigation completes before we
start polling" — which does not explain a missing `isLoading` at all, since the
flag exists whenever the debug interface does. That `catch` now falls through into
the poll loop, so the state probe gets its chance to answer or to produce a better
diagnostic, and the single end-of-budget decision governs both paths. The
preliminary failure is named in the answered-but-unsettled warn with the time it
cost — "the flag was unreadable for the first 10 s" is exactly what explains a
15 s budget that never saw `isLoading` clear, though that figure is
deterministically the clamped preliminary budget rather than a measurement of
anything — but it is not a probe failure: it stays out of the probe counts, and out
of the throw, where the carried probe rejection is both fresher and the better
headline. The loop
became a `do`/`while` so it always probes at least once: the preliminary wait can
cost up to 10 s on its own, and reporting "no probe answered" without having
probed would be a false diagnostic. Its `min(timeout, 10000)` ceiling is now
floored at 1 ms as well, because Playwright reads `timeout: 0` as NO timeout — a
non-positive budget used to park that wait for the whole test, the exact opposite
of what the ceiling is for.

The fall-through's cost is smaller than it first looks, but it is not free. Where
that `catch` returned after `min(timeout, 10000) + 300` ms, the call now spends the
preliminary wait plus one probe deadline plus a poll, so the decision lands ~55 s
after the wait started — on top of everything the spec already spent reaching it,
against the 60 s per-test timeout in `playwright.config.ts`. The scenario that
costs is a page that starves AFTER load, before the nav wait; a page starved from
the start never gets this far, failing earlier in `waitForLuxarReady`'s own wait
with its own message. On such a page Playwright usually expires the test first at
all nine sites: the three whose next statement is an unbounded `page.evaluate`
(directly in `keyboard-input-system.spec.ts`, through the spec-local
`getDimensionValue` twice in `dimension-animation.spec.ts`) hang there either way,
and even the six `spatial-index-accuracy.spec.ts` sites, whose next statement is
the bounded `getLuxarState`, have typically spent enough of the 60 s reaching the
wait that the ~55 s decision lands past it. So the 300 ms return it replaced mostly
bought the same hang one statement later, and the crafted message often never
prints. What the change reliably buys is therefore not a run that ends instead of
expiring, but ATTRIBUTION whenever the decision IS reached: the report prints under
this helper's own name, budget and counts rather than surfacing as the next
statement's failure.

`waitForWebGLError` is bounded rather than split, because it returns data instead
of a verdict: `getWebGLErrors` is a bare `page.evaluate`, so the first unanswered
read blew straight through the helper's 5 s budget to the whole test's. Each read
is now raced against the remaining budget, with the sentinel a Node-allocated
array compared by identity rather than by contents — an empty list is a
legitimate answer here, one a clean GL queue returns on nearly every poll — and no
FURTHER read is dispatched into a remainder shorter than one poll interval, since
`getWebGLErrors` DRAINS the GL queue in-page and an answer discarded for missing
the deadline takes the real errors it already cleared with it. A read that spent
the whole remainder is also no longer followed by one more `pollMs` sleep past the
deadline, so a 1000 ms budget no longer reports 1100 ms elapsed. The first read is
exempt from the sliver-skip, so any positive `timeout`, even one under `pollMs`,
still checks the queue once instead of returning `[]` while warning that nothing
was checked — that exemption is also the one case where the call can still outlast
its budget, since an early answer there is followed by a full `pollMs` before the
guard re-checks. A non-positive `timeout` gets zero reads, the loop guard failing
on entry, and the warn then says nothing was checked, which is true. That trade is inherent to
bounding a helper that returns data; removing it means bounding `getWebGLErrors`
itself — the same treatment #1651 gave `getLuxarState` and `getConsoleMessages` —
which reaches 21 direct call sites across 11 spec files and is left out of scope
here rather than tracked anywhere, #1651 being closed. The helper does not throw on give-up — it warns
once, saying whether any read answered and how many errors the accumulated union
held, so an unsatisfied predicate cannot be read as "the page was healthy and
produced no such error" — but it is not throw-free: a read that rejects, or a page
closed mid-poll, still propagates. It has no call sites today, so that contract
change is forward-looking.

`src/tests/unit/tests/e2e-helpers-silent-waits.test.ts` covers all three helpers
against fake pages, with the per-test redness against the old code recorded in its
header: a page whose probes reject makes both loops throw within their own budget;
a page whose probes never answer at all makes them throw too, carrying the probe's
own starvation diagnostic and a measured elapsed longer than the budget; an
answered-but-unsettled page resolves with exactly one warning carrying the probe
diagnostic, the probe counts, and the preliminary failure when there was one,
while a stale early failure is cleared in EITHER loop without dropping out of the
counts; a `null` answer warns and
returns on both loops rather than being read as no answer; a budget the
preliminary wait consumes whole is still probed exactly once, and a non-positive
one neither hangs in that wait nor claims probes it never attempted; the WebGL
loop accumulates across polls, propagates a rejecting read, and holds its budget
to the millisecond; and the healthy cases stay silent, which is the assertion that
protects the existing call sites.

#### `luxar restamp-lod` migrates a shipped store's LOD thresholds in place

Every LOD ladder in the bundled demo corpus is on the legacy `coverage` selector
— the diagonal metric — because its thresholds were derived before the
`screen-area` one existed. The values are on the wrong scale for the metric the
viewer now prefers, and re-generating a dataset to fix a handful of numbers is
absurd when nothing about the data has changed: only a `selector` attr and one
`coverage_fraction` per ladder child are wrong. The new `luxar restamp-lod`
command rewrites exactly those, in place, without opening a single array (the
`content_hash` restamp that follows a real change is the one exception — see
below).

It walks the store, and for each `kind=lod` group still on `coverage` (or
carrying no `selector`, which historically meant the same) re-derives the
per-child thresholds by screen-occupancy halving and stamps the group
`screen-area`. The anchor follows the tree writers' own rule rather than a
guess, both clauses of it: a ladder gets the fills-screen (per-tile) anchor when
a real multi-part `kind=partition` encloses it, **and** when one of its own
ladder children is a `kind=partition` — the `overview` recipe's coarse cap,
pinned at fills-screen on purpose so the opening framing shows the cap rather
than pulling in the whole dataset. Everything else — including a ladder under a
ONE-part partition, whose single part's bbox is the whole object — keeps the
whole-object anchor. The resolved binding is threaded down to a nested ladder
just as the writers thread it. Children are ordered coarsest→finest by
`child_index`, so a ten-plus-level ladder does not get its finest threshold
handed to `child_10`. A per-recipe round trip (`levels`, `tiles`, `overview`,
`adaptive`: write, age to legacy, restamp) pins the whole point of the command —
a restamped store is indistinguishable from a freshly written one.

The command is a deliberate opt-in and can never be triggered by anything else.
An authored `coverage_fractions=[...]` list and a legacy derived one are
indistinguishable on disk — the reason the compiler's one-part-partition anchor
check only ever warns — so this rewrite may be overriding a choice somebody made
on purpose. It therefore prints the old→new ladder and the anchor for every
group it touches, offers `--dry-run` and a repeatable `--group` to restrict the
pass, and skips (loudly, with a non-zero exit) anything it cannot convert
honestly: a `selector` outside the vocabulary, which wants `luxar gsplat
migrate-format` first, a finest level whose element count the store does not
record, where fabricating a positive would defeat the derivation's own
"finest LOD level is empty" guard, a stored ladder that descends in the
resolved coarsest→finest child order, where the two disagree about which level
is finest and re-deriving would invert the ladder, or a child that carries a
`coverage_fraction` but no scene-node `type` attr, where re-deriving over the
children that do resolve would leave a partial, non-monotonic ladder with that
rung stranded on its legacy threshold.

The exit code covers one further case, in which the rewrite itself succeeded: a
store carrying neither a scene `type` nor a `.gsplats.zarr` `content_hash` — a
bare `kind=partition` root, say — has no digest to restamp, so nothing tells a
warm viewer cache the ladder moved. At zarr format 2, which is what the legacy
corpus this command targets is written in, even the viewer's `zattrs-hash`
fallback digests the root `.zattrs` bytes, and editing a child's ladder does not
move those. The ladders are still written and the run says so plainly, but it
exits non-zero: the store has to be republished under a new URL prefix or the
migration is invisible to every client that already has it.

It is a sibling of `luxar optimize`, not a flag on it: that pass documents that
every attribute is preserved and refuses same-path work, while this one changes
only attributes and works in place. A group already on `screen-area` is skipped,
so a second run changes nothing at all — including the `content_hash`, which is
restamped and re-consolidated only when something really moved, since an
attrs-only edit still has to invalidate a warm viewer cache. That restamp is the
one part of a run that is not free, and the docs now say so: a compiled scene's
digest covers array VALUES, so moving it streams every array in the store once
(linear in the store's size, however few attributes changed), while a standalone
`.gsplats.zarr` gets a metadata-only stamp. The result is then read back and
verified through both the per-node documents and the consolidated index the
viewer fetches, so a consolidation mistake cannot pass silently.

Writes are all-or-nothing. The pass classifies every group in a read-only
planning walk first, and if a write then fails it restores each attribute it had
already rewritten — an absent `coverage_fraction` back to absent — and re-raises
the original error with a note saying what was rolled back. Left unwound, a
mid-walk failure published a torn ladder: screen-area thresholds under
`selector="coverage"`, the two disagreeing about their units with nothing
downstream able to notice.

The recovery restores the store's `content_hash` digests rather than recomputing
them: each is recorded before the hash pass overwrites it, so a legacy store
hashed by an older walk, a hand-edited one, or a scene whose inner groups carry
no per-group digest is not quietly re-digested by a run that FAILED — and the
failure path stays metadata-only instead of streaming every array in the store a
second time. The metadata is re-consolidated only when the run had rewritten the
ROOT document, which at zarr format 3 is the write that destroys the index: a
failure at the first attribute write needs no root write at all, and
re-consolidating there could turn a fully recoverable failure into a published
store with no index, which the viewer loads as an empty scene. On the success
side an index is likewise rebuilt but never introduced — a store handed over
unconsolidated leaves that way, since `is_consolidated` is how `batch-fit` tells
a finished tile from an interrupted one, and the report now carries
`was_consolidated` so an operator can see why.

#### One place decides a LOD ladder's thresholds and the selector that describes them

A `kind=lod` group writes two things that are really one decision: the per-child
`coverage_fraction` thresholds, and the group-level `selector` naming the units
those thresholds are in — the legacy diagonal metric (`"coverage"`, bounded by
`MAX_COVERAGE_FRACTION` = 4.0) or literal screen-area fractions
(`"screen-area"`, anchored at half the screen for a whole object and
fills-screen for a partition tile). Pair them wrongly and nothing raises, because
both spellings are individually valid; every switch point the viewer computes is
simply on the wrong scale.

The rule that picks between them — an explicit `coverage_fractions=[...]` list
keeps the legacy units it was authored in, anything derived is stamped
screen-area — was written out four times (the `add_points` / `add_lines` /
`add_mesh` `substitutive_lod=` wrappers and the `add_gsplats_from_data`
`lod_group=` dispatch) and enforced nowhere. Those four now share one decision,
`lod.group.resolve_lod_ladder`, which returns the selector alongside the
thresholds it describes so a producer has no occasion to name a selector at all;
the previously-dead `DERIVED_LOD_SELECTOR` constant and its new
`LEGACY_LOD_SELECTOR` sibling are what it returns, and the `add_lod_group`
default now reads from the latter instead of repeating the literal. Each call
site keeps its own user-facing length-mismatch message, so no error text moved.

The refactor is behaviour-preserving: all four adders were already pairing
correctly, so nothing a user sees changes. The detached-tree paths are
deliberately untouched and still separate, because they answer a different
question — not "did the caller supply a list?" but "what does a *stored* tree
already claim about its own thresholds?" That one lives in
`gsplats.tree.gate_authored_selector`, shared by
`io/_compiler/gsplat_tree.write_gsplat_node` and
`gsplats_pipeline/from_io.graft_gsplat_node` (the `add_gsplats_from_file` graft
path, which derives its thresholds directly and takes its selector from that
gate).

A new cross-geometry suite pins the rule from both sides for all four adders —
derived ladders stamp screen-area (neither mesh nor gsplats had ever been
asserted), explicit ones stamp legacy (nothing asserted that anywhere) — plus the
consistency invariant that a stamped selector must agree with its own stamped
thresholds, an AST guard that no ladder producer spells a selector out for itself
again, and a discovery guard that a *fifth* `add_lod_group` producer has to be
either routed or explicitly exempted. The suite is a regression fence, not a
detector: it constrains what the library writes from here on and says nothing
about the 209 already-shipped ladders that carry `selector="coverage"` over
derived-looking thresholds (issue #1727) — auditing or migrating those is
separate work.

#### A preset-less content fit is near-lossless again, as it always claimed to be

`gsplat fit --tiling content` without a `--preset` fitted every box at
`cull_retention=0.95`, discarding the bottom 5% of cumulative amplitude after each
box, while the code sitting right there said 0.999. The line meant to install that
default was `fk.setdefault("cull_retention", 0.999)`, and it could never fire:
`load_fit_config` starts from the defaults harvested off `fit_gaussian_splats`'s own
signature, which include `cull_retention=0.95`, so the key was always present by the
time the planner looked. Only the preset-less invocation was affected — every preset
sets 0.999 explicitly — which is exactly the invocation a first content fit tends to
be.

Content tiling keeps its own near-lossless retention, and now actually gets it. Why
content specifically: the library-level sibling `fit_planned` already declared 0.999
for the boxes it fits, so the dead line in the CLI planner was the CLI half of an
intent that already existed downstream — the two halves now share one constant,
`luxar.gsplats.planner.CONTENT_CULL_RETENTION`, and cannot drift apart again. And
content is the `--cal`-driven path, so it is where that 0.95 — one half of the false
`signal_limited` curve `gsplat cal` used to report — is most in play. A per-box cull
also compounds, the merged store losing the weakest splats of every box rather than
of the volume, but that argument does not single content out: `--tiling uniform`'s
default partition merge culls each tile independently too (only its `--flat` merge
culls once, globally), and it stays at 0.95 on purpose. Only the content path moves
here.

The mechanism is a new per-command defaults layer in `load_fit_config`, sitting
directly above the harvested function defaults: the priority chain is now
`CLI flags > YAML config > preset > command defaults > function defaults`. So
`--preset`, a `cull_retention:` in a `--config` and `--cull-retention` all still win
over it — including `--cull-retention 0`, the "keep every splat" escape hatch — and
only the fitter's 0.95 is displaced. The `-j N` box workers resolve the same value
through the same code path, so parallel and sequential content fits cannot diverge.
Nothing else moves: a whole-volume fit (`--tiling none`) and `--tiling uniform` still
fall through to the documented 0.95.

#### The README, the format spec and the viewer's LOD docs describe today's threshold rule (#1732)

Several prose sites still described substitutive LOD selection as it worked
before v3.4. The README told readers the viewer picks a level with
`coverage_fraction = sqrt(N_i / N_finest)` and that the finest level shows once
an object's projected size reaches about half the viewport's fitted screen axis.
Both halves were wrong, and not by relabelling: the count-ratio derivation is
retired, and today's metric is a screen-AREA fraction (projected bbox rect area
over viewport area) where the old anchor was a projected DIAGONAL fraction. No
factor converts one into the other — a rect's area share depends on its own
shape and on the viewport aspect, so the square rect whose diagonal is half the
fitted axis covers ~7% of a 16:9 viewport, not a quarter of it. The paragraph
also said nothing about tiles, which left it subtly wrong for two of the six
recipes tabulated immediately above it.

The rule as the code has it: thresholds are derived by screen-occupancy halving,
count-INDEPENDENTLY (the counts set only the ladder's length), a whole-object
ladder anchoring its finest level at area `0.5` — `[0, 0.125, 0.25, 0.5]` for
four levels — and the two partition-bound recipes, `adaptive` and `overview`,
anchoring one step higher at `1.0`. The old "self-calibrates on any monitor or
aspect ratio" is now "needs no per-resolution or DPI tuning": an area fraction
is exactly resolution-independent but genuinely NOT aspect-invariant, since the
camera framing is fitted to one screen axis, so a wider viewport shows more
world and the same object covers a smaller share of it.

The two v3.2 version-history bullets in `GSPLATS_ZARR_FORMAT.md` each ended with
"the upper bound later widened to `4.0` for partition-bound ladders", which had
the driver backwards: the bound widened so a hand-tuned
`coverage_fractions=[...]` list stayed expressible after the viewer's fill
anchor was loosened — a ×4 rescale that engaged the finest level at a normal
full-frame view instead of only once the object overfilled the screen — and
partition-bound derived ladders then anchored on the already-widened bound.
`MAX_COVERAGE_FRACTION` = 4.0 (a Python-side constant) remains the ceiling on a
`selector="coverage"` ladder, and is only APPROXIMATELY fills-screen in those
legacy diagonal units — a screen-filling object's diagonal is 2.04 fitted axes
at the 16:9 reference, rounded to a plain 2. What it is not is today's anchor,
which under `screen-area` is `0.5` whole-object and `1.0` partition-bound. The
diagonal metric itself arrived in v3.2 for device-independent switching; making
the whole-object anchor aspect-exact was the goal of a later re-anchoring of its
denominator to the fitted screen axis, not of the metric.

Two viewer package READMEs stated the retired rule in the present tense as well
— `src/types/README.md`'s LOD-groups paragraph and `src/scene/README.md`'s
per-frame selector algorithm — as did the `scene/` doc comments the selector is
read through (the hysteresis pick, the cross-fade plan, the mesh freshness
note). They now lead with the derived `screen-area` path and name the diagonal
one as the legacy `selector="coverage"` path it has become, matching the doc
comment in `types/lod-group.ts` that was already correct.

The mesh substitutive-LOD path carried the same premise three more times — the
wrapper docstring, the loop guard that drops a level which fails to reduce the
surface, and the test covering that fallback — each justifying the drop by
saying a duplicate count hands `coverage_fractions` a repeated ratio that is not
strictly ascending and raises. It no longer does: thresholds come from the
ladder's LENGTH, so a duplicate count is not a duplicate threshold. Dropping the
level is still right, for the reason now stated — two identical surfaces would
each claim their own halving of screen occupancy, so the viewer would swap
between them and pay a load for nothing. `decimate_cluster`'s `Raises` block
needed a different correction rather than the same one: it explained why an
empty result is an error by pointing at the `coverage_fractions` raise, which
only fires on an empty FINEST level, while every level that function produces is
a coarse one. The reason is one layer up — an empty return would be dropped in
silence by the wrapper's strictly-ascending guard, and the degenerate mesh would
come out as a plain leaf with nothing naming which mesh caused it.

#### Content-tiled flat fits publish merged quality metrics

Content-adaptive fits now score the merged flat reconstruction against the whole reference volume, for both sequential and parallel box drivers, using the same bounded-memory scorer as uniform tiling. External plans are rejected before fitting when their grid does not match the selected volume.
