When scoring cannot run — including an over-budget volume, a missing or mismatched parallel reference, or the current `kind=partition` result — the fit says why even under `--quiet` and names the `gsplat compare` recourse instead of silently shipping an unscored archive.

#### The demo manifest records both copies of every archive

Every Zenodo-hosted demo archive has been refitted, re-encoded or rebuilt since
the manifest last recorded it, so the pins named files the deposition no longer
holds. A demo would have downloaded the current archive and then failed its own
integrity check.

Recording that truthfully used to be impossible without breaking the repository,
because one `sha256` field served two jobs — "what this repo ships" and "what the
record serves". They were identical by construction until a refit made them
differ. So a truthful hosted pin made the in-repo git-LFS fallback fail its own
checksum, which forced the payloads to be deleted in the same commit, which made
Zenodo the only source, which meant a human had to publish the records before
this change could merge at all.

The two contracts are now separate fields, so both are recorded and both are
true. 23 entries carry a genuine divergence — `sha256`/`bytes` describing the
copy in this repository and `hosted_sha256`/`hosted_bytes` the copy on the
record. Ten hosted-only files (both h2afva variants, the h2afva tp234 stack,
the four decimation cuts, drosophila, and both neuromast channels) have no local
copy for a second field to describe, so their single pin remains the hosted one.
Four entries whose repository and record copies agree carry no second field; an
equal pair contains no additional information.

Each hosted pin was derived from what the deposition holds rather than from a
build log — Zenodo reports an MD5 per file, and every pin comes from a copy whose
MD5 matches. DESI's was re-derived by hashing the hosted object directly, since
its chunk-layout rebuild had been uploaded but never pinned.

The in-repo payloads stay for now. Removing them is no longer entangled with
this change and lands separately.

The blastocyst keys and zebrafish archive have been updated on the draft records.
`scripts/zenodo_migration_audit.py --live` now reports that every pin matches;
publication remains a manual record-side step.

#### A demo that is empty at its default slice can finally be captured

`fractals_4d` and `gsplats_6d_kidney_multichannel_toggles` were the only two
gallery demos with no still and no orbit video. Both died the same way — the full
5-minute capture budget elapsed with nothing on screen — and neither demo was
broken. Each was EMPTY at its default slice position, and the harness could not
reach the one manifest feature that fixes that.

`waitForDataLoaded` gates on `!isLoading && totalElements > 0` and ran BEFORE the
`dimensionNav` step, so a scene that holds nothing until a hidden dimension is
stepped could never get there: the gate waited for elements that only the
navigation produces. `dimensionNav` was structurally unusable for exactly the
demos it exists for, which is why adding it to the manifest alone changed nothing.
The element requirement is now a flag — a `dimensionNav` demo waits only for the
loader to settle, navigates, and is then held to the usual non-empty check, so an
empty canvas still fails rather than being quietly published.

`initialized` (which `waitForLuxarReady` already waits for) is only set after the
initial `loadScene` returns, so dropping the element requirement does not let the
navigation run against a scene that has not loaded yet — it only stops requiring
that the loaded scene have something at its starting slice.

Why each demo is empty is worth recording, because the two causes are unrelated:

`gsplats_6d_kidney_multichannel_toggles` has three binary channel axes
(`nuclei`/`wga`/`actin`, each `range [0,1]`) and one node per channel parked at a
one-hot position — `(1,0,0)`, `(0,1,0)`, `(0,0,1)`. A discrete non-displayed dim
starts at its range minimum with tolerance 0, so the initial slice is the all-off
origin `(0,0,0)`, where no node sits. That is inherent to a toggles demo: all-off
correctly shows nothing. One step on `nuclei` brings up 50,997 splats. The scene
now authors an all-on opening state, so regenerated stores no longer start empty.

`fractals_4d` is a STALE-STORE artefact, not a property of the shipped demo. The
`fractals_4d.luxar.zarr` this was measured on predates #842: `w` was continuous
over `[-2.5, 2.5]` with `step 0.1` (51 navigable positions) while slices existed
only at about `1.0` spacing, so nine in ten positions — including the default
`-2.5` — were empty, and stepping `w` 15 times was what reached `-1.0` and 40,040
points. Since #842 the generator declares `w` discrete on the grid it actually
writes (`step = 2/grid_size`, every slider stop a data plane), so a regenerated
store is populated at its default slice and needs no `dimensionNav` at all. The
manifest keeps the entry, with a note, because it is what makes the demo
capturable on a machine that still has the old store — but its `steps`/`zoom`/
`exposure` are calibrated against that store and want re-deriving once the
dataset is rebuilt. (The drifting step values seen while walking that old axis —
`-2.4000000000000004`, `-1.9000000000000001` — come from the same place: a
CONTINUOUS dimension accumulates `pos + step` without snapping. A discrete dim
rounds to `k·step` on every move, so it does not drift.)

The kidney entry's former `dimensionNav` values were found by walking the
dimension and watching the element count, not guessed; they were removed once
the scene began authoring its populated opening state.

#### A demo's on-scene credit can no longer contradict its own citation

A demo credits its data twice: structurally in `DEMO_META["citation"]`, and
visibly in the `scene.add_text(...)` footer painted onto the scene — which is
the credit a gallery tile actually shows. Nothing kept the two in step, and the
drift was not hypothetical: three footers named the wrong paper and were fixed
by hand in the previous pass, found only because someone happened to read them
side by side.

`test_demo_meta.py` now sweeps every demo that declares a real credit and fails
when an overlay string makes a claim its own `citation["short"]` does not back.
Extraction is static (`ast`, never an import, like the rest of the registry) and
covers plain strings, module-level constants, `+` concatenation, the two branches
of a conditional, and f-strings — for an f-string only the literal segments are
read, with each `{...}` hole left in place as an explicit break so two fragments
that are never adjacent on screen cannot be spliced into a credit nobody wrote.
An overlay is not only an `add_text` call in the demo's own file: a `credit=`
argument to any call is read too, because the six `gsplats_interop` demos paint
their footer through a shared helper. Those six are uncredited today; this branch
starts judging one as soon as it declares a citation, when a demo-file-only reader
would otherwise report green after reading none of its footer.

The comparison is deliberately narrow. A credit footer states two things a
machine can check, a year and the names in front of it: the year must appear in
the declared `short`, and so must at least one of those names, matched on unicode
token boundaries (so `Kim` is not satisfied by `Kimura`, nor `Tan` by `Tanø`) and
case- and accent-insensitively (`Enßlin` ≡ `Ensslin`, `Muñoz` ≡ `Munoz`). Any
name in the group will do, because a footer routinely leads with a title or a
dataset name — `Dip-C, Tan et al. 2018`. The section comment in `test_demo_meta.py`
is the canonical account of what that rule buys, what it costs, and the classes
of drift it cannot see; the corpus shapes a naive rule gets wrong are pinned as
their own tests, and so is the set of credits the real corpus is known to yield,
so the sweep cannot quietly stop reading anything.

#### The gallery manifest carries each tile's credit

`scripts/gallery/manifest.json` gains an optional `citation` string, copied
verbatim from the demo's `DEMO_META["citation"]["short"]` for the 26 gallery
demos that declare one. A tile's attribution is now reviewable in a diff instead
of only on the rendered page.

The manifest cross-check pins it in both directions: a demo with a credit whose
manifest entry has none is a tile that silently dropped its attribution, and a
manifest entry with a credit its demo does not declare is an unsourced claim in
front of readers. A demo that declares no credit therefore carries no key at all
— absence means "unknown or not yet recorded", which is deliberately not the
same statement as `None`'s "procedurally generated, nothing to credit", and a
written-out `null` is rejected rather than read as either. Nothing reads the
field at capture time; it exists to be reviewed and to be pinned.

A `script: null` entry no longer escapes the cross-check either. Such an entry is
resolved by `id` against the demo key, and once it resolves the manifest and the
demo are two descriptions of the same thing, so every comparison runs on it —
credit and structure alike. That is what brought the scriptless entries into this
pass at all: the credit backfill would otherwise have passed straight over them,
leaving the TotalSegmentator README tile without the `Wasserthal et al. 2023` its
demo declares. The structural half turned up a genuinely pre-existing drift at
the same time — the cryo-EM virus capsid tile was filed under `microscopy`
against the `structural` its demo (and both its structural-biology peers)
declares. The manifest is corrected to `structural`. Those entries now carry
their on-disk script paths after #1809; the id fallback remains guarded for any
future `script: null` entry.

#### Scenes can now carry a dataset citation, and 65 demos do

The gallery shows dozens of third-party scientific datasets and credited almost
none of their authors. What attribution existed was in two forms neither the
viewer nor a gallery page could read: a prose block in a module docstring, and a
hand-written `scene.add_text(...)` overlay on five demos.

Attribution is now a property of the *data*. `create_scene(citation=...)` writes
a structured credit into the store's root attributes, so it survives `luxar
export`, a copied `.luxar.zarr`, and anyone who receives the data without this
repo:

```python
scene = compiler.create_scene(
    dimensions=dims,
    citation={"short": "Bui et al. 2013", "doi": "10.1016/j.cell.2013.10.055"},
)
```

Only `short` is required — it is what a tile or viewer renders, so a citation
that cannot be displayed is not a citation. The key is written only when a credit
is owed: an uncredited scene carries no `citation` key at all, so a reader must
treat its absence as "unknown", never as "this data has no author". A malformed
payload raises at `create_scene` time rather than being baked into every copy of
the data, and the rules live in one place (`luxar.core.citation`) shared by the
scene writer and the demo registry, so a demo and a scene cannot disagree about
what a citation is.

`DEMO_META` gains a matching optional `citation` key, populated for 84 demos: 65
real credits and 19 procedural demos marked `None`. `None` is spelled out rather
than left off on purpose — once the key becomes required, adding a demo will mean
deciding whether it owes a credit, and the existing `test_demo_meta.py` will
enforce it.

**Every credit here was resolved through CrossRef or DataCite, or taken from a
credit string the demo's own author wrote — none were pattern-matched out of
prose.** That distinction is the whole point: a citation-shaped regex over the
corpus confidently produces `Prize 1997` for `atp_synthase` (the Nobel Prize),
`Methods et al. 2022` for `cytoself_protein_landscape` (the journal *Nature
Methods*), and `CVPR 2024` for a FlyLight demo (a venue). Misattributing
someone's dataset is worse than omitting the credit, so resolution is a one-off
authoring step whose result is committed and reviewable in a diff, never a
runtime lookup against an API that must be up for the gallery to work.

Deliberately still uncredited, because guessing would be the exact failure this
change exists to prevent: the two ChromaTrace/CHOIR demos
(`chromatrace_choir_umap` and `chromatrace_choir_umap_sequence`), whose upstream
attribution remains unresolved. They are enumerated in #1744.

#### `test-fixtures-rendering.spec.ts` failures say what went unanswered (#1746)

This file ran on the config's 60 s per-test timeout while the helpers it calls
budget far more than that: `page.goto` can spend the 60 s `navigationTimeout`
before a helper even runs, `waitForLuxarReady` allows 45 s, `waitForPointsLoaded`
up to ~90 s (a 45 s loop plus one deliberately unclamped inner `getLuxarState`
probe), and `assertNoConsoleErrors` and `getLuxarState` 45 s each. A wall below
the sum of the phases it is meant to backstop cannot be attributed to any of
them: the run ended as a bare `Test timeout of 60000ms exceeded` with nothing to
say which dataset or which probe was pending — the same failure shape #1651
removed from the helpers. The file now configures 120 s, matching the two other
files that configure this value (`webgl-errors.spec.ts` and
`all-examples-smoke-test.spec.ts`); `frame-pacing.spec.ts` uses the same mechanism
at 300 s. At 120 s the first two phases live inside the wall and report themselves.

Raising a wall is a backstop, not a fix. The fix is that the one unbounded probe
in the file — the 100k-texel element-texture scan in the `lut_uint16` test — is
now raced against a deadline through `raceEvaluate` and throws by name when the
page does not answer, saying the LUT round-trip assertions could not run rather
than passing on an empty read. Its budget is derived from what is left of the
test's own timeout (capped at 45 s, floored at 5 s, with 10 s reserved for the
throw and teardown) instead of being a constant: a fixed 45 s under a 120 s wall
is only reachable when the bounded prefix finishes inside 75 s, and a slower
prefix would let the wall fire mid-scan and reproduce exactly the unattributable
timeout being removed. What exposes this test and not its five siblings is the
scene rather than the probe — it renders 100k points where they render 20 to
1000, so only its page saturates the render loop — and the trade #1651 named
still applies: a bound can cut short a stall that would have ended.

The `test_lut_u16` fixture also drops its point radius from 0.5 to 0.1, which is
a fill-rate change and not a geometry one. The reasoning is in screen pixels: the
point shader clamps `pointSize` to a 1.5 px floor, so at this cloud's default
auto-fit framing a 0.5-radius point rasterizes 9.4 px across and a 0.1-radius one
1.9 px — still above the floor everywhere, so the sprite remains the size the
radius asks for while shedding roughly 25x of the overdraw that made this the one
fixture heavy enough to starve a shared box under the suite's parallel workers.
Smaller is a trap rather than a further saving: at 0.08 the clamp takes over, and
below it the fragment shader compensates the enforced sprite area by squaring
`min(vPointSize / 1.5, 1.0)` into alpha, so peak alpha collapses for no fill-rate
win at all. The point count stays at 100k because that is what puts the encoder
in the `lut_uint16` tier this test exists to exercise.

#### A stacked time or channel axis survives quantization again

`combine_as_new_dimension(sigma=0.0)` is the documented way to stack per-timepoint
fits into a 4D dataset — the docstring recommends `sigma=0.0` for "discrete
dimensions (e.g., time frames)". It gives the new axis an effective sigma of 1e-7,
the epsilon `trils.py` substitutes so the covariance stays positive-definite.
Saving that dataset then destroyed the axis it had just created. Centers are stored
as per-axis uint16 fixed point, whose step is `(hi - lo) / 65535`, so each value
moves by up to half a step; on a 100-frame stack spanning 0..99 that is 7.3e-4, or
**7 320 σ**. Interior frames landed far enough from where they belonged to stop
matching a slice query at all, so they simply did not render — 200 of 5 000 splats
survived. That is the worst possible symptom, because the frames that do land on
the quantization grid land on it exactly: of the 100 frames, four round-trip bit for
bit — the two endpoints, plus frames 33 and 66 where the grid happens to align
(`gcd(65535, 99) = 3`) — so the timelapse always looked perfect wherever anyone
checked it first while 96 of 100 were gone.

Two things made it hard to notice. It was **not** opt-in — `AUTO`, the default,
behaves identically to `MEMORY`, so any stacked dataset saved with default settings
was affected, not just the demos that named a lossy mode. And it is **not** a
large-N problem: the sigma is a fixed constant while the quantization step scales
with the axis, so even a three-frame stack puts the middle frame 153 σ off.

**The primary fix is a grid snap in the encoder.** For an axis whose distinct
values all sit on one regular grid, `hi` is widened to `lo + step·65535` so the
stored quantization grid coincides with the values and they round-trip exactly. A
100-frame stack goes from 7 320 σ of error and 200/5 000 exact splats to zero error
and 5 000/5 000, under `AUTO`, `MEMORY` and `PRECISION` alike. This costs nothing:
`lo`/`hi` are already stored per axis, so it is a scale choice rather than a dtype
change — the store stays 3.01 MB, and the decoder and the format are untouched.
Falling back to float32 instead would also be exact, but centers are one array with
one encoding, so it converts *every* axis: measured at +78% on the same store (+123%
for whole-store `PRECISION`). No demo needs to change its encoding mode.

A grid does not have to be gapless, nor exactly representable in float32, to
qualify. Eligibility is decided by replaying encode→decode over the axis's distinct
values and requiring every one of them back bit-exactly, rather than by testing the
gaps for equality — so frames `0,1,2,7,8,9` (what a spatial tile of a stacked
dataset holds, or what a filter that empties one timepoint in one region leaves
behind) and a 0.1 s frame interval both snap, where a gap-equality test would reject
them and leave them 458 σ and — for a 100-frame stack at that 0.1 s interval —
734 σ off. Ordinary data is left exactly as it was:
continuous coordinates, values on no regular grid, constant (zero-extent) axes, and
axes with more distinct values than the encoding has levels are all untouched. That
selectivity matters, because this code path encodes positions, line vertices, mesh
vertices and splat centers alike. The snap reports through arbol rather than
`warnings.warn`: a warning means the caller should act, and this is a transparent
correctness fix with nothing to do that would otherwise fire on every stacked scene.

**A second, geometry-aware rail backstops what the snap cannot reach.** A snap needs
a grid; a `sigma=0` track stack merged into a fit whose time axis is *continuous*
has none, and neither does an axis with more distinct values than uint16 has levels.
There the splats really are destroyed, and only the Cholesky factors reveal it —
the coordinates alone look perfectly reasonable. `write_gsplat_arrays` is the one
place that holds `centers` and `cholesky_factors` at the same time (both the scene
compiler and the standalone `.gsplats.zarr` tree writer funnel through it), so the
check lives there. Per axis, a splat counts as *unrepresentable* when the worst-case
round-trip displacement — half the grid step — exceeds
`MAX_CENTER_DISPLACEMENT_SIGMAS` (1.0) times that splat's own marginal σ, and the
centers fall back to float32 when more than `MAX_UNREPRESENTABLE_SPLAT_FRACTION`
(0.1%) of the splats are unrepresentable on some axis. The warning names the axis,
the step, the displacement bound, how many splats are affected and their median σ.
The marginal σ is read straight off the packed lower-triangular rows
(`Σ[i,i] = Σ_{j≤i} L[i,j]²`) in one `N·k` pass, without materializing the `(N, d, d)`
matrices.

The rail defers to the snap rather than duplicating its work. An axis that trips the
population gate is tested with the encoder's *own* grid predicate — the same
function, not a proxy — and skipped when the encoder is going to store it exactly;
otherwise a stacked axis, where 100% of the splats are formally unrepresentable,
would escalate the whole centers array to float32 and warn loudly about data that
round-trips bit for bit. The predicate is consulted lazily, only for an axis that
has already tripped, because `np.unique` per axis is real time (0.30 s of a 2.85 s
encode on 5M×3 coordinates) and a tripped axis is rare.

The snap is not the encoder's only exact path, and the rail has to know all of
them: LUT encoding (priority 3) is tried *before* the dtype encoder, stores the
original values verbatim at ~1 B/value, and is skipped in `PRECISION`. Escalating
a LUT-eligible centers array would therefore replace an exact 1 B/value encoding
with an exact 4 B/value one — 240,000 B instead of 60,000 B on a 20,000×3 measured
case — while warning about a displacement that was never going to be applied. A
public `ArrayEncoder.encodes_as_lut` answers that question, asked (like the
grid predicate) only once an offender has been found, so the common path pays
nothing. Separately, a 1-D COORDINATE array used to encode to something nothing
could read back: the per-column reductions produce 0-d rails, which were stored
as bare JSON scalars and rejected on decode. Its rails are always 1-D lists now,
and both sides read a 1-D array as one column of N values.

Both of the rail's numbers are keyed on **harm**, not on jitter. A center moved by
less than one σ is still inside the core the splat was fitted to describe, with the
displacement bounded by the splat's own width rather than by the axis extent, so it
renders essentially where it did. That is not a claim that every query answer
survives — a slice query matches out to roughly `tolerance + coverage_sigma·σ`, so a
splat right on that boundary and pushed the permitted 1.0 σ outward drops out of it,
and because the test is *per axis* a 4-D center may move a full σ on all four at
once (2 σ in Mahalanobis terms for a diagonal Σ) with every per-axis check passing.
What the bound does rule out is the failure the rail is for: past ~1 σ the center
leaves that footprint altogether. A tighter per-splat line would charge 2× the centers
bytes for sub-voxel error — measured on 200,000 splats spread over an 8192-voxel
axis with 5% pinned at the fitter's `sqrt(1/12) ≈ 0.2887` σ floor, the step is 0.125
voxel, so the worst displacement is 0.0625 voxel = 0.217 σ; that is 12.9% of splats
"unrepresentable" at the obvious alternative — a 0.25 σ-of-*jitter* line, i.e. 0.125 σ
of displacement — against 0.03% at this one.

Because the per-splat line is strict, the population gate can be tight. Under the
displacement criterion the benign populations collapse — worst measured axis: 0.015%
for a 20,000-splat random-`U(0, 1)`-Cholesky fixture, 0.0005% for a 200,000-splat
SPZ-like log-normal scale distribution (0.001% with an added σ=1e-6 needle), 0.03%
for the light-sheet case above — so 0.1% clears every one of them by 3× or
more while still catching what a looser 1% gate would miss: a degenerate *minority*.
Merging a 2,000-splat `sigma=0` track stack into a 300,000-splat fit with a real
`σ_t = 3.0` leaves 0.662% of the splats displaced by up to 1,373 σ; at 1% the rail
would stay silent while only 10% of the tracks still landed on their own frame. It
remains a population test, not a minimum: real fits routinely contain a handful of
needle Gaussians — an SPZ import decodes scales as `exp(u8/16 - 10)` with a 4.5e-5
floor — and a single such splat must not double every centers array on disk
(measured: 3.18 MB → 6.23 MB of centers, +54% on a 600k-splat store).

**The residual, and what to do about it.** Up to 0.1% of a store can still be
quantized away with no warning at all — 1,650 splats on a 1.65M-splat fit, or 100
`sigma=0` tracks merged into a 150,000-splat time-axis fit, 61 of which end up off
their own frame while the rail stays silent. Displacement magnitude cannot separate
those two populations (an ordinary `U(0, 1)` Cholesky draw yields σ = 1e-9 and
thousands of σ of displacement), so **a small tracked sub-population that must land
exactly on its coordinate — and that no grid describes — should be saved with
`EncodingMode.PRECISION`** rather than left to the rail.

Three properties of the gate are worth knowing when reading a store's dtypes. A
*fraction* tightens at small N: one unrepresentable splat trips the whole array
whenever N ≤ 999. The verdict is taken per WRITE — that is, per leaf — so a
partitioned or laddered node decides part by part: an 8-tile `tiles` recipe emits
up to eight separate warnings, and within one logical node the centers dtype can
differ between parts, a part whose degenerate splats fall under the gate keeping
uint16 while its sibling escalates. And deferring to the snap sharpens the residual
one more way, deliberately: a gridded stacked axis keeps uint16, where escalating it
would have *incidentally* rescued sub-gate needle populations on the store's other
axes too (centers are one array with one encoding, so escalating for the time axis
would make every axis exact). That side effect is not bought — a stacked store's
spatial axes are held to the 0.1% gate like any other array's.

Only the **centers** escalate. The Cholesky, amplitude and color tiers keep whatever
the caller asked for — the published cell-tracking bundle depends on the Cholesky
staying uint8, and inflating it 4× would buy nothing. An escalated centers array is
also written with `deduplicate=False`. The encoder's content-dedup registry is keyed
on the centers **bytes**, but the rail's verdict depends on a *sibling* array
(`cholesky_factors`) that the registry does not key on. Left in the registry, two
nodes with byte-identical centers and different Cholesky would collapse onto
whichever was written first, and the escalated node would be stored as a `(0, d)`
`array_ref` pointing at the other node's `linear_perchannel_u16` array — reading
back quantized, i.e. the original bug verbatim behind a warning claiming it had been
prevented. Skipping the registry is the whole fix, since `ArrayRefRegistry.check`
both looks up and registers, so an escalated array that never calls it neither
resolves to a lossy target nor becomes one.

The rail also stands down once an axis reaches `COORDINATE_U16_MAX_EXTENT` (2¹⁶, now
single-sourced in `typing_utils.constants` so the two rails cannot drift). The
encoder's extent rail already stores such an array as float32, exactly, and says why
— "extent ≥ 2¹⁶; uint16 fixed-point cannot resolve a unit step" — which is the
useful diagnosis for a scene that is merely very large. Firing here as well would
replace it with one pointing at a degenerate axis that is not there, and would drop
the array's content dedup for a verdict that depends on the centers bytes alone.

Four 4D demos (`cell_tracking_challenge`, `celegans_tracking`, `nexrad_supercell`,
`zebrafish_timelapse`) also cached each per-timepoint fit under `MEMORY` and then
stacked the *in-memory* object rather than what had just been written, while their
cache-hit branch loaded the store back. A cold run and a warm run therefore stacked
different splats. Each now returns what it stored, so the two runs agree — and both
branches load with `include_stats=True`, so the fit's normalization provenance (the
background floor of #1175) still reaches the stacked scene through
`agreed_normalization_stats`.

#### The Layers panel windows each LOD level on its own scalar range (#1753)

The panel has one display-range slider per layer, so it composes one window —
but `LayerApplyEngine.applyComposed` fans that window out over
`collectDataDescendants`, and a layer is very often a `kind=lod` wrapper whose
levels do not share a scalar range. gsplat LOD merging SUMS amplitudes, so a
coarsened level is the same physical signal at a different numeric SCALE, and
the gsplat compiler
(`packages/luxar/src/luxar/io/_compiler/gsplat_assembly.py`) derives
`amplitude_data_range = [min, p99.9]` independently from each splat set's OWN
amplitudes. The layer's reference range is merely whichever descendant
`deriveScalarRangeFromDescendants` picked — the one with the largest `n_splats`,
or, when no descendant declares one (points, lines and mesh write `n_points` and
never `n_splats`) or several tie, simply the first visited. The composed window
went into every level verbatim, so the whole layer rendered on the reference
level's window and every per-level window the producer had stamped was
discarded.

Two things made that worse than a one-off interaction bug. It happened **on
load** — `layers-panel.ts` runs `applyDisplayRange` for every layer while
building the panel — and `applyOpacity` / `applyGamma` / `applyAbsorption` /
`applyBlendingMode` / `applyColormap` all funnel through the same
`applyComposed` afterwards. And a level created lazily AFTER the last commit kept
its own window until the next one, so two levels of the same object could be
windowed differently depending only on load order.

A colormap-active leaf under a LOD ladder now receives the layer's window
re-expressed in its own `scalar_data_range` / `amplitude_data_range`, with the
window's relative position inside the range preserved: the middle 40% of the
layer's signal stays the middle 40% of each level's signal, which is what the
slider means to the user. The per-level window scaling proposed in #1752 (still
in flight) needs exactly this to reach the screen — until now the panel flattened
any per-level window differentiation before it got there.

The remap crosses a LOD ladder and nothing else: every group node from the edited
layer down to the leaf must be `kind === 'lod'`. A partition's parts are disjoint
SPATIAL subsets of one field at the SAME scale, differing only by content, so a
per-part window would be per-tile auto-contrast — the same value rendering as a
different colour in different tiles, with a visible discontinuity at every BSP
seam. (On the repo's own `test_partition_layer.luxar.zarr` fixture the two tiles
are `[0.5000, 0.7455]` and `[0.7542, 0.9998]`, so the field would step white →
black across the seam.) So `adaptive` declines throughout, because the right
reference for a tile's ladder is that tile's own finest level rather than the
layer's, and that is more than #1753 asks for; and a plain `layer=True` group
over two colormapped channels declines too, since two physical fields are not one
field at two scales. Once #1691 / PR #1752 harmonizes `amplitude_data_range`
across a gsplat structure, partition siblings will carry equal ranges and the
equality short-circuit would make this a no-op anyway; the `kind` gate is the
safety net until then, and for every store already written.

An `overview` tree is a **no-op in both branches**, which is worth stating
plainly rather than as half a win. Its tiles decline on the nested partition. Its
coarse cap is structurally eligible, but on a measured
`luxar gsplat lod --recipe overview` store the cap and all four parts carry 432
splats each, and `deriveScalarRangeFromDescendants` breaks that tie with a strict
`count > bestCount` while visiting the cap first — so the cap IS the reference
and the equality short-circuit returns its window untouched. The fine parts
consequently still render on the cap's window (`part_2`'s own
`[0.00059, 0.19962]` on the cap's `[0.000116, 0.44551]`, putting its brightest
splat at LUT 0.45 instead of 1.0). Correcting that needs a per-branch reference,
the same piece `adaptive` is missing.

How big the correction is depends entirely on the ladder, and on a plain gsplat
one it is modest. Measured on a default `luxar gsplat lod --recipe levels -K 4
-L 3` store, the four levels' `amplitude_data_range` top ends are 0.43884 /
0.44417 / 0.43637 / 0.39260 — a ≤13% spread, because the range is `[min, p99.9]`
and mass conservation pins the peak; the bottom ends differ more (~8x: 7.06e-05
vs 5.60e-04). "LOD merging sums amplitudes" is about the mechanism, not the
magnitude. The dramatic case is the MIXED points/lines lift ladder:
`add_points(..., scalars=…, colormap='plasma', layer=True, substitutive_lod=True)`
lifts its coarse levels to gsplats (direct colour, `amplitude_data_range` +
`n_splats`) and keeps the finest level as `points` (colormapped,
`scalar_data_range`, and no `n_splats` — points write `n_points`). Since
`deriveScalarRangeFromDescendants` ranks by `n_splats`, the reference is a lifted
sibling's amplitude range, a different physical quantity from the only
colormapped leaf's scalar: on a real store that pushed an amplitude window of
`[0.037, 2.817]` into a scalar spanning `1.035 … 280.862`, so everything above
2.817 — 99.4% of that span — clamped to the top of the LUT and rendered as one
flat colour. That leaf now gets its own range,
which is what the node factory already hands it at creation.

Mesh ladders never reach any of this, and the reason is the PRODUCER's rather
than the panel's: `core/group/adders/mesh.py::_shared_scalar_window` derives one
window from the whole field before any split or decimation and stamps it on every
part and every level, precisely so "a level or a part that stamps its own subset
min/max" cannot render the same value as a different colour. Mesh siblings
therefore have equal ranges and the equality short-circuit fires. That is also
what makes gsplat LOD the principled exception rather than an inconsistency: mesh
decimation drops vertices without touching the scalars they carry, while gsplat
LOD merging changes the amplitude scale — and only a scale change is something a
window has to be re-expressed across.

The remap is a pure helper (`rendering/display-range.ts::remapWindowToLeafRange`,
beside the `computeUniforms` / `computeDisplayRange` / `resolveColormapWindow`
math it belongs with) and it declines to fire in four cases, each of which would
otherwise produce a _different_ window rather than a refined one. Either range
missing: nothing to map between. Either range non-remappable — degenerate,
inverted, or non-finite. `[x, x]` is legitimate and common (every imported
classical splat file has `amplitudes = 1`); the width floor is the shared
`DEGENERATE_SCALAR_RANGE_EPS`, because below it the two ends of the pipeline have
already collapsed — `computeUniforms` answers a sub-eps span with the identity
gain, so the composed window is `[0, 1]` and not the reference window at all,
while on the leaf side `computeScalarRangeUniforms` answers a sub-eps span with
the LUT MIDPOINT (#631), i.e. one flat neutral colour for every element of that
leaf. Finiteness is a separate arm: `[0, Infinity]` passes any width test and
then `0 × Infinity` sends a NaN window to the shader. The predicate rejects a
NaN-bearing range for free. And the two ranges being equal, which is the
overwhelmingly common case (the finest level IS the reference, and so is every
leaf of an ordinary single-range layer) — short-circuited so an untouched layer's
window stays bit-exact instead of round-tripping through two floating-point
divisions.

The remap also runs only when the composed window really is STATED in the
reference range. `composeEffective` multiplies `intensity` and sums `offset` over
the whole ancestry with live panel state substituted for `layer=true` nodes, so
a window contributed at or below the edited layer leaves the composed one in a
different basis, and remapping it would corrupt a window that was already
correct. `LayerApplyEngine.composedWindowIsInReferenceBasis` declines in four
shapes: the edited layer is off the leaf's ancestry; the edited layer itself
AUTHORED a gain (`layer=True, intensity=0.5` on a wrapper makes `walkSceneGraph`
seed `displayMin/Max` from `computeDisplayRange(0.5, 0)`, a normalized-gain
window with no relation to `scalarDataRange`); a node strictly BELOW the layer is
itself tracked as a LAYER — regardless of its gain, since it owns its own window
and its own panel row (a gain test was a false negative for any nested child
whose range is exactly `[0, 1]`, where `computeUniforms(0, 1)` is the identity
`{1, -0}` and `[0, 1]` is the ordinary range of a normalized scalar, probability
or mask); or a non-layer node below the layer authored an `intensity`, which
mirrors `resolveColormapWindow`'s "non-identity raw leaf gain ⇒ the composed gain
IS the window" rule. A gain on an ancestor ABOVE the layer is deliberately not
gated, and not remapped through either: what gets re-expressed is the layer's OWN
window, the only one actually stated in reference units, with the ancestor gain
re-applied afterwards. That lands on exactly the window the node factory computes
at creation, for every range pair rather than only for ranges that start at 0 —
remapping the composed window instead gives `[-2, 2]` where creation gives
`[0, 4]` for `ref = [1, 3]`, `leaf = [0, 8]` and an ancestor `intensity = 2`.
Both are pinned by tests.

The ancestry chain is walked ONCE per leaf and shared between the composition and
the gate. `collectAncestorNodes` resolves each step with a linear `children.find`
that allocates a string per comparison, so a fan-out over a P-part wrapper costs
~P²/2 comparisons — 7.0 ms at 512 parts, 129 ms at 2000 — and `applyComposed`
runs on every slider tick. Walking it twice would have doubled that.

Nothing else moved. The direct-colour gain/offset route is unchanged, the #936
identity reset on the colour GOG still fires on the colormap path, and the
`identityLayerWindow` route for a mixed direct-colour/colormapped group is
untouched — it only ever fires for a leaf that is NOT colormap-active, so it
cannot overlap the new remap. `applyColormap`'s own `updateScalarRange` write now
goes through the same per-leaf helper: it is immediately superseded by the
`applyComposed` call at the end of that method, but two places pushing a window
by different rules is a trap for the next reader.

#### The shared E2E fixture stops paying for a second opinion on a verdict it already reached

The console-error teardown in `src/tests/e2e/fixtures.ts` ran two gates. The
first is Playwright's own: `page.on('console')` filtered to `msg.type() ===
'error'`, plus `page.on('pageerror')`, matched against
`DEFAULT_ALLOWED_CONSOLE_ERRORS`. The second was `assertNoConsoleErrors(page,
DEFAULT_ALLOWED_CONSOLE_ERRORS)`, which reads the viewer's own in-page
interceptor buffer through a `page.evaluate`. The second one is gone.

It was never a second signal for the question being asked.
`assertNoConsoleErrors` consults `messages.errors` and nothing else — never
`warnings`, `logs` or `all` — so in the fixture it re-decided exactly the verdict
the line above had just rendered, from a strictly narrower source. Every write
into that in-page buffer goes through the interceptor's private
`captureMessage`, which is reachable only from the five `patch()` closures in
`src/utils/console-interceptor.ts`, and each of those unconditionally re-emits
through `this.originalConsole.<method>(...)`: whatever lands in the buffer also
crosses Playwright's console channel. The buffer is narrower on five further
axes — it captures only from `patch()` onward, so a pre-init `ReferenceError` or
a mistyped asset is invisible to it; it is a ring that evicts at
`DEFAULT_MAX_BUFFER_SIZE` where the fixture's array is unbounded; it resets on
navigation; it never sees `pageerror` or browser-generated errors the app did
not route through `console`; and it never sees a web worker's console messages,
which Playwright forwards to the page's `console` event but which the in-page
interceptor — patching the main-thread `console` only — cannot reach.
`console.assert` and `console.trace` are a wash rather than a sixth axis: the
interceptor patches neither, and they arrive over CDP as console message types
`assert` / `trace`, which the fixture's `msg.type() === 'error'` filter drops,
so neither source sees them.

What it did cost was time, on exactly the runs that could least afford it. The
`page.evaluate` round trip is the one part of the teardown a saturated main
thread can withhold: #1651 measured a trivial evaluate unanswered for 5 s twelve
times running, and #1760 reproduced 95 s without a single serviced round trip on
a 2-CPU browser while nineteen console messages arrived through
`page.on('console')` in the same window. Since #1651 that stall is bounded at
45 s rather than eating the whole test budget — the fixture call site that
entry describes is the one deleted here — but 45 s is still 45 s, charged to
each of the 59 of 67 specs that import `test` from `./fixtures`, on precisely the
loaded machine where the whole-suite wall clock is what the E2E daemon kills the
run on. An earlier attempt at this kept the probe and forgave its starvation with
a `testInfo` annotation; that annotation has no consumer (`playwright.config.ts`
reports `html` + `list`, and the daemon's `--reporter=json` parser reads status
and error message only), and it still paid the 45 s. Deleting the call is the
smaller and strictly better change: `getConsoleMessages` keeps its plain `Error`,
and the error class, type guard and description helper that attempt introduced
are not needed.

Specs are unaffected, because the in-page buffer was never only the fixture's.
`assertNoConsoleErrors`, `assertConsoleContains`, `assertConsoleDoesNotContain`
and `assertNoShaderErrors` all read it, the last two over `all` and over
`errors` + `warnings` respectively — buckets with no Playwright-side gate at all
— and `hover-tooltip`, `hover-overlay`, `mouse-interactions` and
`recording-panel` deliberately call `assertNoConsoleErrors(page)` with NO
allow-list from their own `test.afterEach`. That extra strictness is the point of
those calls and is left exactly as it was.

One pre-existing ordering bug is fixed while the teardown is open: `page.off`
for both listeners used to run before the gate filtered what they had captured,
so anything emitted after the gate began could not be seen. They now come off in
a `finally` that runs after the verdict, which also detaches them on the two
early-return paths (the `allow-console-errors` annotation, and a test that
already failed or timed out). With the `assertNoConsoleErrors` await removed the
window this closes is zero-width today — nothing between `use(page)` returning
and the filter yields to the event loop — so this is an invariant made true by
construction rather than an observable fix, and it is what keeps the deletion
safe if an `await` is ever reintroduced there.

The gate's decision is now the exported pure function
`unexpectedConsoleErrors(captured, allowed)` instead of a `filter` buried in the
teardown closure, so it is testable without a browser:
`src/tests/unit/tests/e2e-fixture-console-gate.test.ts` pins that an allowed
pattern drops its entry and an unmatched one survives, that the allow-list is
applied per entry rather than to the joined report string (a gate matching
against the join would let one forgiven 404 pardon a real `TypeError` beside
it), that a `pageerror` is judged exactly like a `console.error`, that every
pattern is tried and capture order is preserved among survivors, that the
function reads no environment of its own, and that an empty capture yields
nothing without throwing. Each of those was checked by mutating the production
line and confirming the corresponding assertion goes red.

#### Failed gsplat file grafts no longer leave empty wrappers

Grafting a nested `.gsplats.zarr` into a scene is now transactional. If a child
write fails after the graft has created its `kind=partition` or `kind=lod`
wrapper, Luxar removes the whole new subtree from both the Zarr store and the
in-memory scene graph, restores compiler-side bounds and warning claims, and
rewinds array-reference deduplication state before re-raising the original
validation error. This covers valid
energy-fraction `additive_lod=` conflicts as well as malformed specifications,
while preserving any node and bounds that existed before the graft began.

#### Batch-fit tasks now read the volumes their plan names

A flat batch channel index is now decoded across every channel-like axis when
`--axes` names layouts such as `camera,time,channel,z,y,x`, instead of applying the
same index to both camera and channel. Batch planning also mirrors the positional
loader's singleton-axis squeeze, so thin 2D timelapses build tile grids and stacked
time barriers in the dimensionality their fit workers actually emit.

The same flat channel decoding applies to direct `gsplat fit` and `gsplat cal`
loads that provide multiple channel-like dimensions through `--axes`. Batch
planning now also rejects unsupported axis labels and multiple time axes before
creating jobs that the fit workers cannot load, and recommends a store's own
valid folded-channel axis labels when positional loading cannot reproduce them.

#### Mesh shading gains an offset key light and specular controls

Mesh surfaces now use an above-left view-space key light and a subtle default
specular highlight. Five mesh-only appearance controls become authorable for the
first time — `specular`, `shininess`, `ambient`, `shade_exponent`, and
`alpha_cutoff` — settable on a mesh node (in authored scenes and the Layers
panel) and refused on non-mesh nodes.

Existing standalone exports bundle their viewer build and retain the previous
shading until they are re-exported.

#### Batch preprocess denoise preserves explicit source axes

Batch denoise calibration and preprocess workers now use the planned source-axis
layout when selecting each timepoint and channel. Fits against the canonical
denoised store receive a rewritten ``t,c,*spatial`` layout, avoiding silent
time/channel swaps for noncanonical and two-dimensional inputs.

#### bioformats2raw stores load instead of crashing on `'Group' has no attribute 'shape'` (#1777)

`bioformats2raw` — the converter most of the OME ecosystem produces its zarr with
— writes one image **group** per series (`0`, `1`, …) with the pyramid levels one
level further down (`0/0`, `0/1`, …), plus an `OME` metadata group at the root.
Three separate places picked the array to read with the same `elif "0" in store:
arr = store["0"]` branch and then asked the result for `.shape`, so such a store
died with `AttributeError: 'Group' object has no attribute 'shape'` in
`discover_ome_zarr_shape` and `load_volume`, and was refused with a
`ValueError` in `open_volume_lazy` — despite its `0/0` being right there and
findable. Both on-disk zarr formats, identically.

The rule now lives in one place, `luxar.io.volume._select_zarr_array`, which all
three call: an explicit `array_key` (nested paths allowed, blank treated as
absent, and a key naming a *group* now descends into it instead of crashing),
else NGFF resolution level `"0"` when that really is an array, else the largest
array found recursively — with a size tie broken on the lowest key path, because
`zarr` does not stabilise key order across opens and the planner and a per-tile
worker are different processes. The three had to move together — had discovery
alone started succeeding, `batch-fit` would have written a whole plan and then
lost every task to the same crash. When `"0"` is a group, resolution is **scoped
to that group**: the store root also holds the other series and the `OME` group,
so a whole-store search could hand back level 0 of a *different image*, which is
a plausible wrong answer rather than an error. Inside the group the candidates
are narrower still — the levels its own `multiscales` block declares, else its
direct array children, else (skipping `labels/`) whatever is nested below —
because NGFF puts an image's segmentation masks at `<image>/labels/<name>/<level>`
and a mask as big as level 0 would otherwise be fitted instead of the image.
Scoping keeps the existing intent: full resolution of the first image, and it is
terminal — an image group holding no array of its own is a `ValueError` naming
the group, not a fall-through to the unscoped whole-store sweep, which would
answer with that image's own mask (a group holding only `0/labels/seg/0`) or with
a different series (an empty one). The owner reported for the selected array is
resolved by one rule as well, the nearest ancestor whose `multiscales` declares
it — for *every* route, the whole-store sweep included. That last one was the
hole: with no `"0"` at the root the sweep reports the level's immediate parent, so
a store whose `img` group declares `res/0` gave `img/res` as owner and only the
no-key spelling fell through to the ndim heuristic, losing the declared axes and
voxel size while `--array-key img`, `img/res` and `img/res/0` all read them. A
rule that skips one route is not a rule: the route left out gives the same array
different axes and a different `batch-fit` fan-out, decided by nothing but the
spelling. The resolution also no longer re-walks a block the search just walked —
a group reported as declaring nothing was already asked, so the ancestor walk
starts above it (a store with a stale four-entry `multiscales` cost 14 group
lookups, five of them exact repeats; now 9 with none).
The terminal "group holds no array" error stopped blaming a key nobody passed:
with no `--array-key` it names the OME-NGFF `"0"` convention that actually chose
that group, and — since the condition is unrecoverable without a key — it lists
the array keys the store *does* hold, so the "`0` is an empty stub, the real image
is at `1`" store answers with `'1/0'` rather than leaving the reader to guess.
A **present but empty** `multiscales` on the owning group is now reported as
"declared but unusable" with the same reason the identical declaration gets on the
root, instead of as "no OME-Zarr/NGFF metadata found" — the one distinction that
notice exists to draw, and it must not depend on which node carries the block.
`_load_zarr_volume` now names the array it actually landed
on (`Using array '0/0'`), where the old "using resolution level '0'" line would
have been a lie.

The metadata half was the quieter half. NGFF `multiscales` was read from the store
ROOT's attributes, but a bioformats2raw store puts that block on the *image* group
and leaves only `bioformats2raw.layout` at the root — so even once the array was
found, discovery would find no `multiscales`, fall through to the shape heuristic,
GUESS the T/C roles (a 4D store is assumed `CZYX`) and recover no voxel size at
all. The root's attributes still stand by default; the group that owns the
selected array now overrides the root's `multiscales`, but only on **evidence**
that its block is about that array — one of the block's own `datasets[*].path`
entries has to resolve to the array that was selected (and the block has to
describe one axis per dimension). A matching axis *count* is not evidence,
because a permuted axis list has exactly the right length: a group can carry a
block describing something else entirely, and adopting that on the strength of
its mere existence would discard good root metadata and rewrite `batch-fit`'s
whole T×C fan-out into a silently wrong plan. An owner block that fails the
evidence gate is *named* in the give-up notice rather than reported as "no
OME-Zarr/NGFF metadata found", which would be a lie about a store that plainly
declares a pyramid — and hides the one detail (its `datasets[*].path` entries do
not resolve to the selected array) that makes it fixable.
The custom (non-NGFF) bare `axes` attribute is the other way round — root first,
owner only as a fallback — because a bare list names nothing, so no such evidence
is obtainable for it; that still fixes bioformats2raw, whose root carries no
`axes` at all.

#### Denoised GSplat batches use the data basis they fit

Tiled normalization ranges and deferred batch background floors now resolve on the denoised intensity basis where possible, so every tile uses the same scale and pedestal as the data it actually fits. Uniform batches also report and reject a whole timepoint/channel slice when an applied floor leaves every spatial tile empty instead of silently dropping that slice from the merge.

For local on-the-fly percentile floors, the deferred resolver calibrates one NLM strength per selected channel and pins those same values into the fit workers so the shared floor and fitted data stay on the same basis. Non-deferred `auto` runs continue to self-calibrate per worker.

#### LOD selectors can use robust published bounds

LOD children may now publish optional `lod_bounds` alongside their complete
`position_bounds`. Both selector metrics size the node from the robust bounds,
falling back per child for existing stores, while frustum gating and eviction
continue to use the complete geometry bounds so sparse visible outliers are not
silently culled.

#### Invalid `extend_to_all` no longer strands wrapper groups

An invalid explicit `extend_to_all` value is now checked before Points, Lines,
or GSplats creates a `kind=partition` / `kind=lod` wrapper, alongside Mesh's
existing preflight. The refusal therefore leaves both the Zarr store and scene
graph untouched instead of stranding a childless wrapper when the first
generated child validates the value.

The shared preflight runs only when a wrapper will actually be written and
keeps each door's kwarg-spec, image-label, and topology checks ahead of it. It
now precedes pre-split channel validation, matching the flat writer's order.
`extend_to_all=None` remains a per-child check, preserving the advisory
candidate warning once per written leaf rather than adding a warning for the
unsplit source array.

#### Reductions refresh the LOD energy stamps they render with (#1789)

A content-changing gsplat rewrite no longer carries the input ladder's
`energy_fraction_cum`, `reference_energy`, `quality` and splat counts onto a
smaller or amplitude-edited artifact. Those values drive the viewer's
progressive brightness compensation and upgrade gate, so the stale metadata was
rendering-visible: a fully loaded reduced level could still be divided by the
input's partial-energy fraction and appear over-bright.

The shared reduction chokepoints now rebuild existing artifact-local stamps from
the rewritten splats. Per-rung counts and cumulative energy fractions are
remeasured and every substitutive level receives the rewritten finest level's
common reference-energy weight. Expensive Torch-based `quality` measurement is
not hidden inside ordinary filtering: stale quality is removed and can be
restored explicitly with `annotate-quality --with-quality`. The operation preserves absence — unannotated and
reveal ladders do not acquire energy compensation — and preserves authored
stamps verbatim for content-neutral rewrites and the `at_substitutive` accessor
used by scene authoring. `level_stats.refine_stats` is removed after a reduction
because its MSE values were measured against a source volume the rewriter does
not have; the descriptive refine method remains.

#### An OME-Zarr level declared as `"./0"` resolves again (#1793)

NGFF lets a `multiscales` block spell its own levels explicitly relative — `"./0"`
is a legal spelling of `"0"` — and writers do emit that form. The
metadata-MATCHING half of the reader already saw through it, but
`_declared_levels` handed the declared path straight to zarr, which rejects a path
holding a `.` segment outright (`ValueError: The path './0' is invalid…`, at both
zarr formats). So an image group whose pyramid is declared `["./0", "./1"]`
resolved *no* level at all.

Everything downstream then degraded together, and plausibly. With no declared
level resolved, the block stops being evidence about the array that was selected,
so the owning group's `multiscales` is rejected as "does not name it" and
discovery falls through to the ndim shape heuristic: a 4D `TZYX` store is read as
`CZYX`, which fans a `batch-fit` out over the wrong axis. The declared voxel size
is lost with it, and selection falls back to the largest array in the group — so a
declared full-resolution level that happens to be smaller than an undeclared
sibling (a projection, a scratch copy) loses to it and the fit runs against the
wrong data. It was loud, at least: a per-level `Skipping declared level` line plus
the give-up notice.

The declared path is now normalised at that one lookup boundary, through the same
`_normalised_dataset_path` rule the matching side uses, so both halves apply the
same rule to any string spelling. A path still holding a `.` segment after the
single leading `./` is removed (`"."`, `"a/./b"`) names no level under any
spelling; those fall back to the slash-stripped original, so the lookup still
fails and is still reported under that spelling rather than vanishing or becoming
a lookup of some other array. The `labels/` exclusion and the returned key path
are both taken from the normalised spelling: a mask declared as
`"./labels/seg/0"` stays excluded, and the key the loader prints
(`Using array '0/0'`) is one a reader can pass straight back as `--array-key`,
which `"0/./0"` would not have been.

**A store that spells its levels `./N` may now select a different array**, and
read different axes off it — that is the point of the fix, but it is a change of
answer for an input that already worked its way through a pipeline. The 4D
`CZYX`→`TZYX` correction changes the T/C fan-out, and a pyramid mixing spellings
(`["./0", "1"]`) used to select the half-resolution level and now selects the
declared full-resolution one. Nothing carries an input fingerprint across that:
`batch-fit run` re-plans from `discover_ome_zarr_shape` on every resume and skips
completed tiles by output filename, so a batch planned before this change and
resumed or merged after it can mix two different `(t, c)` fan-outs, and
`merge --refine volume` would re-open a different array than its tiles were
fitted against — as would `gsplat lod --refine volume --target <store>` against a
pre-fix fit. Re-plan such a batch rather than resuming it.

One adjacent silent drop closed with it: a declared level that resolves to a
*group* is now reported like any other dropped declaration (`names a Group, not
an array`) instead of disappearing into the ndim heuristic unexplained.

#### Culling no longer leaves unwritable empty LOD rungs

A matrix-shaped gsplat reduction can now remove every splat from one step of an
additive ladder without losing the completed result at save time. Empty steps are
dropped when other rungs survive, and the remaining ladder's indices, counts,
cumulative cutpoints, and rung count are rewritten to match the arrays that reach
disk. Pruning removes measurements invalidated by the count change, and energy
stamps are recomputed from the surviving rungs.

#### QEM mesh LOD now covers authored-size surfaces

The topology-preserving mesh decimator no longer runs an SVD for every candidate
edge, repeatedly filters face sets that already contain only active faces, or rebuilds
a complete collapse sequence for every LOD level. A QEM ladder now snapshots all
requested levels from one sequence while still aggregating colours and scalars from
the original vertices at each snapshot. Solved placements outside the collapsing
edge envelope now fall back to an endpoint or midpoint, changing both 3D and nD
output where an ill-conditioned solve would otherwise escape the input bounds. On
the worst-case open-annulus benchmark, a complete three-level K=4 ladder takes 45.9
seconds at 9,882 vertices, so
`method="auto"` now selects QEM through 10,000 source vertices instead of 300 and
retains vectorized clustering above that measured envelope.

#### Size automatic line primitives by total scene load

The viewer now applies the automatic capsule-to-quad threshold to the
concurrent effective line load of the whole scene instead of each line node in
isolation. Large scenes split across many smaller line nodes therefore choose
one consistent primitive and stay within the measured frame budget.

This changes the bundled dMRI tractography demo from capsules to quads: its
scene totals several million effective segments and clears the 2 million
threshold even though its largest line node contains only about 162 thousand.

#### Failed wrapper writes no longer strand partial scene state

Scene geometry additions are now transactional: a failure after a partition or
LOD wrapper starts writing removes the new subtree and restores scene children,
bounds, label flags, warnings, and array-reference deduplication state.
Finalization warns and prunes childless wrapper chains as a structural backstop.
The exported `ZarrWriterProtocol` consequently gains a public
`transaction(path)` context-manager contract for writer implementations.

#### STORM demo separates fitted widefield and measured localization splats

The 3D STORM microtubule demo now fits a compact Gaussian-splat basis to a photon-weighted, diffraction-blurred widefield volume while preserving detector-derived CRLB plus antibody-linkage uncertainty for the super-resolution view. Downloads are size-verified, uncached fits require CUDA explicitly, and both views remain spatially co-registered despite their different axis orders and splat counts.

#### Expand demo credits and gallery coverage

Thirty-nine additional demos now carry structured dataset credits, bringing the
corpus to 65 credited demos, 19 explicitly procedural demos, and two unresolved
ChromaTrace/CHOIR demos. The Tribolium scenes now distinguish the GIANI Zenodo
artifact from the Cell Tracking Challenge source and use the corrected Barry et
al. 2022 paper attribution and DOI throughout.

`Dimension` now normalizes NumPy scalar bounds, steps, scales, and boolean flags
before validation and serialization, preventing array-derived metadata from
leaving a partially written scene. Demo metadata tests also enforce that every
declared credit is passed into scene creation and copied verbatim into any
gallery manifest entry.

The gallery manifest gains 23 additional demo tiles and one corrected title,
with `id` documented as the media/demo key and `dataset` as the authoritative
store path.

#### Bound the DESI demo's finest download

The DESI cosmic-web opening view intentionally starts inside the structure, so
its substitutive selector legitimately chooses the finest child and the
progressive stream eventually downloads that child in full. The demo now authors
a deterministic 1.25-million-point sample from the 9.75-million-object catalog,
matching the previous one-coarser density while preserving camera framing from
the full source. Its intensity is scaled by the sampling ratio so aggregate
brightness stays consistent. The regenerated shipped scene drops from 74.8 MB
to 10.5 MB and keeps five-step progressive ladders on both colorings.

#### Reject unsupported content-batch fit options

Content batch planning now rejects on-the-fly `--denoise` and `--progressive` instead of emitting content-box tasks that silently ignore them. `batch-fit submit --preprocess` remains supported because it denoises to a store before the boxes fit. Direct `fit --tiling content` invocations keep their warned-and-ignored behavior, including hand-run `--plan-box` workers and the explicit `--downscale` flag; a `downscale:` in the fit config remains supported by the content fitter.

#### Numeric NGFF dataset paths resolve consistently

The declared-path rule now also decides what a non-string OME-Zarr/NGFF
`datasets[*].path` may name: real numeric scalars are coerced, while every other
non-string value names nothing. Out-of-spec producers that serialize numeric
level names as numbers therefore retain their declared axes and voxel size,
while a numeric declaration that still cannot resolve is reported instead of
being dropped silently. Malformed values do not become plausible array names
such as ``None`` or ``[]``.

This can change which array and axes an all-numeric malformed pyramid selects.
Re-plan a `batch-fit` run that uses such a source rather than resuming an existing
plan. When numeric and string aliases name the same level, declaration order is
authoritative: the fix makes lookup and metadata agree; it does not prefer the
string declaration.

#### The effective-radii and gsplats TypeScript kernels now round like their Rust twins (#1820)

`src/wasm/typescript/` is not a fallback. Per `CLAUDE.md` it is the PRODUCTION
backend for any dataset above 16 dimensions (the worker's `pickBackend` routes
there unconditionally) and for every browser where the WASM artifact fails to
load, so a viewer can render the same scene through either implementation. Two
of those kernels did their multi-step arithmetic in JS `f64` while Rust
accumulated in `f32`, and the existing parity tests compared with a 1e-5
epsilon — loose enough to hide the entire class.

The divergence was not confined to output digits. `calculate_effective_radii`
compares an `f64` `distanceSquared` against an `f64` `radiusSquared`, so a point
sitting on the rim of its own radius was VISIBLE on one backend and culled on
the other, changing the returned `visibleCount` and the compaction the caller
sizes from it; the discrete-dimension gate could likewise accept in `f32` and
reject in `f64` for the same coordinates. `project_gsplats_nd_to_3d` thresholds
`amplitude × attenuation` against `minAmplitude`, so an unrounded product
changed the EMITTED SPLAT COUNT. Four constants were wrong outright rather than
by an ulp: the degeneracy floor clamped at `Number.MIN_VALUE` (≈5e-324) where
Rust clamps at `f32::MIN_POSITIVE` (2⁻¹²⁶), which regularizes a dead axis four
orders of magnitude apart once `maxDiag × 1e-12` underflows; and
`CHOLESKY_RELATIVE_EPSILON`, `CHOLESKY_EPSILON` and the forward-substitution
epsilon are all `f32` in `common.rs` but were compared as `f64` literals here.
`min_amplitude` and `truncate` are `f32` parameters that wasm-bindgen narrows at
the boundary, which this backend never did.

Every intermediate Rust rounds is now wrapped in `Math.fround` in Rust's
operation order — the idiom already used by `depth-sort.ts` and
`mesh-culling.ts`. The shared `GSPLAT_CHOLESKY_EPSILON` export in
`config/constants.ts` is deliberately left as the `f64` mirror of the source
value (another test pins it); the narrowing happens at the point of use.

Measured against the built WASM module, on the fixtures now committed in
`src/tests/unit/wasm/wasm-vs-typescript.test.ts` (the pre-fix column is the same
fixture with every `Math.fround` stripped and the floor restored to
`Number.MIN_VALUE`): the display marginal Cholesky went from 12 495/120 000
slots differing (up to 3602 ulp) to bit-exact, `calculate_effective_radii` from
633/20 000 outputs differing (up to 1278 ulp) to bit-exact, and
`mahalanobis_distance` at ndim 8 from 5000/5000 trials differing to bit-exact.
The last of those also disproves the file's long-standing note that a multi-step
kernel needs a `sqrt(ndim)`-scaled epsilon; the note is now marked superseded
rather than removed, since a scaled epsilon is still a valid upper bound.

Two residuals remain, documented in place rather than papered over. `Math.exp` /
`Math.log` are not V8-vs-wasm-libm identical — `expf`/`logf` are a different
approximation of the same function — so the shifted-Gaussian attenuation and the
2D phantom axis stay approximate. That is a scope decision, not a wall: a
frounded TypeScript port of musl's `expf` (what `f32::exp` lowers to on wasm32)
measures **0/200 000** mismatches against the real WASM, versus 19 282 (9.64%)
for `Math.fround(Math.exp(x))`. Porting `expf`/`logf` is deferred to **#1830**.
Rounding everything else still collapses the residuals: the emitted attenuated
amplitudes went from 11 907/19 323 differing at up to 1367 ulp to 1734/19 323
bounded by 2·2⁻²⁴ absolute, and the phantom diagonal is within 2 ulp at unit
scene scale (one from `ln`, one from `exp`).

Two limits are worth stating plainly rather than leaving to be rediscovered.
The phantom bound is a property of SCALE, not of the kernel: `phantom =
exp(mean(ln Lᵢᵢ))`, so the relative residual is ≈ `|ln σ|·2⁻²⁴` and the same
fixture measures 2 ulp at unit scale, 16 at µm, 32 at nm and 16 at km — the
parity case sweeps all four. And the visible SET can still differ. At production
defaults (`GSPLAT_DEFAULT_TRUNCATION_RADIUS` 2.75, `MIN_AMPLITUDE` 1e-6),
200 000 splats with amplitudes uniform in [0.2, 1.2] and their hidden coordinate
on the truncation shell emit 94 550 from WASM and 94 540 from this backend — 10
apart. The class is made much
rarer, not removed, and it cannot be removed while `exp` differs at all; the
count-equality assertions in the parity suite therefore hold only on fixtures
whose smallest emitted amplitude clears the residual by a stated margin (410× on
the main attenuation sweep).

The parity suite was rebuilt around that: exact equality wherever exactness is
reachable, a measured ulp/absolute bound where it is not, an amplitude bound
scaled by `invOneMinusC` (which is 1.01 at truncate 3 but 8.51 at truncate 0.5,
and truncate is author-controlled), non-zero slice positions so the subtraction
under test is not exact for free, and coverage for every narrowed constant, for
0/1/2 display dims, and for the interaction of a sub-3D display marginal with a
live attenuation path. It is mutation-validated: deleting any one of the 42
`Math.fround` calls in the two kernels turns 35 of them red, and the 7 survivors
are each proved inert at their definition (halving an f32 is exact; a value
stored into a `Float32Array` is rounded anyway; the phantom's `counted` can only
be 1 or 2).

#### Points overview LOD

`add_points()` now composes an explicit `partition=` with `substitutive_lod=` as an overview topology: mass-preserving coarse Gaussian-splat levels sit above a spatially partitioned Points branch, so large clouds can defer their full-detail payload until zoomed in without giving up the opening overview.

#### Doctor detects partition split planes in the wrong frame

`luxar gsplat doctor` now distinguishes a healthy approximate split tree over
overlapping tiled parts from planes that fall outside the parts' measured
overlap bands and per-axis tolerance floor. The floor preserves the producer's
halo scale when sparse content under-fills one tile. Doctor safely recovers bad
plane positions when possible, reports a coordinate-frame scale only when
repeated cuts support that diagnosis, and otherwise removes an unrecoverable
misleading tree so the viewer falls back to centroid ordering.

#### TypeScript GSplat projection now matches WASM transcendental results

The TypeScript fallback now evaluates the shifted-Gaussian attenuation and phantom-axis geometric mean with the same float32 `exp` and `log` implementations as Rust/WASM. Splats close to the truncation-shell amplitude cutoff therefore no longer appear or disappear depending on whether the WASM backend loaded.

#### TypeScript decode fallback now matches WASM float32 arithmetic

The TypeScript fallback now rounds linear uint8/uint16 bounds and log-scalar arithmetic in the
same operation order as the Rust/WASM decoder. Linear decoding is bit-exact across the full code
range; log decoding remains within one float32 ULP where JavaScript `Math.expm1` differs from
Rust `expm1f`.

#### Accept automatic gsplat device selection

Every `luxar gsplat` command that exposes `--device` now accepts `auto`, matching the advertised CLI and Python API behavior.

#### Validate partition BSP trees in the viewer

The scene loader now checks stored partition split planes against each part's
`position_bounds` before depth sorting uses them. Trees in a different coordinate
frame and malformed trees are discarded so the viewer falls back to centroid ordering
instead of silently applying a wrong painter's order. Tree structure is always validated;
split geometry is checked only when every part has verifiable bounds, so a well-formed tree
without them keeps its stored ordering. Overlapping tiled parts remain valid within their
measured per-axis overlap band. Existing tiled scenes with a rejected tree may therefore
revert to centroid ordering; the viewer does not repair the stored metadata.

#### Screen a built store's LOD ladders against the opening shot (#1839)

`luxar restamp-lod` can re-derive any legacy `coverage` ladder onto the current
`screen-area` selector, but nothing said whether doing so *buys anything on a
given store*. A ladder can only defer detail if the opening framing leaves it
room, and the answer is per-GROUP: a store whose 187 ladders are per-tile has no
single number. The new `luxar.io.lod_screening` measures it — per `kind=lod`
group, at the framing the viewer actually opens with, does the re-derived ladder
pick a strictly COARSER level than the stored one?

It is a read-only report and it can never fail a build. `scripts/check_demo_ladders.py`
gained `--screen` (append the pass to the existing streaming-ladder gate) and
`--screen-only` (skip the gate entirely, always exit 0); the default invocation —
the one `hatch run check` runs — is unchanged.

```
hatch run check-demo-ladders --screen-only datasets/examples/*.luxar.zarr
```

Four things the measurement is careful about, each of which a cruder one gets
wrong:

- **The cut is the group's own anchor, not a flat 1.0.** A derived whole-object
  ladder's finest rung is `WHOLE_OBJECT_FINEST_ANCHOR` = 0.5; only a
  partition-bound one anchors at `PARTITION_FINEST_AREA` = 1.0. A whole-object
  group opening anywhere in `[0.5, 1.0)` still shows full detail on frame one, so
  re-deriving it defers nothing. Which anchor a group gets — and which clause of
  the writers' two-clause rule decided it — is resolved through `lod_restamp`'s
  own `_is_partition_bound` and printed, so the screen and the rewrite can never
  disagree about it. Every refusal is shared the same way: `already-current` is
  decided on the SELECTOR ALONE, exactly as `_plan_lod` decides it (it returns
  before reading a single threshold). A descending stored ladder or an orphan
  `coverage_fraction` child skips a legacy group through `lod_restamp`'s own
  predicates; an already-current group keeps that finding as detail without
  changing buckets. A report that predicted a rewrite the command refuses to
  make would be worse than no report.
- **The two selectors are in different units.** What the store does TODAY is
  scored under its STAMPED selector: the legacy `coverage` metric is an UNCLIPPED
  projected diagonal in pixels over `FILL_FACTOR × min(W, H)`, range ~`[0, 4]`,
  while the re-derived side is always the viewport-clipped area fraction, range
  `[0, 1]`. Feeding either into the other's ladder inverts the answer — a unit
  cube at one framing reads 1.09 (finest under `[0, 0.5, 1.0]`) and 0.148
  (coarsest under `[0, 0.25, 0.5]`) — so the two are never mixed, and a test
  crosses them deliberately to keep it that way.
- **No inherited baseline.** Against an assumed "5.2x" figure a genuine win and a
  no-op look identical, so today's pick is measured, never assumed.
- **Aspect ratio is an input.** Every group is reported at 1:1, 16:9 and 21:9.
  Under the fitted framing the legacy metric happens to be aspect-invariant while
  the area metric is not, so a lone object filling the shot reads 0.56 at 1:1 and
  0.24 at 21:9 — two different levels. Those groups come back `fragile`, their own
  bucket, rather than being filed as a win or a no-op.

The verdicts are `win` / `no-op` / `fragile` / `off-screen` (the frustum gate
fires, so no metric is ever taken) / `already-current` / `skipped` with a reason.
Over a freshly built `datasets/examples` the five LOD stores screen as 1 win, 2
no-ops and 3 already-current: `energy_breakpoints` authors an explicit
`coverage_fractions` list, which pins it to the legacy selector, and it opens on
its finest 8,030-point level where a re-derived ladder would open on its 502-point
one. The three whole-object ladders that are already stamped `screen-area` bucket
`already-current` — the command would not touch them — and `partition_of_lod`'s
two tile-anchored parts already open on their coarse level. Two scenes are skipped because they
author `viewer_config.camera.position`/`target`/`target_node` and so do not open
at the fitted pose the screen models. A scene whose FOV comes from
`cinematic_mode` / `camera.fov_preset` is skipped the same way, with a pointer to
`--screen-render-fov 63`: that value lives in the viewer's own preset table and
guessing it wrong doubles every occupancy.

The camera pose, both metrics, the hysteresis pick, the frustum gate and the
nD→XYZ bounds projection are transcriptions of named viewer functions, each
citing its twin, and each is exported and unit-tested against values derived
analytically rather than snapshotted. Dynamic near/far clipping is deliberately
not modelled: the near-plane hazard that matters is the homogeneous-`w` straddle
inside `projectBoxNdcRect`, which never reads `camera.near`.

#### Match TypeScript log-scalar decoding to Rust

The TypeScript fallback now uses the same float32 `expm1f` algorithm as
Rust/WASM instead of narrowing the host's f64 `Math.expm1` result.

#### Complete gallery coverage for every bundled demo

The 4D cell-tracking challenge now has a gallery tile, bringing the gallery to
all 86 bundled demos. Its capture uses the coverage-selected coarse splat levels
and a measured framing target that keeps the full 3x2 embryo matrix in view.

#### Keep main-thread log-scalar decoding consistent

Log-scalar arrays now use the same float32 operation order in the main-thread decoder and TypeScript worker fallback. Both are bit-exact with the Rust `expm1f` the WASM kernel runs, so all three routes decode a given code to the same float.

#### Linear and geolog arrays now decode identically on every viewer route (#1849)

Large quantized ranges can be decoded in a worker while small ranges and worker
failures decode on the main thread. The main-thread `ArrayDecoder` duplicated
linear and geolog arithmetic with f64 metadata, so that routing choice changed
many output float32 bits within one encoded array. Both paths now call the same
f32-disciplined TypeScript kernels, and the Python-generated round-trip contract
records a second exact hash in viewer-kernel operation order instead of relaxing
cross-language coverage to a few approximate samples.

#### Diagnose partition trees inside scenes

`luxar gsplat doctor` now accepts `.luxar.zarr` scenes as well as standalone
`.gsplats.zarr` datasets, walks every nested partition group, and safely repairs
recoverable split-plane metadata while refreshing the scene root content hash.

#### Core scene authoring no longer needs the `gsplats` extra

`scene.add_gsplats(...)` is part of the core authoring API, but on a plain
`pip install luxar` it died with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'torch'`.
The unconditional trigger is in the compiler: `write_gsplat_arrays`
(`io/_compiler/gsplat_assembly.py`) does `from ...gsplats.utils.trils import
split_tril` on every `add_gsplats`, to split the Cholesky diagonal from the
off-diagonal before writing. `trils` is pure NumPy, but importing that submodule
executes the parent package's `__init__`, which eagerly pulled the torch-only
`device` module. (`core/group/dim_order.py` reaches the same package for
`embed_cholesky_packed` — a second route, but only when the caller passes
`dim_order=`.) The two torch-backed exports (`resolve_torch_device`,
`is_mps_available`) are now resolved lazily through a PEP 562 module
`__getattr__`, with a matching `__dir__` so they stay visible to `dir()` and to
the Sphinx API reference. `from luxar.gsplats.utils import resolve_torch_device`
