still works for the fitting code that needs it, while the core path pays
nothing.

`GSplatData` had the same shape of problem one level up: the container and its
zarr writer are pure NumPy, but `luxar/gsplats/__init__.py` imported them inside
the guard that degrades the whole subsystem to install-hint stubs when the extra
is absent, so a core-only install could not construct or save a `.gsplats.zarr`
even though nothing about doing so requires the extra. `GSplatData`,
`AdditiveSubLOD` and `SubstitutiveLevel` are now imported unguarded. The scope
of that exception is constructing, saving, loading, geometrically transforming,
and grafting into a scene. Content-EDITING still needs the extra: intensity
rescaling, a reducing `filter`/`filter_by` and the heuristic `cull` methods
(hence a bare `cull()`, whose `auto` resolves to `cumulative`) recompute stats
through `luxar.gsplats.lod`, which imports `scipy.sparse`, while the
rendering-based `cull` methods `error_budget`/`redundancy` hit `import torch`
sooner still. The package docstring now states exactly where that line falls.

The `gsplats` extra is `scipy` *and* `torch`, so the subprocess regression test
blocks both: it compiles a real four-geometry scene plus a standalone
`.gsplats.zarr` with the whole extra made unimportable by a `sys.meta_path`
finder, then reads the store back and asserts the arrays. The contract is "core
authoring works without the extra", not merely "the module imports".

While here, `gsplats/interop/tracksdata.py` drops its inlined `_unpack_tril`
copy — it existed only to avoid the eager torch import this change removed — and
calls `luxar.gsplats.utils.trils.unpack_tril` directly.

#### Native scene partitions retain their BSP split planes

`add_points`, `add_lines`, `add_mesh`, and `add_gsplats` now store the recursive
split planes used by `partition=` on the wrapper as `bsp_tree`. The viewer can
therefore traverse freshly compiled parts in stable BSP back-to-front order
instead of falling back to whole-part centroid sorting, which could pop at part
seams as the camera moved. The planes exactly separate points and splats; lines
and mesh are split by polyline or face centroid, so their vertex bounds may cross
a plane and the order is correspondingly approximate. Trees are pruned and
renumbered against the parts actually written, so an empty region cannot leave a
valid-looking tree pointing at the wrong child.

#### Content-planned partitions publish merged quality metrics

The default `gsplat fit --tiling content` partition output now records whole-volume `psnr_db`, `ssim`, `mse`, and foreground quality metrics at the archive root in both sequential and parallel modes. Scoring renders and sums the surviving core-disjoint box parts, matching their additive reconstruction without flattening the splats, and retains the existing memory-budget decline diagnostics.

#### Cinematic scenes frame with their resolved lens

The viewer now resolves a scene-authored or cinematic field of view before
automatic camera fitting, so first-load framing uses the lens that will actually
render the scene. Returning visitors keep their stored per-scene FOV precedence,
and invalid authored values fall back to the configured default.

#### Demo captions now carry compact attribution

Every bundled demo scene now writes the same bottom-right caption overlay, and
credited demos append a compact reference so attribution survives screenshots.
The citation contract gains an optional, authoring-time-validated `ref` field
for cases where the full `short` byline does not fit the caption; references
longer than 40 characters are refused rather than truncated.

An AST guard keeps every authored scene on the shared caption helper, rejects
hand-authored bottom-right overlays, and verifies that every cited demo has a
footer-sized reference. Existing generated demo stores remain unchanged until
the batched regeneration tracked in #1879.

#### GSplat chunk bounds contain decoded centers on continuous barrier axes

GSplat spatial indexes now add the center encoder's per-axis round-trip slack to
`chunk_bounds`, including on top of the tight epsilon used for `slice_dims`.
This closes a silent under-fetch where a non-gridded time/channel coordinate
could move farther during uint16 decoding than its barrier bound was padded and
therefore make its own chunk unreachable. Exact gridded axes, LUT encodings and
centers escalated to float32 keep their previous bounds.

#### Points and lines chunk bounds include decoded radii and widths

Point radii and line widths may be quantized as positive scalars, so their
decoded values can be slightly larger than the authored values used to build
spatial chunk bounds. The encoder now reports one conservative round-trip slack
for a positive-scalar array, and the points/lines ordering writers add it to
spatial radius/width pads. This keeps decoded geometry inside the bounds the
viewer uses to decide which chunks to fetch; categorical barrier dimensions
remain unexpanded.

Point `radii` and line `widths` also no longer use cross-array deduplication, so
their footprint slack cannot be replaced by another array's quantization grid.

#### Reject unknown `partition=` dictionary keys

Scene authoring now raises a clear `ValueError` when a `partition=` dictionary
contains keys other than `max_elements` or `rule`, instead of silently ignoring
misspellings and falling back to the default partition size.

#### Tribolium embryo demo renders volumetrically

The `gsplats_3d_tribolium_embryo` demo composited its splats with `normal`
alpha-over, which gave the embryo the look of a shell of surface peaks rather than
a solid body. It now uses `volumetric` emission–absorption, where absorption
(kappa 3.13, well above the 1.0 identity) supplies the front-to-back depth cueing
and the tissue reads as dense.

Volumetric integrates emission along every ray, and this light-sheet volume carries
a heavy diffuse background, so the layer's own opacity comes down to 0.06 to keep
that integral in range — absorption, not brightness, does the shaping. Absorption
and opacity are therefore a single dialled-in setting rather than two independent
knobs, and the display window (0–1.085, a slight roll-down on this direct-colour
node) moves the brightest accumulated cores a little farther into Neutral's
shoulder. The scene's `Neutral` / `exposure=1.97` pin is unchanged.

These values were dialled in against the fit as it stood, and the same release
then removes most of that diffuse background at fit time (see the floor entry).
Nuclei brightness barely moved, so the pairing is inherited rather than
re-verified; read the low opacity as one half of a tuned absorption/emission
balance rather than as compensation for haze that is no longer there.

#### Tribolium demos no longer fit the specimen's background haze

The four demos that share the tribolium fit (`gsplats_3d_tribolium_embryo`,
`gsplats_lod_tribolium`, `gsplats_recipes_tribolium`, `gsplats_lod_embryo_line`) were
spending most of their splat budget reconstructing background rather than nuclei.

The stack carries two background levels: a ~204-count detector offset in the medium
outside the embryo, and the specimen's own ~675-count autofluorescence inside it. The
default `floor="auto"` takes the histogram mode over the whole box, and since roughly
56% of this field of view is empty medium (~44% embryo), the narrow 204-count peak is
the tallest bin — so `auto` stripped the detector offset and stopped, leaving 75.6% of
the embryo's interior mass as haze to be fitted. The median cap could not correct it
either, because the mode sat below the median.

The fit now subtracts the measured specimen level. Background reconstruction drops by
~4700x, nuclei-to-background contrast goes from 4x to over 12000x, and the dim nuclei
that were previously indistinguishable from haze (1.7x above it) now stand 784x clear of
it. Two separate measurements, since they answer different questions: the scene's total
emitted mass falls to 16% of its former value (so about 84% of what it emitted was
background), and independently, the share of the reconstruction landing in voxels the
source calls pure background drops from 54.6% to 0.06% while the share on nuclei rises
from 29.3% to 94.2%. Nuclei brightness is essentially unchanged, but the volumetric
absorption/opacity pairing was dialled on the pre-floor fit and still needs a live A/B
against the replacement.

The floor is measured in camera counts, where it can be checked against a histogram, and
converted to the fit's normalised space at the point of use. The value is documented
in-place alongside the sweep that chose it, including the arm that over-floors and
destroys the dim band, so it cannot be raised casually.

A fit records the floor it used, so all four demos check the cache on load and
warn when they find a pre-floor one rather than quietly rendering the haze. Run any of
these demos once with `--recompute` to replace it; the downloaded archive and extracted
TIFF are reused when already present.

#### Viewer fixture generation no longer builds the full development environment

Viewer tests now generate their Python fixtures in a dedicated CPU-only Hatch
environment instead of installing the CUDA and desktop-tooling dependencies from
the default development environment. This substantially reduces fixture setup
time and disk/cache pressure while keeping the real gsplat recipe pipeline in use.

#### Float16 arrays keep their dynamic range when quantized

Scalar and RGB quantization now perform their affine maps in float64 before rounding
or truncating to integer codes. Previously a float16 input multiplied by the 65,535
levels of the uint16 tier overflowed to infinity, so positive, bounded, log-scaled,
and RGB arrays could silently decode as one constant value; the same change also
improves the accuracy of the uint8 tier. Existing affected stores already contain
the flat codes and cannot be repaired while reading, so re-author those scenes from
their source arrays.

#### Keep authored camera positions paired with their scene FOV

Returning visitors now receive an authored camera position together with its
resolved scene field of view, even when per-scene rendering settings exist in
localStorage. Stored FOV settings remain authoritative for auto-framed scenes.

#### `optimize` decides a payload-name collision from a listing, not a lookup

A store whose group carries a payload attr naming a case-shifted zarr metadata
document — `image_file = "Zarr.json"` — with no such file behind it is skipped
with a notice, on every platform. It used to be refused on macOS and Windows,
and the refusal quoted the wrong bytes.

`_copy_payload_files` has to separate two stores that spell a payload the same
way: one whose attr dangles, which the re-chunk should skip (the output is then
exactly as complete as its input), and one that really holds a distinct file
called `Zarr.json`, which it must refuse, since writing that key on a
case-insensitive filesystem replaces the document the whole node is read
through. It told them apart by trying to READ the name — and that is the one
question an open-by-name cannot answer here, because the OS resolves it: on the
very filesystems the branch exists for, `Zarr.json` folds onto the group's own
`zarr.json` and comes back full of bytes. So the skip was unreachable there, a
merely incomplete store was stranded instead of re-chunked, and the refusal
reported the node document's size while advising the user to rename a payload
file that does not exist. The CI filesystem does not fold, so the existing
regression test passed there and failed on a developer's laptop.

The verdict now comes from a directory listing compared case-sensitively in
Python. `_zarr_compat.list_raw_keys` reports the key names stored directly under
a group's own prefix — store-agnostic, like its `read_raw_bytes` neighbour, and
verified against `LocalStore`, `MemoryStore` and `ZipStore`. A listing is not
folded, so the copy consults it first and only reads a name the store really
holds — which is what keeps the dangling case visible on every platform. It
reports every immediate child, subdirectories included, so the read still has
the last word: a name held by a child group rather than a file has no bytes to
drop and no file to rename, and takes the same skip as a dangling attr. The
hasher's name gate is deliberately untouched: it feeds the content hash, and
tightening it would move the digest of every store carrying such a name.

#### Hover picking follows camera projection changes

Changing the field of view or clipping planes now invalidates the cached GPU pick buffer, so hover labels and tooltips cannot report geometry that the visible camera projection has moved or clipped away.

#### Clicking a picked element can now open a link or copy a string (#1917)

A labelled element could be **named** on hover and nothing else. Left- and
right-click on the canvas did nothing at all: outside the camera controls
nothing in the viewer listened for `click`, `contextmenu`, `mousedown` or
`pointerdown`, and both controls implementations already suppress the native
context menu, so a right-click was swallowed and replaced by nothing.

Three new per-node attrs make an element actionable. They are plain `.zattrs`
values riding the existing `**attrs` pass-through, so no adder signature
changed:

```python
scene.add_gsplats(
    "organs", centers=..., labels=organ_names,
    link="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search={hover_label}",
    copy="{hover_label}",     # optional — defaults to the bare label
    link_target="_blank",     # optional — the default
)
```

Left-click (no drag) opens the resolved URL; right-click (no drag) opens the
shared context menu with `Copy "<text>"`, `Open link in new tab` and `Copy link
address`, omitting whatever the element does not offer and not opening at all
when it offers nothing. The hover placeholder vocabulary is reused verbatim, so
there is one substitution to learn; it now lives in one place
(`utils/hover-template.ts`) shared by the tooltip, the link and the copy string,
with the escaping — and only the escaping — differing per consumer. The
totalsegmentator CT demo adopts it: every organ links to a lookup of its own
name.

Templates are authored per **node** rather than per hover overlay because a
scene has effectively one overlay but many layers, and the target is a property
of the data ("these are UniProt accessions"), not of the tooltip's presentation.

A click acts on the settled hover pick rather than taking a fresh one. That is
partly honesty — it is the element whose name the user just read — and partly
necessity: there is no synchronous pick, and awaiting a GPU readback risks
spending the browser's transient user activation, turning "open the link" into
"popup blocked". Staleness is covered by counters `PickingSystem` already
maintains: `pickGeneration` (camera move, resize, ortho swap, FOV edit, mouse
move, leave, dispose) and the new public `visibleSignature`, which catches a
layer-visibility toggle — the one invalidator that deliberately does not dirty
the pick buffer. `suppress()` pointedly does *not* advance the generation,
because pointerdown → `start` → suppress is the first half of an ordinary
click; a test pins that, since the failure mode would be every click silently
refusing itself.

Making that list true required one fix outside the feature: `setCamera` — the
perspective↔orthographic swap — set the pick buffer's dirty flag directly and
advanced no counter, so a cached pick survived a change that reprojects every
element on screen. Hover an element, toggle ortho without moving the mouse
(nothing fires `mousemove`), click, and the click acted on whatever used to be
under the cursor. It now routes through `markDirty`, which also fades the
now-stale tooltip. Same family as the FOV gap in #1916, found by enumerating
every mutation that can invalidate a pick and checking each against the two
counters.

Click is told from camera gesture by movement, never by button: which button
orbits and which pans is platform-dependent (`naturalDrag` defaults to macOS,
and ortho maps RIGHT to nothing), so any button-based rule would be wrong on
half the installs. A press that moves ≤4 px is a click. The menu opens on
`pointerup`, not on the `contextmenu` event, because on macOS the latter fires
at press time and a right-drag to rotate would pop a menu as the drag began;
macOS Ctrl+primary-click is treated as secondary, as in every native app.

Both halves of a link are untrusted — the template is author-supplied and the
substituted values are per-element data — so the guard is layered: values are
percent-encoded (a label may contribute content to a URL but never structure),
the result is parsed with no base so a relative template is refused rather than
resolving against the viewer's own origin, the scheme must be `http`/`https`
(an allowlist, deliberately stricter than the denylist used for *rendered*
markup — this URL gets navigated to), embedded credentials are refused
(`https://good.example@evil.example/` reads as one host and navigates to
another, including in the menu's own `Copy link address`), the length is
capped, and links open with `noopener,noreferrer` to a target restricted to the
two keywords that imply it.
The Python writer runs the equivalent check, so a bad `link=` fails the write
instead of becoming a click that silently does nothing. A referenced
placeholder that resolves empty suppresses the action rather than leaving a
hole — `https://uniprot.org/{hover_label}` with no label is a valid URL to the
wrong place, and that is the *normal* case at coarse levels of a substitutive
LOD ladder, whose synthesised gsplat levels inherit the node attrs but carry no
labels.

Also included: a `pointer` cursor over a linked element; Shift+F10 and the
ContextMenu key as the keyboard path the UI design guide requires of every
context menu; `element-click` / `element-contextmenu` embedder events carrying
the element, the gesture and the resolved link; and a kill switch —
`allowLinks: false` or `?noLinks` — that suppresses navigation, the link menu
items and the cursor while leaving `Copy` working, for embedders showing scenes
they did not author.

One provisioning subtlety worth knowing: picking is only stood up when
something will consume it, and both new sources of demand had to be added to
that test. A node declaring `link` or `copy` now counts as a consumer in its
own right, in the early-return gate and the live `shouldPick` predicate alike —
a layer with a link but no labels (a link built from `{hover_index}` is
perfectly usable) auto-injects no hover overlay either, so without that it
would never pick and the link would never fire. An `element-click` /
`element-contextmenu` listener counts too, on the same terms as `selection`, so
a host driving its own behaviour on an unlabelled scene gets events rather than
silence.

Touch is out of scope: there is no hover, so the cached-pick path has nothing
to act on and a tap does nothing. A follow-up would need tap → async pick →
in-tab navigation (the awaited readback may have spent the user activation) and
long-press → menu.

#### Per-element `keys=`, so a link can be built from an id the tooltip does not show (#1917)

The click actions added alongside this substitute the hover vocabulary into a
URL, which works only when the visible label IS the linkable id. Across the demo
corpus it almost never is. Of the 27 demos that pass `labels=`, essentially all
build composite prose — `"P04637 · DNA-binding cluster"`,
`"Blinding Lights — The Weeknd (pop)"` — and in four of them the id is not in
the label at all, because it was never fetched. A template over `{hover_label}`
would produce a percent-encoded blob of the whole sentence.

So there is now a second per-element string channel. `labels` stays what a
reader sees; `keys` is what a machine reads:

```python
scene.add_points(
    "proteins", positions,
    labels=[f"{acc} · {cluster}" for acc, cluster in ...],   # unchanged, readable
    keys=accessions,                                          # "P04637"
    link="https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/{hover_key}/entry",
)
```

It is stored as a CSR pair (`key_offsets` / `key_bytes`, flagged by
`has_keys`) — the same structure as labels, written by the same serializer with
a channel parameter rather than a near-copy of it, and read by the same viewer
loader constructed on the `'keys'` channel. That sharing is deliberate: keys
follow the same spatial permutation as labels (a key must stay paired with its
element), the same all-or-nothing rule across an additive ladder, the same
per-`part_<i>` slicing under a partition, and the same union-CSR-on-the-parent
placement for a ladder. Anything that treats them differently would be a bug,
so the code cannot express the difference.

The two channels are otherwise independent: a node may carry either, both or
neither, and a `link` built purely from `{hover_index}` needs no strings at all.
Keys are also much cheaper than the obvious alternative of storing a whole URL
per element — a six-character accession is ~7 bytes against ~45, and the viewer
decodes the entire CSR into memory on first hover, so a 3M-element scene would
otherwise hold hundreds of MB of near-identical prefixes.

Eleven demos adopt it: arXiv embeddings, CAFA5 and ESM3 proteins, Spotify tracks,
earthquakes, FlyWire, CAIDA, HuRI, asteroids, Tabula Sapiens, and the Gaia
landmarks. Each keeps readable hover prose while its bare identifier drives the
link/copy template; demos with missing or synthetic identifiers suppress the
link instead of offering a broken destination.

Two smaller fixes fell out of the threading. The ladder writers requested each
level's spatial permutation only when the ladder was *labelled*, so a keys-only
ladder asked for a union with zero permutations; they now request it when either
channel is present. And the gsplats writer imported its string validator inside
the `if labels is not None:` branch, which left the keys check referencing an
unbound name — the import is hoisted to cover both.

#### Changed (breaking) — one arXiv demo, and it now shows all 3,286,365 papers

We shipped two arXiv-embedding demos. `arxiv_papers_semantic_scholar` could
never show more than about 1,200 papers, and `arxiv_papers_kaggle` was showing
the oldest 15% of its corpus. The first is **deleted**; the second now
visualizes the whole thing.

**`arxiv_papers_semantic_scholar` is gone (key, script, test, README section,
gallery-manifest entry, complexity-baseline entries, built scene).** Its
`search_papers_by_field()` paged Semantic Scholar's `/paper/search`, which
enforces `offset + limit <= 1000`; requests past that are 400s the demo's
`except RequestException: break` swallowed. So `DEFAULT_PAPERS_PER_FIELD =
200000` across 5 fields — a nominal 1,000,000 papers — resolved to at most 5,000
raw hits and, after the demo's own citation/abstract filter, **1,231**. That is
the upstream API's design, not a bug we can fix here; the unauthenticated
endpoint now 429s on the first request besides, and `query=<field name>` was a
full-text relevance search rather than a field filter, so its 1,000 hits were
the documents most textually similar to the *word* "Physics". Delete the
`arxiv_semantic_scholar` cache directory and any
`datasets/demos/arxiv_papers_semantic_scholar.luxar.zarr` by hand.

**`arxiv_papers_kaggle` defaults to the full corpus.** `vectors.dat` holds
exactly 3,286,365 unit-norm `float32[3072]` rows — 2,902,228 arXiv, 308,367
bioRxiv and 75,770 medRxiv papers through 2025-12 — and the demo used to read
the first 500,000 with `pd.read_csv(nrows=...)`. `papers.csv` is sorted by
ascending ID, so those were arXiv submissions from 2007-04 to roughly 2012-03:
a five-year slice in which computer science is 8.7% of the points, because the
CS/ML growth happens entirely after the cut. The "Year" view, which colours by
`update_date`, spanned 2007–2025 and hid it.

Four changes make the whole corpus routine rather than impossible:

- **Blockwise decode.** `np.frombuffer` over multi-MB blocks replaces a
  `struct.unpack` + `list()` + `append` per paper. The ZIP itself streams at a
  measured 204 MiB/s, so all 37.6 GiB of vectors decompress in ~3 minutes; the
  decode loop was the entire bottleneck.
- **Streamed PCA pre-reduction.** UMAP ran on the raw 3072-D vectors, an
  `N x 3072 x 4 B` working set that is 40 GB at full scale. A randomized PCA
  fitted on a 300k-row uniform subsample now projects every row on the fly to
  `--pca-dim` (default 128, ~58% of variance) into a 1.6 GB cached memmap. Peak
  RSS is bounded by the fit subsample; the cache is keyed on `--pca-dim` alone,
  so the 3072-D vectors are not re-read. `papers.csv` still comes from the ZIP,
  so keep the archive.
- **`--sample=N` is a uniform random sample**, seeded and reproducible, instead
  of a prefix. The default is now the whole corpus.
- **Optional GPU UMAP.** `--device=auto|cpu|gpu` uses RAPIDS cuML when it
  imports. Measured on an RTX PRO 6000: **56 s** for 3,286,365 x 128 -> 3D.
  cuML is in no Luxar extra and its absence stays a quiet fall-back to
  `umap-learn`, not an install instruction.

The **Year** view now means what it says. Years used to come from the Cornell
snapshot's `update_date` — the LAST REVISION — and nothing in that snapshot
predates 2007, so the 400,803 papers submitted from 1991 through 2006 were all
painted 2007-or-later and 35 years of arXiv were squeezed into 19. The year is
decoded from the identifier instead: `0704.0001` and `hep-lat/0506004` both
carry their submission month, a bioRxiv/medRxiv DOI carries a full date, and all
2,902,228 arXiv rows decode. Titles and categories still come from the snapshot,
which is the only thing that has them.

Two smaller correctness fixes ride along. Point radii are now derived from the
**measured** median nearest-neighbour distance of the reduced cloud rather than
from constants hand-tuned at 500k: median spacing falls as roughly `N^(-1/3)`,
so the old ramp was ~1.9x too large over the full corpus and would have merged
the spheres into white — the same failure its own comment documented for the
ramp before it. And the 384,137 bioRxiv/medRxiv papers, which the arXiv-only
Cornell snapshot cannot match, are coloured as `biorxiv` / `medrxiv` instead of
being dumped into grey `other`, taking their year from the date in their DOI;
the 68,138 legacy accessions that carry no date anywhere report no year and are
painted neutral in the Year view rather than being assigned one.

The `arxiv_kaggle` bundle cache is bumped to `version=3`: a v1 bundle is a
date-ordered prefix with no spacing measurement, and a v2 bundle carries
`update_date` years. The bundle STORES the years, so changing how they are
derived invalidates it exactly as changing the UMAP would; neither may be
reused. `pandas` also stops being a requirement of this demo — its only caller
was the `read_csv(nrows=...)` the streaming reader replaced.

#### `H` and `O` are toggles again: panels no longer autofocus their filter field

`InputHandler.onKeyDown` drops every key except `Escape` while focus is on a
typing surface, which is what lets a user type into a search box without
flipping dimensions or cycling camera modes. Two panels then autofocused a text
filter as they opened — the help overlay handed focus to its filter on a 0 ms
timer, and the dataset browser had a one-shot "first successful listing claims
focus" block — so each panel's own toggle key became one-way: `H` opened the
help overlay, but the second `H` was swallowed as typing and the overlay never
closed. Nothing was trapped (Escape, the close button and clicking away all
worked, and the rail button closed it because a pointer click blurs the filter
first), but the docs, the binding description and the rail tooltip all promised
a toggle.

Both panels now park initial focus on the panel **container** instead. A
`<div role="dialog">` is not a typing surface, so the guard never engages and
the toggle key reaches its global binding. Type-to-filter is preserved by a new
shared helper, `ui/help-overlay/type-to-filter.ts`: a container-level `keydown`
listener forwards the first printable keystroke into the filter — focusing it,
appending the character and dispatching the `input` event the panel's existing
filter handler already listens for — so filtering still starts on the very first
key the user presses, whenever a filter is on screen at all (the dataset browser
hides its search bar while loading, on an error and in an empty directory; keys
pressed in those states are contained by the modal, since there is nothing to
narrow and nothing behind the panel should hear them). `Tab` still reaches the
focus trap,
`ArrowDown` still moves into the dataset listing (from the container now, since
the search field no longer has focus to hand off), a keystroke that opens an IME
composition focuses the filter without preventing the composition — so CJK and
European dead-key layouts keep their first character — and an AltGr-composed
printable (`AltGr+2` = `@`, which Windows reports as ctrl+alt) types like any
other character rather than being mistaken for a shortcut. `Space` is not a
filter character: a leading space matches nothing and it scrolls a
`tabindex="-1"` container. The dataset browser's manual-entry fallback — the
form shown for a server that cannot be listed at all (S3/CloudFront, nginx with
`autoindex off`) — no longer autofocuses its path field either, but it is
deliberately *not* wired into type-to-filter: that field takes a URL, not a
filter query, so stray keystrokes should not be routed into it. Focus stays on
the container and the user clicks or tabs into the field, which is a deliberate
act; from there the ordinary typing guard applies exactly as it does for every
other text field in the app, `Enter` still submits and `Escape` still closes the
panel.

Dropping the autofocus removed something nobody had noticed it was doing: the
focused text field was the only thing keeping global shortcuts out of the scene
behind an `aria-modal` panel, because no panel pushes an `InputContext`. So the
container listener now contains them itself, and the rule is unconditional on
focus: every key that bubbles up to the panel container is `stopPropagation`ed
— from the shell, from a listing row, from the filter, from a breadcrumb alike
— so `Home`/`End` no longer jump the selected dimension and `Shift`+arrows no
longer change the animation speed while a panel is open, not even after a
single `Tab`. A key an inner handler already consumed (`preventDefault` without
`stopPropagation`, which is how the listing's arrow navigation is written) is
contained too rather than released to the globals; the inner handlers
themselves are unaffected, since they run first on the way up.

There are exactly three exceptions. `Escape` (panel dismissal), `Tab`/`Shift+Tab`
(the focus trap), and the keys the panel *advertises* — which is now more than
its own toggle: containment silences everything else, so a shortcut a panel
offers as a **live affordance** must be declared or it is dead. The dataset
browser's welcome banner shows an `H` Help chip you are meant to press right
there, so it declares both `O` and `H`; the help overlay declares `H`. The rule
is about affordances, not about every `<kbd>` on screen: the help overlay's
reference table lists `O`, `V`, `F`, `R`, `B`, `1`–`9` and the rest as a
*catalogue* of what those keys do when the panel is closed, and they are
correctly inert while it is open — as they already were before this change,
when the autofocused filter fed them to the typing guard.

That exemption is gated on the event target being the container itself, so once
focus has moved into a field or a row those keys are ordinary characters again
and typing `o` into the path field cannot close the browser.
Containment is `stopPropagation` only, never `preventDefault`, so panel
scrolling with `Home`/`PageDown` and every browser-level shortcut (`Ctrl+F`,
`Cmd+W`, `F5`, the function keys) keep working.

One character genuinely cannot serve both masters. Forwarding the first `h`
into the help overlay's filter would re-break exactly the toggle this change
fixes, so a panel's own toggle key is passed through to the global binding and
cannot be the *first* character of a filter query. It types normally once the
filter has focus, `Shift`+that key types it even as the first character (the
global lookup spells the shifted form `"h+shift"`, which no binding registers,
so passing it through would only make it a dead key), and matching is
case-insensitive — so no query is unreachable, and "help" is also found by
typing `elp`.

While the wording was under review anyway: `O` has toggled the dataset browser
since the shortcut was wired through `installBrowserShortcut`, but the binding
description, the help overlay row, the viewer guide and the viewer README all
still said "Open dataset browser". Now that the keyboard round-trip actually
works, they say "Toggle".

`trapFocus` gained an `autoFocusFirst` option because the two mechanisms would
otherwise fight: the trap parks initial focus on the container's first focusable
element via its own 0 ms timer, which would fire after the panel's synchronous
container focus and silently win. The filtered panels pass `false`; the error
overlay is unchanged. The trap also learned to steer `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` inward
when focus is on the container itself — otherwise the browser default would walk
Shift+Tab straight out of a modal whose focus now starts on a `tabindex="-1"`
element — and to skip focusables that are not rendered, since the dataset
browser hides its whole search row while a directory loads and `Shift+Tab` would
otherwise aim at a `display: none` input, which a real browser refuses to focus.

Finally, the trap's cleanup now restores focus to the element it recorded on
entry only when focus is still *inside* the container it is releasing. Modals
stack: open the help overlay from the rail, then open the dataset browser on top
of it, then press `H` (which the browser declares as a passthrough) — that
closes the help overlay, and an unconditional restore sent focus back to the
rail button, i.e. straight out of the still-open browser dialog, where the
global shortcuts start reaching the scene again. That is precisely the invariant
this change exists to establish, so the restore is now conditional.

Dataset-browser rerenders preserve the same invariant: when a navigation
loading state, breadcrumb rebuild or cancelled path edit removes the focused
child, focus returns to the panel only if it fell back to `null` or `<body>`.
That narrow check keeps modal containment active without taking focus from a
dialog stacked on top.

#### Two dataset-browser E2E guards were waiting on the wrong readiness signal

The `first-time-ux` specs that exercise the `O` shortcut gated on
`window.__luxarDebug.app`, which the bootstrap publishes at construction — before
`LuxarApp.init()` has finished. At the time, the window-level
`open-dataset-browser` listener was installed only at the _end_ of `init()`, after
the awaited dataset load, so the `O` keypress dispatched its event into the void and
both tests died on their first assertion. The listener now installs before dataset
routing, while the readiness wait still protects the input binding and routing
assertions.

What that cost is worth recording: the Escape exemption in `InputHandler.onKeyDown`
— the one that lets Escape reach the context manager even while focus sits in a text
input — had no `onKeyDown`-side guard (the context manager's half of the routing is
unit-tested; the chain through to a panel actually closing was not), and neither did
the `O` toggle's reopen-after-Escape path, which depends on `DatasetBrowser.close()`
firing `onClose` so the next press does not toggle a phantom browser shut. Both are
guarded again.

The tests now gate on `waitForLuxarReady`, focus the canvas through the shared
`focusCanvas` helper instead of a bare click whose failure was swallowed, and assert
explicitly that a `?src=` load does not auto-open the browser — an assertion that has
to come before the focus click, which would Escape the browser away and make it
vacuous.

#### The lift-parity spec now brackets the peak-mode divergence instead of noting it

Points and their lifted-gsplat twin agree on the ray mass in every sum mode, but
peak projection (`max`, `normal`, `opaque`) is still uncalibrated: the lift bakes
one amplitude for both shader branches and only the sum branch applies the ray
integral. The parity spec asserted that gap with a one-sided `> 1.1` on the crop
MEAN — a bar that sat inside the 10% parity band's own width, so it could not
tell a real 30× divergence from measurement noise, and a one-sided one at that.
The peak arm now reads the crop PEAK (the quantity peak projection actually
calibrates, and the one immune to `opaque`'s depth-driven coverage collapse) and
brackets it two ways: by DIRECTION per mode, and by a per-mode, per-radius
EXPECTED magnitude within a factor of 1.5 either way. An effect-C change now
goes red and its message names the value that moved.

Each cell also prints mean, peak and coverage side by side. A mean ratio alone
cannot say WHY it moved — under `opaque` a gsplat quad stamps one depth across
its whole footprint, so faint tails depth-reject the bright cores behind them and
coverage collapses on peaks that are bit-identical to `max`'s. The table is
emitted before the guards run, so a dead cell is diagnosed against the rows
measured either side of it rather than throwing mid-build and printing nothing.

Measuring the peak also surfaced the independent point/line `opaque` blending
defect fixed by #1994. With alpha-over restored, the points peak grows with
radius while the gsplat peak retains effect C, so the ratio crosses parity and
the lifted twin becomes increasingly dimmer toward the coarse radii. The opaque
arm therefore asserts the measured r=0.15 and r=0.40 cells rather than the two
fine cells used by `max` and `normal`.

#### The LOD cross-fade sweep now actually moves the camera (#1930)

`lod-group.spec.ts`'s volumetric cross-fade test swept 61 camera distances and
found "a single level at opacity 1" — because the sweep never left the opening
framing. Two independent reasons, both of which fail silently:
`__luxarDebug.controls` is the `ControlsManager`, which has no `target` field, so
`debug.controls?.target ?? {x:0,y:0,z:0}` read the world origin instead of the
real pivot; and `runUpdateStep` step 8 re-applies the controls' own
target/orientation/distance to the camera every frame, so a bare
`camera.position.set()` is overwritten on the next line unless `reinitialize()`
re-derives the orbit state from it first. All 61 iterations therefore sampled the
same settled pose — which sits outside both bands of the fixture's 0 / 0.5 / 1.0
ladder, so one level at full opacity was the correct answer for the pose the test
was in. Nothing was wrong with volumetric cross-fading.

`helpers.ts` gained the one definition of the placement idiom:
`placeCameraAt(page, position, { target, up })` writes the position, aims at the
active controls' pivot, `reinitialize()`s and `update()`s, and returns the
post-clamp pose plus a `viaOrbitControls` flag saying whether any controller
actually re-derived the write — so a caller can PROVE the camera moved instead of
assuming it. `getCameraPivot` reads the pivot for poses expressed relative to the
content centre, and THROWS when there is none rather than answering with the
world origin: a silent origin fallback is half of what hid this bug, so the
helper written to end it does not ship one. Both are thin wrappers over a page-side
`window.__luxarE2ECamera`, so the lod-group sweep — which places the camera 61
times inside ONE `page.evaluate` — and `ortho-mode.spec.ts`'s `putCameraOffAxis`,
converted here, drive the same routine rather than three copies of it.

`withOrbitDistanceLimits` (widen the orbit distance clamp for the duration of a
body, restore in a `finally`) is kept but demoted to DEFENSIVE, because the
original rationale was overstated: the clamp is
`[D / 1000, D × 10000]` around the framing distance `D`
(`ZOOM_IN_FACTOR`/`ZOOM_OUT_FACTOR`), measured as `[0.0138, 137990]` on the
`test_lines` fixture. The lod sweep spans `0.15·D … 15·D` and the line
placement sits at `~D/3`, both two-plus decades inside it, so the clamp could
not have fired at either site — the missing `reinitialize()` was the whole
cause. The wrapper is kept on the lod sweep only because that sweep's range is
a knob that could be widened past `D/1000`. It now THROWS when the widening
could not be applied (non-orbit
controls) instead of silently running the body under the original clamp.

The reworked sweep records every step's distance scale, post-clamp camera
distance and `{idx, opacity}` vector, attaches the whole trace to the Playwright
report as JSON, and renders it into the failure message of the assertions that
can go red — so a future failure distinguishes "the band exists but is narrow"
from "the opacities are only ever 0 or 1". Most importantly it now asserts that
the camera moved at all — observed distance spread > 10x across a requested ~100x
span, and every placement re-derived by orbit controls — which is exactly the
failure mode that hid here. Each observed band is also checked as a DISSOLVE
rather than just a pair of partial weights: within a band the finer level's
opacity must fall monotonically as the camera retreats, and must actually vary.
Adjacency + strict partiality + `sum ≈ 1` are all satisfied by an inverted weight
mapping and by a constant 50/50 split (a pop at each band edge — the very defect
the cross-fade prevents), and the trace already carries the distance needed to
rule both out. The blend-state read was
moved inside the widened-limits window and parked at the pose where the blend was
observed, so it samples the cross-fading pair rather than whatever the far end of
the sweep left on screen.

With the camera finally moving, the trace exposed a second defect the old
assertion could not see: it was DISCONTINUOUS. The 0↔1 band cross-faded, but the
1↔2 band — which the fixture's ladder puts squarely inside the swept range — was
missing entirely, because the sweep outran the loader. The registry requests a
level's chunks only when that level is first needed and holds the resident level
at opacity 1 until the replacement has arrived, so a fast sweep crosses the
boundary before the incoming level exists and the band never happens (the server
log showed `child_1`'s chunks arriving ~4 s after `child_0`/`child_2`'s). The
sweep now runs a bounded residency warm-up first: coarse passes over the same
range (every 4th step) repeated until every level published by the scene has been
observed VISIBLE at least once — the in-page proxy for "resident" — bounded by a
12 s WALL CLOCK and nothing else, so a page that never settles still runs the
measuring pass and reports what was actually observed instead of hanging. The
clock is the only bound on purpose: residency is gated on chunk fetches, so the
only useful response to "not resident yet" is to keep the loop turning, and an
incomplete warm-up therefore always spent its entire budget — which is what makes
incompleteness mean "the data did not arrive in 12 s" and nothing else. Typical
cost is a few seconds of wall clock.

The assertion was tightened to match: instead of "some cross-fade happened
somewhere", the sweep collects EVERY crossing that meets the cross-fade contract
and requires each adjacent pair — derived from CONSECUTIVE observed level
indices, with a contiguity check so a level the probe cannot see fails loudly
rather than quietly shrinking the contract — to have been seen fading. That is
the assertion that would have caught the loader race, and it makes the test a
per-boundary cross-fade guard. Contiguity is checked against the lod group's own
`children.length` as well as against `0…n`, because `[0, 1]` is contiguous: a
nested `kind=lod`/`kind=partition` child attaches as an ANONYMOUS placeholder
group, and the finest level is the natural place for one, so a missing tail is
invisible to a name-matching probe.

The strength of that claim follows the evidence, because per-boundary residency
is not an implementation invariant: the registry hard-swaps instead of blending
on several legitimate paths (partner not yet loaded, never-downgrade display
hold, off-screen pinning, `?noLodFade`, a manual level lock), and the warm-up
compensating for that is bounded by a clock. So the strict per-boundary
assertion holds only when the warm-up reached residency AND the sweep was not
truncated. What replaces it otherwise is a NARROWER contract, not the absence of
one: a run whose warm-up came up short still requires a genuine cross-fade for
every adjacent pair among the levels that DID become resident. That is nearly as
strong — every pair that does not touch the missing level still has to fade — and
it cannot go red on a healthy product, because a level that never arrived cannot
fade. A never-displayed END level costs the contract one pair; a MIDDLE one costs
two, so on the three-level fixture a missing level 1 leaves no pair to claim and
the run falls to the floor ("something was displayed"), which the annotation says
in as many words. Only a TRUNCATED sweep, which never visited
part of the distance range and so implies no particular subset of pairs, falls
all the way back to the pre-change contract of at least one genuine cross-fade
with every per-blend invariant still enforced. Each narrowing is said loudly, in
the failure text and in a `degraded` annotation that names the levels which were
never displayed. The failure messages name the missing pairs and
print the warm-up and sweep summaries next to the trace, so "the fade is broken",
"the level was never resident" and "the sweep ran out of time" are
distinguishable at a glance. The test also raises its own timeout to 150 s: its
in-page budgets (12 s warm-up + 90 s sweep) can outlast the suite-wide 60 s one,
and being killed mid-`page.evaluate` discards the very attachment the test exists
to produce. The sweep now STOPS at its deadline (recording the truncation) rather
than paying one more frame per remaining step — and that deadline is sized from
the budget actually available, because truncation costs assertion strength and
must stay exceptional: 61 steps of paced frames on a single-worker,
software-rendering runner are plausibly the same order as the 20 s first tried,
which would have made the degraded path the normal CI outcome.

Two more inert camera sites were converted to the same helper:
`gsplat-rendering-visual.spec.ts`'s "camera rotation does not produce shader
errors" (four rotations that all rendered the same pose) and
`line-rendering-visual.spec.ts`'s near-camera line test (whose camera never
reached the scene origin it claims to sit at). Both now ASSERT the returned
placement — non-null, orbit-re-derived, coordinates where they asked — so a
regression in the helper makes them fail instead of going quietly inert again.
The line test's "no full-screen artefact" check was unfalsifiable while it was
there: the fixture's vertices carry a red→blue gradient (green is 0 on every
vertex), so its `r>240 && g>240 && b>240` on all four corners could never be
true. It now asserts a TWO-SIDED contract: at least one central sample is painted
(something rendered) and at least one canvas corner still reads as background
(it did not paint the whole viewport). The corner half is what the artefact
actually DESTROYS, and needs no colour threshold to defend — but four background
corners are equally consistent with an EMPTY frame, so on its own it would stay
green through a regression in the very mechanism the test names, `uNearCull`
degenerating every segment. The central half, sampled with the same 3×3 grid
idiom as the cap-factor test in the same file, is the complement. A
colour-uniformity threshold would not have worked either: adjacent vertices
differ by ~28/255 in R and B across a single segment, so an artefact that keeps
any of the line's own interpolation is wider than any spread bound tight enough
to mean something. Both sample sets are logged on every run, so "the healthy
frame really does paint the middle and leave a corner dark" is checkable from the
run log instead of assumed.

#### Reject degenerate custom log-scalar encodings

The `log_scalar_uint8` and `log_scalar_uint16` custom encoders now reject empty,
non-finite, negative, and zero-range data instead of writing invalid values or
metadata that the decoder cannot read.

#### Apply authored camera FOV presets

Apply an authored named `camera.fov_preset` lens to the viewer camera even when no numeric `camera.fov` is provided, keeping the live lens and rendering-controls label in sync.

#### Content hashes now converge across case-insensitive filesystems

A payload attr that named a case-shifted zarr metadata document, such as
`image_file = "Zarr.json"`, could make `content_hash` depend on its own previous
value on macOS and Windows. The hasher's semantic name gate rejects `zarr.json`
exactly, but the shifted spelling passed; an open-by-name then case-folded onto
the group's real `zarr.json`, whose bytes include the hash being restamped.
Repeated compiles or `luxar optimize` runs therefore produced a different digest
each time, while the same store converged on a case-sensitive Linux filesystem.

The hasher now asks the store's immediate-child listing whether this narrow
collision class exists with the exact authored spelling before reading it. A
dangling shifted name folds the same `absent:` term on every platform, while a
store that genuinely holds a distinct case-shifted payload still hashes its
bytes. Ordinary payload names retain the existing store-native lookup semantics;
the listing is not used to enumerate payloads.

Affected macOS and Windows directory stores receive a one-time hash migration to
the platform-independent digest on their next compile or re-chunk; the same
store's digest is unchanged on a case-sensitive filesystem. Republishing the
migrated store invalidates warm viewer caches keyed by the old digest. Subsequent
rewrites converge, and stores without a case-shifted metadata-document payload
name keep their existing hashes.

#### `luxar mesh import` reads VTK XML PolyData (`.vtp`)

`.vtp` is what ParaView, VTK and PyVista write for a surface, and what a
marching-cubes isosurface comes out of a segmentation pipeline as — so it was the
conspicuous gap in an importer that already read PLY, OBJ, STL and glTF. It now joins
them, on the same terms: NumPy plus the standard library (`xml.etree`, `base64`, `zlib`)
and no new dependency, so it works on a bare `pip install luxar`.

Every encoding the format allows is decoded, because a `.vtp` in hand is whichever one
its writer chose: `ascii`, inline base64 (`format="binary"`), and an appended section in
either `raw` or `base64` form, each optionally `vtkZLibDataCompressor`-compressed, with a
`UInt32` or `UInt64` block header and either byte order. `Polys` are fan-triangulated and
`Strips` triangulated with the alternate winding a strip requires; `Verts` and `Lines`
carry no surface and are dropped; `PointData` normals and colours come across.

Three of those are traps that misparse *without erroring*, which is why each is handled
explicitly and tested on decoded geometry rather than on bytes. ParaView's default
`<AppendedData encoding="raw">` puts arbitrary binary inside the document, so an XML
parser refuses the whole file, header included — the stream is split on the literal
`<AppendedData` first and only the header portion parsed, by a pull parser that hands back
a usable tree even though the closing tags never arrive. A *compressed* base64 block is
two concatenated base64 streams, the block header encoded separately from the payload, so
a single `b64decode` of the element text yields plausible garbage. And `offsets` are
cumulative *end* offsets with no leading zero, which read as starts merely rotates the
polygon list. An LZ4- or LZMA-compressed file is refused by name rather than inflated as
zlib, and a `.vtu` (UnstructuredGrid) is named as the volume mesh it is, with a pointer at
ParaView's *Extract Surface*, instead of failing thirty lines deeper in the PolyData
parser.

Two structural features of the format come across as well. A PolyData may hold several
`<Piece>`s, each numbering its own points from 0; they are concatenated into one surface
with every index rebased, bounded against its own piece first so an over-running index
cannot quietly stitch itself to a neighbouring piece's geometry, and `PointData` is taken
all-or-nothing across them rather than inventing rows for the pieces that lack it. And
every tag may sit in an XML namespace, prefixed or default — tags are matched by local
name throughout, and the header parser reads the tree ElementTree already built rather
than reconstructing source spellings, which is not possible in general because one
namespace URI may legally have two in-scope prefixes at once.

#### Keep the dataset browser responsive during startup

The Datasets rail control and `O` shortcut can now open the browser during startup. Dataset choices made before initialization finishes leave the browser open with a retry hint, without changing the configured source or starting an overlapping load.

#### Theme visual tests wait for viewer readiness before keyboard input

The theme visual-regression spec now uses the shared Luxar readiness gate before every
keyboard-driven panel toggle. Its dataset-browser snapshots wait for the welcome browser
to auto-open instead of conditionally pressing `O` during initialization, where the
shortcut listener is not installed yet and the keypress can be dropped. The readiness
gate resolves only after the no-dataset initialization path mounts the welcome browser,
so the visibility check no longer races its auto-show.

#### Report successful demo teardown on macOS

`luxar demo stop` now recognizes process groups containing only unreaped
zombies on macOS, avoiding the full signal escalation delay and false failure
report after the demo was successfully stopped.

#### Built demo stores are checked for their declared attribution

`hatch run check-scene-credits` now compares each built demo store with its
registry citation. It catches missing or malformed citation records and drift
in the attribution-bearing `short`, `doi`, and `license` fields, using Luxar's
shared zarr metadata reader so stale consolidated format-2 metadata cannot hide
what the viewer actually sees. The check is part of `check-static` and remains a
clean no-op when no demo stores have been built.

#### Unpublished Chromatrace work is absent from the public gallery

The `chromatrace_choir_umap` and `chromatrace_choir_umap_sequence` demos remain
available in the repository, but their gallery manifest entries are removed so
unpublished work is not presented on the public site.

#### Rebuild a demo scene when its builder changes, and warn before a node overflows its element texture

`ocean_currents_earth` was reported with a hard-edged wedge of missing
streamlines over the North Atlantic. The data was never missing: the scene on
disk had been built before the ribbons were partitioned, so all 11,440,000
segments sat in one Lines node — above the 11,173,888 a single node can hold on
a 16384-class GPU. The viewer clamped the tail, and because segments are stored
in Hilbert order the lost 2.3% was one contiguous spatial lobe rather than a
scatter, which is why it read as a hole in the ocean instead of a capacity
limit. The partitioning fix had landed three weeks earlier; nothing rebuilt the
stale store, because a demo reused its output whenever the path merely existed.

Four source-built demo scenes now include a builder fingerprint — a hash of
that demo module's source — in either the scene root or their existing build
marker, and rebuild when it no longer matches. `--keep-stale` remains an escape
hatch when a source-only mismatch may not justify an expensive reassembly. The
DESI galaxies demo is the exception: it may unpack a shipped prebuilt scene
with no local builder fingerprint, so it retains its targeted stale-ladder
diagnostic rather than forcing a ~1 GB download and rebuild on every run. The
fingerprint check gates scene assembly only: downloads, gsplat fits and
precomputed bundles keep their own caches, so an edit costs a scene rebuild and
never a re-fetch or a re-fit.

The compiler now also warns at authoring time when a node exceeds what one
element texture can render on a 4096-class GPU — 2,793,472 segments, 5,591,040
points or 4,194,304 splats — including the concatenated total of an additive
ladder. The warning names `partition=dict(max_elements=…)` for scene-authored
geometry and also points standalone GSplat datasets to
`luxar gsplat lod --recipe tiles`. The caps live in
`luxar.typing_utils.constants` alongside the derivation that mirrors the viewer
layout.

The Rivers of Earth terrain is now partitioned under the 5,591,040-point bound,
with each part retaining its own stream ladder.

`ocean_currents_earth` itself picks up the appearance it was meant to have: the
globe renders `opaque` (the only mode that leaves the viewer's sorted
transparent set and unconditionally depth-writes, so it is the only one that
reliably composites *under* the ribbons in front of it) and the currents sit at
opacity 0.77. Its opening camera now targets the origin — the centre of the
Earth — instead of a point just below the near surface, so the globe starts
centred and the first drag orbits the planet about its axis rather than swinging
it about a surface point.

#### A refit no longer hands the scene a flat fit

`milkyway` writes a `levels` archive with four substitutive levels;
`cryoem_virus` now writes a four-rung additive `stream` archive. Both then
returned the flat pre-LOD fit to the caller that builds the scene. Their warm
path loads the archive back and gets the hierarchy, so only a
local refit (`--recompute`, or a machine without the precomputed archive) was
affected: it produced a flat single-leaf scene from the same code that produced
a `kind=lod` group on a later cache hit. Milkyway's display gain is documented
as calibrated against the finest level of that group.

Both now return what was STORED, the way `nexrad_supercell` already did and
documented: a re-read carries the levels (verified — four in, four out) and also
picks up the lossy cache encoding, so a local refit and a later cache hit agree
on bytes as well as topology rather than merely on splat count.

A gate covers the shape, because this is the third distinct way a topology can be
paid for and then discarded and the other two already have one. It fires only
where the return value can actually reach the scene as geometry, so a demo that
grafts the path with `add_gsplats_from_file` — cmu1 — is correctly left alone.

#### 4D zebrafish timelapse: one node, seventeen times the splats, and a cage to read it against

The zebrafish gastrulation demo wrote one flat gsplats node per timepoint,
pinned to its frame with `fill={"time": t}` — 64 sibling nodes, no level of
detail, no shared appearance and a Layers row each. It now stacks the
per-timepoint fits into a single 4D `GSplatData` whose fourth centre column is
time, and gives that node a substitutive LOD ladder in which time is a hard
coarsening barrier, so a coarse level never blends one frame's cells into the
next. Timepoints are still fitted independently and cached one by one; only the
thing that is shipped and displayed changed.

The fit itself was starving, in two independent ways.

It asked for 2,000 seeds and then took the fitter's bare defaults — 1,000
iterations, below what the `draft` preset would give, and `cull_retention=0.95`,
which throws away most of the splats along with the last 5% of amplitude. A busy
timepoint shipped a few hundred splats, and whole cells were missing from the
render. A measured sweep put the plateau at ~13,000 splats (32,000 seeds, 5,000
iterations, retention 0.9999); doubling the seeds again moves the
reconstruction by 0.13 dB, because the cull and not the seed budget is what sets
the count on data this heavy-tailed.

And it was subtracting a background floor that was not background. `--floor
auto` takes the histogram mode of the NON-ZERO voxels, capped at their median —
correct where the non-zero population is a camera pedestal, and inverted here,
where 98.7–99.8% of voxels are exactly zero so that population is the specimen
itself. The level landed at 26/255 at the first timepoint and climbed to 91/255
as the embryo brightened, deleting between a quarter and 56% of the image
energy before fitting began. Turning it off is worth up to +7.6 dB global and
+10.7 dB foreground.

Together with the budget, the fit this demo now does is +6.8 dB global and
+10.2 dB foreground on the frame both were measured on. It also fits all 151
timepoints at full XY resolution — the old stride arithmetic took 64 frames and
stopped at frame 126, so the last 50 minutes of gastrulation were never in the
demo at all.

The shipped archive is now a single 19.2 MB `.gsplats.zarr.zip` holding all 151
timepoints in four substitutive levels (19k / 78k / 317k / 1.27M), replacing a
1.6 MB bundle of 64 per-frame zips.

Because the labelled endoderm occupies under 2% of the imaged voxels, the scene
now draws the acquisition volume as a toggleable wireframe cage ruled every
100 µm. The Time slider reads in minutes, from the LSM's own 120 s frame
interval, and the acquisition geometry is checked against the file on the refit
path rather than assumed.

Three things only the viewer showed. The Time axis steps by exactly 2.0 min
rather than the recorded 2.0001470947: a discrete dimension becomes an
`<input type="range">` whose value snaps onto `min + k*step`, and with the raw
interval the browser clamps the final timepoint out of reach — 1.3 s of drift
over five hours buys an axis whose last stop exists. The `Dimensions` list is
ordered X, Y, Z, because that order is what the viewer maps onto screen x/y/z
and listing Z first showed an 859 × 859 × 316 µm slab edge-on as a tall narrow
column. And the cage's colours were roughly halved, because additive lines over
a specimen filling 2% of the frame out-shone the thing they exist to measure.

`--show-roundtrip` is gone. It rendered splats fitted in physical coordinates
onto a voxel-indexed grid, so every PSNR it printed was measuring a coordinate
mismatch rather than the fit. The per-timepoint quality the fitter stamps for
itself is reported instead.

#### Fitting demos choose their cached LOD topology

The remaining fitting demos now route recomputed Gaussian-splat caches through
the shared LOD policy, producing a deliberate streaming ladder instead of
inheriting whichever topology their fitter happened to return.

#### Correct the particle-collision track physics

The static and animated collision demos now share one charged-track sampler
whose initial tangent, helix pitch, and charge-dependent turn direction follow
the generated particle momentum. Tight low-momentum tracks use geometry-aware
angular sampling instead of an artificial radius floor, while retaining the
documented 2x rendered-radius scale for readability. Stiff tracks can reach the
outer detector before the shared arc budget ends. Their on-screen particle
legend is also generated from the same color table used to draw the tracks.

#### Exact-storage scalar bounds include the viewer cast

Broadcast and LUT positive-scalar encodings now include the viewer's float32
narrowing in their chunk-bound pad when the authored dtype is wider. Constant
float64 point radii and line widths can no longer decode just outside a bound
that was computed from the authored value.

#### Make nD keyboard dimension selection visible

Digit keys now report unavailable nD navigation targets with an on-screen toast, while the dimension-sliders panel shows which non-displayed dimension the `[` and `]` keys currently control. Repeated stepping at a dimension bound also reports the minimum or maximum value reached. The help overlay and nD transform bench now make the navigable-subset numbering explicit, and the bench carries an exhaustive expected-value audit across every frame and channel.

#### Keep partition draw order stable while streaming

Order-dependent partition parts now keep unique back-to-front `renderOrder`
values throughout progressive loading. The coordinator also preserves each
visible part's BSP rank while blending-mode changes or late worker recovery
temporarily invalidate its commit stamp.

#### Compare scores partitioned gsplat fits directly

`luxar gsplat compare` now materializes the default-rendered leaves of a
partitioned or nested gsplat tree in memory, so the default output of tiled
uniform and content fits can be scored without first writing a flattened copy.

The advice that assumed otherwise is gone with it: when a tiled or planned merge
declines to score itself (no reference volume, or a peak over the memory budget),
the notice now points straight at `luxar gsplat compare` for every tree shape
instead of routing a partition through a full-disk `luxar gsplat flatten` copy
first.

#### Make partition command failures actionable

`luxar gsplat render` now reads the default-rendered leaves of partition and nested gsplat trees directly, while `luxar gsplat napari` materializes the same selection for inspection. Matrix-based rewrite commands (`partition`, `cull`, `filter`, `slice`, `decimate`, and `merge`) now reject those trees cleanly and direct users to `luxar gsplat flatten` instead of printing an internal matrix-shape error and traceback.

#### Keep streamed GSplat ladders in one coherent draw order

Progressive GSplat appends no longer combine the previous depth-sorted prefix with a newly loaded storage-order suffix while the fresh worker sort is pending. The texture upload remains suffix-only, but the enlarged node temporarily uses one identity permutation, hardening the additive-LOD load window against detached alpha-over populations while the original gastrulation report remains unconfirmed.

#### A timelapse step no longer flashes through the coarsest LOD

Stepping the Time slider on a 4D substitutive LOD group dropped the display from
the finest level to the **coarsest** and climbed back, on every step. Measured on
a 151-timepoint gsplat timelapse: 6,900 splats → 108 → 6,900 in ~70 ms, four
frames at 1.6% of the geometry — so playing the axis was a strobe, even though
the fine level's data for the new timepoint was already cached (the 70 ms is
decode, not fetch).

The registry's slice-aware fallback shows the coarsest fresh level the instant a
scrub invalidates the aspiration, so the new slice appears immediately at low
detail. That is right when the aspiration is seconds away and wrong when it is
milliseconds away — and the coarse level wins the race precisely because it
carries almost nothing. The never-downgrade gate could not help: its rule is that
staleness beats quality, so what is on screen is released the moment the view
version moves.

The registry now holds the previous slice instead, but only when the fresh
fallback is below half the committed elements of what is already displayed — not
a coarser view of the new slice but a token of it. For a timelapse step the held
frame is the previous frame, which is what a video player leaves up while the
next one decodes. The hold is bounded to 250 ms, spent from when it starts and
not refreshed by later version bumps, so a continuous drag still degrades to live
coarse geometry exactly as before.

#### Opaque Points and Lines preserve opacity and soft-edge photometry

The viewer's `opaque` blend state now uses explicit SrcAlpha/OneMinusSrcAlpha
custom blending while remaining depth-writing and in Three.js's opaque render
list. Three.js otherwise replaces `NormalBlending` plus `transparent: false`
with `NoBlending`, which made Points and Lines discard layer opacity,
soft-edge falloff, sub-pixel compensation, and per-element alpha. Negligible
alpha-weighted fragments are discarded before they can occlude visible geometry
behind them. Opaque Point/Line sprite shells that previously tiled into flat,
full-bright surfaces now retain their soft edges and layer opacity while
continuing to write depth.

#### Mandelbulb structure is visible in colour and shading (#1972)

The Mandelbulb demo now colours its surface with a plane orbit trap instead of
the narrow iteration-count band that collapsed almost entirely to cyan. The
trap is equalized through the `magma` ramp and retains local spatial coherence,
so neighbouring folds vary smoothly rather than reading as palette noise.

Distance-estimator normals now drive baked ambient occlusion and a fixed key
light for the emissive point geometry. Crevices remain darker than exposed
surface regions throughout the cinematic orbit, while four full-depth AO probes
avoid the inaccurate-normal tail of shortened escape loops and remove the fifth
probe that measured as visually negligible.

#### E2E rejects stale generated examples

Generated example fixtures now carry the builder, writer, zarr environment, and
output inventory that produced them. Makefile E2E entrypoints rebuild stale
fixtures, while Playwright's global setup rejects stale stores even when invoked
directly; unrelated stores in `datasets/examples/` are preserved.

#### A pre-publish gate for the Zenodo records

`scripts/zenodo_migration_audit.py` grows a `--live` mode: read-only (its only
verb is GET, and a test asserts the source contains no mutating verb and no
publish call) and run immediately before a human publishes the drafts. It checks
every hosted file against its pin **in both directions**, that no scratch or
probe object was left behind, that the contents table matches the file count, and
that the size claims in the prose agree with the files.

Each check exists because that mistake was made. The size audit alone found
**20 of 23** size claims in the record descriptions stale — they predated the
refit and rebuild campaign — including one that described a build that was
evaluated and rejected, down to its tile count and per-level splat totals.

It lands in the existing audit rather than as a fourth Zenodo script, because
"is this ready?" is the question that audit already owns, and because the audit
already resolves the `files` vs `variants.*.files` duality that any pin walk
needs. The default stays entirely local and offline.

The one check that is not a size comparison: when nearly every pin disagrees with
the records, it says so as a diagnosis — *this is probably not the manifest that
will ship* — rather than reporting the mismatches as that many broken files. That
came out of a real incident where an audit run against a superseded manifest
reported the records stale everywhere and was believed; the records were ahead,
and the re-pin was sitting in an unmerged branch. Correct-looking output about the
wrong input is otherwise indistinguishable from a real defect.

#### Separate what the repo ships from what the record serves

`data_manifest.json` file entries gain an optional `hosted_sha256` alongside
`sha256`, and `ensure_dataset` now understands both. `sha256` describes the copy
this repository ships — for a git-LFS file it is literally the pointer's oid —
while `hosted_sha256` describes what the Zenodo record serves.

These were the same number by construction, so nothing ever had to choose between
them, and the manifest's one field quietly served both jobs. A refit broke the
identity: the hosted artifact and the in-repo copy became different bytes. Since
the fetch treated that field as the authority at every step, pinning the hosted
digest truthfully made the in-repo fallback fail its own checksum — so the LFS
payloads had to be deleted in the same change, so Zenodo became the only source,
so the record had to be published before the PR could merge. Publication ended up
on the critical path of every demo-data change, and there are eight more refits
queued.

Bytes already in hand are now accepted if they satisfy *either* contract: hosted
first (canonical, silent), then local (usable, reported as "the record hosts a
newer build"). Both the cache leg and the in-repo leg had to agree on this, since
the cache slot is keyed on `(dataset, variant, basename)` with no record of which
source filled it — a cache check stricter than the leg that wrote it would
quarantine its own copy and re-make it on every run. Only the download leg is
strict, and strictly on the hosted digest: bytes from the record must be the
record's bytes. Nothing changes for the datasets whose two digests agree, which
is most of them, and a `hosted_sha256` equal to its `sha256` is indistinguishable
from having none.

The generator carries `hosted_sha256` forward rather than deriving it, because it
cannot: `_checksum` reads a pointer's oid or hashes local bytes, and what a record
serves has no source on disk. Without that, a dataset whose data directory
happens to be *visible* would silently lose its hosted pin on the next
`make gen-data-manifest`, while a dataset with nothing on disk kept its own — a
field surviving in some rows and evaporating in others is worse than one that
never worked.

Consequence worth knowing: while an in-repo payload is present it wins over a
newer hosted artifact, so a checkout with a stale LFS object keeps serving the
older generation (loudly). That is the trade that lets the pins be truthful while
the payloads are still in the tree, and it ends when they are removed — which is
now an independent change rather than something sequenced around a human
publishing a record.

#### Measure the demo archives once, commit the figures, render from those

`gen_zenodo_records.py` read each archive's `fitting/` stamps at render time. That
worked while the archives lived in the repository, and the migration to Zenodo is
removing them — so the text could only be generated on a machine holding ~400 MB
of demo data, and on a partial checkout it reported "no PSNR" for archives whose
hosted copies are fully stamped. Publishing an absent figure for data that has
one is the failure the generator exists to prevent, occurring in its own output.

Measurement is now separate from rendering. `--refresh` reads whatever archives
are present and writes `scripts/demo_archive_characteristics.json`; rendering
reads that. It is 16 KB of committed text, so it survives payload removal, needs
neither network nor git-LFS content, and the next refit re-stamps it as part of
the upload step.

Record tables now quote the hosted download size rather than the repository
copy's size. Tree archives that do not stamp a root count derive their finest
element count from the tree groups, so datasets such as `ct_atlas` report
647,083 splats instead of a dash.

Two things the separation made necessary, both learned by measuring rather than
reasoning. `--archives-root` searches a staging tree first, because the repo and
cache copies are the PRE-REFIT generation for every dataset the campaign touched:
8 of 27 local archives carry a PSNR and **none** carry a foreground PSNR, while
the staged generation gives 17 of 18 with both. And a measurement taken from the
staged copies outranks one taken locally, because without that a later local
`--refresh` silently replaces every refitted dataset's figures with the stale
ones — the staleness this file exists to end, reintroduced by its own tool.

Each entry records the `measured_sha256` it came from, so `--check` can now say
when a figure was measured from bytes the manifest no longer pins. That is the
drift a refit causes, and the hand-written descriptions had no guard against it.

Measured effect: archives that would publish an incomplete row fall from 28 to
11, and 17 rows across the three records gain both a PSNR and a foreground PSNR
where they previously printed a dash.

#### Rebuild demo scenes after writer changes

The four cached demos that carry builder fingerprints now include Luxar's production
Python sources and Zarr writer environment in that stamp, so encoder, store-writer, and
format changes invalidate scenes produced by older code instead of silently reusing
incompatible data.
Playwright now applies the same production-source freshness gate to its generated
viewer fixtures instead of checking only that fixture directories exist, and
`make test-e2e` repairs stale or incomplete fixture artifacts before running.
Example datasets and demos now share the same production-source fingerprint helper;
the next `make run-examples` rebuilds examples stamped by the older implementation.

#### Mesh imports no longer frame vertices outside the surface

The default welded `luxar mesh import` path now removes vertices that no surviving
triangle references, remaps the index buffer, and slices normals and colours through
the same compaction. Non-surface points can no longer inflate scene bounds, camera
framing, or the picking ordinal range. `--no-weld` remains the explicit opt-out and
keeps the vertex list produced by the reader, including unreferenced points.

#### Visual baselines now have one reproducible platform policy

The viewer's checked-in screenshot corpus is now Linux Chromium only, with a
dedicated local command for comparison and updates. Playwright ignores snapshot
creation on other platforms across every entry point, and a browserless policy
test prevents unsupported tracked baselines from returning.

#### Import time-indexed mesh directories as nD meshes

`luxar mesh import` and `luxar.mesh.interop.import_mesh_directory` can now stack
`T<number>` mesh files into one node with hidden time and optional `Ch<number>` channel
dimensions, avoiding manual vertex concatenation and face-index rebasing.

#### Move consumer-exclusive utilities to their owning packages

The public `luxar.utils.spatial_hash` module moved to
`luxar.gsplats.spatial_hash`, alongside its only production consumers. Update
direct imports to the new path; the old module path has no compatibility shim.

#### Restore modified keyboard shortcuts on fly-control keys

Context routing now evaluates modifier-aware bindings before applying bare
fly-control passthrough. Animation speed adjustment with Shift+ArrowUp or
Shift+ArrowDown and viewer-state export with Ctrl+Shift+S are reachable again,
while unmodified WASD and arrow keys continue to route to fly controls.

#### Custom mesh directory indices

`luxar mesh import --index-regex` and `import_mesh_directory(..., index_regex=...)`
can derive directory time/channel coordinates from required named `t` and optional named
`c` regex captures when filenames do not use the built-in uppercase `T`/`Ch` tokens.

#### Warn when overlapping nodes have incompatible depth behavior

Scene finalization now reports overlapping geometry pairs where a defaulted
`additive` node ignores depth written by another layer, or where two
independently order-dependent transparent nodes have view-dependent cross-node
order. Explicit `additive` is treated as intentional X-ray rendering. The
diagnostic follows composed transforms, nD slider dimensions, viewer-compatible
scene-root semantics, inherited opacity and blending mode, and mutually
exclusive LOD branches. Partition parts and LOD chunks are named and deduplicated
as the author-facing node that owns them. To avoid pairwise noise from coarse
bounds, the order-dependent case requires containment and rolls up repeated hits
when either node was already reported; the additive/depth-writer case still uses
